pages.title: The Cognitive Triangle & the Thought Record
pages.html:
The Cognitive Triangle & the Thought Record

This is the single most portable idea in the whole CBT toolkit, and the one clients remember. Events don't directly cause feelings — our interpretation of events does. The counselor's job is to make that interpretation visible and testable. The cognitive triangle is the diagram of this claim; the thought record is the worksheet that operationalizes it. Together they are the practical core of theory-cbt-practice (the theory is Unit 2's theory-cbt).

The triangle: thoughts ⇄ feelings ⇄ behaviors

The three points influence each other, but CBT's founding move is to insert a step between the situation and the feeling:

Situation → automatic thought → emotion / behavior

The canonical example : a friend walks past you in a hallway without saying hello.

  • Thought "He hates me / I did something wrong" → feeling: hurt, anxious → behavior: withdraw, ruminate.
  • Thought "He's in a hurry / didn't see me" → feeling: neutral → behavior: text him later.

Same event, different thought, different feeling. The event didn't change; the interpretation did. This is liberating for a client because it locates a point of leverage: you can't always change the situation, but you can examine the thought. Behavior is on the triangle too — how you act feeds back into what you think and feel, which is the bridge to concept-behavioral-activation.

Three levels of cognition (why the same situation hits some people harder)

Automatic thoughts don't come from nowhere; they're generated by deeper beliefs :

  1. Automatic thoughts — immediate, unbidden, surface-level ("I'm going to fail this"). The most accessible; where a thought record starts.
  2. Intermediate beliefs — conditional rules and assumptions ("If I don't do everything perfectly, I'm a failure"). Often unstated.
  3. Core beliefs / schemas — global, absolute self-judgments formed early ("I am inadequate," "I'm unlovable," "the world is dangerous"). They act as a lens that generates the automatic thoughts.

Beginning CBT works at the automatic-thought level (accessible, testable); deeper work reaches for the schemas over time. You don't open with "let's examine your core belief that you're unlovable."

Cognitive distortions: the catalog of thinking errors

Teaching a client to name systematic distortions lets them catch thoughts in real time :

  • All-or-nothing / dichotomous thinking — no middle ground ("if I'm not perfect I'm a failure").
  • Catastrophizing — assuming the worst-case and treating it as certain.
  • Overgeneralization — one event becomes "always / never / everyone."
  • Mind reading — assuming you know what others think (usually badly).
  • Personalization — taking responsibility for things outside your control.
  • Emotional reasoning — "I feel worthless, so I must be."
  • "Should" statements — rigid rules that generate guilt and pressure.

Naming is not dismissing: the point isn't "your thought is a distortion, so ignore it," but "this looks like a catastrophizing pattern — let's check it against the evidence."

The thought record (the workhorse)

The thought record turns the triangle into a repeatable procedure — the tool you'll actually assign as homework . Columns:

SituationAutomatic thoughtEmotion (0–100)Evidence forEvidence againstBalanced alternativeRe-rate emotion
Friend walked past"He hates me"anxious 80he didn't wavehe was on his phone; he texted later; we're fine"He probably didn't see me; one moment isn't the friendship"anxious 30

The move is collaborative empiricism (theory-cbt-practice): you don't hand the client the "balanced alternative," you use Socratic questioning to help them generate it — "What's the evidence on the other side? What would you tell a friend who thought this? Is there another explanation?" . A client who produces their own reframe believes it more (the generation effect from the learning-science rulebook) than one who is told.

The stance traps

  • Correcting instead of testing. "That thought is irrational" argues with the client and re-enacts the fix-it reflex. The move is to test together, not to overrule. Distortion labels are hypotheses, not verdicts.
  • Toxic positivity / "just think positive." CBT is about accurate thinking, not cheerful thinking. Sometimes the evidence supports the negative thought — and then the work shifts to problem-solving or acceptance, not to a forced silver lining.
  • Invalidating real adversity. If a client's situation genuinely is bad (poverty, discrimination, loss), reframing the thought without acknowledging the reality is a way to miss the person. The thought record complements, not replaces, seeing the situation clearly (cf. Unit 4 on not psychologizing structural harm).

Connects to

  • theory-cbt-practice — the session structure and full toolkit this technique sits inside.
  • theory-cbt (Unit 2) — the theory (Beck/Ellis, ABC model, the cognitive model).
  • concept-behavioral-activation — the behavior corner of the triangle, and the confusable partner (change the thought vs. change the behavior).
  • concept-mood-disorders and concept-anxiety-disorders (Unit 6) — the disorders CBT most targets.
  • concept-act — the third-wave contrast: ACT does not try to change the thought's content; it changes your relationship to it (defusion).

Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy, CBT techniques II (thought record, Socratic questioning, distortions). StatPearls, CBT (the hallway example; automatic thoughts). pages.title: Confidentiality and Its Limits
pages.html:
Confidentiality and Its Limits

The idea: counseling works because clients can say anything. The Supreme Court put it plainly: effective psychotherapy "depends upon an atmosphere of confidence and trust," and "the mere possibility of disclosure may impede development of the confidential relationship necessary for successful treatment." Confidentiality is therefore the profession's central promise — and because it is not absolute, you must know its limits cold and tell clients about them up front.

Three words that aren't synonyms

TermWhat it isWho enforces it
Privacythe client's underlying right to control access to themselves and their informationconstitutional/common-law right
Confidentialitythe professional's ethical duty not to disclose what the client reveals (B.1.c)ethics code, licensing board
Privileged communicationthe legal protection against forced disclosure in courtevidence law; belongs to the client, not the counselor

Privilege is the narrowest: it only matters in legal proceedings, it is created by statute or case law, and the client (not you) holds it — the client can waive it; you can't. Jaffee v. Redmond (1996) established the psychotherapist–patient privilege in federal courts, explicitly including licensed clinical social workers; states have their own privilege statutes, which vary.

The promise (ACA Code, B.1)

  • B.1.b: request private information only when it benefits the counseling.
  • B.1.c: "Counselors disclose information only with appropriate consent or with sound legal or ethical justification."
  • B.1.d: at initiation and throughout, inform clients of the limitations — and flag foreseeable situations where confidentiality must be breached.

The exceptions (B.2 — the part to know cold)

  1. Serious and foreseeable harm (B.2.a) — disclosure "required to protect clients or identified others from serious and foreseeable harm." Covers danger to self (suicide — see concept-suicide-risk-assessment) and danger to others (concept-duty-to-warn). Note the 2014 wording: serious and foreseeable, not "imminent" — a deliberate change to a more workable standard. When in doubt, consult.
  2. Legal requirements (B.2.a) — chiefly mandated reporting of suspected abuse/neglect of children and vulnerable adults (concept-mandated-reporting).
  3. Contagious, life-threatening diseases (B.2.c) — may (not must) disclose to an identifiable third party at serious, foreseeable risk of contracting the disease, after assessing whether the client intends to inform them; state laws govern.
  4. Court-ordered disclosure (B.2.d) — first seek the client's written informed consent, or take steps to prohibit or narrow the disclosure as much as possible.
  5. End-of-life decisions (B.2.b) — counselors working with terminally ill clients considering hastening death have the option to maintain confidentiality, within applicable law and after consultation.

Plus the quieter, everyday "exceptions" clients should know about: supervision and interdisciplinary treatment teams (B.3.b), subordinates/office staff (B.3.a), third-party payers (B.3.d — insurers require a diagnosis), and consultation. These aren't breaches; they're the ordinary plumbing of care — but consent should cover them.

The overriding rule: minimal disclosure (B.2.e). When you must disclose, clients are (where possible) told beforehand and involved in the decision, and "only essential information is revealed." You breach the seal, never the whole vault — you tell the necessary person the necessary fact, not the client's history.

The confidentiality speech (the syllabus practice rep — worked model)

Write yours first, then compare:

MINE: Let's go over confidentiality. The main idea is that I can't tell anyone anything you say, unless there are legal or ethical concerns. Those concerns are narrow, but pretty understandable: if you present a clear threat to your own or someone else's life, then I have to report that. If you are neglecting or abusing children or special needs adults, I need to report that. If I am asked to testify in court, I will ask you for permission and then say whatever you have allowed me to say with the above exceptions in mind. Any time that I would disclose something, I always keep the details as narrow as possible. Only giving out information that is absolutely necessary. This is all so that you can feel confident being completely honest with me, which is the only way this is gonna work.

"One more thing before we start, and it's important. What you say in this room stays in this room. I don't tell your family, your employer, or anyone else that you're even here. There are a few exceptions, and I'd rather you hear them now than be surprised later. If I believe you're in real danger of seriously hurting yourself, or someone else is in danger from you, I'm required to act to keep people safe — and I'd involve you in that as much as I possibly could. If you tell me a child or a vulnerable adult is being abused or neglected, the law requires me to report that. And in rare cases a judge can order me to release records — if that ever happened I'd fight to keep it as narrow as possible. Also, I meet with a supervisor to make sure you're getting good care, and if you use insurance, they require a diagnosis. That's the whole list. Everything else is between us. What questions do you have?"

Notice what makes it work: plain words, no legalese, the reason for each exception, the promise to involve the client, and an invitation to ask. Compare the failure mode — mumbling through "there-are-limits-to-confidentiality-per-state-law" at speed because the topic is awkward. Clients hear the discomfort, not the content. Saying it calmly is a skill; rep it out loud.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • How much to say up front. Exhaustive warnings would be "time prohibitive and unnecessarily frightening," and clients don't retain them anyway — hence: a clear summary at intake, revisited when a limit becomes live. Some forensic writers (Darby & Weinstock's "dialectical principlism") even argue full re-warning mid-crisis can be ethically withheld when safety demands honest risk assessment; that's a debated position, not settled doctrine.
  • Does warning clients chill disclosure? The worry is real but the evidence is mixed; the field has settled on candor because discovering an unstated exception after a breach is far worse for trust.
  • Privilege varies by state and by profession — who is covered (LPCs? interns?) and what exceptions apply (the "dangerous patient" carve-out) differ by jurisdiction.

Connects to

  • concept-informed-consent — the speech lives inside the consent conversation (B.1.d ↔ A.2.b).
  • concept-duty-to-warn and concept-mandated-reporting — the two big exceptions, unpacked.
  • study-tarasoff — where the harm exception's legal teeth came from.
  • Unit 8 (crisis) — operationalizes "danger to self": risk assessment, safety planning.

Sources

2014 ACA Code of Ethics, B.1–B.3 (verbatim). Jaffee v. Redmond, 518 U.S. 1 (1996), Cornell LII. StatPearls, Duty to Warn. Darby & Weinstock (2018), PMC. APA Services, Mandatory reporting. Full notes in ../research/unit03-ethics-law-sources.md.

pages.title: Congruence (Genuineness, Self-Disclosure & Immediacy)
pages.html:
Congruence

Congruence (also called genuineness or realness) is the third of Rogers' core conditions: the therapist is transparent and real rather than hiding behind a professional façade — "transparently conveys their feelings and thoughts to genuinely relate to the client." It is often called the master condition, because it's what keeps the other two honest: UPR and empathy that aren't genuinely felt become a performance, and clients can usually tell.

Two layers: internal and external

Congruence has an inside and an outside, and both are required:

  • Internal congruence (self-awareness). The therapist is in contact with their own experience — aware of what they're actually feeling in the room, not defended against it. You can't be transparent about a feeling you won't let yourself notice.
  • External congruence (transparency). What the therapist shows matches what they feel — no professional mask, no pretending. The client meets a real person, not a role.

Incongruence in the therapist (saying "go on" while visibly bored, projecting warmth over irritation) is exactly the kind of mismatch a client's observation picks up, and it quietly erodes trust.

Congruence is not "say whatever you feel"

The single biggest misreading: genuineness does not mean unfiltered honesty or dumping every reaction on the client. Congruence is disciplined, not impulsive. Two skills channel it:

  • Immediacy — talking openly about what's happening between you and the client in the present moment ("I notice I feel pushed away when we get near this topic — does that fit for you?"). Immediacy is congruence aimed at the relationship itself, and it's one of the most powerful (and advanced) uses of genuineness. It's also the skill that lets you name an alliance rupture instead of ignoring it.
  • Therapist self-disclosure — revealing something of your own experience. Used sparingly and for the client's benefit it can normalize, build the bond, or model openness. Used carelessly it shifts focus onto the counselor — the same failure mode as sympathy. The guideline: disclose to serve the client's work, not to relieve your own feelings, and keep it brief and relevant.

The tension with UPR (a real one)

Congruence and UPR can pull against each other: what if you genuinely feel judgment or irritation? The resolution is not to fake regard (that's incongruent) and not to unload the judgment (that's unregarding). It's to (a) work your own reaction — often it's your material, addressed in supervision — and (b) where relevant, voice it as immediacy in a way that keeps the client's worth non-contingent. Naming "I notice myself wanting to jump in and fix things when you talk about this" is congruent and preserves regard; "you're being self-destructive and it's frustrating" is neither. Holding all three conditions at once is the actual skill, and it's why they're taught together.

Why it matters in the room

Congruence is what makes the relationship feel real rather than clinical, and realness is a precondition for the client risking anything. It's also, quietly, an ethical stance: it resists the temptation to manage the client with a technique-shaped mask. And it protects the therapist — chronic incongruence (performing warmth you don't feel, session after session) is a fast route toward the depletion Unit 8 treats as a competence issue.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • How much to show is genuinely debated. Classical person-centered therapy leans toward high transparency; more cautious traditions worry that therapist disclosure burdens the client. The safe default: congruence as not-faking first, active disclosure only when it clearly serves the client.
  • Genuineness is culturally inflected. How much directness and self-revelation reads as "real" versus "unprofessional" or "intrusive" varies across cultures — another place Unit 4 complicates a naïve rule.

Connects to

  • concept-core-conditions — the synthesis hub; congruence is one of the three conditions and the one that keeps the other two honest.
  • concept-unconditional-positive-regard and concept-empathy — the conditions congruence protects from becoming technique.
  • concept-therapeutic-alliance — immediacy is the skill that names and repairs ruptures.
  • person-carl-rogers — congruence as the therapist-side expression of Rogers' larger self-theory.

Sources

StatPearls, Person-Centered Therapy, NCBI (congruence as transparency). CounsellingTutor, Rogers' core conditions (orientation on genuineness/immediacy/disclosure). pages.title: Rogers' Core Conditions (Overview)
pages.html:
Rogers' Core Conditions

Carl Rogers argued that a particular therapist attitude — not a technique — is what frees a client to grow. He named three therapist-side conditions, which sit at the base of the microskills hierarchy: no amount of skillful questioning compensates for their absence. This page is the overview and synthesis; each condition has its own page with the depth.

The three conditions (at a glance)

ConditionOne-line coreDeep page
Unconditional positive regardPrizing the client's worth independent of behavior — not approval, not agreement, not liking.concept-unconditional-positive-regard
EmpathyUnderstanding from inside the client's frame and conveying it — the "as if," measurable on Carkhuff's levels.concept-empathy
CongruenceBeing transparent and real — the "master condition" that keeps the other two from becoming a performance.concept-congruence

(The classic empathy-vs-sympathy-vs-interpretation distinction now lives on concept-empathy, where it belongs.)

How the three fit together

They are not a checklist of separate moves; they interlock. Congruence is the ground: if the therapist isn't genuinely feeling regard and understanding, the other two become technique, and clients detect the gap. UPR sets the safety — worth that won't be withdrawn — that makes it safe for the client to be understood. Empathy is the understanding itself, delivered inside that safety. Rogers' wager was that a client held in all three will re-contact their own experience and move toward growth on their own — the actualizing tendency doing the work once the conditions of worth are lifted.

The model underneath (Rogers' six conditions)

The famous "three" are the therapist-side attitudes within Rogers' (1957) six necessary-and-sufficient conditions for change. The full six:

  1. Therapist and client are in psychological contact.
  2. The client is in a state of incongruence (a gap between self-concept and experience).
  3. The therapist is congruent in the relationship.
  4. The therapist experiences unconditional positive regard for the client.
  5. The therapist experiences empathic understanding of the client's frame.
  6. The client perceives (at least minimally) the therapist's empathy and UPR.

Condition 6 is the one beginners forget: regard the client doesn't notice does no work. What matters is the condition as received, not as intended — which is why the Barrett-Lennard Relationship Inventory measures the client's perception.

Why this matters in the room

These are the attitudes a client is unconsciously scanning for in the first few minutes. Get them right and the client opens up; fake them and the relationship stays shallow. The hardest part for anyone with a fix-it reflex is that UPR and empathy both require withholding the solution and staying with the person's experience first. (See the stance note in unit01-helping-skills.)

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Rogers claimed the conditions were necessary and sufficient — all that's required for change. The mainstream view today treats them as necessary but not sufficient: vital ground to stand on, but most clients also need active methods on top. Rogers' own Wisconsin schizophrenia project (1967) is part of why the "sufficient" claim was tempered — the conditions did not produce dramatic gains with hospitalized patients.
  • Critics note the principles can be "too vague" to operationalize, and the efficacy evidence is mixed (e.g. not inferior to CBT for depression at 6 months, possibly inferior at 12). Rapport is necessary, not a proof of superiority.

Connects to

  • concept-unconditional-positive-regard · concept-empathy · concept-congruence — the three conditions in depth.
  • person-carl-rogers — the self-theory these conditions come from (actualizing tendency, conditions of worth).
  • theory-person-centered (Unit 2) — these conditions are the change engine of person-centered theory, treated as a full school.
  • concept-microskills-hierarchy — the conditions are the foundation the skills are built on.
  • theory-common-factors — Rogers' conditions were the original common-factors hypothesis.
  • concept-therapeutic-alliance — UPR/empathy/congruence are how you build Bordin's bond.

Sources

StatPearls, Person-Centered Therapy (Rogerian Therapy), NCBI Bookshelf (three conditions; the six; necessary-and-sufficient debate). Penn State, Counseling Microskills (conditions as the base of the hierarchy). Full notes in ../research/unit01-helping-skills-sources.md.

pages.title: Counselor Self-Care as an Ethical Competency
pages.html:
Counselor Self-Care as an Ethical Competency

The syllabus is blunt about this: counselor self-care is "not optional — it's an ethical competency." That framing is the whole point of this page. Self-care is not a wellness add-on or a reward for surviving a hard week; it is the professional obligation to remain fit to practice, and it is written into the ethics code. The chain is short: vicarious trauma, secondary traumatic stress, and burnout impair judgment and boundaries → an impaired counselor harms clients → the ACA Code prohibits practicing while impaired → therefore preventing and addressing your own distress is an ethical duty, not a personal luxury .

The ethics hook: ACA C.2.g (Impairment)

The ACA Code of Ethics standard C.2.g requires counselors to monitor themselves for signs of impairment from their own physical, mental, or emotional problems, to refrain from offering or providing services when impaired, to seek assistance, and — if necessary — to limit, suspend, or terminate their professional responsibilities until it's safe to resume . Unaddressed VT/STS is exactly the kind of emotional impairment this standard covers. This is the same competence-and-fitness thread from Unit 3's concept-scope-of-practice: staying within your competence includes staying fit to practice it. An exhausted, cynical, boundary-slipping counselor who keeps a full trauma caseload isn't being tough — they're committing a slow ethical breach.

Prevention is organizational, not just personal

The most important — and most frequently missed — point: preventing counselor trauma is a shared responsibility, not a matter of individual willpower . "Just practice self-care" placed entirely on the individual is itself part of the problem; agencies that employ trauma counselors have a duty to reduce VT, and the research names concrete organizational levers:

  • Caseload management. Limiting the number of trauma clients per week measurably reduces VT — it is not the difficulty of the population but the traumatic content and its dose that drives the harm .
  • Supervision and consultation as a standard, funded resource — not a favor.
  • Training in "traumatology" — counselors trained in trauma's effects (including its effects on them) experience less VT .
  • Benefits that matter: adequate pay, paid vacation, coverage for the counselor's own personal counseling .

If you only "self-care" your way around an agency that hands you thirty trauma intakes a week, you will lose. The individual practices below sit on top of a workplace that shares the load.

Peer supervision: the counselor's version of a safety plan

Of all the individual strategies, peer supervision and consultation is the best-supported — in one study it was the most common coping method (85%) among trauma counselors . It does several jobs at once:

  • Normalization — hearing that colleagues have the same reactions lessens the shame that keeps VT hidden and cumulative.
  • Schema repair — a colleague's outside perspective corrects the distorted beliefs VT installs ("everyone is dangerous," "I'm useless at this").
  • Ethical debriefing. This one is subtle and important: confidentiality limits mean you cannot debrief a hard session with your partner or friends — but peer supervision is a setting where you can process the material ethically . It's the counselor's release valve that doesn't violate the client's privacy (concept-confidentiality-limits).

The personal layer

On top of the organizational and supervisory layers, the individual practices that reduce VT are unglamorous and real :

  • Work / play / rest balance — genuine time off, leisure, physical activity, creative outlets; rest and vacations are restorative, not indulgent.
  • A strong social support network — VT erodes trust and intimacy, so relationships both prevent and repair it.
  • Reconnection practices — journaling, meditation, personal counseling, emotional support that lets you feel again after numbing.
  • Meaning and spirituality — VT often works by draining meaning (cynicism, nihilism, a fractured worldview); actively tending a sense of meaning counters that specific damage.

Track the balance, not just the damage: the ProQOL frames it as compassion satisfaction and the costs (burnout + STS) — the goal isn't zero cost, it's keeping the reward of the work larger than its toll (concept-vicarious-trauma).

The stance traps

  • Treating self-care as a personal virtue. It's an ethical obligation (C.2.g) and an organizational responsibility — framing it as "am I disciplined enough" both misplaces the burden and misses the ethics.
  • The martyr reflex. The belief that a good counselor absorbs unlimited pain is the belief that produces impaired counselors. Herman's observation stands: helpers can end up "engulfed in anguish" — and then they help no one .
  • Waiting until you're impaired. By the time boundaries slip and errors show, VT is already cumulative. Prevention (supervision, caseload limits, balance) is the intervention; treatment is the fallback.
  • Debriefing with people you shouldn't. Venting a session's details to a partner breaks confidentiality; take it to peer supervision instead.

Connects to

  • concept-vicarious-trauma — the problem this page responds to; the confusable-terms cluster.
  • concept-scope-of-practice and unit03-ethics-law — C.2.g impairment; fitness-to-practice as part of competence.
  • concept-confidentiality-limits — why peer supervision (not friends/family) is the ethical place to debrief.
  • aux-psychological-first-aid — "helper load" and Ring Theory ("comfort in, dump out") are the acute-support version of this.

pages.title: Cultural Humility
pages.html:
Cultural Humility

The idea: you can complete a training; you cannot complete a culture. Tervalon & Murray-García (1998), writing about physician training, argued that "cultural competence" smuggles in a false promise — that another person's culture is a finite body of knowledge a professional can master, be certified in, and be done with. Their replacement is a stance, not a curriculum: cultural humility, defined as "a lifelong commitment to self-evaluation and self-critique, to redressing the power imbalances … and to developing mutually beneficial and non-paternalistic … partnerships with communities."

Three commitments, worth memorizing as a set:

  1. Lifelong self-evaluation and self-critique — no endpoint, no certificate. The work is noticing your own assumptions each time, with each client.
  2. Redressing the power imbalance in the clinician–client dyad — the client is the expert on their own experience; knowledge about a culture never outranks the person from it.
  3. Institutional accountability / non-paternalistic partnership — humility scaled up: programs and agencies, not just individuals, answer to the communities they serve.

Not modesty — an other-oriented stance

When counseling researchers operationalized the construct, they defined it interpersonally: an other-oriented (rather than self-focused) stance, marked by respect and the absence of superiority toward the client's cultural background (Hook, Davis, Owen, Worthington & Utsey, 2013). Humility here is not thinking poorly of your skills; it's the orientation that the client's frame, not yours, is the working map.

The evidence is the striking part. In Hook et al.'s studies, client-rated therapist cultural humility predicted a stronger working alliance and better therapy outcomes — with the alliance mediating the effect. Two things to notice: the mechanism runs through Unit 1's concept-therapeutic-alliance, and the rating that matters is the client's. Given that therapist self-reported multicultural competence is contaminated by social desirability and barely predicts anything (theory-tripartite-model), the empirical case for humility is almost self-demonstrating: the data say you can't accurately grade yourself — which is what humility claimed all along.

What it sounds like in the room

The failure mode isn't ignorance; it's applied knowledge without humility — treating a cultural generalization as a fact about the individual. Contrast:

Counselor A (competence as mastery): "I did a training on Latino family culture — I know familismo is central for you, so let's make sure any plan keeps your family's approval front and center."

Counselor B (humility): "I've read about how strongly family can figure into these decisions in some Latino families — and I don't know how much that describes your family, or you. What's true in your house?"

Counselor A is warm, informed — and has replaced the client with a category (a move sometimes called a stereotype with good intentions). Counselor B holds the same knowledge but as a hypothesis the client can veto. That veto power is dimension 2 — the power redress — done at conversational scale.

The same stance governs mistakes. A counselor who mispronounces a client's name, misgenders them, or assumes their partner's gender doesn't collapse into self-flagellation (which recenters the counselor — self-focused, the exact opposite pole of other-oriented); they correct, briefly own it, and return the session to the client. Repair over performance. (For repairing a microaggression specifically, see concept-microaggressions.)

Humility vs. competence: the debate, resolved-ish

The field's official documents still say "competencies" (concept-msjcc); its training culture increasingly says "humility." The mainstream resolution treats them as complements rather than rivals — competencies name the learnable content (awareness, knowledge, skills, action), humility names the stance that keeps the content from hardening into stereotype-with-a-syllabus. But know the genuine tension for exams and essays: Tervalon & Murray-García's critique was aimed at the competence framing itself, and "moving beyond the debate" is its own small literature.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Is "humility vs. competence" a false dichotomy? Most current writers say yes (complements); the original 1998 article says the framing matters because endpoint thinking changes behavior. Be able to argue both.
  • Measurement inherits the old problem in mirror image: humility is client-rated by design, which fixes the self-report validity issue but means the construct is only observable through the client's eyes — a feature ethically, a limitation psychometrically.

Connects to

  • theory-tripartite-model — the framework humility corrects; together they're the standard curriculum pairing.
  • concept-msjcc — imports humility's power analysis (quadrants) and its non-paternalism clause (advocacy domain).
  • concept-therapeutic-alliance — the mediator: humility works through the bond.
  • concept-core-conditions — Rogers' stance (client as expert, not-knowing) anticipates humility; this page is where that stance meets culture.

pages.title: DBT Skills (the four modules)
pages.html:
DBT Skills (the four modules)

Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) is the other major third-wave therapy, built by Marsha Linehan for the clients other treatments were failing: chronically suicidal people and those with borderline personality disorder (BPD) (concept-personality-disorders) — people whose central problem is pervasive emotion dysregulation. Linehan's insight was that these clients needed something CBT alone didn't provide: a therapy that took their pain seriously enough to accept it while still pushing for change. That tension is in the name. This page focuses on the four skills modules — the part of DBT a foundations counselor is most likely to encounter and borrow — while noting that full DBT is a larger, structured program.

The dialectic: acceptance and change

"Dialectical" points to the core stance: holding two apparent opposites together. The central dialectic is acceptance AND change . A purely change-focused therapy (like a naïve CBT) tells a dysregulated, self-invalidating client that their reactions are wrong and must be fixed — which the client experiences as the same invalidation that helped create the problem. A purely acceptance-focused therapy leaves them stuck. DBT insists on both at once: "You are doing the best you can, AND you need to do better" — validation and a demand for change, held simultaneously. This resolves the fix-it paradox for exactly the clients where fixing-without-accepting backfires most.

The four skills modules

DBT skills split cleanly into two acceptance modules and two change modules — the dialectic, built into the curriculum:

Acceptance-oriented skills:

  1. Mindfulness — the core module, taught first and returned to throughout. Nonjudgmental awareness of the present moment: the "what" skills (observe, describe, participate) and "how" skills (nonjudgmentally, one-mindfully, effectively). The foundation the other three rest on. (Shared DNA with ACT's present-moment/defusion work.)
  2. Distress Tolerance — how to get through a crisis without making it worse (without self-harm, substance use, or an impulsive blow-up) when a problem can't be solved right now. Skills like TIPP (Temperature, Intense exercise, Paced breathing, Paired muscle relaxation), distraction, self-soothing, and radical acceptance of what can't be changed. This is the module most relevant to the crisis stance in Unit 8.

Change-oriented skills:

  1. Emotion Regulation — identifying and labeling emotions, reducing vulnerability to "emotion mind" (via sleep, eating, exercise), and opposite action (acting against an unjustified emotion's urge — e.g., approaching when fear says avoid, which is behavioral-activation and exposure logic).
  2. Interpersonal Effectiveness — asking for what you need and saying no while keeping the relationship and your self-respect; taught with mnemonics like DEAR MAN, GIVE, and FAST. Close kin to assertiveness training.

Full DBT is more than a skills group

The four modules are usually taught in a skills-training group — in the ASGW taxonomy a psychoeducational group (concept-group-types), curriculum-based and skills-focused rather than a here-and-now process group — but comprehensive DBT has four components working together :

  • Individual therapy (weekly),
  • the skills-training group,
  • phone coaching (in-the-moment skills help between sessions),
  • and a therapist consultation team (support for the clinicians, because these cases are hard).

A foundations counselor may borrow DBT skills (distress-tolerance and mindfulness skills are widely useful) but should not claim to be doing DBT without the full program and training — a scope-of-practice point (concept-scope-of-practice).

The evidence

DBT is the most established treatment for BPD and chronic suicidality, and one of the few therapies with strong RCT evidence for reducing suicide attempts and self-harm:

  • Linehan 1991 (the original RCT vs. treatment-as-usual): DBT patients were less likely to attempt suicide, had fewer and less medically severe self-harm episodes, and dropped out less .
  • Linehan 2006 (a 2-year RCT vs. therapy by non-behavioral experts): DBT roughly halved suicide-attempt rates and reduced ER visits and hospitalizations — and crucially, it beat expert therapy, ruling out "just any good clinician" as the explanation .

This evidence is why DBT is often called the gold standard for BPD, and why its skills have been adapted for eating disorders, substance use, and adolescents .

The stance

DBT's whole architecture is a rebuke to the fix-it reflex applied to dysregulated clients: it validates first (radical genuineness about the client's pain and effort) and only then asks for change, because change demanded without validation is the invalidation that harms. For a helper inclined to jump straight to solutions, DBT is a structured lesson in why acceptance has to come first — and how to still get to change.

What's contested

  • Third-wave ≠ superior in general. DBT is the clear front-runner for BPD/self-harm, but it hasn't been shown to outperform standard CBT for garden-variety depression or anxiety; use it where emotion dysregulation is central, not as a default upgrade .
  • "DBT-informed" vs. DBT. Widespread borrowing of DBT skills means a lot of practice labeled "DBT" is really skills-borrowing without the four-component structure or fidelity — a real quality caveat .

Connects to

  • concept-act — the paired third-wave therapy (third-wave-skills compare): both acceptance-and-mindfulness based, but ACT targets psychological flexibility broadly while DBT is a skills program for emotion dysregulation, with the strongest evidence in BPD.
  • concept-personality-disorders (Unit 6) — BPD, the disorder DBT was built for.
  • concept-suicide-risk-assessment and concept-safety-planning (Unit 8) — DBT's distress-tolerance and the chronic-suicidality population overlap directly with the crisis unit.
  • concept-behavioral-activation — "opposite action" is the same approach-the-avoided logic as activation and exposure.
  • concept-scope-of-practice (Unit 3) — borrowing skills is fine; claiming to deliver full DBT without training is not.

Sources

Linehan et al. (1991), Archives of General Psychiatry — original DBT RCT (fewer/less-severe attempts vs. TAU). Linehan et al. (2006), Archives of General Psychiatry — 2-year RCT vs. experts (attempts roughly halved). Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual + Psychwire (four modules: mindfulness/distress-tolerance acceptance-side, emotion-regulation/interpersonal-effectiveness change-side; four treatment components; dialectic). Hayes & Hofmann (2017), "third wave." Full notes in ../research/unit09-modalities-sources.md.

DBT is the clear front-runner for BPD/self-harm , but it hasn't been shown to outperform standard CBT for garden-variety depression or anxiety; use it where emotion dysregulation is central, not as a default upgrade S20 . "DBT-informed" vs. DBT. Widespread borrowing of DBT skills means a lot of practice labeled "DBT" is really skills-borrowing without the four-component structure or fidelity — a real quality caveat S19 . pages.title: Crisis Intervention & De-escalation Models
pages.html:
Crisis Intervention & De-escalation Models

A crisis is not defined by the event. It's defined by the person's perception of an event or situation as an intolerable difficulty that overwhelms their current resources and coping . Two people lose the same job; one problem-solves and one falls apart — the difference is in the appraisal and the resources, not the event. This matters because it tells you the intervention target: crisis work restores enough coping and control to get the person through the acute period, not to solve the underlying problem. This page covers the two things that show up in practicum: a general crisis-intervention model (the structure for helping someone in acute crisis) and verbal de-escalation (the specific skills for an agitated, escalating person).

The through-line: safety is not a step, it's the thread

Across every model below, client safety is continuous, not sequential . It's tempting to read a step model as "do step 1, then step 2," but in crisis work safety is re-checked at every moment — because it can change in seconds. Hold that as the frame for everything that follows.

James & Gilliland's six-step model (the anchor)

The unit's anchor text organizes crisis intervention as three listening steps and three acting steps :

Listening

  1. Define the problem — from the client's point of view, using core microskills (open questions, reflection, empathy). You cannot help with a crisis you've defined for them.
  2. Ensure client safety — the continuous first priority; assess and reduce danger to self and others (this is where concept-suicide-risk-assessment and concept-means-reduction live).
  3. Provide support — be present, non-judgmental, and unconditionally accepting; the person needs to know someone is with them.

Acting

  1. Examine alternatives — mobilize situational supports, coping mechanisms, and constructive thinking the person may not see in the tunnel of crisis.
  2. Make plans — concrete, collaborative, doable next steps that restore a sense of control (this is where the safety plan gets built).
  3. Obtain commitment — a clear, realistic agreement to act on the plan.

The acting steps are collaborative — the counselor is more directive than in ordinary therapy (a crisis is not the time for pure non-directiveness) but still works with the person to restore their own agency, not to take over.

Roberts' seven-stage model (the same logic, finer grain)

Roberts' Seven-Stage Crisis Intervention Model covers the same territory with more granularity : (1) assess lethality and biopsychosocial risk; (2) establish rapport; (3) identify the major problems (including the "last straw" precipitant); (4) deal with feelings (validate, actively listen); (5) generate alternatives; (6) develop an action plan; (7) follow-up. Note the shared spine with James & Gilliland — assess/safety first, rapport, alternatives, plan, follow-up — which is the pattern to actually remember. The models differ in how finely they slice the same sequence, not in what they tell you to do.

Verbal de-escalation: Project BETA's ten domains

When the person is agitated and escalating — not (only) in despair but keyed up, angry, or on the edge of losing control — you need the specific skills of verbal de-escalation. The Project BETA consensus (American Association for Emergency Psychiatry) frames the goal in three moves: verbally engage the person → build a collaborative relationship → talk them down out of the agitation. Its ten domains :

  1. Respect personal space — keep at least two arms' lengths, and keep an exit clear for both of you.
  2. Do not be provocative — calm posture, hands visible, no staring down, no challenge; your body says "not a threat."
  3. Establish verbal contact — only one person talks to the patient (multiple voices escalate and confuse).
  4. Be concise — short sentences, simple words; an agitated brain processes language poorly. Repeat as needed.
  5. Identify wants and feelings — "What would help right now?" Often the agitation has a concrete, meetable need behind it.
  6. Listen closely — active listening; "Miller's law" (assume what they say is true from their perspective); reflect it back ("Tell me if I've got this right…").
  7. Agree or agree to disagree — find something true to agree with ("You're right that the wait has been ridiculous"); you don't have to win.
  8. Set clear limits — matter-of-factly and respectfully, without threats ("It's okay to be angry; it's not okay to hurt anyone here").
  9. Offer choices and optimism — give real alternatives to violence and honest hope; choices restore control.
  10. Debrief — afterward, with the patient and staff, to repair the relationship and learn from what happened.

Restraint is a last resort — and here's the reasoning

Coercion, physical restraint, and forced medication are the last resort, not a shortcut . Beyond the injury risk, restraint tends to reinforce the idea that violence is how conflict gets resolved, is associated with longer stays and worse outcomes, and ruptures the very relationship that makes future help possible. Successful verbal de-escalation preserves the person's dignity and returns control to them, which is both more humane and more effective. This is the same logic as everywhere else in the unit: the counselor's job is to restore the person's agency, not to override it.

The stance traps

  • Getting bigger when they get bigger. Matching agitation with your own raised voice or squared shoulders escalates. The skill is to get calmer and smaller as they get louder.
  • Reasoning with an escalated brain. Long explanations and logic fail during high arousal; be concise, meet the need, de-escalate first, then problem-solve.
  • Skipping safety because the model looks sequential. Safety is continuous; re-check it constantly.
  • Winning the argument. "Agree or agree to disagree" — being right is not the goal; getting to calm is.

Connects to

  • concept-suicide-risk-assessment, concept-safety-planning, concept-means-reduction — the danger-focused content that "ensure safety" and "make plans" point to.
  • concept-microskills-hierarchy and unit01-helping-skills — de-escalation is microskills under pressure; the relational engine is the same.
  • aux-psychological-first-aid — PFA is crisis intervention for the acute aftermath of disaster/loss; shares the stabilize-first logic.

pages.title: Death Notification — Telling Someone Their Person Has Died
pages.html:
Death Notification — Telling Someone Their Person Has Died

The hardest sentence in acute care: someone asks "Where is she?" and the answer is that she is dead. This page covers how that news is delivered — and how to answer the question honestly when you don't yet know. It sits between concept-pfa-core-actions (this is Core Action 2, Safety and Comfort, in its most extreme form) and concept-supporting-the-bereaved (everything that happens after the words).

The one rule that governs everything here: never lie, and never stall with soothing vagueness. False reassurance feels kind for thirty seconds; when the truth arrives it retroactively poisons everything else you said and did. The NCTSN field guide is explicit that premature reassurance about a missing loved one is a harm to avoid.

Who delivers it (role boundary first)

Formal notification belongs to whoever holds confirmed knowledge and the authority to speak it — medical staff, police, a chaplain or medical examiner's office. Law-enforcement practice codifies five principles: in person, in time, in pairs, in plain language, with compassion. "In time" matters more than comfort: the family should hear it from a person, not the news or social media. "In pairs" exists because the reaction may need two sets of hands — one for the bereaved, one for logistics or for another family member who collapses.

If you are a lay helper and the death is not confirmed to you, notification is not your job — but stonewalling isn't either. Your job is the honest-uncertainty script below, plus visibly fetching the person who does know.

In plain language: the "D-words"

Every protocol converges on the same instruction: say "died" or "dead." Not "passed," "lost," "didn't make it," "gone," "expired." This is not bluntness for its own sake — under acute shock, people take euphemisms literally or refuse to parse them ("lost? then go find her"), and ambiguity forces the bereaved to do the inferential work of concluding their child is dead, which is crueler than the word. The MADD/DOJ curriculum calls the euphemisms what they are: "words of denial."

The clinical protocol: GRIEV_ING

The emergency-medicine standard, from Hobgood et al. — training built on it measurably improved physicians' notification skill and confidence. The underscore is a step:

LetterStepWhat it looks like
GGatherGet the family together, seated, in a private space
RResourcesCall in support — chaplain, other family, friends
IIdentifyYourself, the deceased by name, and what the family already knows
EEducateBriefly: what happened, what was done
VVerifySay it: "died" / "dead." No euphemisms
_(Space)Stop talking. Let it land. Tolerate the reaction
IInquireInvite and answer every question
NNuts and boltsViewing the body, belongings, funeral steps, organ donation
GGiveYour contact info — questions will come later

Note the shape: the actual news is one plain sentence in the middle, wrapped in preparation before and presence after. Most of the protocol is not the sentence.

The three scenarios (the discrimination that matters)

What you say to "Where is my child?" depends on which situation you are in — and confusing them is where helpers do damage.

1. Death is confirmed, and they don't know yet. Warning shot, then plain words, then the name:

"Mrs. Alvarez, I have very hard news. … Sofia died in the accident. She's dead. I am so sorry."

Then stop talking and stay. Collapse, screaming, flat denial, anger at you — all are normal first responses; none need correcting. If the person is flooded past function, this is exactly the stabilization skill of concept-pfa-core-actions (Core Action 3): calm presence, time, grounding — not more information.

2. You genuinely don't know (missing person, unconfirmed). Honesty about uncertainty, in both directions — no "I'm sure she's fine" and no grim hinting:

"I don't know where Sofia is right now. Here is what I do know: rescue teams are searching that building. Here is what I'm going to do: I'll find the person keeping the family list, and I will come back to you either way."

Then actually do it. Addressing the concrete concern is the stabilization.

3. They were told, and they're asking again — shock, dissociation, or the first crash of denial. Answer truthfully every time, gently, without escalating detail and without irritation:

"She died, remember — she's at the hospital now. I'm right here with you."

Repetition is not a failure to hear you; it is the mind metering out something unbearable (concept-grief-models — accepting the reality of the loss is Worden's task, not an event).

Side-by-side — instinct vs. practice:

Instinct saysSay instead
"She's being taken care of." (she's dead)"I have very hard news. Sofia died."
"I'm sure they'll find him.""I don't know yet. Here's what I know, and I'll come back to you either way."
"She passed on." / "We lost her.""She died."
Answering "where is she?" with silence or a subject changeThe truth, then presence.
Re-explaining the medical details when asked againThe same plain sentence, again, kindly.

"Can I see her?" — viewing the body

Answer the literal question too: where the body is, and whether they can see their person. The evidence supports an offered, prepared, genuine choice — neither pushing viewing nor shielding people from it. In Chapple & Ziebland's study of 80 people bereaved by suicide or other traumatic death, most who viewed said it was the right decision (35 of 49; only 2 regretted it, both with badly damaged bodies and no real choice), while some who didn't view were later haunted by not knowing. Their conclusion: relatives should have the opportunity to view, with preparation for what they will see, time to decide, and room for different family members to choose differently — and "clinicians should not assume that relatives will be harmed by seeing a bruised or damaged body." For a bereaved parent specifically, being able to see and hold their child is often part of grasping that the death is real — but it is their choice, made with honest preparation, never a prescription.

After the words

The notification ends; the accompaniment begins. Everything in concept-supporting-the-bereaved applies from this minute — presence over fixing, the child's name, concrete help, no timelines. Do not hand a freshly notified parent a pamphlet and leave; linkage (Core Action 8) means a warm connection to a person, and GRIEV_ING's final Give step — a name and number for the questions that arrive at 2 a.m. — is the clinical version of "keep showing up."

Connects to

  • concept-pfa-core-actions — Safety and Comfort (Core Action 2) houses death notification; Stabilization (3) handles the flooded reaction that may follow.
  • concept-supporting-the-bereaved — what helps and harms from the moment after notification.
  • concept-grief-models — why denial and re-asking are normal first minutes, not pathology.
  • aux-psychological-first-aid — module hub and stance.
  • Unit 8 — crisis response, and notification after suicide specifically.

pages.title: Managing Difficult Group Members
pages.html:
Managing Difficult Group Members

Every group produces a handful of recurring problem roles, and how a counselor handles them separates a working group from a stalled one. The central reframe — and the stance lesson of this page — is this: a "difficult" member is almost never a person to be managed out of the way so the real work can proceed. Their difficult behavior is the work. What they do in the group is usually a live re-enactment of the very interpersonal pattern that causes them trouble outside it (the social microcosm, theory-yalom-factors) — which means the group is the one place that pattern can be seen, named, and revised. The reflex to smooth things over or take the difficult member aside protects the group's comfort at the cost of its therapeutic power. Yalom's Theory and Practice catalogues these prototypes; the ones below are the ones you'll meet .

The prototypes

The monopolist

Talks compulsively, fills every silence, and dominates the group's airtime — often narrating endless detail or giving everyone advice. Underneath it is usually anxiety: silence feels dangerous, so they rush to fill it. The cost is real: other members disengage, resent the monopolist, and stop doing their own work; the group's energy drains. The move: not simply cutting them off (which shames them and teaches the group the leader will police airtime). The therapeutic move works on two levels at once — help the group look at why it has allowed one person to carry all the talking ("I'm curious what it's like for the rest of you to be so quiet while Tom does all the work"), and help the monopolist examine what the talking protects them from. Both the behavior and the group's collusion with it become here-and-now material.

The silent member

The opposite pole — withdrawn, minimally participating. Silence is easy to ignore because it doesn't disrupt, but it is quietly costly: silent members tend to gain little, and prolonged silence can pull the group into either over-protecting them or scapegoating them. The silence has many possible meanings — fear of self-disclosure, feeling one's contributions don't matter, cultural norms around speaking in a group, shame, or a trauma history. The move: understand before you push. Gentle invitation and here-and-now curiosity ("I notice you've been taking a lot in today — I'd be interested in what's stirring for you") without coercion. Pressuring a silent member to perform usually deepens the withdrawal; the goal is to make participation safe, not mandatory.

The help-rejecting complainer ("yes, but…")

The member who repeatedly presents problems, solicits the group's help, and then rejects every solution offered — "yes, but that won't work because…" They pull the group into a fruitless cycle of trying to fix them and being defeated, which eventually breeds frustration and withdrawal. The move: stop feeding the content-level rescue attempts and shift to process. The pattern itself is the material: the member is enacting a relationship in which they simultaneously demand and defeat help — a pattern that surely operates outside the group too. Naming that dynamic gently and curiously ("I notice we keep offering ideas and they keep not fitting — I wonder if what happens in here happens in your life too") is far more useful than another doomed suggestion. This is the group's purest case for "resist the urge to fix": the entire trap is baited to pull the fix reflex out of the group, and the way out is to decline the bait.

The scapegoat / the group deviant

Sometimes the group unconsciously funnels its collective tension onto one member — the person who becomes the target of the group's frustration, blamed for the group's stuckness. Scapegoating is a group-level phenomenon (it says as much about the group as about the target) and, left unaddressed, it can genuinely harm the scapegoated member. The move: protect the member (an ethical duty — concept-group-ethics-and-formation) and illuminate the process: what is the group doing by putting everything on this one person? The scapegoat is usually carrying something for the whole group.

Characterologically difficult members

Members with borderline, narcissistic, or schizoid features (Unit 6, concept-personality-disorders) bring their interpersonal patterns into the group vividly — the narcissistic member needs to be special and central; the borderline member may split the group into all-good and all-bad; the schizoid member stays affectively remote. These are the same patterns that make individual relationships hard for them, now visible and workable — but they also test the leader's ability to protect the group and manage their own countertransference.

The through-line: work the process, protect the members

Three principles cover almost every difficult-member situation:

  1. Address the process, not just the content. The behavior is data about how this person relates, not merely a nuisance to suppress. Turn it into examinable here-and-now material (concept-group-leadership).
  2. Use the group, don't do it alone. The difficult behavior is happening to the group, so the group is your best resource — surface how members are experiencing it rather than handling it as a private transaction between you and the difficult member. This also keeps the difficult member from becoming your patient inside the group (the "individual therapy in front of an audience" trap).
  3. Protect while you work. Making a pattern examinable never licenses letting a member be attacked or humiliated. The leader's protective function (screening, safety, limits) is the floor beneath all of this — an ethical duty, not a nicety (concept-group-ethics-and-formation).

What's contested / cautions

  • These are heuristic prototypes, not diagnoses. "The monopolist" is a role a person is playing in this group at this time, not a label for who they are — and roles are partly created by the group, not just carried in by the individual. Reifying the prototype (writing someone off as "our monopolist") is itself an error.
  • The behavior may be about the leader. A group full of "resistant" or silent members is, in encounter-group terms, often a signal about leadership (concept-group-leadership) — an over-controlling or over-stimulating leader manufactures the very difficulty they then complain about. Check your own contribution first (the Unit 9 theory-motivational-interviewing "discord, not resistance" reframe applies here too).
  • Culture shapes what looks "difficult." Norms about self-disclosure, deference, and speaking in a group vary widely (Unit 4). A member read as "silent" or "resistant" may be behaving exactly as their cultural context prescribes — a cultural-humility check belongs before any labeling.

Connects to

  • unit10-group — the hub; the "difficult member is an opportunity" stance.
  • theory-yalom-factors — the social microcosm: why the difficult behavior is a live re-enactment.
  • concept-group-leadership — process illumination is the tool; a "difficult group" may be a leadership signal.
  • concept-personality-disorders (Unit 6) — the characterologically difficult member's patterns.
  • concept-group-ethics-and-formation — the protective duty and how screening prevents some problems.

Sources

Yalom & Leszcz (2020), The Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy, ch. on problem group members (the monopolist, the silent member, the help-rejecting complainer, characterologically difficult members; work the process, use the group). Corroborated by StatPearls (group roles; leader management of the emotional climate; countertransference) and Psychology Town (the social microcosm as the reason the behavior is workable). pages.title: The DSM-5-TR: Structure, History, and How to Use It
pages.html:
The DSM-5-TR: Structure, History, and How to Use It

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is the common language of American mental-health care: a catalog of disorders, each defined by explicit criteria. The syllabus's advice is exact — you don't read it cover to cover; you learn its structure and use it as a reference. This page is that structure.

A short history that explains the present

  • DSM-I (1952): 106 diagnoses in 130 pages, organized on a scheme the U.S. Army built in WWII — psychoanalytic in flavor, thin on criteria.
  • DSM-III (1980): the revolution. Explicit, symptom-count diagnostic criteria replaced theory-laden descriptions so two clinicians could (in principle) reach the same diagnosis. Size jumped to 265 diagnoses / 886 pages.
  • DSM-IV (1994) → DSM-5 (2013): DSM-5 carries 237 disorders (fewer than DSM-IV's 297 — consolidation, e.g., the autism merger), dropped the Roman numeral, and made the structural changes below.
  • DSM-5-TR (2022): a text revision that went beyond text: prolonged grief disorder added; free-standing symptom codes for suicidal behavior and nonsuicidal self-injury (recordable with or without any diagnosis — a preview of Unit 8); unspecified mood disorder; criteria or specifier tweaks to 70+ disorders; terminology modernized ("experienced gender"), with the whole text reviewed by an Ethnoracial Equity and Inclusion Work Group.

Two removals mark the field's self-corrections: homosexuality was deleted as a diagnosis in 1973 — the standing proof that what counts as "disorder" is partly a social decision — and the bereavement exclusion was deleted in 2013 (the debate lives on concept-mood-disorders).

How the manual is organized

By lifespan, in one list. DSM-5 scrapped the old "disorders of infancy, childhood and adolescence" chapter and ordered the manual developmentally: chapters that typically emerge early (concept-neurodevelopmental-disorders) come first; neurocognitive disorders of later life come last. Chapters are grouped so that neighbors are plausible differentials — the schizophrenia spectrum sits beside bipolar, which sits beside depressive disorders; the anxiety chapter is followed by obsessive-compulsive and related disorders and then trauma- and stressor-related disorders, both of which DSM-5 moved out of the anxiety chapter into families of their own.

Each disorder entry contains the diagnostic criteria plus supporting text: diagnostic features, prevalence, development and course, risk factors, culture- and gender-related features, and differential diagnosis — the entry is a small literature review, not just a checklist.

When criteria don't quite fit: DSM-IV's "not otherwise specified" became two options — other specified disorder (you name the reason the presentation misses full criteria) and unspecified disorder (you don't). Clinically honest vagueness beats a forced fit.

What DSM-5 removed: the multiaxial system

DSM-IV diagnoses came in five axes: I clinical disorders; II personality disorders and intellectual disability; III relevant medical conditions; IV psychosocial/environmental stressors; V the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF, 0–100). DSM-5 dropped the whole apparatus for nonaxial documentation — all disorders and relevant conditions in one list, ordered by clinical priority. The GAF died of "conceptual lack of clarity … and questionable psychometric properties," replaced (optionally) by the WHO's WHODAS 2.0 disability measure; Axis IV's job passed to expanded V/Z codes for psychosocial and environmental problems (housing, abuse, relational distress).

Why counselors still care: the axes forced every diagnosis to sit inside a picture of the person's body, stressors, and functioning. The counseling literature's warning is that without the structural prompt, context becomes optional — and the profession's whole identity is "strength-based and developmentally, culturally and contextually sensitive" work. The fix is a habit, not a form: document stressors, functioning, and strengths anyway (the concept-biopsychosocial-model is the natural frame).

DSM and ICD — who's who

The DSM is an American Psychiatric Association product; the ICD (WHO's International Classification of Diseases) is the world's. Worldwide, "the ICD is more frequently used for clinical diagnosis, whereas the DSM is more valued for research" — and in U.S. practice the two are welded together: the codes you write on claims are ICD codes, listed beside each DSM diagnosis. That's also the honest answer to "why diagnose at all?" in many settings: reimbursement generally requires a covered diagnosis, a structural pressure counselors must notice (it pushes toward diagnosing, and toward "covered" diagnoses) and manage ethically — diagnosis should record clinical reality, not billing convenience.

Culture in the manual

DSM-5 retired "culture-bound syndrome" for three sharper ideas :

  • Cultural syndromes — recognized symptom clusters in a cultural group (e.g., ataque de nervios; susto).
  • Cultural idioms of distress — shared ways of talking about suffering ("nerves," heat in the chest) that don't map one-to-one onto criteria.
  • Cultural explanations — causal models (e.g., susto as soul loss after a fright).

The Outline for Cultural Formulation (five domains: identity; explanations of illness; psychosocial environment; the clinician–client relationship; overall assessment) and the 16-question Cultural Formulation Interview (CFI) operationalize this. The stakes are misdiagnosis in both directions: "behavior that is aberrant in one culture can be standard in another" — apparent paranoia can be a rational stance for a migrant from state surveillance, spiritual experiences are not hallucinations by default, and acculturative stress can look like disorder. This is unit04-multicultural doing diagnostic work.

How to actually use it (the counselor's algorithm)

  1. Start from the presentation, not the manual — what does the client say is wrong, in their words?
  2. Generate 2–3 candidate categories; read the differential diagnosis text, not just criteria.
  3. Check the gates: duration, impairment, substance/medical rule-outs, culture (would this be unremarkable in the client's context?).
  4. Prefer honest uncertainty (other specified/unspecified, provisional) over premature precision.
  5. Write the diagnosis down as a hypothesis to revisit — Unit 7 turns it into a case conceptualization; it is not the end of thinking.

Sources

OpenStax §15.2. First et al. (2022). Kress et al., TPC. NCBI NBK519711. StatPearls PTSD. StatPearls OCD. SAMHSA TIP 59. Full notes in ../research/unit06-psychopathology-sources.md.

pages.title: Dual Relationships & Boundary Management
pages.html:
Dual Relationships & Boundary Management

The idea: a dual (multiple) relationship exists when a counselor holds more than one role with a client — therapist and friend, business partner, professor, in-law, fellow congregant. Terminology note: APA's code says "multiple relationships"; the ACA Code mostly speaks of "nonprofessional relationships" and boundary management. The 2014 ACA Code's key move is that not all dual relationships are unethical — some are prohibited outright, the rest are managed with a risk–benefit analysis, consent, consultation, and documentation.

The prohibited list (A.5 — bright lines)

  • A.5.a — Sexual/romantic relationships with current clients: absolutely prohibited. Extends to the client's romantic partners and family members, and to electronic as well as in-person contact. No risk–benefit analysis applies; this is the profession's clearest rule.
  • A.5.c — Former clients: prohibited for 5 years after the last professional contact — and even after five years, only with documented forethought that the relationship isn't exploitive and holds no potential to harm. (The APA code's parallel rule uses 2 years; know whose code you're quoting.)
  • A.5.d — Don't counsel friends or family with whom you can't remain objective.
  • A.5.e — No personal virtual relationships with current clients — don't friend/follow your clients on personal social media.

The managed list (A.6 — judgment + paperwork)

  • A.6.a — previous relationships: accepting an acquaintance as a client requires weighing risks and benefits, plus precautions (informed consent, consultation, supervision, documentation).
  • A.6.b — extending boundaries: attending a client's wedding or graduation, buying a client's product, visiting a hospitalized family member — potentially beneficial, never automatic.
  • A.6.c — document boundary extensions before the interaction (when feasible): rationale, potential benefit, anticipated consequences. If unintended harm occurs, show evidence of attempting to remedy it.
  • A.6.d — role changes (individual → couples counseling; evaluator → therapist) require fresh informed consent and the right to refuse.

Boundary crossing vs. boundary violation (the discrimination that matters)

Boundary crossingBoundary violation
Definitiondeparture from standard practice that is not harmful or exploitative — may even serve the workdeparture that harms or exploits the client or puts the work at serious risk
Examplesshaking an offered hand; extending a session for a client in crisis; attending a client's graduation (documented); appropriate self-disclosuresexual contact; entering business deals with a client; using client information for personal gain
Verdictjudgment call — sometimes good practiceunethical, sometimes illegal

The heuristic embedded in the codes: ask whose need does this meet? A crossing serves the client's interest; a violation serves the counselor's. Violations also rarely start as violations — the "slippery slope" pattern (small unexamined crossings drifting toward exploitation) is why A.6.c makes you write the rationale down before acting: documentation forces the examination.

The rural/small-community reality

The blanket "avoid all dual relationships" advice of older codes collapsed on contact with real communities: in a small town, on a military base, in a tight-knit cultural or religious community, or in recovery communities, the counselor will share a grocery store, a church, and a school with clients. Overlap there is unavoidable and refusing all overlapping clients would deny care. The modern standard is therefore manage, don't merely avoid: minimize role mixing where possible, talk about unavoidable overlap openly, and document.

What it sounds like: "Since we live in the same town, we're going to run into each other — at Kroger, at games. Here's how I handle that: I won't greet you first, so you never have to explain who I am. If you say hi, I'll say hi. And anything we see or say out there stays out there — we can talk about it in here if you want, but I won't bring it up. Does that work for you?"

That's boundary management as an informed-consent conversation — which is exactly what A.6 intends (concept-informed-consent).

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Where the crossing/violation line sits is contextual — the same act (a hug, self-disclosure, a gift) can be therapeutic with one client and harmful with another; culture changes the meaning too. Zur and others argue rigid "risk-management" boundary avoidance can itself harm care; more conservative voices emphasize slippery-slope risk. The codes deliberately split the difference (bright lines for sex and exploitation; judgment for the rest).
  • Post-termination romance: ACA says 5 years + documented non-exploitation; APA says 2 + a heavy multi-factor test; some ethicists argue "once a client, never a partner." Know the rule and that it's debated.

Connects to

  • concept-informed-consent — every managed boundary runs through consent and documentation.

pages.text: Dual Relationships & Boundary Management The idea: a dual (multiple) relationship exists when a counselor holds more than one role with a client — therapist and friend, business partner, professor, in-law, fellow congregant. Terminology note: APA's code says "multiple relationships"; the ACA Code mostly speaks of "nonprofessional relationships" and boundary management. The 2014 ACA Code's key move is that not all dual relationships are unethical — some are prohibited outright, the rest are managed with a risk–benefit analysis, consent, consultation, and documentation. S1 S11 S12 The prohibited list (A.5 — bright lines) A.5.a — Sexual/romantic relationships with current clients: absolutely prohibited. Extends to the client's romantic partners and family members, and to electronic as well as in-person contact. No risk–benefit analysis applies; this is the profession's clearest rule. S1 A.5.c — Former clients: prohibited for 5 years after the last professional contact — and even after five years, only with documented forethought that the relationship isn't exploitive and holds no potential to harm. (The APA code's parallel rule uses 2 years; know whose code you're quoting.) S1 S11 A.5.d — Don't counsel friends or family with whom you can't remain objective. S1 A.5.e — No personal virtual relationships with current clients — don't friend/follow your clients on personal social media. S1 The managed list (A.6 — judgment + paperwork) A.6.a — previous relationships: accepting an acquaintance as a client requires weighing risks and benefits, plus precautions (informed consent, consultation, supervision, documentation). S1 A.6.b — extending boundaries: attending a client's wedding or graduation, buying a client's product, visiting a hospitalized family member — potentially beneficial, never automatic. S1 A.6.c — document boundary extensions before the interaction (when feasible): rationale, potential benefit, anticipated consequences. If unintended harm occurs, show evidence of attempting to remedy it. S1 A.6.d — role changes (individual → couples counseling; evaluator → therapist) require fresh informed consent and the right to refuse. S1 Boundary crossing vs. boundary violation (the discrimination that matters) Boundary crossing Boundary violation Definition departure from standard practice that is not harmful or exploitative — may even serve the work departure that harms or exploits the client or puts the work at serious risk Examples shaking an offered hand; extending a session for a client in crisis; attending a client's graduation (documented); appropriate self-disclosure sexual contact; entering business deals with a client; using client information for personal gain Verdict judgment call — sometimes good practice unethical, sometimes illegal The heuristic embedded in the codes: ask whose need does this meet? A crossing serves the client's interest; a violation serves the counselor's. Violations also rarely start as violations — the "slippery slope" pattern (small unexamined crossings drifting toward exploitation) is why A.6.c makes you write the rationale down before acting : documentation forces the examination. S1 S11 The rural/small-community reality The blanket "avoid all dual relationships" advice of older codes collapsed on contact with real communities: in a small town, on a military base, in a tight-knit cultural or religious community, or in recovery communities, the counselor will share a grocery store, a church, and a school with clients. Overlap there is unavoidable and refusing all overlapping clients would deny care. The modern standard is therefore manage, don't merely avoid : minimize role mixing where possible, talk about unavoidable overlap openly, and document. S11 S12 What it sounds like: "Since we live in the same town, we're going to run into each other — at Kroger, at games. Here's how I handle that: I won't greet you first, so you never have to explain who I am. If you say hi, I'll say hi. And anything we see or say out there stays out there — we can talk about it in here if you want, but I won't bring it up. Does that work for you?" That's boundary management as an informed-consent conversation — which is exactly what A.6 intends ( concept-informed-consent ). What's contested (don't over-learn it) Where the crossing/violation line sits is contextual — the same act (a hug, self-disclosure, a gift) can be therapeutic with one client and harmful with another; culture changes the meaning too. Zur and others argue rigid "risk-management" boundary avoidance can itself harm care; more conservative voices emphasize slippery-slope risk. The codes deliberately split the difference (bright lines for sex and exploitation; judgment for the rest). S11 S12 Post-termination romance: ACA says 5 years + documented non-exploitation; APA says 2 + a heavy multi-factor test; some ethicists argue "once a client, never a partner." Know the rule and that it's debated.
