pages.title: Duty to Warn / Duty to Protect
pages.html:
Duty to Warn / Duty to Protect

The idea: when a client poses a serious danger of violence to an identifiable other person, the counselor's obligation to protect that person can override confidentiality. The doctrine comes from the Tarasoff case (study-tarasoff); Justice Tobriner's formulation is the line every program quotes: "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins."

Warn vs. protect — the distinction exams love

These are not synonyms, and the difference is the history:

  • Duty to warn (Tarasoff I, 1974): the original, narrower ruling — the clinician must warn the intended victim of the threat.
  • Duty to protect (Tarasoff II, 1976): the rehearing replaced warning with a broader duty to "take reasonable precautions to protect" the third party. Warning is now just one option on a menu — often not the best one.

The menu of reasonable protective steps:

  • increase session frequency; intensify treatment
  • arrange removal of weapons from the client's home (means restriction — reappears in Unit 8)
  • initiate or adjust medication (via a prescriber — see concept-helping-professions-compared)
  • voluntary or involuntary hospitalization
  • involve family or other third parties in the treatment
  • notify the identifiable victim and/or police — when less intrusive measures won't suffice

This matters clinically: "duty to warn" framing pushes new clinicians toward the most relationship-destroying option first. The actual duty, in most formulations, is to do something effective, with warning as a last resort — and with minimal disclosure governing what you say if you do warn (concept-confidentiality-limits, B.2.e).

When is the duty triggered?

The classic threshold (per APA's 1987 formulation, echoed in most statutes):

  1. a clear threat of killing or seriously injuring
  2. a specific, identifiable victim (generalized anger at "everyone" typically doesn't trigger Tarasoff duties — though it absolutely triggers clinical risk work),
  3. intent and ability to carry it out, with some imminence.

The ACA Code's own standard (B.2.a) is broader and simpler: disclosure permitted/required "to protect clients or identified others from serious and foreseeable harm" — and consult when in doubt. Consultation plus documentation is the universal safety net: it converts "my judgment" into "the professional standard of care."

The legal reality: it depends on your state

There is no single national duty. As compiled by StatPearls (2012-era count, still the standard citation): 23 states mandate warn/protect by statute; ~10 impose it through common law; ~11 make it permissive (you may disclose without liability, but aren't required); and a handful provide no guidance. Two extensions worth knowing: Jablonski v. United States (duty includes reviewing prior treatment records for violence history) and Ewing v. Goldstein (in California, a credible threat communicated to the therapist by the client's family can trigger the duty — not just the client's own words).

Keep the duties straight (duty-concepts cluster): duty to warn/protect concerns danger to an identifiable third party and involves clinical discretion in most states. Mandated reporting (concept-mandated-reporting) concerns abuse of protected classes (children, vulnerable adults), is statutory in all 50 states, and involves essentially no discretion — suspicion itself triggers the report. Confusing these two is the classic Unit 3 exam error.

What it looks like in the room

Client: "I swear, if I see him with her again I'm going to put him in the ground. I have my brother's gun."

Weak response (avoid): "Let's take a breath — I'm sure you don't mean that." (Minimizes; no assessment; if he does mean it, you've closed the door.)

Stronger response: "I hear how much rage is in that. I need to take it seriously, and I want to understand exactly where you are with it. When you say put him in the ground — is that a plan you've thought about, or the size of the anger talking? … You remember when we started, I said if I ever believed someone was in real danger I'd have to act to keep people safe. I want us to work this together so nobody gets hurt and you don't lose your future to this."

Note the sequence: take it seriously → assess (plan, means, intent, timeline) → recall the already-disclosed limit (this is why the informed-consent speech matters) → prefer collaborative protective steps; warn/notify only as needed. Then document the assessment and consult.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Prediction is the weak link. StatPearls is blunt: "guidelines on accurately predicting and assessing dangerousness are lacking." The law demands a judgment the science can't make reliably — which is exactly why consultation + documentation, not clairvoyance, is the standard.
  • Did Tarasoff chill treatment? A long-running debate: critics argue duty-to-protect rules deter dangerous clients from disclosing (or entering treatment at all); defenders note the catastrophic alternative. Empirical evidence is thin either way.
  • Scope creep: some jurisdictions have extended protect-duties to property, to self-harm-adjacent situations, or to disease exposure — boundaries remain unsettled.

Connects to

  • study-tarasoff — the case itself; facts, holdings, aftermath.
  • concept-confidentiality-limits — the exception this doctrine lives inside (B.2.a).
  • concept-mandated-reporting — the confusable sibling duty; see box above.
  • Unit 8 — suicide risk assessment applies the same logic to danger-to-self, with its own tools.

Sources

pages.title: Feeding & Eating Disorders
pages.html:
Feeding & Eating Disorders

Three disorders carry this chapter's clinical weight, and they sort on two questions: is body weight significantly low? and is there compensation after binges? Hold those two hinges and the discriminations fall out. What must never fall out of view: anorexia nervosa is among the deadliest diagnoses in the entire manual — this chapter is medical, not cosmetic.

Anorexia nervosa (AN)

Three criteria, all required :

  1. Restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight (for age, sex, development).
  2. Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behavior that prevents weight gain — a fear that, tellingly, intensifies as weight falls.
  3. Disturbance in how body weight/shape is experienced, undue influence of weight/shape on self-worth, or persistent failure to recognize the seriousness of the low weight.

Two subtypes: restricting (dieting, fasting, exercise only) and binge-eating/purging (with binge or purge behavior — still AN, not bulimia, because weight is low). Lifetime prevalence 0.3–1%, mostly female, onset in late adolescence/early adulthood.

The mortality warning deserves its own line: all-cause mortality is sharply elevated — medical complications (cardiac, electrolyte) plus suicide, which accounts for roughly a quarter of AN deaths. Denial is close to criterial (criterion 3): the disorder is typically ego-syntonic — the client may experience the restriction as achievement and the helpers as the threat, which is why motivation work precedes everything and why outpatient counseling always runs alongside medical monitoring (concept-scope-of-practice; coordinated care).

Bulimia nervosa (BN)

Recurrent binge eating — a discrete period of objectively large intake with a sense of loss of control — plus recurrent inappropriate compensatory behavior (self-induced vomiting, laxatives/diuretics, fasting, driven exercise), both at least weekly for 3 months, with self-worth unduly tied to shape/weight. The weight criterion is the AN/BN line: in BN, weight is normal or above. Same behaviors at low weight → AN binge-purge subtype. Medical risks concentrate around purging (electrolyte disturbance, esophageal damage, dental erosion). Unlike AN, BN is usually ego-dystonic — shame-soaked and hidden, often for years; asking directly and without disgust is the whole screening skill.

Binge-eating disorder (BED)

Recurrent binges with loss of control and marked distress — eating rapidly, until uncomfortably full, without hunger, alone out of embarrassment, followed by disgust/guilt — without compensatory behavior (that absence is the BN line). At least weekly for 3 months. New as an official diagnosis in DSM-5, and the most common eating disorder in the U.S.; more gender-balanced than AN/BN.

The rest of the chapter, briefly

ARFID (avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder): restriction with nutritional consequences but no body-image disturbance — sensory aversion, fear of choking, low interest (common alongside autism); it is what separates "extreme picky eating with impairment" from AN. Plus pica and rumination disorder.

In the room

Distinguish the disorder from the culture that grows it: dieting, "clean eating," and body talk are normative — which both camouflages early eating disorders and means your own casual comments about food/weight/appearance are clinical acts in this population. Screen behaviorally ("Do you ever eat in a way that feels out of control?" "What happens after?") rather than by appearance — most people with eating disorders are not visibly underweight (BN and BED by definition), and compliments on weight loss can reinforce restriction. Body dysmorphic disorder is the near neighbor: appearance obsession without the eating pathology.

Sources

StatPearls Anorexia Nervosa (AN/BN/BED distinctions in-page). Full notes in ../research/unit06-psychopathology-sources.md.

pages.title: Effect Size, Statistical Significance & Clinical Significance
pages.html:
Effect Size, Statistical Significance & Clinical Significance

Three different numbers get collapsed into one vague idea — "the study found something" — and keeping them apart is the most transferable statistical skill a counselor can have. A study can be statistically significant (unlikely to be a fluke), have a large effect size (the difference is big), and still be clinically insignificant (it doesn't help a real person enough to matter) — or any combination of those. Three questions, three numbers:

  • Is it real / not just noise? → the p-value (statistical significance).
  • How big is it? → the effect size.
  • Does it matter to this person? → clinical (practical) significance.

You will almost never compute these. You need to read them and know which question each answers .

The p-value: what it is, and the misreadings to unlearn

A p-value is the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true . By convention, p < .05 is called "statistically significant" — but .05 is an arbitrary line, not a law of nature.

The misinterpretations are so common the American Statistical Association issued a formal statement to correct them . A p-value is not:

  • the probability that the null hypothesis is true (or that the finding is "due to chance"),
  • the probability that the hypothesis/treatment is correct (p < .05 does not mean "95% chance it works"),
  • a measure of how big or important the effect is.

That last point is the one that bites clinically. Because the p-value depends on both the effect size and the sample size, a huge study can make a trivial effect "significant." A weight-loss drug that produces an average loss of half a pound will be wildly "significant" in a 50,000-person trial and still be clinically pointless. "Statistically significant" answers whether, never how much .

Effect size: the "how big" number

Effect size quantifies the magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size — which is exactly what the p-value can't do. The two you'll see most :

  • Cohen's d — a standardized mean difference (how far apart two group means are, in standard-deviation units). Rule-of-thumb: ≈0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large (below ~0.2 is trivial).
  • Pearson r — the strength of a correlation, from −1 to +1; ≈0.1/0.3/0.5 small/medium/large. (*r*² is the proportion of variance shared.)

Treat the thresholds as conventions, not verdicts — Cohen himself warned against them, and what counts as "large" depends on the field and the stakes (a d of 0.2 for a cheap, safe, population-wide intervention can matter more than a d of 0.8 for an expensive, risky one). Effect sizes are also what make studies comparable and are the currency of meta-analysis (concept-evidence-based-practice). This is the number behind claims you've already met: psychotherapy's alliance–outcome correlation (r ≈ .28, Unit 1), antidepressants' modest average benefit (d ≈ 0.3, Unit 11), and the down-weighted SFBT effect sizes (Unit 9).

Confidence intervals: precision, not just a verdict

A 95% confidence interval gives the plausible range for the true effect, capturing the estimate's precision . It's more informative than a bare p-value for two reasons: it shows how big the effect might be (its width = how much uncertainty), and if the interval excludes the null value (0 for a difference, 1 for an odds ratio), the result is "significant" at .05 anyway — so the CI contains the p-value's information and the magnitude. A narrow CI far from zero is a strong, precise result; a wide CI straddling zero is "we don't really know." Best practice is to report effect size + CI + p-value together, because no one of them tells the whole story .

Clinical (practical) significance: does it matter to a person?

Statistical significance is about populations; a clinician treats a person. Clinical significance asks whether a change is large enough to matter in real life — and psychotherapy research has a precise tool for it. Jacobson and Truax defined clinically significant change as moving from a score typical of the dysfunctional population to one typical of the functional population, paired with the Reliable Change Index (RCI) — the change divided by the standard error of the difference, which asks whether an individual moved more than measurement error alone would produce .

Combine the two and every client sorts into one of four outcomes: recovered (reliable change and crossed into the functional range), improved (reliable change but still in the clinical range), unchanged (no reliable change), or deteriorated (reliably worse). This is the statistical backbone of measurement-based care and outcome monitoring — the individual-client meaning of "did therapy work," and the direct methods-level answer to Unit 7's repeated PHQ-9 question ("their score dropped 3 points — is that real, or noise?"). It lives on concept-single-case-design as a practice.

The stance: the nomothetic–idiographic gap

Hold the whole page together with one idea. All of this machinery is nomothetic — about group averages and populations. Your work is idiographic — about one particular person. A large average treatment effect is real and leaves some clients unchanged or worse; a non-significant group finding doesn't mean it can't help this individual. That gap is not a flaw to be fixed; it's the permanent condition of applying research to a person, and it's why "the number is not the person" is the unit's stance. Effect sizes and significance inform the clinical decision; they don't make it.

Connects to

  • concept-evidence-based-practice — effect sizes are the currency of meta-analysis and the evidence hierarchy; "significant but tiny" is a core appraisal skill.
  • concept-single-case-design — reliable change and clinical significance are how you read one client's outcome data.
  • concept-validity-threats — statistical-conclusion validity is the home of p-values, power, and over-reliance on .05.
  • concept-screening-tools and concept-treatment-planning (Unit 7) — the repeated-measure the RCI interprets; measurement-based care in practice.
  • concept-psychotropic-classes (Unit 11) — antidepressants' "real but modest" (d ≈ 0.3) effect is this page's distinction in action.

Three questions, three numbers: Is it real / not just noise? → the p-value (statistical significance). How big is it? → the effect size . Does it matter to this person? → clinical (practical) significance . You will almost never compute these. You need to read them and know which question each answers S7 S8 . The p-value: what it is, and the misreadings to unlearn A p-value is the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed, if the null hypothesis were true S8 . By convention, p < .05 is called "statistically significant" — but .05 is an arbitrary line, not a law of nature. The misinterpretations are so common the American Statistical Association issued a formal statement to correct them S9 . A p-value is not : the probability that the null hypothesis is true (or that the finding is "due to chance"), the probability that the hypothesis/treatment is correct (p < .05 does not mean "95% chance it works"), a measure of how big or important the effect is. That last point is the one that bites clinically. Because the p-value depends on both the effect size and the sample size, a huge study can make a trivial effect "significant." A weight-loss drug that produces an average loss of half a pound will be wildly "significant" in a 50,000-person trial and still be clinically pointless. "Statistically significant" answers whether , never how much S7 S9 . Effect size: the "how big" number Effect size quantifies the magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size — which is exactly what the p-value can't do. The two you'll see most S7 : Cohen's d — a standardized mean difference (how far apart two group means are, in standard-deviation units). Rule-of-thumb: ≈0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large (below ~0.2 is trivial). Pearson r — the strength of a correlation , from −1 to +1; ≈0.1/0.3/0.5 small/medium/large. (*r*² is the proportion of variance shared.) Treat the thresholds as conventions, not verdicts — Cohen himself warned against them, and what counts as "large" depends on the field and the stakes (a d of 0.2 for a cheap, safe, population-wide intervention can matter more than a d of 0.8 for an expensive, risky one). Effect sizes are also what make studies comparable and are the currency of meta-analysis ( concept-evidence-based-practice ). This is the number behind claims you've already met: psychotherapy's alliance–outcome correlation ( r ≈ .28, Unit 1), antidepressants' modest average benefit ( d ≈ 0.3, Unit 11), and the down-weighted SFBT effect sizes (Unit 9). Confidence intervals: precision, not just a verdict A 95% confidence interval gives the plausible range for the true effect, capturing the estimate's precision S8 . It's more informative than a bare p-value for two reasons: it shows how big the effect might be (its width = how much uncertainty), and if the interval excludes the null value (0 for a difference, 1 for an odds ratio), the result is "significant" at .05 anyway — so the CI contains the p-value's information and the magnitude. A narrow CI far from zero is a strong, precise result; a wide CI straddling zero is "we don't really know." Best practice is to report effect size + CI + p-value together, because no one of them tells the whole story S8 S9 . Clinical (practical) significance: does it matter to a person? Statistical significance is about populations ; a clinician treats a person . Clinical significance asks whether a change is large enough to matter in real life — and psychotherapy research has a precise tool for it. Jacobson and Truax defined clinically significant change as moving from a score typical of the dysfunctional population to one typical of the functional population, paired with the Reliable Change Index (RCI) — the change divided by the standard error of the difference, which asks whether an individual moved more than measurement error alone would produce S10 . Combine the two and every client sorts into one of four outcomes: recovered (reliable change and crossed into the functional range), improved (reliable change but still in the clinical range), unchanged (no reliable change), or deteriorated (reliably worse). This is the statistical backbone of measurement-based care and outcome monitoring — the individual-client meaning of "did therapy work," and the direct methods-level answer to Unit 7's repeated PHQ-9 question ("their score dropped 3 points — is that real, or noise?"). It lives on concept-single-case-design as a practice. The stance: the nomothetic–idiographic gap Hold the whole page together with one idea. All of this machinery is nomothetic — about group averages and populations. Your work is idiographic — about one particular person. A large average treatment effect is real and leaves some clients unchanged or worse; a non-significant group finding doesn't mean it can't help this individual. That gap is not a flaw to be fixed; it's the permanent condition of applying research to a person, and it's why "the number is not the person" is the unit's stance. Effect sizes and significance inform the clinical decision; they don't make it. Connects to concept-evidence-based-practice — effect sizes are the currency of meta-analysis and the evidence hierarchy; "significant but tiny" is a core appraisal skill. concept-single-case-design — reliable change and clinical significance are how you read one client's outcome data. concept-validity-threats — statistical-conclusion validity is the home of p-values, power, and over-reliance on .05. concept-screening-tools and concept-treatment-planning (Unit 7) — the repeated-measure the RCI interprets; measurement-based care in practice. concept-psychotropic-classes (Unit 11) — antidepressants' "real but modest" ( d ≈ 0.3) effect is this page's distinction in action. S9 Wasserstein & Lazar (2016), the ASA statement on p-values. S10 Jacobson & Truax (1991), clinical significance and the Reliable Change Index. Full notes in ../research/unit12-research-sources.md .

pages.title: Empathy (Accurate Empathy & Carkhuff's Levels)
pages.html:
Empathy

Empathy is the second of Rogers' core conditions: understanding the client's experience from inside their frame of reference and conveying that understanding back so the client feels gotten. Rogers called the fully-developed version accurate empathy — "the therapist conveys an accurate understanding of the patient's private world." It is the most studied and most operationalized of the three conditions.

Two components, and the "as if"

Empathy has both an affective side (sensing the client's feeling) and a cognitive side (comprehending it and its meaning). The classic guardrail is Rogers' phrase "as if": you sense the client's world as if it were your own without ever losing the "as if" quality. Lose it and you've stopped empathizing and started merging — over-identifying, taking the feeling on as yours, which helps no one (see the limits below).

Empathy vs. sympathy vs. interpretation

Empathy is routinely confused with two near-neighbors, and the confusions degrade the response in opposite directions. Keeping them apart is a CACREP-level skill.

  • Empathy — understanding the emotion from inside the client's frame and reflecting it: "It sounds like that left you frightened." Stays in their frame.
  • Sympathy — feeling sorrow or concern for the client from outside their experience: "I'm so sorry that happened to you." It's a real emotional response, but for them rather than with them. Clark (2010) warns that misapplying sympathetic responses as empathic ones can interfere with the counseling relationship — it can position the counselor above the client and quietly shift the focus onto the counselor's reaction. Watches from outside the frame.
  • Interpretation — adding your own explanation of cause or meaning, going beyond what the client said: "I wonder if that frightens you because it echoes something older." This is an influencing skill (higher on the microskills hierarchy, more risk), not a core condition. Leaves the frame.

Also worth separating from compassion (empathy plus a motivation to help relieve suffering) and pity (feeling sorry for someone from a position of superiority — the coldest of the set). Only the first item on the list — staying in the frame — is what Rogers meant.

Carkhuff's five levels: empathy as a measurable, teachable skill

Rogers described empathy; Robert Carkhuff (1969), building on Truax & Carkhuff (1967), made it gradable. His five-level scale was the first to operationalize empathy into observable helper behaviors, expressly to teach it. It's the rubric counselor-education still uses to rate a response.

LevelNameWhat the response does
1Non-empathicDetached or dismissive; ignores or misreads the feeling. Leaves the client unheard.
2SubtractivePartial/superficial; responds to content but subtracts from the felt meaning.
3InterchangeableAccurately reflects the client's expressed content and feeling — no more, no less. The minimum for effective helping.
4Additive (skilled)Adds to the client's expression — names and clarifies a feeling they were reaching for but hadn't quite said.
5Additive (highly skilled)Surfaces emotion the client hasn't yet articulated; deepens self-understanding.

The load-bearing idea: Level 3 is the floor, not the ceiling. Levels 1–2 subtract from what the client offered; Level 3 is interchangeable (a good paraphrase-of-feeling); Levels 4–5 are additive (this is Ivey's "advanced accurate empathy"). A beginner who reliably hits Level 3 is already helping; the growth edge is moving from interchangeable to additive without sliding into premature interpretation. The difference between an additive reflection and an interpretation is that additive empathy still names what is implicitly present in the client's own experience, whereas interpretation imports an explanation from outside it.

Why it matters in the room

Empathy is what a client is unconsciously scanning for in the first minutes: does this person get it? Get it right and they open up; miss it and the session stays on the surface. For anyone with a fix-it reflex, accurate empathy is hard because it requires withholding the solution and staying with the person's experience first — reflect the feeling, then stop talking (see the stance note in unit01-helping-skills).

What's contested / the limits (don't over-learn it)

  • Empathy can be faked and clients can tell. Reflected feeling that isn't backed by congruence reads as a technique. The three conditions work together.
  • Cultural empathy isn't automatic. Accurately entering another's frame is harder across large cultural distance; assuming you already understand can be its own failure (this is where Unit 4's cultural humility complicates a naïve "just be empathic").
  • Over-identification (losing the "as if") collapses the helpful distance and can lead to burnout and boundary loss — Unit 8's vicarious trauma is partly what happens when empathy loses its "as if" over time.

Connects to

  • concept-core-conditions — the synthesis hub; empathy is one of the three conditions.
  • concept-unconditional-positive-regard and concept-congruence — the other two.
  • concept-microskills-hierarchy — reflection of feeling is empathy made into a teachable skill; interpretation is its higher-risk neighbor.
  • concept-attending-and-listening — you can't be accurately empathic without first attending and observing.
  • theory-common-factors — empathy is one of the best-supported common relationship factors.

pages.title: Evidence-Based Practice, the Evidence Hierarchy & the Replication Crisis
pages.html:
Evidence-Based Practice, the Evidence Hierarchy & the Replication Crisis

"Evidence-based" is one of the most-used and most-misused phrases in the field. It is invoked to sell trainings, to win insurance approval, and sometimes to shut down a conversation ("but is it evidence-based?"). This page does three things: says what evidence-based practice actually means (it's an act of integration, not a trump card), gives you the hierarchy for ranking what counts as strong evidence, and — crucially — hands you the humility to read that evidence critically, because the field has learned the hard way that a lot of published findings do not hold up.

What EBP actually is: three legs, integrated

The APA's official definition, which Unit 9 already leaned on, is worth holding verbatim: evidence-based practice in psychology is "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences" . Three co-equal legs:

  1. Best available research evidence,
  2. Clinical expertise (the counselor's trained judgment), and
  3. Client characteristics, culture, and values/preferences.

The load-bearing word is integration. EBP is not "research evidence overrides everything else"; a treatment with the best RCT support is not evidence-based practice for a client who won't do it, can't access it, or whose culture it ignores. This is the definition that keeps "evidence-based" from becoming a cudgel — and it's the same three-legged stool wherever you meet the phrase. Don't confuse EBP with an EST (below): an empirically supported treatment is a specific therapy shown to work in trials (one input to leg 1); evidence-based practice is the whole integrative process.

The evidence hierarchy: ranking "best available research"

Not all evidence is equal, and the evidence pyramid ranks study designs by how resistant they are to bias , strongest at the top:

  1. Systematic reviews & meta-analyses — rigorous syntheses of all the good studies on a question (a meta-analysis pools their effect sizes).
  2. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) — the strongest single-study design for a treatment claim (concept-experimental-vs-correlational).
  3. Cohort studies — follow groups over time (observational, no randomization).
  4. Case-control studies — compare people with/without an outcome, looking back.
  5. Cross-sectional studies / case series.
  6. Case reports & expert opinion — weakest; a single anecdote or authority.

As you climb, the evidence gets less susceptible to bias but also rarer. Two caveats keep the pyramid honest: it ranks design, not execution — a poor meta-analysis is not automatically better than a well-run RCT, and quality-appraisal systems like GRADE exist precisely to judge quality within a level; and the top designs can still have poor external validity (concept-validity-threats), so "highest on the pyramid" is the starting question, not the final word.

Empirically supported treatments (ESTs) apply this logic to name specific therapies. Chambless and Hollon's criteria are the standard: well-established = efficacy shown in ≥2 good between-group experiments by independent research teams (guarding against a single lab's bias); probably efficacious = a lower tier with fewer or non-independent studies . Note what the label means and doesn't: "empirically supported" is a floor ("this has been shown to work for this problem"), not a ranking that makes unlisted approaches worthless — and the common-factors / dodo-bird finding (Unit 9) shows technique differences are often small once the alliance is accounted for.

The reason to stay humble: the replication crisis

Here is the fact that should recalibrate how you read any single exciting study. In 2015, the Open Science Collaboration tried to replicate 100 psychology studies from top journals. Although ~97% of the originals reported significant results, only about 36% of the replications reached significance, and effect sizes shrank by about half . This is the empirical core of the replication crisis, and its causes are now well understood:

  • Publication bias (the file-drawer problem) — journals prefer positive, novel results, so null findings and failed replications go unpublished, making the visible literature look stronger than the real one.
  • p-hacking / researcher degrees of freedom — the many small, defensible-looking analytic choices (when to stop collecting data, which covariates to include, which outcomes to report) can be flexed — usually unconsciously — until p dips below .05. Simmons and colleagues showed this can push the false-positive rate far above the nominal 5% .
  • HARKing — presenting a post-hoc finding as if it had been the hypothesis all along.
  • Allegiance bias — the developer's own trials tend to report the biggest effects (the SFBT-effect-size caution in Unit 9; the enthusiasm behind new group and neuro claims in Units 10–11).

The field's response is the open-science movement: preregistration and registered reports (committing to hypotheses and analyses before seeing the data, and getting publication guaranteed regardless of outcome), larger samples, open data, and — the culture change that matters most — valuing replication and null results.

The takeaway is not cynicism ("psychology is fake"). It's calibration: a single, splashy, un-replicated study earns provisional interest, not belief; a replicated effect with a preregistered design and a meaningful effect size earns real confidence. Being a discerning consumer of the field's competing claims — the syllabus objective — is this calibrated skepticism.

Where this lands clinically

When a workshop, a rep, or a headline pitches you an intervention, this page is the checklist: What's the evidence — an RCT, a meta-analysis, or a testimonial? Who ran the studies — independent teams or the developer? How big is the effect, and has it replicated? And does it fit this client's values and access (concept-effect-size, the three legs)? That is not academic caution; it's how you avoid wasting a client's time and money on the confidently-marketed-but-unsupported, which the field produces in abundance.

Connects to

  • concept-experimental-vs-correlational — the designs the hierarchy ranks; why RCTs and their syntheses sit on top.
  • concept-effect-size — meta-analysis pools effect sizes; "significant but tiny" and allegiance-inflated effects are read here.
  • concept-validity-threats — why even top-of-pyramid studies can mislead (external validity; execution ≠ design).
  • concept-program-evaluation — EBP's "does it work for my program/clients" cousin.
  • unit09-modalities and theory-solution-focused (Unit 9) — the three legs and the allegiance-bias caution, first met there.
  • theory-yalom-factors (Unit 10) — "group ≈ individual" (Burlingame) and "groups can harm" as evidence-appraisal claims.

Sources

Open Science Collaboration (2015) + Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn (2011) — the replication crisis, p-hacking, publication/allegiance bias. Full notes in ../research/unit12-research-sources.md.

pages.title: Experimental vs. Correlational (vs. Quasi-Experimental) Designs
pages.html:
Experimental vs. Correlational (vs. Quasi-Experimental) Designs

The single most useful thing this unit can give you is a reflex that fires every time you read a claim: what kind of study is this, and does it license the claim being made? Ninety percent of bad science reporting — and a fair amount of bad clinical reasoning — is one specific error: treating a correlational finding as if it proved causation. "People who journal are less depressed" is not "journaling reduces depression." Learning to tell the designs apart, and to know exactly what each one can and cannot support, is the core literacy skill.

The one question that separates the designs: was something manipulated, and was assignment random?

Two yes/no questions sort essentially every quantitative design:

  1. Did the researcher manipulate a variable (deliberately assign an intervention/condition), rather than just measure what was already there?
  2. Was assignment to conditions random?
  • True experiment — yes to both. The researcher manipulates the independent variable and uses random assignment to conditions. Only this design supports a causal claim .
  • Quasi-experiment — yes to manipulation, no to random assignment. There is an intervention, but people fall into groups by a pre-existing feature (clinic A vs. clinic B, this school year vs. last). It sits between the other two on internal validity .
  • Correlational (non-experimental) — no manipulation at all. The researcher measures two or more variables as they naturally occur and looks at their relationship. It supports claims of association, not causation .

The randomized controlled trial (RCT) — the design at the top of the treatment-evidence hierarchy (concept-evidence-based-practice) — is simply a true experiment applied to a treatment: participants are randomly assigned to the therapy vs. a control/comparison, so that (on average) the groups differ only in the treatment.

Why only the experiment gets to say "caused"

A causal claim requires three things, and correlational designs can only ever deliver the first :

  1. Covariation — the two variables actually move together. (Correlation gives you this.)
  2. Temporal precedence — the cause comes before the effect. (Correlational snapshots often can't establish which came first.)
  3. No plausible alternative explanation — nothing else explains the covariation. (This is the one random assignment is built to buy.)

Random assignment is the engine. By allocating people to conditions by chance, it makes the groups equivalent on average at the outset — on everything, measured or not, including confounds you never thought of. So if they differ afterward, the manipulation is the only systematic difference left standing. That is what "control" means and why the experiment earns the word caused .

The two traps of correlational data

A correlation of r between X and Y can arise three ways, and the data alone cannot tell you which:

  • X → Y (what the headline assumes),
  • Y → X — the directionality problem (maybe less-depressed people have the energy to journal, not the reverse),
  • Z → both X and Y — the third-variable problem (a lurking common cause — e.g., having free time and stability drives both journaling and lower depression) .

This is why "correlation does not imply causation" is the unit's mantra. Correlational research is not bad — it is essential when manipulation is impossible or unethical (you cannot randomly assign people to trauma, poverty, or a diagnosis), it is often the only ethical option, and it generates the hypotheses experiments then test. It just cannot, by itself, support a causal verdict.

Random assignment vs. random sampling — a beginner's-mistake pair

These sound alike and do opposite jobs (this is a classic exam confusable):

  • Random assignment — dividing your participants into conditions by chance. It serves internal validity (equating the groups → causal inference). An experiment without it is not a true experiment.
  • Random sampling / selection — drawing your participants from the population at random. It serves external validity (a representative sample → generalizable results) — see concept-validity-threats.

A study can have one without the other: a tightly randomized experiment on 200 undergraduates (strong assignment, weak sampling) vs. a national survey with no manipulation at all (strong sampling, no assignment).

Where this lands clinically

You will read all three kinds of study, and the design tells you how much weight to put on the claim. An RCT showing a therapy beat a control supports "this treatment works." A correlational study linking a parenting style to an outcome supports "these tend to go together — worth exploring," not "this parenting causes that." A quasi-experiment comparing two clinics is suggestive but confounded (the clinics' clients differ). Matching the strength of your belief to the strength of the design is the skill — and it hands directly to how you rank and appraise evidence in concept-evidence-based-practice.

Connects to

  • concept-validity-threats — the four validities and the threats each design is vulnerable to; internal (causal) vs. external (generalizability) validity is the axis behind assignment vs. sampling.
  • concept-evidence-based-practice — the evidence hierarchy ranks these designs by how well they support a treatment claim (RCT and its syntheses on top).
  • concept-single-case-design — a true experiment can be run on one person; the design logic here scales down.
  • concept-reliability-validity (Unit 7) — measurement quality is the other half of a trustworthy study; a perfect design with an invalid measure still fails.
  • unit09-modalities (Unit 9) — why RCTs anchor "empirically supported" while the common-factors caution keeps "supported" from meaning "best."

pages.title: Grief Models & the Normal/Prolonged Boundary
pages.html:
Grief Models & the Normal / Prolonged Boundary

You don't need a theory to sit with a grieving person — but a wrong theory will make you unhelpful, because you'll start correcting their grief against a script. The clinically useful move is to hold loose, descriptive models (this is roughly what grief does) and drop the rigid, prescriptive one (grief should march through these stages).

The five stages — and why clinicians have largely retired them

Elisabeth Kübler-Ross's denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance is the most famous grief framework in the culture — and the most over-applied. The critiques are serious:

  • She derived the stages from interviews with terminally ill people facing their own deaths, not from the bereaved — so generalizing them to mourning was never well-founded.
  • Grief does not proceed in a fixed order, and many people never show several of the stages.
  • The biggest practical harm: presented as an itinerary, the stages make grieving people (and their helpers) feel they are "doing it wrong" when their experience doesn't fit — "I'm not at acceptance yet," "I skipped bargaining."

Keep the stages only as a vocabulary for common reactions that can occur, never as a path someone should be on. Better models follow.

Worden's Four Tasks of Mourning (active, non-linear)

William Worden reframed grief from passive stages to tasks the mourner works — which restores agency and doesn't imply an order.

  1. Accept the reality of the loss — move from intellectual to emotional acknowledgment that the person is gone.
  2. Process the pain of grief — feel it rather than avoid or numb it.
  3. Adjust to a world without the deceased — external (roles, tasks), internal (identity, "who am I now"), and spiritual adjustments.
  4. Find an enduring connection with the deceased while embarking on a new life — not "let go" or "get over," but relocate the person into a continuing bond and keep living.

That fourth task is the modern correction to an older "sever the ties / achieve closure" view: healthy grief usually keeps a continuing bond, it doesn't erase one.

The Dual Process Model (the best everyday mental model)

Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut's model describes what grieving actually looks like hour to hour: an oscillation between two kinds of coping.

  • Loss-oriented coping — confronting the loss itself: the yearning, the crying, looking at photos, missing the person.
  • Restoration-oriented coping — dealing with the changed world: practical tasks, new roles, paying bills, returning to work, building a different daily life.

The key insight is the oscillation: a healthy griever moves back and forth — leans into the pain for a while, then takes a break to handle life or simply rest, then back again. This is why a grieving parent can be sobbing one hour and organizing the funeral catering the next, and neither is denial or "being strong" — both are normal coping. Crucially: taking a break from grief is not avoidance. A helper who expects unbroken devastation may misread restoration-oriented moments as coldness; that misreading damages support.

Normal grief vs. Prolonged Grief Disorder

Most grief — even shattering grief — is not a mental disorder and does not need treatment; it needs time, support, and presence. But a minority develop a persistent, disabling condition that DSM-5-TR now names Prolonged Grief Disorder (PGD) — housed with the trauma- and stressor-related disorders (Unit 6), which also carries the grief-vs-depression discrimination (concept-mood-disorders). The boundary is drawn by time + persistence + impairment, not by intensity of early grief:

  • Time threshold: the death was at least 12 months ago for adults (6 months for children and adolescents). Before that, intense grief is expected, not pathological.
  • Core symptoms: persistent, pervasive intense yearning/longing for the deceased and/or preoccupation with them, most days, to a clinically significant degree — plus symptoms like identity disruption, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, emotional numbness, feeling life is meaningless, and intense loneliness.
  • Function: the grief causes clinically significant distress or impairment and exceeds cultural/contextual norms.

Risk factors that should raise your antenna: loss of a child, sudden/violent/unnatural death, and being unprepared for the death are among the strongest predictors of PGD. A parent whose child has just died sits squarely in the high-risk group — which is a reason to stay connected and watch over time, not a reason to pathologize their early, normal devastation.

Why this matters in the room

These models do one job for the helper: they stop you from imposing a shape on someone's grief. You won't tell a parent they "should be at acceptance," won't read their practical, functional moments as not caring, and won't either over-pathologize ordinary acute grief or miss the time-and-impairment signs that warrant a referral. See concept-supporting-the-bereaved for what that looks like in practice.

  • aux-psychological-first-aid — the module hub.

pages.title: Stages of Group Development
pages.html:
Stages of Group Development

A group is not a fixed thing you lead the same way every week — it is a developing organism with predictable phases, and the single most common beginner mistake is to treat every session as if the group were at the same maturity. Conflict in week three is not a sign the group is failing; it is usually a sign the group is on schedule. Knowing the stages lets you read what a group needs right now and, crucially, stops you from mislabeling normal developmental turbulence as a problem to be smoothed over. Two frameworks matter: Tuckman's generic sequence and Corey's counseling-specific stages. They describe the same arc.

Tuckman: forming, storming, norming, performing (+ adjourning)

Bruce Tuckman (1965) reviewed the small-group literature and named a four-stage sequence that has proven remarkably durable; Tuckman & Jensen (1977) added a fifth :

  1. Forming — orientation. Members are anxious, polite, and dependent on the leader. They test the water, look for acceptance, and want to know the rules and whether they're safe. Little real work happens; the task is inclusion and safety.
  2. Storming — conflict. As comfort grows, differences surface: members jockey for position, challenge one another and often the leader's authority, and the group feels tense or unsafe. This is the hardest stage for a beginner to tolerate — and the most important not to suppress. Conflict, handled well, is how the group earns real trust.
  3. Norming — cohesion. The group works through its conflicts and settles into shared norms and roles. Trust and belonging rise; members start to feel like an "us." Cohesiveness (theory-yalom-factors) consolidates here.
  4. Performing — the working stage. The group functions as a productive unit: members take risks, give and receive honest feedback, and use one another. This is where the therapeutic factors do their heaviest lifting.
  5. Adjourning (added 1977) — termination/mourning. The group ends; members process loss, consolidate gains, and say goodbye. Skipping this stage wastes the ending's therapeutic potential.

Corey: the counseling-specific version

Counselor-education texts (Corey) reframe the same arc for therapy and counseling groups, adding a stage before the group even meets :

  • Pre-group (formation). Before session one: screening, selection, preparation, and informed consent (concept-group-ethics-and-formation). Yalom's research is emphatic that this stage — often skipped by beginners — strongly predicts who stays and who drops out. The group's fate is partly decided before it convenes.
  • Initial stage — orientation and exploration (Tuckman's forming). Establishing trust, goals, and norms; addressing confidentiality immediately. Members are tentative and watching the leader.
  • Transition stage — the counseling name for storming. Anxiety, defensiveness, resistance, and the struggle for control come to the surface; members may challenge the leader or each other. The leader's task is to help the group work through conflict, not around it — to model that the group can survive disagreement. Mishandled, this stage stalls the group; handled well, it produces the trust the working stage runs on.
  • Working stage — cohesion and productivity (Tuckman's norming+performing fused). Trust is at its highest; members take real risks, address difficult material, and hold each other accountable in a way that feels supportive rather than judgmental.
  • Final stage — consolidation and termination. Reviewing progress, saying what needs saying, and planning how to transfer the learning to life outside the group.

The leader's job changes by stage

The reason stages matter practically: what a good leader does is stage-dependent (concept-group-leadership).

  • Initial/forming — high executive function and structure: set norms, protect members, reduce anxiety, model inclusion. The group can't self-regulate yet.
  • Transition/storming — tolerate and contain conflict without fleeing it. The instinct to rescue the group from its own tension (or to side with whoever challenges you) is the trap; the move is to make the conflict examinable and safe. Resisting the urge to smooth it over is the stance skill of this stage.
  • Working/performing — step back. Let members do the therapeutic work on each other; the leader's over-involvement here starves the group. This is the group version of the whole curriculum's "resist the urge to fix": as the group matures, the leader deliberately decenters.
  • Final/adjourning — surface the ending, help members grieve it, and consolidate what they'll take with them.

What's contested (don't over-apply the ladder)

  • Stages are a heuristic, not a law. Real groups don't march cleanly forward; they recycle — a new member, a crisis, or a rupture can throw a "working" group back into storming, and open-ended groups (members joining and leaving continuously) never sit still in one stage at all . Use the model to read a group, not to grade it against a timetable.
  • Tuckman's evidence is mostly non-clinical. The 1965 model was a literature review across many group types (including training and work groups), not a study of therapy groups. It transfers well as a lens; it is not a validated clinical mechanism.
  • "Storming = failure" is the costly misread. The most damaging error the model prevents is a beginner reading normal transition-stage conflict as the group breaking down and reflexively suppressing it — which robs the group of the trust that only comes from surviving conflict together.

  • concept-group-leadership — the leader's functions are dialed up or down by stage.
  • concept-group-ethics-and-formation — the pre-group stage: screening, preparation, consent.
  • theory-eriksons-stages (Unit 5) — the same idea that development proceeds in stage-specific tasks, one organism up.

Yalom's research is emphatic that this stage — often skipped by beginners — strongly predicts who stays and who drops out. The group's fate is partly decided before it convenes. Initial stage — orientation and exploration (Tuckman's forming ). Establishing trust, goals, and norms; addressing confidentiality immediately . Members are tentative and watching the leader. Transition stage — the counseling name for storming . Anxiety, defensiveness, resistance, and the struggle for control come to the surface; members may challenge the leader or each other. The leader's task is to help the group work through conflict, not around it — to model that the group can survive disagreement. Mishandled, this stage stalls the group; handled well, it produces the trust the working stage runs on. Working stage — cohesion and productivity (Tuckman's norming + performing fused). Trust is at its highest; members take real risks, address difficult material, and hold each other accountable in a way that feels supportive rather than judgmental. Final stage — consolidation and termination. Reviewing progress, saying what needs saying, and planning how to transfer the learning to life outside the group. Tuckman Corey (counseling) The group's core task — Pre-group screen, prepare, consent Forming Initial trust, safety, norms, goals Storming Transition survive conflict; earn real trust Norming Working (early) cohesion consolidates Performing Working risk-taking, feedback, the real work Adjourning Final consolidate gains, grieve, transfer learning The leader's job changes by stage The reason stages matter practically: what a good leader does is stage-dependent ( concept-group-leadership ). Initial/forming — high executive function and structure: set norms, protect members, reduce anxiety, model inclusion. The group can't self-regulate yet. Transition/storming — tolerate and contain conflict without fleeing it. The instinct to rescue the group from its own tension (or to side with whoever challenges you) is the trap; the move is to make the conflict examinable and safe. Resisting the urge to smooth it over is the stance skill of this stage. Working/performing — step back. Let members do the therapeutic work on each other; the leader's over-involvement here starves the group. This is the group version of the whole curriculum's "resist the urge to fix": as the group matures, the leader deliberately decenters . Final/adjourning — surface the ending, help members grieve it, and consolidate what they'll take with them. What's contested (don't over-apply the ladder) Stages are a heuristic, not a law. Real groups don't march cleanly forward; they recycle — a new member, a crisis, or a rupture can throw a "working" group back into storming, and open-ended groups (members joining and leaving continuously) never sit still in one stage at all S7 S8 . Use the model to read a group, not to grade it against a timetable. Tuckman's evidence is mostly non-clinical. The 1965 model was a literature review across many group types (including training and work groups), not a study of therapy groups. It transfers well as a lens; it is not a validated clinical mechanism. "Storming = failure" is the costly misread. The most damaging error the model prevents is a beginner reading normal transition-stage conflict as the group breaking down and reflexively suppressing it — which robs the group of the trust that only comes from surviving conflict together. pages.title: Group Ethics & Formation (Screening, Preparation, Confidentiality)
pages.html:
Group Ethics & Formation

A large share of a group's outcome is decided before the first session — in who is selected, how they are prepared, and what norms are set. This is also where group work departs most sharply from individual ethics (Unit 3), because a group has a feature a dyad does not: other clients in the room. That one fact reshapes confidentiality, consent, and the counselor's protective duty. The ASGW Best Practice Guidelines organize the whole job into three phases — planning, performing, and processing — and the two that beginners underweight are the bookends: planning (formation) and processing (reflection) .

Screening and selection (the pre-group task)

Both the ACA Code (A.8) and ASGW require the counselor to screen prospective members . The standard: select members whose needs and goals are compatible with the group's purpose, who will not impede the group process, and whose well-being will not be jeopardized by the group experience . Screening is a two-way fit judgment — it protects the candidate (a fragile or acutely-in-crisis person may be harmed by, or unable to use, a particular group) and it protects the group (a member whose needs are radically mismatched can derail it, and the wrong mix produces the "difficult member" dynamics of concept-difficult-group-members). The intensity of screening scales with the depth of the group (concept-group-types): light for a psychoeducational class, careful and clinical for a reconstructive psychotherapy group.

Composition is part of selection: homogeneous groups (members share a problem — e.g., a bereavement group) cohere faster and normalize a specific struggle; heterogeneous groups offer a richer social microcosm and more varied feedback. Neither is universally right — the choice follows the group's aim.

Preparation: the pre-group meeting

Yalom's research is emphatic and often-skipped: pre-group preparation improves outcomes and reduces dropout . Before the group starts, meet with members to demystify the process — explain how group works, what to expect (including that early sessions can feel awkward and that conflict is normal — concept-group-development-stages), correct misconceptions ("I'll just be talked at" / "I'll be forced to bare my soul"), set realistic expectations, and establish norms. Prepared members drop out less and engage sooner. Formation is not paperwork; it is the first therapeutic act.

Informed consent in groups

Group informed consent (concept-informed-consent) carries everything individual consent does — purpose, risks and benefits, the leader's qualifications, voluntary participation and the right to leave — plus group-specific elements: the norms and expectations, the risks unique to groups (exposure to others' distress, the possibility of conflict or of feeling pressured), and, above all, the limits of confidentiality. A special case is the involuntary or mandated member (court-ordered groups are common in addiction and domestic-violence work): they must still be told what is and isn't required, what will be reported to the referring body, and what genuine choices remain — consent is meaningful even when attendance isn't optional.

The confidentiality limit that is unique to groups

This is the single most tested point in group ethics, because it inverts an individual-therapy assumption. In individual therapy the counselor controls confidentiality (within its legal limits — Unit 3, concept-confidentiality-limits). In a group, the other members are not bound by the counselor's ethics code — and the counselor cannot guarantee that they will keep what they hear private.

The ACA Code B.4.a states it precisely :

"In group work, counselors clearly explain the importance and parameters of confidentiality for the specific group being entered."

Parse what that does and doesn't promise. The counselor's duty is to explain confidentiality's importance, set it as an explicit group norm, describe the parameters (what confidentiality means here, why it matters, the consequences of breaching it), and often have members agree to it — but the counselor can only promise their own confidentiality, not the members'. Honesty about this limit is itself part of consent: members decide what to disclose knowing the room is not sealed. A further legal wrinkle: privilege (the legal protection that can keep therapy communications out of court) generally does not apply to group treatment — the presence of third parties can waive it — unless a specific state statute preserves it . So the honest framing to members is: "I will keep what's said here confidential and I'll ask the same of everyone, and we'll treat it as a firm expectation — but I can't guarantee others will, and the law may not protect it the way it protects one-on-one therapy."

The protective duty

Because a group can harm — the encounter-group casualty finding (concept-group-leadership) is the evidence — ACA (A.8.b) charges the counselor to take reasonable precautions to protect members from physical, emotional, or psychological trauma . In practice: screen out foreseeable bad fits, set and enforce safety norms, intervene when a member is being scapegoated or attacked (concept-difficult-group-members), and keep the group's intensity within tolerable bounds (the moderate-not-maximal stimulation finding). Protection is not softness; it is the floor that makes the risk-taking of real group work safe enough to attempt.

Processing (the underweighted back end)

The third ASGW phase, processing, closes the loop: the leader reflects on each session (ideally with a co-leader or supervisor), tracks each member's trajectory, and attends to endings — helping members consolidate gains and transfer learning out of the group (concept-group-development-stages final stage). Skipping processing is how groups drift and how casualties go unnoticed.

pages.title: Group Leadership
pages.html:
Group Leadership

Leading a group is not "doing individual therapy with more people in the room." The leader's real product is not the help they personally deliver but the culture and process they cultivate so that members help one another. This page covers the two frameworks every group counselor is expected to know — the four leadership functions (and the striking finding that more is not always better) and the leader's core technical job, activating and illuminating the here-and-now — plus the classic leadership styles.

The four leadership functions (Lieberman, Yalom & Miles)

The most-cited empirical study of what group leaders actually do — Lieberman, Yalom & Miles' Encounter Groups: First Facts (1973), across 18 groups — reduced leader behavior to four basic functions :

  1. Emotional stimulation — challenging, confronting, self-disclosing, modeling risk, drawing out feeling. The leader as activator.
  2. Caring — support, warmth, acceptance, encouragement, protection. The leader as holder.
  3. Meaning-attribution — explaining, clarifying, interpreting, giving members cognitive frameworks to make sense of their experience. The leader as translator.
  4. Executive function — setting limits, rules, norms, goals; managing time, pacing, and structure. The leader as manager.

The finding that matters: more is not always better

The study's famous result is not the list but the shape of each function's relationship to outcome :

  • Caring and meaning-attribution have a linear relationship — more is better. You essentially cannot over-supply warmth or over-supply sense-making. A leader should max these out.
  • Emotional stimulation and executive function have a curvilinear (inverted-U) relationship — a moderate amount is best; too much or too little produces worse outcomes. Too little stimulation and the group is flat and safe to the point of inertia; too much and members are overwhelmed and flooded. Too little executive management and the group is chaotic and unsafe; too much and the leader is a traffic cop running a series of dyads, suffocating the group's own process.

The best-supported leader profile: moderate emotional stimulation, moderate executive function, high caring, high meaning-attribution .

Leaders can harm

The same study is the field's key evidence that group leadership can produce casualties — members who left worse off. The damage clustered under one profile: the "aggressive stimulator" — high emotional stimulation, intrusive, charismatic-authoritarian, low on caring . This is the empirical backbone of the unit's stance warning (unit10-group): the leader whose personality dominates the group, who confronts hard and cares little, is not merely ineffective — they are dangerous. It is a direct argument for humility, for screening (concept-group-ethics-and-formation), and for prioritizing warmth over charisma.

The core technical skill: activate and illuminate the here-and-now

Yalom locates the leader's central task in the here-and-now — the group's immediate, present-moment interactions, as opposed to the "there-and-then" of members' outside lives . It has two tiers, and both are required:

  1. Activation — steering the group's attention into the present. When a member reports a conflict with their spouse (there-and-then), the leader looks for its live echo in the room: "You said your wife dismisses you — I wonder if you felt dismissed by the group just now when the topic changed." The outside story becomes usable data about how the member relates here.
  2. Process illumination (the self-reflective loop) — after the group experiences an interaction, the leader helps it reflect on the interaction itself: what just happened between us, and what does it reveal? Process is the relationship-level meaning of what's said, as distinct from content (the topic). "I notice that every time Maria opens up, someone rushes to fix it — what's that about in here?" is a process comment. Experience without reflection is just events; reflection without experience is dry intellectualization. The therapeutic engine is the loop.

This is where the social microcosm (theory-yalom-factors) gets its payoff: members enact their patterns in the here-and-now, and process illumination is how those patterns are made examinable. It is also the group form of Unit 1's microskills (concept-microskills-hierarchy) — reflection, immediacy, and observation — aimed at the space between members, not just from counselor to client.

Yalom frames the leader's broader tasks the same way: create and maintain the group (get the right members in the room and keep them there — the formation work), build the culture (shape norms of honesty, feedback, and here-and-now focus; the leader is the group's norm-setter, mostly by modeling), and activate and illuminate the here-and-now.

Leadership styles

The classic Lewin/Lippitt/White typology of leader style (1939) is still standard shorthand in group texts:

  • Authoritarian / autocratic — the leader directs, decides, and controls. Efficient and sometimes necessary early or in crisis, but it fosters dependence and suppresses the group's own agency.
  • Democratic — the leader facilitates shared decision-making and draws out the group. Generally associated with the best group climate and member satisfaction; the default aim for most counseling groups.
  • Laissez-faire — the leader is hands-off and minimally directive. Can free a mature working group, but applied to an early or anxious group it reads as absence and leaves members unsafe and rudderless.

The style should flex with the stage (concept-group-development-stages): more structure early (an initial group can't self-direct), less as the group matures and can carry its own process. Rigidly holding one style regardless of what the group needs is the error.

The stance thread: decenter yourself

Everything on this page points one way. The leader's growth is away from being the hub of every exchange. The high-skill move, over and over, is to turn the work back to the group — "Does anyone else recognize that?" instead of answering yourself — because the member-to-member exchange is where universality, altruism, and interpersonal learning live. The curriculum's "resist the urge to fix" here becomes "resist the urge to be the one who helps." Over-functioning as a leader isn't generosity; it's theft of the group's own therapeutic power.

  • concept-group-development-stages — the functions and styles are dialed by stage.
  • concept-difficult-group-members — leadership put to the test; the difficult member as a here-and-now opportunity.

pages.title: Types of Group Work (ASGW)
pages.html:
Types of Group Work (ASGW)

"Group" is not one thing. A corporate task force, a divorce-recovery skills class, an outpatient interpersonal-growth group, and an inpatient group for chronic psychiatric conditions are all "groups," but they differ in purpose, depth, membership, and the leader's role. The Association for Specialists in Group Work (ASGW) — the ACA division that sets group standards — organizes the field into four specializations, distinguished primarily by focus and depth of aim . Knowing which type you're running (and which you're trained to run — a scope-of-practice question, concept-scope-of-practice) determines everything downstream: who you admit, how you lead, and what "success" means.

The four types

1. Task / work groups

Aim: accomplish an identified work goal external to the members — get something done. Examples: committees, task forces, planning groups, teams, community organizations, study circles. Focus: the task and the group's process in service of the task (a skilled task-group leader still attends to dynamics — a committee tears itself apart on process just like a therapy group — but the point is the product, not the members' personal growth). Depth: shallowest with respect to members' inner lives; members are there for the work.

2. Psychoeducational (guidance) groups

Aim: prevent and educate — impart information and build specific skills, usually around a known theme. Examples: a stress-management class, a parenting-skills group, a divorce-adjustment group, an anger-management or social-skills group, a psychoeducational group about managing depression. Members: typically relatively well-functioning people who want knowledge or skills for a life role or stressor. Focus: structured, often curriculum-based, leader as teacher/facilitator. Prevention and growth, not remediation of deep pathology. (This is the ASGW type that most resembles the classroom — and it borrows heavily from Unit 9's structured skills, e.g. a concept-dbt-skills skills group.)

3. Counseling groups

Aim: interpersonal problem-solving and personal/interpersonal growth — address the "problems of living" (ASGW's phrase). Members: people dealing with conscious, situational, developmental concerns — not severe or entrenched dysfunction. Focus: the here-and-now (concept-group-leadership), member-to-member interaction, growth and prevention/remediation of common life difficulties. Not aimed at major personality change. This is the bread-and-butter group of a counseling practicum.

4. Psychotherapy groups

Aim: remediation and reconstruction — treat deeper, more severe or enduring psychological dysfunction, including personality-level change. Members: people with significant, often long-standing psychological problems (and, historically, more acute or serious diagnoses). Focus: may work with unconscious material, developmental history, and repetitive dysfunctional patterns, not only conscious problems of living. Requires the most advanced training. (Yalom's Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy is fundamentally about this type — though its therapeutic factors and here-and-now method inform all four.)

The distinction that gets tested: counseling vs. psychotherapy groups

CACREP exams and supervisors press on the counseling-vs-psychotherapy hinge because the line is real but easily blurred :

Counseling groupPsychotherapy group
Aimgrowth, prevention, problem-solvingremediation, reconstruction
Depthconscious, situational "problems of living"deeper, enduring dysfunction; may work with the unconscious
Membersrelatively well-functioning, developmental concernsmore severe / entrenched problems
Personality change?not a goalcan be a goal
Setting (typical)schools, colleges, community agenciesclinical / inpatient / intensive outpatient

The two share a great deal of method — both run on cohesion, the here-and-now, and the therapeutic factors — so in practice they sit on a continuum of depth rather than in sealed boxes. The reason the distinction still matters is competence and scope (concept-scope-of-practice): running a reconstructive psychotherapy group requires training a psychoeducational-group leader may not have, and the deeper the aim, the more careful the screening must be (concept-group-ethics-and-formation).

Why the type drives everything else

Picking the type is not a labeling exercise; it sets the parameters:

  • Screening tightens as depth increases — a stress-management class needs light screening; a psychotherapy group needs careful selection so members won't be harmed or won't derail the group (concept-group-ethics-and-formation).
  • Leadership shifts from teacher (psychoeducational) toward process facilitator (counseling/psychotherapy) — more here-and-now, less curriculum (concept-group-leadership).
  • What "difficult member" means changes: a monopolist derails a psychotherapy group's process (concept-difficult-group-members) but may barely matter in a one-off task meeting.
  • The therapeutic factors (theory-yalom-factors) are strongest in counseling and psychotherapy groups, where cohesion and interpersonal learning have time to develop; a single task meeting rarely touches them.

  • concept-scope-of-practice (Unit 3) — running a group type you aren't trained for is a competence/scope problem.
  • concept-group-ethics-and-formation — screening intensity scales with the group's depth of aim.
  • concept-group-leadership — the leader's role shifts across the four types.
  • concept-dbt-skills (Unit 9) — a common psychoeducational/skills-group content.

pages.title: The Helping Professions Compared
pages.html:
The Helping Professions Compared

The idea: four (plus) professions all "do therapy," but they differ in degree, training length, license, professional identity, and — most concretely — who can prescribe medication. You need this map to refer well, to coordinate care, and to explain your own role to clients (a genuine informed-consent element, A.2.b).

The comparison table (learn this cold)

Professional counselor (LPC/LMHC/LCMHC)Clinical/counseling psychologistClinical social worker (LCSW)Psychiatrist (MD/DO)
Degreemaster's in counseling (~2–3 yrs; CACREP-accredited programs are the standard)doctorate — PhD (research-heavy), PsyD (practice-heavy), or EdD (4–6 yrs + internship)master's in social work (MSW, ~2 yrs)medical degree + 3–4 yr psychiatry residency
Post-degree licensure path~2 yrs supervised practice + exam (e.g., NCE/NCMHCE)1–2 yrs supervised practice + EPPP exam~2–3 yrs supervised clinical work + exammedical licensing + board certification
Signature lenswellness, development, prevention — the person in their life contextpsychological science: assessment, testing, diagnosis, therapyperson-in-environment: systems, resources, advocacy alongside therapybiological/medical: brain, body, medication
Distinctive functionscounseling/psychotherapy; strong identity around the therapeutic relationshippsychological testing/assessment (IQ, personality, neuropsych) is largely their turftherapy plus case management, connecting clients to concrete resourcesprescribing; medical workups; hospitalization decisions
Psychotherapy?yesyesyestrained in it; in practice many focus on medication management
Prescribes?no (no state)no, except specially trained psychologists in a handful of states (see below)noyes

Adjacent roles worth recognizing: psychiatric-mental-health nurse practitioners (PMHNPs) prescribe in every state and provide much of real-world medication management; marriage & family therapists (LMFTs) are master's-level clinicians with a systems specialty; school counselors hold a distinct master's credential; "psychotherapist" is, in most states, not a protected title by itself — the license behind it is what matters.

The prescribing exception (RxP) — and why the number keeps changing

Psychologists with a postdoctoral master's in clinical psychopharmacology, supervised practice hours, and a national psychopharmacology exam can prescribe in a small set of states: New Mexico (2002, first), Louisiana (2004), Illinois (2014), Iowa (2016), Idaho (2017) — APA's page stops there, but Colorado (2023) and Utah (2024) have since joined (≈7 states as of 2024–25, a moving target as bills advance elsewhere). Appropriately trained psychologists may also prescribe in the military (DoD), the U.S. Public Health Service, and the Indian Health Service.

For everyone else, the answer to "can you give me something for this?" is a referral — typically to a psychiatrist, PMHNP, or the client's primary-care physician (who in fact write the majority of psychotropic prescriptions in the U.S.). Coordinating with prescribers is a core counselor skill (Unit 11 covers the medications themselves).

Counselor professional identity (the CACREP angle)

"Professional counseling orientation" is a CACREP core area partly because counseling had to carve an identity distinct from psychology and social work. The distinguishing story programs teach: counseling grew from the guidance/vocational movement (Frank Parsons, early 1900s) and the humanistic tradition (theory-person-centered), so its center of gravity is developmental and wellness-oriented — clients are people navigating problems of living, not primarily patients with pathology. In practice the professions' day-to-day work overlaps heavily (all four diagnose and treat in most settings); identity shows up in emphasis, training, and advocacy priorities more than in what the hour with a client looks like.

Choosing a referral (the applied skill)

  • Needs medication evaluation → psychiatrist / PMHNP (or PCP for straightforward cases).
  • Needs IQ, learning-disability, ADHD, or neuropsychological testing → psychologist.
  • Needs housing, benefits, elder services, discharge planning alongside therapy → LCSW.
  • Needs weekly psychotherapy for anxiety/depression/adjustment → any of the therapy professions; fit and availability matter more than the letters (theory-common-factors).

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • RxP itself is contested: organized medicine (and some psychologists) oppose psychologist prescribing on safety/training grounds; proponents cite rural access gaps and the military's decades of safe experience. Expect the state list to keep changing.
  • Turf boundaries are legislative, not scientific — who may test, diagnose, or take insurance varies by state and payer, and the borders move under lobbying pressure. Treat any tidy "counselors do X, psychologists do Y" as a tendency, not a law of nature.

Connects to

  • concept-scope-of-practice — this page is scope at the profession level; that one is scope at the personal level.
  • concept-duty-to-warn — the protective-steps menu (hospitalization, medication) routinely requires knowing who does what.
  • concept-psychotropic-classes (Unit 11) — psychotropic medication classes; what you're coordinating about.

Sources

APA Services, About prescribing psychologists (+ 2024–25 reporting for CO/UT; flagged as dated in sources file). Full notes in ../research/unit03-ethics-law-sources.md.
