pages.title: Informed Consent
pages.html:
Informed Consent

The idea: clients have the right to choose — freely and knowledgeably — whether to enter and whether to stay in counseling. Informed consent is how that right is honored: the counselor reviews, in writing and verbally, what counseling is, what it costs, what could go wrong, and what the limits of the promise are. It is grounded in the principle of autonomy.

What the Code requires (A.2)

A.2.a — consent is a process, not a signature. "Informed consent is an ongoing part of the counseling process, and counselors appropriately document discussions of informed consent throughout the counseling relationship." The intake paperwork starts consent; it doesn't finish it. When the work changes — a new technique, a role change (A.6.d), a disclosure decision — consent is revisited.

A.2.b — what must be explained. Counselors "explicitly explain to clients the nature of all services provided," including, but not limited to:

  • purposes, goals, techniques, procedures of services;
  • limitations, potential risks, and benefits (yes — counseling has risks: distress can rise before it falls, relationships can change);
  • the counselor's qualifications, credentials, relevant experience, and approach;
  • continuation of services if the counselor is incapacitated or dies;
  • the role of technology;
  • fees and billing;
  • confidentiality and its limits — the piece clients most need and least expect (concept-confidentiality-limits);
  • the client's right to refuse services or any recommendation, and the consequences of refusal.

A.2.c/A.2.d — capacity and culture. Consent language must be developmentally and culturally appropriate. When a client cannot legally consent (minors, adults under guardianship), counselors seek the guardian's consent and the client's assent — their agreement, sought in terms they can understand — and include them in decisions to the extent possible.

A.2.e — mandated clients (court-ordered) get told what will be shared with whom, before the work starts, and retain the right to refuse services — knowing the consequences of refusing.

What it sounds like in the room

Not a form read aloud — a conversation. Contrast:

Counselor A (form-first): "Before we start, sign here, here, and initial here. Standard stuff — limits of confidentiality, fees, that kind of thing. Okay! So what brings you in?"

Counselor B (consent as conversation): "Before you tell me your story, I want you to know how this works, because you get to decide if it works for you. What you say here stays here — with a few exceptions I'll spell out, because they matter. I'm a counselor-in-training, which means I meet weekly with a supervisor who oversees my work. We'd meet weekly, and we'll check in regularly on whether this feels useful — if it doesn't, we'll change course or I'll help you find someone who fits better. What questions do you have about any of that?"

Counselor A got a signature; Counselor B got consent — and, research on the alliance suggests, the beginning of trust (concept-therapeutic-alliance). Note B disclosed trainee status and supervision: that's A.2.b's "qualifications" requirement working.

Why "ongoing" is not just a nicety

Patients demonstrably don't retain consent information: studies find clients and surrogate decision-makers "not remembering relevant information weeks after" it was given. A one-time recitation therefore can't carry the ethical load; the fix is briefer, clearer initial disclosure plus revisiting the relevant limit when a situation makes it live — e.g., re-explaining the harm exception before asking detailed risk questions. The counterweight: exhaustively listing every rare exception up front would be "time prohibitive and unnecessarily frightening" — so the skill is calibrated candor, not a legal recitation.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • How much detail up front is genuinely debated (see above) — plain-language summary + process view is the consensus, but where exactly to draw the line is judgment.
  • Consent for minors varies by state — some states let minors consent to outpatient mental health care at specific ages, especially for substance use or crisis; check your statute.

Connects to

  • concept-confidentiality-limits — the single most important content inside the consent conversation.
  • concept-therapeutic-alliance — consent done well is an early alliance intervention (Bordin's goals and tasks agreement is basically structured consent).
  • concept-dual-relationships — boundary extensions and role changes each require fresh, documented consent (A.6.c, A.6.d).

Sources

2014 ACA Code of Ethics, A.2, A.6 (verbatim). Darby & Weinstock (2018), PMC. Child Welfare Information Gateway (state-statute variation). Full notes in ../research/unit03-ethics-law-sources.md.

pages.title: The Intake / Clinical Interview
pages.html:
The Intake / Clinical Interview

The intake is the first full session with nearly every client, and it does two jobs at once that beginners think are separate: it gathers the information you'll build everything on, and it begins the relationship that makes the information trustworthy. Sommers-Flanagan's frame is that the clinical interview is the foundational assessment method — not one tool among many but the one all the others hang from — and that rapport and data-collection are not a trade-off: a client who feels judged, rushed, or processed hands you a thinner, more defended history . The interview is an intervention. Being carefully heard is the first dose of the common factors from unit01-helping-skills.

How structured? A dial, not a switch

Interviews range along a spectrum :

  • Unstructured — you follow the client, few fixed questions. Maximal rapport and richness; weak coverage (you may miss a whole domain) and poor reliability (two clinicians get different pictures).
  • Structured — a fixed script (research and some diagnostic instruments work this way). Maximal coverage and reliability; can feel like an interrogation and starve the alliance.
  • Semi-structured — a checklist of domains you will cover, asked conversationally and in whatever order the client's story opens them. This is where most skilled clinical intakes live: the structure lives in your head, not on the page between you.

The skill is holding a mental map of what must be covered while staying responsive to the person — structure serving the relationship, not overriding it.

What an intake covers: three areas, one history

Sommers-Flanagan collapses the intake into three core areas :

  1. The presenting problem — what brings them in, in their words, and its story.
  2. The biopsychosocial history — the context the problem grew in.
  3. Current functioning — how they're doing right now, including the mental status exam and a risk screen.

1. The presenting problem

Start here, and start in the client's language, not the diagnostic translation. Useful structure without leading:

  • What is the problem (their description, then a specific recent example)?
  • When did it start, and why now — what changed that made today the day they called? (This is your first read on precipitating factors — see concept-case-conceptualization.)
  • Course — getting better, worse, or cycling? Frequency, intensity, duration.
  • Impact — what can't they do now that they could before? (The impairment that Unit 6's definition of "disorder" hinges on, and the thing insurers reimburse — concept-treatment-planning.)
  • What have they tried, and what happened?
  • Why help-seeking now may itself be culturally loaded — for some clients "telling a stranger your feelings" is foreign or shameful (concept-acculturation); the fact of arriving can be data.

2. The biopsychosocial history

The organizing frame is concept-biopsychosocial-model from Unit 5 — the three domains keep you from tunneling on symptoms:

  • Biological — medical history and current conditions, medications, substance use (ask everyone, matter-of-factly — substances mimic and co-travel with nearly everything; concept-substance-use-disorders), sleep/appetite, family history of mental illness, pregnancy/ birth/developmental history where relevant.
  • Psychological — prior mental-health treatment and diagnoses, trauma history (screen, don't push for the narrative — concept-trauma-stressor-disorders), coping style, prior episodes, attachment history (concept-attachment-styles), strengths.
  • Social — family and relationships, work/school, housing and finances, culture/religion/identity, legal issues, supports and community. This is also where you catch the protective factors a strengths-based plan is built on.

The old DSM-IV multiaxial system forced this context onto every diagnosis; DSM-5 dropped the scaffold (concept-dsm-structure), so gathering context is now a habit you supply, not a form that prompts you.

3. Current functioning (and the risk screen)

  • The mental status exam — a structured description of present state (concept-mental-status-exam).
  • Screening measures where indicated — a PHQ-9, a GAD-7 (concept-screening-tools) — to baseline severity and enable measurement-based care.
  • A risk screen — every intake, non-negotiable. Item 9 of the PHQ-9 (thoughts of death/self-harm) or a direct question. Asking about suicide plainly and non-anxiously does not plant the idea; freezing is not an option (full treatment in Unit 8). This is also where the limits of confidentiality get spoken — informed consent and the confidentiality speech usually open the intake (concept-informed-consent, concept-confidentiality-limits).

Opening and closing the intake

  • Open with informed consent and the confidentiality-and-its-limits speech — the client can't give you an honest history without knowing where the walls are (concept-confidentiality-limits).
  • Close by summarizing what you heard (a microskill doing assessment work — see concept-microskills-hierarchy), offering an initial impression tentatively, checking it against the client's sense of fit, and agreeing on next steps. Ending with the client's own goals seeds concept-treatment-planning.

The stance traps

  • Interrogation drift. Rapid-fire closed questions fill your form and empty the room. Lead with open questions and reflections; let the history come through the relationship.
  • "I need all the data." The completeness reflex serves the counselor's anxiety. You do not need the trauma narrative to screen, to assess safety, or to start — pushing for it before trust and stability exist is how helpers re-traumatize (concept-trauma-stressor-disorders). Screening is asking plainly and accepting the answer.
  • Premature formulation. Diagnosing in the first ten minutes and then interviewing to confirm it is confirmation bias with a notepad. Hold the impression as a hypothesis to revisit (concept-dsm-structure).

Sources

Sommers-Flanagan & Sommers-Flanagan, Clinical Interviewing (via the author's Clinical Interview as an Assessment Tool). Context frames from IOM psychological-testing overview. Full notes in ../research/unit07-assessment-sources.md.

pages.title: Research Ethics & the IRB — the Belmont Report
pages.html:
Research Ethics & the IRB — the Belmont Report

Every rule protecting research participants today was written in response to research that harmed people. That history is not incidental — it's the reason the ethics have the shape they do, and knowing it is what keeps "get IRB approval" from feeling like bureaucratic box-checking. This page is the research-world analog of Unit 3: the same duty of care you owe a client — honesty, consent, confidentiality, non-exploitation — owed instead to the person who agrees to be studied. For a counselor, it matters in two concrete ways: you may one day conduct or assist with research (a thesis, a program evaluation meant for publication, an agency study), and you constantly read research whose credibility depends on whether it was done ethically.

The abuses that built the rules

The modern framework is a direct reaction to specific scandals :

  • Nazi medical experiments in WWII concentration camps → the Nuremberg Code (1947), whose first principle is that "the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential."
  • The Declaration of Helsinki (1964, WMA, revised since) — the medical profession's own standards for research on human subjects, extending Nuremberg.
  • The Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972) — the U.S. Public Health Service tracked hundreds of Black men with syphilis, deceived them about their condition, and withheld penicillin even after it became the standard cure, so as to study the untreated disease. Its exposure was the American scandal that forced reform: the National Research Act (1974), the commission that wrote the Belmont Report, and the IRB / Common Rule system.

The pattern in every case: vulnerable or captive people, no real consent, harm accepted in the name of knowledge. The principles below are the point-by-point answer to that pattern.

The Belmont Report: three principles, three applications

The Belmont Report (1979) is the foundational U.S. statement of research ethics. It names three principles, and — this is the part worth memorizing, because it's the clean discrimination the unit quizzes — each maps to a concrete application :

PrincipleWhat it meansIts application
Respect for personsPeople are autonomous agents; those with diminished autonomy (children, prisoners, cognitively impaired) get extra protectionInformed consent — voluntary, informed, with the right to decline or withdraw
BeneficenceMaximize benefits, minimize harms ("do no harm" + actively protect)Risk/benefit assessment — the study's risks must be justified by its benefits
JusticeThe burdens and benefits of research must be distributed fairlyFair subject selection — don't load the risks onto the vulnerable/convenient, or reserve the benefits for the privileged

Justice is the principle Tuskegee most flagrantly violated (poor Black men bore the entire burden for knowledge that would benefit others), and it's the one most easily forgotten, so it's worth anchoring: who bears the risk, and who gets the benefit?

The IRB and the Common Rule

The Institutional Review Board (IRB) is the enforcement mechanism. Under the Common Rule (45 CFR 46), research involving human subjects must be reviewed and approved by an IRB before it begins — a panel that checks the study against the Belmont principles: adequate informed consent, a defensible risk/benefit ratio, protections for vulnerable populations, and privacy/confidentiality safeguards . Review is prospective (before data collection, not after — you can't retroactively make an unethical study ethical), and studies posing more than minimal risk get fuller scrutiny. The IRB is to a research participant what informed consent and confidentiality protections are to a client — the structural guarantee that the power imbalance won't be exploited.

ACA Section G: the counselor's research ethics

The ACA Code of Ethics, Section G (Research and Publication) is the counseling profession's own version, and it will read as familiar because it mirrors the clinical-ethics sections you studied in Unit 3 :

  • Informed consent to research — voluntary participation; the purpose, procedures, risks, and any experimental elements disclosed; the right to decline or withdraw without penalty.
  • Confidentiality of research data — the same protection research participants get that clients get.
  • Avoiding harm and honest reporting of results — no fabrication, don't bury unfavorable findings, correct errors, and give proper publication credit (research-integrity duties that connect straight to the publication-bias problem — burying null results is both an ethics violation and a distortion of the evidence base).
  • Boundaries with participants — a specific flag: when participants are also students, supervisees, or clients, they must be free to decline without cost to that relationship — the research version of Unit 3's dual-relationship rule (the power differential makes "voluntary" consent suspect).

The stance: consent is the through-line

The single idea that unifies this page with the whole ethics thread of the curriculum: the person's informed, voluntary, revocable agreement is the floor, not a formality. Every abuse above is, at bottom, a consent failure. Every protection above — Belmont's respect for persons, the IRB's review, ACA's Section G — is a way of guaranteeing that a participant, like a client, is a person who agreed, understanding what they agreed to and free to stop. That's the same conviction under Unit 3's informed consent, now extended to the research relationship — which is a fitting place for the final unit of the spine to close: the methods that let us know things, bounded by the ethics that keep the knowing from costing people their dignity.

Connects to

  • concept-informed-consent and concept-confidentiality-limits (Unit 3) — the clinical originals of research consent and confidentiality; same duty, different relationship.
  • concept-dual-relationships (Unit 3) — the student/supervisee/client-as-participant boundary in Section G.
  • concept-evidence-based-practice — honest reporting vs. publication bias; research integrity is both an ethics and an evidence-quality issue.
  • concept-program-evaluation — the research-vs-evaluation line that helps determine when IRB review is required.
  • unit03-ethics-law (Unit 3) — the whole professional-ethics framework this page is the research chapter of.

Sources

The Belmont Report (1979), OHRP — respect for persons / beneficence / justice and their applications; the IRB. Nuremberg Code, Declaration of Helsinki, Tuskegee, the Common Rule (45 CFR 46). ACA Code of Ethics (2014), Section G: Research and Publication. Full notes in ../research/unit12-research-sources.md.

pages.title: Mandated Reporting
pages.html:
Mandated Reporting

The idea: every U.S. state designates certain professionals — mental health professionals included — as mandated reporters who must report suspected abuse or neglect of a child (all 50 states + DC) and, in most states, of elders and vulnerable adults. This is a statutory legal duty: it is not optional, not a clinical judgment call about what's best for the client, and it overrides confidentiality by design.

The elements (learn the italicized words)

  • Trigger: reasonable suspicion, not proof. You report when you have reasonable cause to suspect — you do not investigate first, and you don't need to be sure. Investigation is the child-protective agency's job, not yours. Reporting on suspicion that turns out unfounded is the system working as intended.
  • Timing: immediate. Statutes typically require prompt reporting (often an oral report within 24–48 hours, followed by a written one — specifics vary by state).
  • Immunity: good faith. All states and DC provide immunity from liability for good-faith reports — even ones that prove unfounded.
  • Penalty for failure: criminal charges (misdemeanor to felony), fines or jail, civil liability for harm that follows a failure to report, and licensure consequences.
  • Who's protected: minors everywhere; elder adults and dependent/vulnerable adults (adults unable to protect themselves due to age or disability) in most states.
  • What counts: physical abuse, sexual abuse, neglect, and in many states emotional abuse and exposure to specified dangers; some states require reporting past abuse disclosed by adult survivors under some circumstances — a genuinely tricky area; know your statute.

Mandated reporting vs. duty to warn (the confusable pair)

Mandated reportingDuty to warn/protect
Sourcestatute, all 50 statescase law/statute, varies by state (study-tarasoff)
Protectschildren, elder/vulnerable adultsidentifiable third party threatened by client
Triggerreasonable suspicion of abuse/neglectserious, foreseeable threat of violence
Discretionessentially none — suspicion → reportsubstantial clinical judgment (assess, choose protective steps)
You tellchild protective services / adult protective servicesvictim, police, or take other protective action

The deep difference: mandated reporting is a bright-line rule (the legislature already made the judgment call); duty to protect is a standard (you exercise judgment against it). New clinicians reverse these — agonizing over whether to report clear-suspicion abuse (don't agonize; report) while treating a specific threat as a formality (don't; assess carefully).

What it sounds like in the room

The stance challenge: making a report while keeping the relationship. It is usually possible — and usually best — to tell the client, unless doing so would endanger the child. Contrast:

Avoidant (common failure): say nothing, report secretly, hope it never comes up. (When the client finds out — they usually do — the alliance rupture is far worse than honesty would have been.)

Honest and warm: "I need to stop us for a second, because something you just said matters a lot. You remember at the start I told you that if I heard a child might be being hurt, I'm required by law to report it? What you've described about how your boyfriend disciplines your son is in that category. I have to make that call. I want to do it with you if you're willing — and I want you to know this doesn't end our work. My job is still to be in your corner. Let's talk about what happens next."

Note the moves: recall the pre-disclosed limit (concept-informed-consent doing its job) → name the duty plainly (no apology for the law, no blame of the client) → offer to make the report collaboratively → recommit to the relationship. Research and practice lore agree the relationship often survives a well-handled report — it rarely survives a concealed one.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Does mandatory reporting deter help-seeking? A live policy debate: some researchers argue broad mandates discourage struggling parents from disclosing and flood the system with unfounded reports; defenders point to detection gains. As a clinician your duty is unambiguous either way — the debate is about the law, not your compliance with it.
  • State variation is real: who is mandated (in ~18 states, everyone is), what standard applies, whether clergy/attorney privileges carve out — the Child Welfare Information Gateway maintains the state-by-state compilation; read yours before practicum.

Connects to

  • concept-confidentiality-limits — this is the "legal requirements" arm of B.2.a; it belongs in the confidentiality speech verbatim.
  • concept-duty-to-warn — the confusable sibling; table above.
  • Unit 8 — abuse discovery often co-presents with crisis; the reporting conversation is itself a crisis-communication skill.

Sources

2014 ACA Code of Ethics, B.2.a. StatPearls, Duty to Warn. Darby & Weinstock (2018). APA Services, Mandatory reporting — categories, suspicion standard, immunity, penalties. Child Welfare Information Gateway, Mandatory Reporters of Child Abuse and Neglect (State Statutes Series). Full notes in ../research/unit03-ethics-law-sources.md.

pages.title: Means Reduction (Lethal-Means Safety Counseling)
pages.html:
Means Reduction (Lethal-Means Safety Counseling)

Of everything in this unit, means reduction is the intervention with the clearest life-saving logic — and the one beginners are most likely to skip because the conversation feels intrusive. Means reduction (lethal-means safety counseling) is collaboratively putting time and distance between a suicidal person and the most lethal methods, until the crisis passes . It is step 6 of the safety plan, but it deserves its own page because the reasoning behind it is not obvious and, once understood, changes how you run the conversation.

Why it works: four facts that make method access decisive

  1. Case fatality varies enormously by method. Roughly 85–90% of firearm suicide attempts are fatal, versus a few percent for overdose or cutting . The method a person reaches for in a crisis largely determines whether they live — so the same person with the same intent has a very different chance of surviving depending only on what's within reach.
  2. Suicidal crises are often brief and impulsive. The interval between deciding and acting is frequently minutes to an hour. If a highly lethal method isn't at hand during that window, the acute urge often passes .
  3. Substitution is incomplete. The common objection — "they'll just find another way" — overstates it. Many people do not switch to an equally lethal method when the first is unavailable; removing the most lethal option is not simply redirected .
  4. Most attempt survivors don't die by suicide. About 9 in 10 people who survive an attempt do not go on to die by suicide later . Getting someone through the acute crisis alive is not a stopgap — for most people, it is the outcome.

Put together: because crises are transient and lethality is method-dependent, buying time by reducing access to the most lethal means saves lives at the population level, even accounting for some substitution. This is why it is a public-health strategy, not just a clinical nicety.

What the conversation actually is

It targets the two most important categories for most clients :

  • Firearms — the highest-priority means because of case fatality. Best option: temporary off-site storage with a trusted person, a gun shop, a range, or a police department while the person is at risk. If off-site isn't possible: locked, unloaded, with ammunition stored separately — and ideally the key/combination held by someone else.
  • Medications — limiting quantities on hand, locking them up, using a lockbox, and disposing of excess (many overdoses use what's already in the house).

The framing is collaborative and explicitly time-limited: "While things are this hard, can we make it so the most dangerous options aren't right there? We can get your firearm stored with your brother for a few weeks and get it back when you're through this." It is not confiscation, not a demand, and not permanent — it's a favor the person does for their future self, arranged with them and, for firearms, with a responsible other actually holding the item.

Do it even when it's uncomfortable

The evidence-practice gap here is stark: one survey found that while ~78% of emergency departments assess whether a patient has access to lethal means, only ~35% actually provide means counseling . The assessment question ("do you have access to a firearm?") is easy; the counseling — helping arrange to reduce that access — is what gets dropped, usually out of the clinician's discomfort, not the client's. Counselors' worry that raising firearms will rupture the alliance is generally unfounded when the tone is collaborative and concerned rather than confiscatory. Skipping the conversation to spare your own discomfort is the failure mode, and it's the same avoidance reflex that keeps clinicians from asking about suicide directly (concept-suicide-risk-assessment).

The stance traps

  • Assessing access without acting on it. Knowing there's a gun in the house and doing nothing about it is the most common — and most consequential — miss.
  • Confiscation framing. "You have to get rid of your guns" invites a fight. "Let's store them somewhere safe for a few weeks" invites cooperation.
  • Treating it as optional politeness. This is the highest-yield step in the safety plan; it is not the throwaway last line.
  • Only counting the client's action. For highly lethal means, safety depends on a responsible other physically holding or securing the item — not on the at-risk person's willpower.

Connects to

  • concept-safety-planning — means reduction is step 6; this page is that step in depth.
  • concept-suicide-risk-assessment — "access to means" is a practical contributor to capability in the ideation-to-action model, which is why removing it lowers acute risk.
  • aux-addiction — overdose risk and naloxone are the substance-use parallel to means safety.

Sources

Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Means Matter program, Lethal Means Counseling; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions. Full notes in ../research/unit08-crisis-trauma-sources.md.

pages.title: The Mental Status Examination (MSE)
pages.html:
The Mental Status Examination (MSE)

The MSE is to psychiatry what the physical exam is to medicine: a structured, cross-sectional description of the client's current state, written in a shared vocabulary so another clinician reading your note sees roughly what you saw. Two things it is not: it is not a diagnosis (it describes present state; it only supports a diagnosis when combined with history, substance/medical history, and collateral data), and it is not objective — it is "a subjective assessment … which may vary significantly between clinicians based on their observation skills" . The discipline is to describe, not interpret: "tearful, avoided eye contact, spoke slowly" is an observation; "depressed" is a conclusion the MSE feeds but does not equal.

Most of the MSE is gathered by watching and listening during the interview — you're doing it whether or not you call it that — with only a few items (orientation, memory, attention, abstract reasoning) requiring you to ask specific questions.

The domains

A common ordering (memory hooks vary — some use "ASEPTIC" or similar; the content matters more than the mnemonic) :

DomainWhat it capturesObserved or asked?
Appearanceapparent age, dress, grooming, hygiene, marks (scars, tattoos)observed
Behavior / attitudecooperativeness, eye contact, distress, redirectability, psychomotor agitation/retardationobserved
Motor activitygait, posture, tremor, tics, abnormal movementsobserved
Speechrate, rhythm, volume, fluency (pressured? slurred? impoverished?)observed
Moodthe client's self-reported emotional stateasked (verbatim)
Affectthe observed emotional expressionobserved
Thought processthe form of thinking — how thoughts connectobserved (inferred from speech)
Thought contentwhat is thought about — themes, preoccupations, ideationobserved / asked
Perceptionhallucinations, illusions, depersonalization/derealizationobserved / asked
Cognitionalertness, orientation, attention, memory, abstract reasoningasked / tested
Insightthe client's understanding of their own conditioninferred / asked
Judgmentcapacity to make sound decisionsinferred / asked

The three distinctions beginners flatten

These are the MSE's confusable pairs — and the reason it has its own cluster.

Mood vs. affect

Mood is what the client tells you; affect is what you see.

  • Mood — subjective, self-reported, documented in the client's own words: "I feel empty," "fine, I guess." It's the client's report of their emotional weather.
  • Affect — the clinician's observation of expressed emotion, described on several axes: quality (euthymic, dysphoric, euphoric, anxious), range (full, constricted, blunted, flat), stability (labile = rapidly shifting), and congruence with mood and content.
  • The mismatch is the signal. A client who says "I'm doing great" (mood) while tearful and trembling (affect) shows incongruent affect — and that gap is often more diagnostic than either alone. Flat affect points toward psychosis or severe depression; labile affect toward mania or intoxication.

Memory hook: mood is the climate (what they report over time), affect is the weather right now (what you observe).

Thought process vs. thought content

Process is the shape of thinking; content is the subject. They dissociate completely — you can have a perfectly organized thought process delivering a floridly delusional content, and vice versa.

  • Thought process (form) — the connections between ideas: linear/goal-directed (normal), circumstantial (over-detailed but eventually returns to the point), tangential (wanders off and never returns), flight of ideas (rapid, loosely connected — mania), loose associations (no logical link — psychosis), perseveration (stuck on one idea), thought blocking (abrupt stops).
  • Thought content (subject) — what the thinking is about: delusions (fixed false beliefs — paranoid, grandiose, somatic, thought insertion/broadcasting), obsessions, phobias, and — always assessed — suicidal and homicidal ideation (passive vs. active; plan; intent; means).

Insight vs. judgment

Insight is understanding the illness; judgment is deciding well about it. They also dissociate — a subtle, exam-favorite point.

  • Insight — does the client recognize they have a condition, and grasp its nature? Rated poor / limited / fair / good. Example: fair insight = knowing the voices aren't real; poor insight = denying obvious symptoms.
  • Judgment — can the client make sound, safe decisions and anticipate consequences? Assessed from history and observed choices (the old "what would you do if you smelled smoke in a theater?" is crude and largely abandoned in favor of real-life decisions).
  • The dissociation: a person with poor insight ("I'm not ill") can still show fair judgment (takes the medication anyway, to avoid another hospitalization) — and someone with good insight can repeatedly make dangerous choices. Don't collapse the two.

Cognition, briefly

Screened, not exhaustively tested, in a counseling intake: alertness (alert → drowsy → stupor), orientation (person / place / time / situation — acute disorientation suggests delirium or intoxication, an easily-missed medical emergency, not primary psychiatric illness), attention (serial 7s, spelling "world" backward), memory (immediate / recent / remote), and abstract reasoning (similarities, proverbs — concrete interpretations flag psychosis or neurocognitive impairment). Suspected cognitive impairment routes to a fuller instrument (MoCA, MMSE, Mini-Cog) and a medical referral, not a counseling formulation.

Why counselors document it

  • A shared, portable snapshot. Your MSE lets the next provider — and future-you — see the baseline and detect change. It is the natural companion to the severity scores and to measurement-based care.
  • A change detector. "Affect brighter, thought process now linear, no longer responding to internal stimuli" is progress you can point to.
  • Read it against the baseline. An MSE means little without the developmental and cultural norm it's measured against — apparent guardedness can be rational (unit04-multicultural), and what's odd at one age is ordinary at another (unit05-development). Describe; don't pathologize the difference.

Sources

StatPearls, Mental Status Examination (NBK546682). MSE-as-one-input-to-diagnosis corroborated by Sommers-Flanagan. Full notes in ../research/unit07-assessment-sources.md.

pages.title: Microaggressions (and the Debate About Them)
pages.html:
Microaggressions (and the Debate About Them)

The idea: Sue et al. (2007), in American Psychologist, defined racial microaggressions as "brief and commonplace daily verbal, behavioral, or environmental indignities, whether intentional or unintentional, that communicate hostile, derogatory, or negative racial slights and insults." Three features do the conceptual work: they are small (each instance deniable), they are cumulative (the cost is the drip, not the drop), and they are usually delivered by people who believe themselves unprejudiced — which is what connects this page to concept-privilege-power's invisibility problem.

The taxonomy (the testable core)

TypeDefinitionIntentExample
Microassaultexplicit, old-fashioned derogation — name-calling, deliberate exclusion, displaying hostile symbolsusually conscious/deliberateusing a slur; refusing service
Microinsultsubtle rudeness or insensitivity that demeans identityoften unconscious"You're so articulate." (to a Black professional — the compliment contains the low expectation)
Microinvalidationcommunications that negate or nullify the person's experiential realityoften unconscious"I don't see color." · "Anyone can succeed here if they work hard." · "Where are you really from?"

Discrimination hooks: microassault = closest to overt racism (the intent is there); microinsult = demeans (an insult wearing a compliment's clothes); microinvalidation = erases (tells the person their reality didn't happen). The third is the counselor's occupational hazard — "I treat everyone the same" and premature reassurance ("I'm sure they didn't mean anything by it") are both microinvalidations available in-session, with a warm voice.

In the room: rupture and repair

Sue et al.'s paper is subtitled Implications for Clinical Practice because the clinical claim is the sharp one: microaggressions occur inside therapy, and each one is an alliance rupture (concept-therapeutic-alliance) with a client who may already be deciding whether counseling is safe — one plausible contributor to the minority dropout gap (unit04-multicultural).

The skill is repair without self-recentering (concept-cultural-humility's other-oriented stance). A client says, "When you said my standards for my kids were 'maybe a little intense,' it felt like you were writing off how our family does education":

Counselor A (defensive/invalidating): "Oh — that's not what I meant at all! I'm honestly the least judgmental person about parenting styles. I just meant intense in a good way!" (Denies, recenters the counselor's innocence, and — by explaining the client's reaction away — commits a microinvalidation while apologizing for one.)

Counselor B (repair): "Thank you for telling me — I can see that landed as a judgment on your family's values, and I'm sorry. I think I was measuring against my own defaults without noticing. Can you tell me more about what those standards mean in your family?" (Owns it briefly, names the mechanism, returns the floor.)

Ruptures repaired this way can strengthen the alliance — the client learns difference is discussable here, which is broaching's promise kept under pressure (concept-privilege-power).

The critique (know this side too)

Lilienfeld (2017), Perspectives on Psychological Science: the microaggression research program makes strong claims on inadequate evidence. The load-bearing objections: definitions are elastic (almost anything can qualify post hoc); classification rests on subjective report alone (no observer-independent criteria); the "aggression" label imputes motives the data can't show; members of the same minority group disagree about whether a given remark is offensive; and the causal claim (microaggressions → mental-health harm) rests on correlational, self-report designs. His proposed fix: the more neutral term "perceived racial slight" and a moratorium on strong claims pending better research. Notably, Sue's rejoinder conceded many of these points while defending the value of documenting lived experience; Williams (2019) answered Lilienfeld point-by-point, and the argument continues in print.

How to hold both: the phenomenon (subtle, cumulative, deniable slights that wear on people) is well-attested experience and a real clinical concern; the research program's strong causal and taxonomic claims outrun current evidence. In session, the epistemology debate barely matters — if your client experienced your remark as a slight, the alliance took the hit regardless of what the construct is named, and repair is the same move either way. In a paper, cite both sides.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Everything in the section above — this is the unit's flagship live controversy. A program will expect the taxonomy; a good program will also expect Lilienfeld.
  • Base rates and thresholds — how common, how harmful, and where slight ends and microaggression begins are all unsettled empirically.

Connects to

  • concept-privilege-power — invisibility of privilege explains unintentional delivery; broaching is prevention, repair is cure.
  • concept-cultural-humility — the repair stance (own it, don't recenter).
  • concept-therapeutic-alliance — rupture-and-repair is the frame that makes this clinical.
  • concept-msjcc — intrapersonal advocacy includes helping clients process internalized microaggressions.

Sources

Sue et al. (2007), American Psychologist. Lilienfeld (2017), Perspectives on Psychological Science (+ Sue's rejoinder; Williams 2019). Day-Vines et al. (2007). NIMHD + PMC disparities data. Counseling Today MSJCC article. Full notes in ../research/unit04-multicultural-sources.md.

The load-bearing objections: definitions are elastic (almost anything can qualify post hoc); classification rests on subjective report alone (no observer-independent criteria); the " aggression " label imputes motives the data can't show; members of the same minority group disagree about whether a given remark is offensive; and the causal claim (microaggressions → mental-health harm) rests on correlational, self-report designs. His proposed fix: the more neutral term "perceived racial slight" and a moratorium on strong claims pending better research. Notably, Sue's rejoinder conceded many of these points while defending the value of documenting lived experience; Williams (2019) answered Lilienfeld point-by-point, and the argument continues in print. S12 How to hold both: the phenomenon (subtle, cumulative, deniable slights that wear on people) is well-attested experience and a real clinical concern; the research program's strong causal and taxonomic claims outrun current evidence. In session, the epistemology debate barely matters — if your client experienced your remark as a slight, the alliance took the hit regardless of what the construct is named, and repair is the same move either way. In a paper, cite both sides. S6 S12 What's contested (don't over-learn it) Everything in the section above — this is the unit's flagship live controversy. A program will expect the taxonomy; a good program will also expect Lilienfeld. S6 S12 Base rates and thresholds — how common, how harmful, and where slight ends and microaggression begins are all unsettled empirically. S12 Connects to concept-privilege-power — invisibility of privilege explains unintentional delivery; broaching is prevention, repair is cure. concept-cultural-humility — the repair stance (own it, don't recenter). concept-therapeutic-alliance — rupture-and-repair is the frame that makes this clinical. concept-msjcc — intrapersonal advocacy includes helping clients process internalized microaggressions. pages.title: Ivey's Microskills Hierarchy
pages.html:
Ivey's Microskills Hierarchy

Allen Ivey's contribution (microcounseling, ~1967–71) was to take the vague instruction "build rapport" and break it into discrete, teachable, observable skills arranged as a pyramid — you master the lower ones before the higher ones do any good. The model has been studied extensively.

The ladder (base → top)

  1. Foundation — the core conditions + ethics + cultural competence. Genuineness, empathy, UPR (concept-core-conditions) are the ground the whole pyramid stands on.
  2. Attending behavior. The physical basics of being present: eye contact, vocal qualities (tone, pace), verbal tracking (following the client's topic, not yours), and open body language. This is "the foundation skill" — clients talk more when attended to. Treated in depth (SOLER, the three Vs + B, the use of silence) on concept-attending-and-listening.
  3. Observation skills. Noticing how the client communicates — especially mismatches between words and nonverbals (saying "I'm fine" while tearing up).
  4. Questions. Open questions ("What was that like?") to expand, closed questions ("How many?") to pin down specifics. Beginners over-rely on questions; used too much they turn a session into an interrogation.
  5. Reflecting skills — encouragers/minimal encouragers, paraphrasing, reflecting feeling, summarizing. The workhorse listening skills (see the distinctions below).
  6. Influencing skills (top, higher-risk) — interpretation, self-disclosure, confrontation, directives. Powerful, but they impose the counselor's frame, so they require the lower skills to be solid first.

From skills to a session: Ivey's five-stage interview

The microskills are the notes; Ivey also gave a structure for a whole session — a five-stage arc that any theoretical orientation can fill in. It's a useful map for "what do I actually do for 50 minutes?"

  1. Empathic relationship — build rapport and structure ("Hello — here's how we'll work today").
  2. Story and strengths — draw out the client's concern and their resources (not just the problem).
  3. Goals — establish what the client wants ("What would you like to happen?").
  4. Restory — help the client generate new ways of thinking about and narrating the situation.
  5. Action — move toward change the client will carry outside the room.

Notice the sequence: relationship and story come before goals and action — the same discipline as the stance note below, built into the shape of the session.

The distinction that trips everyone up: reflect vs. paraphrase vs. interpret

These look similar and are constantly confused. The difference is how far you go beyond the client's words.

SkillWhat you doStays inside the client's frame?
Paraphrase (reflect content)Restate the content of what they said in fresh wordsYes — mirrors their meaning
Reflect feelingName the emotion underneath, matched to its intensityYes — surfaces what's implicit but present
SummarizeCondense several paraphrases/reflections; used at start/endYes — broadest of the three
InterpretAdd your read of meaning, cause, or need — beyond what they saidNo — you leave their frame
  • Paraphrase ("So the deadline got moved up and now the whole plan is in question") — content, no new meaning added.
  • Reflection of feeling ("It sounds like that left you anxious and a little betrayed") — names emotion the client implied but didn't label. Requires a wide feeling vocabulary.
  • Interpretation ("I wonder if this keeps happening because you say yes before you've checked what you can handle") — introduces an explanation the client didn't offer. It's an influencing skill: it can deepen a session or, if premature, feel presumptuous. Earn it with the lower skills first.

The stance payoff

The single most useful move in this unit is reflect feeling, then go quiet. A reflection invites the client to say more; a question or an interpretation steers them toward your agenda. If your instinct is to fix, default down the ladder to a reflection and let silence do the rest. (See unit01-helping-skills stance note.)

Connects to

  • concept-core-conditions — the foundation layer of the pyramid (and the deep pages concept-unconditional-positive-regard / concept-empathy / concept-congruence).
  • concept-attending-and-listening — the attending/observation layer in depth (SOLER, silence).
  • concept-empathy — reflection of feeling is empathy made teachable; interpretation is its higher-risk neighbor one rung up.
  • concept-therapeutic-alliance — these skills are how you build the bond.
  • concept-oars (Unit 9) — Motivational Interviewing's OARS is this same listening engine reused, given a direction (drawing out change talk). The named "Microskills ↔ OARS" cross-unit thread.

Sources

Penn State, Counseling Microskills. iResearchNet, Allen Ivey. counseling.education, Reflecting & Listening Skills. Full notes in ../research/unit01-helping-skills-sources.md.

pages.title: Mood Disorders: Depressive & Bipolar
pages.html:
Mood Disorders: Depressive & Bipolar

DSM-5 split the old "mood disorders" chapter into two — depressive disorders and bipolar and related disorders — but clinically they form one discrimination problem: is this depression, is it grief, and has there ever been a manic or hypomanic episode? Getting that last question wrong is the most consequential routine error in this territory.

Major depressive disorder (MDD)

The anchor criteria set of the whole unit — and one of the syllabus's "big three" to be explainable in two minutes. Five or more of nine symptoms, nearly every day for at least two weeks, at least one of which is (1) depressed mood or (2) anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure), causing significant distress or impairment, with no history of mania/hypomania and no substance/medical explanation. The nine :

  1. depressed mood (in children/adolescents, may be irritable mood)
  2. anhedonia
  3. significant appetite/weight change
  4. insomnia or hypersomnia
  5. psychomotor agitation or retardation
  6. fatigue / loss of energy
  7. worthlessness or excessive guilt
  8. poor concentration / indecisiveness
  9. recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation

Lifetime prevalence ~12%, roughly twice as common in women; untreated episodes typically run 6–12 months. The recurrence staircase is worth memorizing because it changes treatment conversations: ~50% recur after a first episode, ~70% after a second, ~90% after a third. Depression is also potentially lethal — suicidal ideation is a criterion symptom, and risk assessment (concept-suicide-risk-assessment) is inseparable from this diagnosis.

Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is the low-grade, long-haul variant: depressed mood more days than not for ≥2 years (1 year in youth), with milder symptom load. A person can carry both ("double depression").

Depression vs. grief — the emblem discrimination

DSM-IV barred diagnosing MDD in the first two months of bereavement; DSM-5 removed that exclusion, reasoning that bereavement-triggered depression doesn't demonstrably differ in nature, course, or outcome from depression after any other precipitant — and that depression kills, so withholding the diagnosis from the bereaved "risks closing the door on potentially life-saving interventions." Critics answered that this medicalizes mourning. The working discriminations, whatever your stance :

Ordinary griefMajor depression
self-esteem preservedworthlessness, self-loathing
comes in waves, with positive memories betweenpervasive misery
consolable by support and connectionlargely inconsolable
oriented to the lossoriented to the self

Grief that stays intense, impairing, and yearning-centered ≥12 months out is its own DSM-5-TR diagnosis — prolonged grief disorder, housed with the trauma- and stressor-related disorders and covered from the support side in the PFA elective's concept-grief-models.

The bipolar side: episodes first, disorders second

Bipolar diagnoses are built out of episodes:

  • Manic episode: abnormally elevated or irritable mood with increased energy/activity, lasting ≥7 days (or any duration if hospitalization is required), plus 3+ symptoms (4+ if the mood is only irritable): grandiosity, decreased need for sleep (rested after 3 hours — not insomnia, which is wanting sleep and failing), pressured speech, flight of ideas/racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity or agitation, and high-risk behavior (spending sprees, sexual indiscretion, reckless ventures). Marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychosis makes it manic by definition.
  • Hypomanic episode: the same symptom picture but ≥4 days, observable by others yet without marked impairment, hospitalization, or psychosis.

Then: Bipolar I = at least one manic episode, ever (depression common but not required). Bipolar II = at least one hypomanic episode plus at least one major depressive episode, and never a full manic episode — not a "milder" illness; its depressive burden is heavy. Cyclothymic disorder = ≥2 years of hypomanic-ish and depressive-ish symptoms that never reach either episode threshold.

The screening habit that protects clients: people with bipolar disorder mostly seek help while depressed; correct diagnosis lags first contact by ~6–10 years on average, and 20–30% of "MDD" presentations transition to bipolar within 3 years. An antidepressant given to undetected bipolar depression can destabilize mood. So before anyone concludes "unipolar depression," ask about lifetime highs: Has there ever been a stretch of days when you needed almost no sleep and still felt full of energy? Suicide risk in bipolar disorder runs ~20–30× the general population — this category and Unit 8 are never far apart.

In the room

Depression's presentation is often the stance problem this curriculum keeps flagging: a person whose motivation, hope, and concentration are symptoms — met by a helper itching to fix. Behavioral prescriptions bounce off anhedonia; the alliance (concept-therapeutic-alliance) and accurate empathy are what make later structured work (concept-behavioral-activation, Unit 9) possible. And an energized, grandiose client is not "finally doing better" — always read energy against the episode grammar above.

Sources

OpenStax §15.2. First et al. (2022). StatPearls MDD. StatPearls Bipolar Disorder. Pies (2014). Full notes in ../research/unit06-psychopathology-sources.md.

pages.title: The Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies (MSJCC)
pages.html:
The MSJCC (Ratts et al., 2015)

The idea: the profession's current framework for multicultural work — developed by Ratts, Singh, Nassar-McMillan, Butler & McCullough, endorsed by AMCD (June 29, 2015) and by ACA (July 20, 2015) as the official revision of the 1992 theory-tripartite-model. Two upgrades define it: intersectionality (everyone, counselor included, holds privileged and marginalized identities at once) and social justice (competence includes acting on the conditions around the client, not only the conversation with them).

The architecture (learn this cold — it's diagram-question bait)

Four quadrants. The 1992 model quietly assumed a majority counselor and a minority client. The MSJCC crosses counselor × client status explicitly:

Marginalized clientPrivileged client
Privileged counselorQuadrant IQuadrant II
Marginalized counselorQuadrant IVQuadrant III

The point isn't to file yourself in one box — identities are fluid and intersectional (a White gay male counselor is privileged and marginalized simultaneously, on different axes), so the quadrants describe moments and dimensions of a relationship, not fixed types of people. Power, privilege, and oppression run through every dyad — including Quadrant II, where two privileged people can jointly fail to notice anything.

Four developmental domains, in deliberate order:

  1. Counselor self-awareness — your own values, biases, privileged/marginalized statuses.
  2. Client worldview — the client's cultural context and identity development.
  3. Counseling relationship — how the combination (the quadrant dynamics) plays out in the dyad itself.
  4. Counseling and advocacy interventions — doing something about it, in and beyond the office.

The order encodes the theory of change: self-awareness precedes understanding others, both precede the relationship, and all three precede intervention. Skipping to domain 4 without domains 1–3 is activism without a clinician attached; stopping at domain 3 is insight without consequences.

AKSA — the aspirational competencies. Within each of the first three domains, competence develops across Attitudes & beliefs, Knowledge, Skills — the tripartite triad — plus the MSJCC's signature addition: Action. The 1992 model asked you to be aware, informed, and skilled; the 2015 model asks what you did about it.

Six socioecological levels structure the advocacy domain, from inside the client outward: intrapersonal → interpersonal → institutional → community → public policy → international/ global. Worked examples from the authors: helping a client process internalized microaggressions (intrapersonal); a school counselor getting a wheelchair-accessible route fixed so a student stops losing instructional time (institutional); connecting a client to identity-affirming community organizations (community); advocacy on trans-inclusive public-facility policy (public policy).

What "advocacy" changes about the job

The MSJCC's most consequential sentence is structural: problems are not always inside the client. When a client's distress is being produced by an inaccessible building, a discriminatory workplace, or a hostile policy, culturally competent treatment of the feelings alone quietly locates the pathology in the person suffering it. Advocacy "with, and on behalf of" clients is the framework's answer — and it deliberately echoes the counselor stance debate from theory-postmodern (the client is not the problem; the problem is the problem).

The fix-it caution (see unit01-helping-skills) cuts both ways here. Advocacy is a fix-it move — and this is the one place the curriculum licenses it. But the discipline still applies: advocacy done for a client without their steering can recreate the paternalism it means to correct ("non-paternalistic" is written into concept-cultural-humility's definition for exactly this reason). Empower first; act with; act on behalf of only where asked or where the client can't.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Scope of the advocacy mandate. How far a counselor's role properly extends into policy and political action is debated within the profession; the MSJCC names six levels but leaves the judgment to you. Programs vary in how activist a reading they teach.
  • Empirical youth. The MSJCC is a values-and-consensus document; the outcome evidence (unit04-multicultural: Tao r ≈ .29; Hook's humility findings) mostly predates it and tests adjacent constructs, not the framework as a whole.

Connects to

  • theory-tripartite-model — the 1992 ancestor; MSJCC = tripartite + intersectional quadrants + action + advocacy.
  • concept-cultural-humility — supplies the stance for domains 1 and 3 (and the "non-paternalistic" guard rail for domain 4).
  • concept-privilege-power — the quadrants operationalize privilege inside the dyad; broaching is the domain-3 skill.
  • concept-therapeutic-alliance — domain 3 is Bordin's bond/goals/tasks under cultural load.

Sources

MSJCC official PDF (Ratts et al., 2015; AMCD/ACA endorsements). Counseling Today practical-applications article (same authors). Tervalon & Murray-García (1998). Hook et al. (2013). Tao et al. (2015). Full notes in ../research/unit04-multicultural-sources.md.

pages.title: The Neurobiology of Trauma (a working model)
pages.html:
The Neurobiology of Trauma (a working model)

You do not need to be a neuroscientist to do trauma-informed work, but you need a working model — enough to understand why a trauma survivor's reactions are involuntary and physiological, not choices or character flaws. The one sentence to carry: in trauma, the brain's alarm system gets stuck on and its braking and context systems get turned down, so the body reacts to the past as if it were the present. Everything below fleshes out that sentence. Read the direction of the findings as solid and the decimals as provisional — this is an area where the popular story runs ahead of the settled science (see the caveats at the end) .

Three structures: an alarm, a context-stamp, and a brake

StructureNormal jobIn trauma
Amygdalathreat detection — the smoke alarmhyperactive; fires at over-generalized cues; excitatory to the stress axis
Hippocampusmemory + context — time-stamps events as pastreduced volume/function; fails to mark the memory as over, so it intrudes as if now; inhibitory to the stress axis
Prefrontal cortex (mPFC)top-down regulation — the brake on the amygdalareduced activity; can't dampen the alarm → "regulatory failure"

The result is a system out of balance: the amygdala keeps sounding the alarm, the hippocampus can't file the experience away as finished, and the prefrontal cortex can't apply the brake . Clinically, that is the picture of PTSD — hypervigilance, flashbacks that feel present, and difficulty calming down once triggered.

The HPA axis: the stress hormone loop

The body's slower stress response is the HPA axis: the hypothalamus releases CRH → the pituitary releases ACTH → the adrenal glands release cortisol, which mobilizes energy for threat. Normally the loop is self-limiting: cortisol and hippocampal output feed back to shut off CRH (negative feedback) . Chronic or early trauma dysregulates this loop. Here honesty matters: the findings are inconsistent — some studies show elevated cortisol, others show blunted/low morning cortisol — and "dysregulated responses are not consistently associated with psychopathology" . So the takeaway is dysregulation of the stress axis, not a clean "high cortisol = trauma" biomarker. McEwen's allostatic load frames it well: chronic stress shifts the body's whole set-point, and running the emergency system too long wears the body down.

Two memory systems: why the story is fragmented

A key working idea: trauma is encoded differently from ordinary experience .

  • Explicit memory (hippocampus-dependent): conscious, verbal, narrative, time-stamped — "this happened last year."
  • Implicit memory (amygdala-dependent): non-conscious, sensory, emotional, and bodily — a smell, a posture, a surge of dread.

Under the extreme arousal of trauma, explicit encoding is disrupted while implicit encoding is strengthened. That's why a survivor may have fragmentary sensory images and intense somatic/emotional reactions without a coherent story — and why a trigger (a sound, a smell) can launch the body into full alarm before any conscious memory arrives. This is the defensible core of the popular phrase "the body keeps the score": the body reacts before the narrative catches up. It also reframes a client's self-blame ("my memory is patchy, so maybe it wasn't that bad" or "why can't I just tell the story?") as normal trauma encoding, not evasion or exaggeration — which is directly why trauma-informed care says don't force the narrative.

Fight, flight, and freeze — freeze is not a choice

The threat response is usually taught as fight or flight, but the third — freeze / tonic immobility — is the one that matters most clinically. It's an involuntary shutdown (the deer in headlights; the assault victim who couldn't move or scream), mediated below conscious control . Survivors routinely blame themselves for it ("why didn't I fight back / run / say no?"), and naming freeze as an automatic, hardwired response — not consent, not weakness, not a failure of will — is often itself therapeutic.

The window of tolerance (a clinical heuristic)

Siegel's window of tolerance is the arousal band in which a person can stay regulated — think, feel, and stay present without being overwhelmed :

  • Above the window = hyperarousal (fight/flight): panic, rage, racing thoughts, hypervigilance.
  • Below the window = hypoarousal (freeze/shutdown): numbness, dissociation, flatness, collapse.

Trauma narrows and destabilizes the window, so small triggers push a survivor out of it. The clinical use is concrete: notice which side the client is on and help them back into the window before doing any content work — grounding and slowing for hyperarousal, gentle re-orienting/re-engagement for hypoarousal. This is trauma-informed pacing made operational. Treat the window of tolerance as a useful map, not a measured brain state — it's a heuristic that organizes what you observe, not a validated neural construct.

What's contested — read carefully

  • Direction solid, details soft. Amygdala-up / hippocampus-and-PFC-down and the explicit/implicit split are well supported in direction; exact volumes and cortisol patterns vary across studies .
  • "The body keeps the score" is a metaphor with a real core and an overstated edge. The real core: implicit/somatic encoding and physiological reactivity. The overstated edge: the strong claim that trauma is literally "stored in the body," and sweeping claims about repressed/recovered memory — memory science rejects the memory-as-videotape view; trauma memory is reconstructive and suggestible, not a sealed recording. van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score is popular-press: excellent for orientation and empathy, but corroborate its mechanisms against peer-reviewed work (done here) .
  • Polyvagal theory (Porges) — the vagal/social-engagement account behind a lot of trauma pop-neuroscience — is clinically popular but its specific neurophysiological claims are scientifically contested. Use its language ("the nervous system feels unsafe") as a bridge to clients, not as established fact .

Connects to

  • concept-trauma-informed-care — the neurobiology is why the informed-care stance (safety, choice, don't-force-the-narrative) is what it is.
  • concept-trauma-stressor-disorders (Unit 6) — the PTSD/ASD diagnoses whose mechanisms this page supplies.
  • concept-stress-response and concept-autonomic-nervous-system (Unit 11) — the stress response and autonomic nervous system in full; this page is the working-level preview (note source_units: [8, 11]).
  • concept-de-escalation — hyperarousal in the room is the window-of-tolerance model in action.

Sources

Siegel, The Developing Mind — window of tolerance. van der Kolk (2014), The Body Keeps the Score — popular-press, flagged. Full notes in ../research/unit08-crisis-trauma-sources.md.

pages.title: Neurodevelopmental Disorders: ADHD & Autism Spectrum
pages.html:
Neurodevelopmental Disorders: ADHD & Autism Spectrum

The manual's first chapter — first because these conditions onset in the developmental period and are, at core, atypical developmental trajectories rather than acquired episodes. That makes this the chapter where unit05-development does the most direct work: every diagnosis here is a claim that a child's development deviates from age norms beyond the (wide) normal range, which you cannot judge without knowing the norms. The chapter also holds intellectual disability, specific learning disorder, communication disorders, and tic disorders; counseling practice most often meets ADHD and autism spectrum disorder, so they get the depth here.

ADHD

A persistent, impairing pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity. Criteria mechanics :

  • 6+ of 9 inattention symptoms (careless mistakes, can't sustain attention, doesn't seem to listen, doesn't finish, disorganized, avoids sustained mental effort, loses things, distractible, forgetful) and/or 6+ of 9 hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms (fidgets, leaves seat, runs/ climbs inappropriately — "an internal motor," can't play quietly, talks excessively, blurts, can't wait turns, interrupts). Age 17+: 5+ suffices.
  • Several symptoms before age 12, present in 2+ settings (the two-setting rule screens out context problems — a child inattentive only at school may have a classroom problem, not ADHD), with clear functional interference.
  • Three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive, combined. The inattentive presentation — historically underdiagnosed, especially in girls — has no behavioral fireworks; it looks like daydreaming and "not living up to potential."

Adult prevalence ~3–6%; a substantial share of childhood cases attenuate by adulthood (roughly half "grow out of" the full syndrome, especially with treatment), while others persist with the hyperactivity turned inward (restlessness, disorganization).

The differential trap runs both directions: anxiety and depression impair concentration and can be misread as ADHD; ADHD's demoralized, scattered adult can be misread as anxious or depressed. The discriminator is the timeline — ADHD is lifelong and cross-context (childhood onset, multiple settings); an attention problem that started at 30 alongside low mood is not ADHD.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD)

Two symptom pillars, both required, onset in the early developmental period :

  1. Persistent deficits in social communication and interaction — all three areas: social-emotional reciprocity (back-and-forth conversation, sharing of interests/affect); nonverbal communication (eye contact, gesture, facial expression); developing, maintaining, and understanding relationships.
  2. Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities — at least 2 of 4: stereotyped/repetitive movements or speech; insistence on sameness and routines; highly restricted, intense fixated interests; sensory hyper- or hypo-reactivity (the DSM-5 addition — sound sensitivity, indifference to pain, sensory seeking).

DSM-5's big consolidation: autistic disorder, Asperger's disorder, and PDD-NOS were merged into the single spectrum, graded by severity levels 1–3 ("requiring support" → "requiring very substantial support") and specifiers (with/without intellectual or language impairment). Prevalence estimates have climbed steeply — CDC 2020: ~1 in 36 eight-year-olds — a rise that mixes broadened criteria, better detection, and possibly true increase; it's also Exhibit A in Frances's diagnostic-inflation argument (concept-categorical-vs-dimensional). Comorbidity is the rule: ~74% have at least one co-occurring condition.

Discriminations: social anxiety (concept-anxiety-disorders) wants connection but fears judgment, with intact social understanding; ASD involves differences in the social-communication machinery itself, from early development. Schizotypal oddity (concept-personality-disorders) emerges in adolescence/adulthood; ASD is lifelong.

In the room

Counselors are often the first professional a struggling family or a "why is everything harder for me than everyone else?" adult consults — your job is usually recognition and referral for formal evaluation (concept-scope-of-practice), then support around it. Two stance notes: the neurodiversity conversation is live (many autistic adults frame autism as difference to be accommodated, not deficit to be cured — hold the DSM's deficit language and the client's self-understanding without forcing either), and with children, always ask what the environment demands before locating the whole problem in the child — the concept-biopsychosocial-model applies to eight-year-olds too.

Sources

StatPearls ADHD. StatPearls Autism Spectrum Disorder. Frances (2013). Full notes in ../research/unit06-psychopathology-sources.md.

pages.title: The Neuron & Neurotransmission (the substrate)
pages.html:
The Neuron & Neurotransmission (the substrate)

Everything else in this unit — the stress response, the medications, the way therapy changes the brain — is built out of one repeating event: one neuron passing a signal to the next across a tiny gap. You need a working picture of that event, and a working vocabulary for the chemicals that carry it, because that is the level medications act on and the level the "chemical imbalance" story either does or doesn't hold up at. This page is the substrate; the rest of the unit stands on it.

The neuron and the synapse, in one pass

The brain is roughly 86 billion neurons, each a cell specialized to receive, integrate, and send signals. A neuron receives input on its branching dendrites, sums it in the cell body, and — if the input crosses a threshold — fires an electrical impulse (the action potential) down its axon. The signal is electrical within a neuron but chemical between neurons: axons don't touch the next cell. They stop just short, at a junction called the synapse, separated by a gap (the synaptic cleft).

Here is the whole handoff, and every drug in this unit acts somewhere along it:

  1. The action potential reaches the axon terminal and triggers calcium-evoked release of tiny sacs (vesicles) of neurotransmitter into the cleft .
  2. The neurotransmitter diffuses across and binds receptors on the next (postsynaptic) neuron — like a key in a lock. Binding either excites that neuron (makes it more likely to fire) or inhibits it (less likely).
  3. The signal is then cleared so it doesn't fire forever: the neurotransmitter is either broken down by enzymes in the cleft or pumped back into the sending neuron by reuptake transporters to be recycled .

That third step is worth holding onto. Reuptake is how most transmitters are switched off — and blocking reuptake is exactly how the most-prescribed antidepressants work (see below and concept-psychotropic-classes).

The neurotransmitters worth knowing

You do not need the full catalog. You need the handful that psychiatric medications target and that clients hear names for. The single most important distinction is excitatory vs. inhibitory — the brain runs on a balance of accelerators and brakes.

NeurotransmitterExcitatory / inhibitoryWorking glossClinical association
Glutamatethe master excitatorythe brain's main "go" signal; central to learning/memory and plasticity too much = excitotoxicity (Alzheimer's, stroke); implicated in schizophrenia, and the target of ketamine
GABAthe master inhibitorythe brain's main "stop" signal; ~40% of inhibitory processing the calming system benzodiazepines and alcohol enhance; anxiety, insomnia, epilepsy
Dopaminemodulatoryreward/motivation, movement, executive function too much (mesolimbic) → psychosis; too little (nigrostriatal) → Parkinson's; reward circuit in addiction; ADHD
Serotoninmodulatorymood, sleep, appetite, and gut (~90% is in the GI tract) depression/anxiety; the target of SSRIs — though the causal story is contested (below)
Norepinephrinemodulatoryarousal, alertness, attention, the stress response anxiety, PTSD, ADHD, depression; the "NE" in SNRIs; the sympathetic transmitter (concept-autonomic-nervous-system)
Acetylcholineexcitatory (mostly)muscle movement, memory/learning, the parasympathetic transmitter Alzheimer's (memory); the ANS's dominant chemical

Two of these — glutamate and GABA — are the workhorses (the accelerator and the brake that most of the brain actually runs on). The famous ones — dopamine and serotonin — are modulators: they don't carry most of the traffic, they tune it. That distinction matters for the myth-busting later: "your serotonin is low" treats a fine-tuning knob as if it were the main power supply.

How drugs act: agonist, antagonist, reuptake blocker

Almost every psychotropic works by nudging one of the steps above, and there are only a few ways to do it. This vocabulary carries the whole medication page:

  • Agonist — mimics or boosts a neurotransmitter's action (turns the system up). E.g., a direct dopamine agonist in Parkinson's.
  • Antagonist — blocks a receptor so the neurotransmitter can't act (turns the system down). E.g., antipsychotics are dopamine (D2) antagonists .
  • Reuptake inhibitor — blocks the recycling pump, so the transmitter lingers in the cleft and keeps acting (an indirect way to turn the system up). E.g., SSRIs block serotonin reuptake; SNRIs block serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake .
  • Positive allosteric modulator — binds a different site and makes the receptor more responsive to the real transmitter (doesn't act on its own). E.g., benzodiazepines make GABA-A receptors more responsive to GABA .

Notice these are mechanisms, not outcomes: "turns the serotonin system up" is not the same as "fixes depression." Which brings us to the honest caveat.

The honest caveat: the immediate-effect / delayed-benefit gap

Here is a fact that quietly undermines the simple "low chemical, top it up" story. An SSRI blocks serotonin reuptake within hours — synaptic serotonin rises almost immediately. But the antidepressant effect takes 2–6 weeks . If depression were simply low serotonin and the drug simply raised it, the mood should lift in a day. The lag is the tell: the benefit appears to come not from the raised chemical itself but from slow, downstream adaptations — receptor changes, increased BDNF (a growth factor), and synaptic plasticity/neurogenesis . In other words, the medication may work by the same route therapy does — by changing the brain's wiring over weeks (concept-neuroplasticity-therapy) — not by refilling a tank. This is the neurochemical seed of the "chemical imbalance is a myth, but medication can still help" position developed in concept-psychotropic-classes.

Connects to

  • concept-psychotropic-classes — the drugs that act on every step above; the agonist/antagonist/reuptake vocabulary is used there in earnest.
  • concept-autonomic-nervous-system — where acetylcholine and norepinephrine do their body-wide work.
  • concept-neuroplasticity-therapy — glutamate as the "primary mediator of plasticity"; the delayed-benefit gap resolved as neuroplasticity.
  • concept-neuroscience-of-addiction (addiction elective) — dopamine and the reward circuit in detail.
  • unit11-neuroscience — the hub; the "biology is one lens" stance.

Sources

StatPearls, Physiology, Autonomic Nervous System (ACh/NE in the ANS). NIMH, Mental Health Medications (SSRIs act on reuptake; 4–8 week onset). SSRI pathway + "From Serotonin to Neuroplasticity" (reuptake mechanism; the delayed-onset/BDNF/plasticity account). StatPearls, benzodiazepines as GABA-A positive allosteric modulators.
