pages.title: Reliability, Validity & Screening Statistics
pages.html:
Reliability, Validity & Screening Statistics

Every number this unit produces — a PHQ-9 score, an IQ, a personality profile — is only as good as the instrument behind it, and there are exactly two questions to ask of any instrument: is it consistent (reliability)? and does it measure what we think it measures, for the use we're putting it to (validity)? Get the relationship between those two backwards and you'll either trust a number you shouldn't or discard one you should. This page is the psychometric floor under concept-screening-tools, and it's where culture-fair assessment and Unit 12's research methods meet clinical practice.

Reliability — is it consistent?

Reliability is the stability and consistency of scores . Four kinds, by what could vary:

  • Test–retest reliability — same test, same person, two time points. Does the score hold when the trait hasn't changed? (Confounded if the trait does change between administrations.)
  • Internal consistency — do the items hang together, all tapping the same construct? Measured by split-half correlation or, standardly, Cronbach's α (0–1; ~0.70+ is the usual acceptable floor, ~0.80+ good) . This is the number quoted for the PHQ-9 (α ≈ .86) and GAD-7 (α ≈ .88).
  • Inter-rater reliability — do two clinicians scoring the same client agree? Matters most for judgment-based ratings (an MSE, a structured interview). Poor inter-rater reliability is exactly the crack the dimensional critics drove through DSM categories (concept-categorical-vs-dimensional).
  • Parallel/alternate-forms — do two versions of the test agree? (Relevant when you need to re-test without practice effects.)

Validity — does it measure the right thing, for this use?

Validity is "the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses" — and the key subtlety is that validity attaches to the interpretation and use, not to the test itself . The same test can be valid for one purpose and invalid for another. Kinds of validity evidence, roughly weakest to strongest:

  • Face validity — does it look like it measures the thing? (Weakest; about appearance/buy-in, not evidence.)
  • Content validity — do the items cover the whole construct, not just part? (A depression scale that omitted sleep and appetite would have poor content validity.)
  • Criterion validity — does the score correlate with an external benchmark (the "criterion")? Two timings: concurrent (correlates with a criterion measured now — e.g., PHQ-9 vs. a structured diagnostic interview) and predictive (predicts a future outcome — e.g., a risk scale predicting later attempts).
  • Construct validity — does the test behave the way the theory of the construct says it should? Supported by convergent evidence (correlates with things it should — GAD-7 with the BAI, r≈.69) and discriminant evidence (does not correlate with things it shouldn't) .

The one relationship to never get backwards

Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A test can be reliable without being valid — but it cannot be valid without being reliable.

The dartboard image: reliable but invalid = a tight cluster of darts in the wrong corner (consistent, consistently wrong — a bathroom scale 10 lb heavy every time). Valid requires the darts cluster on the bullseye — which means they must cluster at all (reliable) and land in the right place. So reliability is the floor: an unreliable measure is just noise, and noise can't be valid; but a rock-solid reliable measure can still measure the wrong construct entirely. Consistency is not correctness.

Standardization and norms — the quiet third requirement

A number is meaningless without a comparison group. Standardization = fixed administration procedures (same instructions, same conditions) plus a representative normative sample the score is compared against . This is where clinical assessment collides with Unit 4: a test validated and normed on one population can misfire on another. A "score in the clinical range" means "clinical relative to these norms" — apply it outside that population and the interpretation may be invalid even if the test is impeccable. Psychometric quality does not license use: trustworthy assessment needs reliability + validity evidence + standardized administration + representative norms + qualified interpretation + fairness across groups . This is cultural humility in numeric form.

Screening statistics: sensitivity, specificity, and predictive value

A slightly different question: not "is the scale consistent?" but "when it flags someone, how much should I believe it?" Four terms :

  • Sensitivity = of everyone who has the condition, the fraction the test catches (true positives). A sensitive test, when negative, helps rule OUT — SnNOut.
  • Specificity = of everyone who doesn't, the fraction the test correctly clears (true negatives). A specific test, when positive, helps rule IN — SpPin.
  • PPV / NPV — of those the test flags positive/negative, the fraction who truly are/aren't. Unlike sensitivity/specificity, PPV and NPV depend on prevalence: the same test yields a lower PPV in a low-prevalence setting (more of its positives are false alarms).

The trade-off, and why screens are built to over-flag

Sensitivity and specificity trade off: move a cut-point to catch more cases and you catch more false alarms too . Screening instruments are deliberately tuned toward high sensitivity — missing a case (a suicidal client cleared as fine) is worse than a false positive (a well client sent for a closer look). That's why the PHQ-9/GAD-7 cut-points feel low and why a positive screen is a flag to assess further, never a diagnosis (concept-screening-tools). A diagnostic test (or, here, the clinical interview) can afford higher specificity because it comes after the screen has already narrowed the field.

Sources

IOM, Overview of Psychological Testing (NBK305233). StatPearls, Sensitivity and Specificity (NBK557491). Rutter & Brown (2017), GAD-7 psychometrics. Research Methods in Psychology, 2nd Canadian Ed. (OER). Full notes in ../research/unit07-assessment-sources.md.

pages.title: Collaborative Safety Planning
pages.html:
Collaborative Safety Planning

Once risk is assessed, the question becomes what do we build together so this person survives the next crisis? The answer is a safety plan, and the answer is emphatically not a "no-suicide contract." The Safety Planning Intervention (SPI), developed by Barbara Stanley and Gregory Brown, is a brief, collaborative, clinician-assisted written plan: a prioritized list of coping strategies and supports the person can move through when a suicidal crisis begins to build . It is one of the most evidence-supported brief interventions in suicide prevention — in a study of emergency-department patients, the SPI plus structured follow-up calls was associated with ~45% fewer suicidal behaviors over six months versus usual care , and it is endorsed by the Joint Commission, the VA/DoD guideline, and the Zero Suicide framework.

The six steps, in order

The order is the point. The plan moves from what the person can do entirely alone toward external and professional help, so the earliest steps are always available even when no one else is :

  1. Warning signs. The personal thoughts, images, moods, and behaviors that signal a crisis is starting — in the client's own words ("when I start replaying the breakup and stop answering texts"). Naming these is what tells the person when to open the plan.
  2. Internal coping strategies. Things the client can do on their own, without contacting anyone, to ride out and distract from the urge — walk, cold water, music, exercise, a specific show. These come first because they build the sense that I can get through a wave myself.
  3. Social contacts and settings for distraction. People and places that take the mind off the crisis — a sibling to text about nothing, a coffee shop, a gym — without disclosing the suicidal thoughts. The job here is distraction and connection, not disclosure.
  4. People to ask for help. Family or friends the client will actually tell they're in crisis. This is the first step that involves disclosing the crisis to someone.
  5. Professionals and agencies to contact in a crisis. The counselor, the local emergency department, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) — with names and numbers written down, because a person in crisis will not go looking for them.
  6. Making the environment safe. Reducing access to lethal means — the means-restriction step. For highly lethal means (especially firearms), this is done with responsible others, not left to the person alone.

Why it is built with the client, not handed to them

A safety plan photocopied and handed over is nearly worthless. The intervention is the collaborative conversation: eliciting the person's own warning signs, testing whether each coping strategy is realistic ("would you actually call your brother, or would you not want to worry him?"), and troubleshooting the barriers. A strategy the client didn't help choose is a strategy they won't use at 2 a.m. The plan is also a living document — revisited and revised as circumstances and risk change, not a one-time form . And it dovetails with the ideation-to-action logic: steps 3–4 raise connectedness and step 6 lowers practical capability, which are exactly the two things you can change tonight (concept-suicide-risk-assessment).

Safety plan vs. no-suicide contract — the discrimination that matters

Beginners (and older training materials) reach for the "no-suicide contract" — a client's verbal or written promise not to harm themselves. Drop it. The two look superficially similar and are opposites in what they do :

No-suicide contractSafety plan (SPI)
What it asksa promise ("I won't kill myself")a plan ("here's what I'll do when the urge comes")
Who it servesthe clinician's anxiety / liabilitythe client's survival
Evidencenone that it reduces suicide or attemptsRCT/cohort support for reduced suicidal behavior
Failure modefalse reassurance; defensive, not therapeutic; gives the client nothing to dorequires ongoing collaboration and revision

A contract extracts a promise and offers nothing in return; when the crisis comes, the person has a broken promise and still no plan. Worse, it can lull the clinician into thinking the work is done. A commitment to safety is fine as a stance — but the deliverable is the plan, the concrete list of what the client will do and whom they will reach.

The stance traps

  • Handing over a form. If you filled it out and gave it to them, you skipped the intervention. The value is in the co-construction.
  • Skipping means reduction to avoid an awkward conversation. Step 6 is the step most likely to save a life and the one most often rushed or dropped (concept-means-reduction).
  • Confusing a promise with a plan. "They contracted for safety" is not a safety plan. Ask: does the client know what to do, and whom to call, when the warning signs start?
  • One and done. Risk changes; the plan has to change with it.

Connects to

  • concept-suicide-risk-assessment — the assessment that precedes and calibrates the plan.
  • concept-means-reduction — step 6 in depth.
  • concept-confidentiality-limits — when risk is high enough that the plan is not sufficient and you must act on the danger-to-self exception.
  • aux-psychological-first-aid — the acute-support stance the plan is delivered within.

Sources

Stanley & Brown (2012), Cognitive and Behavioral Practice; Stanley-Brown SPI template. Stanley et al. (2018), JAMA Psychiatry; Rudd, Mandrusiak & Joiner (2006), The Case Against No-Suicide Contracts. Full notes in ../research/unit08-crisis-trauma-sources.md.

pages.title: Scope of Practice & Competence
pages.html:
Scope of Practice & Competence

The idea: you may only do work you are qualified to do. Two related but distinct fences enforce this — one drawn by the state, one drawn by your own training:

Scope of practiceCompetence
Drawn bythe law — your license statute defines what your profession may doethics — what you personally are trained to do (C.2)
Question it answers"May a counselor do this at all?""May I do this?"
Example violationan LPC prescribing medication, or administering/interpreting tests reserved to psychologists in that statea counselor trained only in adult work taking on a 6-year-old with encopresis

You can be inside your profession's scope and still outside your personal competence — that's the subtler, more common failure.

What the Code requires (C.2)

  • C.2.a — Boundaries of competence. "Counselors practice only within the boundaries of their competence, based on their education, training, supervised experience, state and national professional credentials, and appropriate professional experience." Note what's not on the list: enthusiasm, having read a book, or a weekend webinar certificate. The same standard makes multicultural counseling competency required across all specialties — cultural competence is not a specialty; it's floor-level (Unit 4 takes this up).
  • C.2.b — New specialty areas only after appropriate education, training, and supervised experience — and while developing the new skill, take steps to ensure competence and protect others from harm. The path into (say) trauma work or play therapy is coursework → training → supervision, not "learn on the client."
  • C.2.d — Monitor effectiveness continually; seek peer supervision to evaluate your efficacy.
  • C.2.f — Continuing education — maintain awareness of current science and best practices, including for diverse populations. Licensure boards make a version of this legally mandatory (CE hours per renewal cycle).
  • C.2.g — Impairment. Monitor yourself for impairment from physical, mental, or emotional problems, and refrain from providing services when impaired. Seek help; if needed, limit, suspend, or terminate your practice. This is the ethical root of the self-care material in Unit 8 — burnout management isn't a wellness perk, it's a competence obligation.

The referral reflex (and its limits)

The classic answer to "a client presents beyond my competence" is refer — with an appropriate warm handoff, not abandonment (A.11 governs termination and referral; abandonment is prohibited). But two cautions keep the reflex honest:

  • Referral isn't rejection. Done well it sounds like: "What you're describing — the flashbacks, the nightmares — deserves someone with specific trauma training, and that's not yet me. I'd like to connect you with someone excellent, and I'll stay in the loop so nothing falls through the cracks." Competence-based referral, honestly explained, models integrity.
  • Values are not a competence issue. A 2014-era bright line (added after the Ward v. Wilbanks litigation): counselors may not refer merely because a client's identity, beliefs, or behavior conflicts with the counselor's personal values (A.4.b, A.11.b) — you refer for lack of skill, never lack of approval. This distinction is heavily tested in programs.

The stance note

Scope discipline runs against two self-reliant reflexes: "I can figure this out" (in many fields self-teaching is a virtue; in clinical work, unsupervised self-teaching is the ethics violation), and "more tools = better" (in clinical work, a technique you half-know is a liability, not an asset). The professional habit to build instead: know the edges of what you know, say them out loud, and treat supervision as the safeguard — the thing that catches the errors you can't see from inside your own perspective.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • How much training makes you "competent" in a modality is genuinely fuzzy — there's no bright-line hour count for most specialties; certification schemes vary wildly in rigor. The defensible answer is always the C.2.b triad (education + training + supervision) plus consultation.
  • Scope battles between professions (who may diagnose, who may test, who may prescribe) are live legislative fights that vary by state — see concept-helping-professions-compared.

Connects to

  • concept-helping-professions-compared — scope of practice at the profession level.
  • concept-dual-relationships — the other self-discipline standard: knowing where your role ends.
  • Unit 8 — impairment, vicarious trauma, and self-care as ethical competencies (C.2.g is the hook).

pages.text: Scope of Practice & Competence The idea: you may only do work you are qualified to do. Two related but distinct fences enforce this — one drawn by the state, one drawn by your own training: Scope of practice Competence Drawn by the law — your license statute defines what your profession may do ethics — what you personally are trained to do (C.2) Question it answers "May a counselor do this at all?" "May I do this?" Example violation an LPC prescribing medication, or administering/interpreting tests reserved to psychologists in that state a counselor trained only in adult work taking on a 6-year-old with encopresis You can be inside your profession's scope and still outside your personal competence — that's the subtler, more common failure. S1 S7 What the Code requires (C.2) C.2.a — Boundaries of competence. "Counselors practice only within the boundaries of their competence, based on their education, training, supervised experience, state and national professional credentials, and appropriate professional experience ." Note what's not on the list: enthusiasm, having read a book, or a weekend webinar certificate. The same standard makes multicultural counseling competency required across all specialties — cultural competence is not a specialty; it's floor-level (Unit 4 takes this up). S1 C.2.b — New specialty areas only after appropriate education, training, and supervised experience — and while developing the new skill, take steps to ensure competence and protect others from harm. The path into (say) trauma work or play therapy is coursework → training → supervision, not "learn on the client." S1 C.2.d — Monitor effectiveness continually; seek peer supervision to evaluate your efficacy. S1 C.2.f — Continuing education — maintain awareness of current science and best practices, including for diverse populations. Licensure boards make a version of this legally mandatory (CE hours per renewal cycle). S1 C.2.g — Impairment. Monitor yourself for impairment from physical, mental, or emotional problems, and refrain from providing services when impaired . Seek help; if needed, limit, suspend, or terminate your practice. This is the ethical root of the self-care material in Unit 8 — burnout management isn't a wellness perk, it's a competence obligation. S1 The referral reflex (and its limits) The classic answer to "a client presents beyond my competence" is refer — with an appropriate warm handoff, not abandonment (A.11 governs termination and referral; abandonment is prohibited). But two cautions keep the reflex honest: Referral isn't rejection. Done well it sounds like: "What you're describing — the flashbacks, the nightmares — deserves someone with specific trauma training, and that's not yet me. I'd like to connect you with someone excellent, and I'll stay in the loop so nothing falls through the cracks." Competence-based referral, honestly explained, models integrity. Values are not a competence issue. A 2014-era bright line (added after the Ward v. Wilbanks litigation): counselors may not refer merely because a client's identity, beliefs, or behavior conflicts with the counselor's personal values (A.4.b, A.11.b) — you refer for lack of skill , never lack of approval . This distinction is heavily tested in programs. S1 The stance note Scope discipline runs against two self-reliant reflexes: "I can figure this out" (in many fields self-teaching is a virtue; in clinical work, unsupervised self-teaching is the ethics violation), and "more tools = better" (in clinical work, a technique you half-know is a liability, not an asset). The professional habit to build instead: know the edges of what you know, say them out loud, and treat supervision as the safeguard — the thing that catches the errors you can't see from inside your own perspective. What's contested (don't over-learn it) How much training makes you "competent" in a modality is genuinely fuzzy — there's no bright-line hour count for most specialties; certification schemes vary wildly in rigor. The defensible answer is always the C.2.b triad (education + training + supervision) plus consultation. S1 Scope battles between professions (who may diagnose, who may test, who may prescribe) are live legislative fights that vary by state — see concept-helping-professions-compared . S7 S8 Connects to concept-helping-professions-compared — scope of practice at the profession level. concept-dual-relationships — the other self-discipline standard: knowing where your role ends. Unit 8 — impairment, vicarious trauma , and self-care as ethical competencies (C.2.g is the hook). unit04-multicultural — multicultural competence as required-for-everyone (C.2.a). pages.title: Screening & Outcome-Monitoring Tools (PHQ-9, GAD-7, and others)
pages.html:
Screening & Outcome-Monitoring Tools (PHQ-9, GAD-7, and others)

A screening tool is a brief, standardized self-report that turns a fuzzy clinical impression into a number you can compare — across clients, and across weeks for the same client. Two of them, the PHQ-9 and the GAD-7, are so common in real practice that you'll administer them constantly, so learn them cold. But the load-bearing idea comes first, because it's the one that's easy to get wrong: a screen is not a diagnosis. It flags a domain of distress and grades its severity; the diagnosis is still made by the clinical interview (concept-intake-interview) and the criteria (unit06-psychopathology).

The PHQ-9 (depression)

The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 — Kroenke, Spitzer & Williams (2001) :

  • 9 items, one for each of the nine DSM major-depression symptoms, each scored 0–3 ("not at all" → "nearly every day") over the last two weeks → total 0–27. (Because the nine items are the nine criteria, the PHQ-9 doubles as a criteria refresher — concept-mood-disorders.)
  • Severity anchors: 5 / 10 / 15 / 20 = mild / moderate / moderately severe / severe (0–4 minimal).
  • Cut-point ≥10: sensitivity 88%, specificity 88% for major depression . Scoring ≥10 makes a depression diagnosis 7–14× more likely; ≤4 drops it below ~1-in-25 .
  • Reliability: Cronbach's α ≈ 0.86–0.89 (good internal consistency) .
  • Item 9 is a suicide-risk trip-wire — "thoughts that you would be better off dead, or of hurting yourself." Any non-zero answer obligates a direct, in-person risk follow-up; never let a self-report scale substitute for the conversation (concept-suicide-risk-assessment).
  • Free and public-domain, in 30+ languages — a real reason it's everywhere.
  • PHQ-2 = the first two items (mood + anhedonia) as an ultra-brief pre-screen; a positive PHQ-2 (≥3) prompts the full PHQ-9.

The GAD-7 (anxiety)

The Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 — Spitzer, Kroenke, Williams & Löwe (2006) :

  • 7 items, each 0–3 over the last two weeks → total 0–21.
  • Cut-points: 5 / 10 / 15 = mild / moderate / severe.
  • Cut-point ≥10: sensitivity 89%, specificity 82% for GAD . Internal consistency α ≈ 0.83–0.92 across samples .
  • It is not GAD-specific. Though built for GAD, it also screens positive for panic disorder (~74%), social anxiety disorder (~72%), and PTSD (~66%) — the clean illustration that a positive screen names a broad domain of distress, not a diagnosis. A high GAD-7 sends you to the interview to find out which anxiety, not to write "GAD." (GAD-2 = the first two items as the brief pre-screen.)

A starter kit of other instruments

You don't need to memorize these, but recognize them — they populate the same measurement-based-care workflow :

ToolScreens forNotes
PC-PTSD-5PTSD5-item primary-care trauma screen (Unit 8)
AUDIT / AUDIT-Calcohol useAUDIT-C = 3 items; ties to concept-substance-use-disorders
C-SSRSsuicide riskColumbia protocol — structured risk, not a "score" (Unit 8)
MoCA / MMSE / Mini-Cogcognitive impairmentwhen the MSE flags cognition — a screen, then referral
CFIcultural contextthe DSM's Cultural Formulation Interview (concept-dsm-structure)

Screen once — then keep measuring (measurement-based care)

The highest-value use of these tools isn't the one-time intake flag; it's repeated administration to track change. Measurement-based care (MBC) = giving a validated scale (PHQ-9, GAD-7, …) at each visit and using the score to steer treatment . Why it matters:

  • It catches non-response and deterioration earlier than clinical impression — clinicians relying on unaided judgment routinely fail to notice a client is worsening, and the benefit of MBC is strongest precisely for the patients who would otherwise quietly not improve .
  • It closes the loop with the plan: the same instrument that flagged the problem now defines a measurable goal ("PHQ-9 from 18 to <10 in 12 weeks") and shows whether you're getting there (concept-treatment-planning). This is the outcome-monitoring thread Unit 12 picks up.

The trap: a number is a flag, not a verdict

Screens are deliberately tuned toward high sensitivity — better to over-flag and assess than to miss a case (concept-reliability-validity) — which guarantees false positives. So:

  • Never diagnose from a score. A PHQ-9 of 16 is a reason to interview carefully, not a diagnosis of MDD. The score can't tell grief from depression, or a bad week from an episode (concept-mood-disorders).
  • Cut-points are population-dependent, not laws. ≥10 is the standard flag, but ≥8 is optimal in some psychiatric samples — a calibrated setting, not a threshold of truth.
  • Read the score in context. Self-report is filtered through culture, language, literacy, and motive-to-present (unit04-multicultural); a validity coefficient earned in one population may not travel (concept-reliability-validity).
  • Don't let the form run the session. MBC serves the work; a client is a person, not a trend line — the same "measure, don't be captured by the measure" discipline the whole unit teaches.

Sources

Kroenke et al. (2001), PHQ-9. Spitzer et al. (2006), GAD-7. APA, PHQ-9 & PHQ-2. Rutter & Brown (2017), GAD-7 psychometrics. Fortney et al. (2017), measurement-based care. Full notes in ../research/unit07-assessment-sources.md.

pages.title: Single-Case Designs & Progress Monitoring
pages.html:
Single-Case Designs & Progress Monitoring

Group research answers "does this work on average, across people?" But a counselor sits with one person, and often wants to know something a group study can't tell them: "is this working for this client?" Single-case methods are built for exactly that question — and the surprising, useful fact is that you can run a genuine experiment on a single participant, with real internal validity, without a control group. This is also the design tradition (from applied behavior analysis and special education) closest to everyday clinical practice, which is why the course-map flags it as a discrimination target and why counselors report doing single-case and outcome evaluation more than any other kind .

The core move: repeated measurement across phases

A single-case (single-subject) experimental design measures the outcome repeatedly over time, dividing the study into labeled phases — conventionally A for baseline and B for treatment :

  • Baseline (A) — repeated measurement with no treatment, continued until the behavior is stable (the "steady state"). The baseline is the comparison the whole design rests on: it's what the client's trajectory looks like without the intervention.
  • Treatment (B) — the intervention is introduced and measurement continues.

A bare AB design (baseline, then treatment) shows change, but can't rule out history or maturation — maybe the client would have improved anyway. The experimental single-case designs add controls that defend the causal claim.

The two workhorse designs

Reversal (ABAB / withdrawal) design. Introduce treatment (B), then withdraw it (return to A), then reintroduce it (B). If the behavior improves under treatment, drifts back toward baseline when it's removed, and improves again when it's reapplied, the treatment — not some coincidental outside event — is almost certainly the cause. That tracking-with-the-phases is the strongest single-case demonstration of causation . Its limits are obvious and important: you can't (and shouldn't) withdraw a treatment for a dangerous behavior, and some gains don't reverse (a skill, once learned, stays learned) — in both cases reversal is the wrong tool.

Multiple-baseline design. The ethical and practical fix. Instead of withdrawing treatment, stagger its onset across several baselines — across behaviors (same person, different targets), settings (same person, different contexts), or people. If each baseline changes only when treatment reaches it — and not before — the staggered pattern rules out history/maturation just as convincingly, without ever removing an effective treatment . This is the design of choice when reversal is unethical or impossible.

How you read the data: visual inspection

Single-case data are judged primarily by visual inspection of the graph — not (mainly) by inferential statistics — along three features :

  • Level — the average height of the outcome within a phase (did it jump?).
  • Trend — the slope across observations (was it already climbing, or did treatment bend the line?).
  • Latency — the time between the phase change and the change in behavior (a fast, tight response to each phase change is more convincing than a slow, ambiguous drift).

A convincing single-case result shows changes in level/trend that are large, immediate, and repeated at each phase change. (Statistical methods for single-case data exist and are growing, but remain supplementary to the visual analysis.)

Single-case design vs. a case study — don't confuse them

A perennial mix-up (and a clean exam discrimination): a case study is descriptive — a rich narrative account of one person, with no manipulation and no baseline logic, so it cannot support a causal claim (it sits near the bottom of the evidence hierarchy, concept-evidence-based-practice). A single-case experimental design systematically manipulates the intervention against a stable baseline with repeated measurement, so it can support causal inference. Same "N = 1," opposite evidentiary weight. (Confusingly, both are sometimes called "case" work — read for the baseline + manipulation, which only the experimental design has.)

The clinical cousin: progress monitoring / measurement-based care

Strip a single-case design down to its most usable core — repeated measurement of one client, plotted over time — and you have progress monitoring, the practice-level tool this whole thread has been building toward. In everyday care it's usually an AB design (no reversal, no staggering), which means it is good enough to guide this client's care but not to prove the therapy caused the change — and that's the correct trade for clinical work.

Measurement-based care (MBC) formalizes it: routinely administer a brief outcome measure (the PHQ-9 / GAD-7 from Unit 7's concept-screening-tools), plot the scores, and use them to adjust treatment — the "golden thread" of concept-treatment-planning made continuous. Its payoff is specific and evidence-backed: MBC and feedback-informed treatment improve outcomes especially by catching the client who is not on track — the quietly deteriorating person whom clinical intuition, left alone, tends to miss . And the question "is this 4-point drop real or just noise?" is answered by the reliable change index on concept-effect-size. This is measurement in service of the relationship, not a reduction of the person to a number — the unit's stance, made concrete.

Connects to

  • concept-experimental-vs-correlational — single-case designs are true experiments scaled to one participant; baseline logic replaces the control group.
  • concept-validity-threats — reversal/multiple-baseline are ways to defend internal validity (rule out history/maturation) without a between-groups control.
  • concept-effect-size — the reliable change index / clinical significance is how you read one client's outcome data.
  • concept-evidence-based-practice — where single-case (and the case study it's confused with) sit on the evidence hierarchy; well-controlled single-case series can even support EST status.
  • concept-screening-tools and concept-treatment-planning (Unit 7) — the instruments and the golden thread that progress monitoring runs on.

pages.title: Stages of Change: The Transtheoretical Model
pages.html:
Stages of Change: The Transtheoretical Model

The most useful answer to "how do you break an addiction?" is: not all at once, and not from a standing start. Prochaska & DiClemente's Transtheoretical Model (TTM) — the "stages of change" — describes change as a process a person moves through, and gives the helper the single most important diagnostic question they can ask: not "how do I get them to quit?" but "where are they right now?" Matching your move to the stage is the whole game; pushing action on someone who is still precontemplative is the classic way to create "resistance."

The five stages (plus the loop)

  1. Precontemplation — not considering change in the foreseeable future (next ~6 months). Often unaware or minimizing ("I can stop anytime," "it's not a problem"). May be there because they've tried and failed before. Others usually see the problem first.
  2. Contemplation — aware and ambivalent. Sees pros and cons of changing and is stuck between them ("I know I should, but…"). Can sit here for a long time. This is the home of ambivalence, the target of theory-motivational-interviewing (Unit 9; applied to substance use in concept-treatment-and-recovery).
  3. Preparation — intending to act soon (within ~a month) and taking first steps: telling someone, researching options, cutting back, making a plan.
  4. Action — actively changing the behavior — the visible, effortful phase (quitting, entering treatment). Where outsiders think "change" begins, but it rests on the three stages before it.
  5. Maintenance — sustaining the change and working to prevent relapse; the new pattern is becoming the default but still takes work. This is where concept-relapse-prevention lives.

Relapse / recycling is treated as an expected event, not a stage failure: most people cycle back to an earlier stage and go around again.

It's a spiral, not a staircase

Prochaska & DiClemente originally drew discrete stages, but the field now models change as a spiral: people loop through the stages several times before change sticks, each pass usually starting from a bit further along rather than back at zero. The clinical consequence is a posture, not just a fact: a return to use is a normal turn of the spiral to be learned from, not proof the person "can't change" — which is the same reframing concept-relapse-prevention makes at the level of a single slip.

Decisional balance: the pros and cons tip

Movement across the early stages tracks a shifting decisional balance — the person's felt weight of the pros vs. cons of changing. In precontemplation the cons of change dominate (using still "works" for them); progress looks like the pros of change gaining weight until they tip the scale. You rarely tip it for someone by adding arguments (that triggers the righting reflex backlash — see concept-treatment-and-recovery); you help them voice their own pros of change.

Matching the intervention to the stage

The model's practical core: different stages need different help.

StageWhat the person needsWhat backfires
PrecontemplationInformation, concern, a relationship — raise doubt, don't demand actionUltimatums, lectures ("just quit")
ContemplationHelp tipping the balance — explore ambivalence, evoke change talkPushing a plan before they're ready
PreparationConcrete options, a plan, first-step supportVagueness; withholding practical help
ActionSkills, structure, active treatment, reinforcementAssuming they're "cured"; disappearing
MaintenanceRelapse-prevention skills, cue management, support networkTreating it as finished

Delivering the right help at the wrong stage is a leading cause of stalled change — action-oriented advice to a precontemplator reliably produces defensiveness, not motion.

Why this matters in the room

The single most common helper error in addiction work is stage mismatch: pressing action on someone who hasn't yet resolved whether to change. It feels like helping; it produces argument. TTM reframes the goal from "get them to quit today" to "help them take one step along the spiral," which is both more effective and more humane — and it means a precontemplative client who leaves merely doubting their use has moved, even though nothing visible changed.

pages.title: The Stress Response (SAM, HPA, and allostatic load)
pages.html:
The Stress Response (SAM, HPA, and allostatic load)

Stress is not a feeling; it's a coordinated whole-body program for meeting a demand, and it runs on two systems at two speeds. This page is the full version of the working-level preview Unit 8 gave in concept-neurobiology-of-trauma (which is flagged source_units: [8, 11] for exactly this handoff). The through-line to carry: the stress response is adaptive — it's supposed to fire. The problem is almost never that a client has a stress response; it's that theirs fires too easily, too hard, or won't shut off. Distinguishing the healthy program from its dysregulation is the clinical point.

Two systems, two speeds

A threat (real, remembered, or imagined — the brain doesn't cleanly distinguish) triggers two stress cascades that work in sequence :

SAM axis (fast)HPA axis (slow)
Full nameSympathetic-Adreno-MedullaryHypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal
Speedsecondsminutes
Chemicaladrenaline / noradrenaline (catecholamines)cortisol (a glucocorticoid)
Routenerves → adrenal medulla → bloodstreamhormones → adrenal cortex → bloodstream
Feelthe instant jolt: pounding heart, dry mouththe sustained mobilization: energy, focus, wakefulness

The SAM arm is the sympathetic branch's adrenaline shortcut from concept-autonomic-nervous-system — the "fight or flight" jolt in the first second. The HPA arm is the endocrine follow-through, and it's worth knowing as a chain because medications and dysregulation both act on it:

Hypothalamus releases CRH → tells the pituitary to release ACTH → tells the adrenal cortex to release cortisol → cortisol mobilizes glucose, sharpens attention, and (crucially) feeds back to the hypothalamus and hippocampus to shut CRH off . That last step — negative feedback — is the off-switch. A working stress response turns on fast and turns off cleanly. Much of stress-related pathology is a failure of the off, not the on.

The brain circuit that gates it

The two axes don't fire at random; they're gated by a small circuit you already met in Unit 8 :

  • Amygdala — the smoke alarm. Detects threat and drives the stress axes.
  • Hippocampus — the context-stamp and a brake. It time-stamps events ("this is happening now / this already happened") and inhibits the HPA axis (it's rich in cortisol receptors, part of the negative-feedback loop).
  • Prefrontal cortex (PFC) — top-down regulation. The rational brake that can appraise a threat as false and dampen the amygdala.

Under acute threat this circuit is adaptive: amygdala up, energy mobilized, and then — once safe — PFC and hippocampus bring it back down. Under chronic stress the balance shifts the wrong way (a hyperactive amygdala, an under-functioning hippocampus and PFC), which is precisely the picture Unit 8 draws for trauma. This unit's addition is the endocrine half of that story (the HPA hormones), where Unit 8 emphasized the memory half.

Acute vs. chronic: allostasis and allostatic load

The single most useful idea here is Bruce McEwen's :

  • Allostasis = "stability through change." The body doesn't hold one fixed set-point; it shifts its set-points to meet demand — raising blood pressure, cortisol, and glucose to handle a stressor, then returning them. This is healthy and efficient.
  • Allostatic load = the cumulative wear and tear the body accrues when the allostatic systems (SAM + HPA) are run too often, too long, or fail to shut off — "how chronic stress gets under our skin and skull." Chronically elevated (or, confusingly, chronically blunted) cortisol, worn-down feedback, and a rewired amygdala/hippocampus are allostatic load. It links chronic stress to a long tail of physical and mental-health outcomes.

The clinical translation: acute stress is a feature; allostatic load is the bug. A client's tension headaches, gut problems, poor sleep, and constant edginess can be the somatic signature of an alarm system that never fully stands down — worth naming, because it reframes "it's all in my head" as a real, whole-body process. It's also the biological argument for why self-care and recovery aren't optional luxuries: they are how the system discharges load.

What's contested — read carefully

  • There is no clean cortisol biomarker for stress or trauma. This is the honest limit carried straight from Unit 8: cortisol findings are inconsistent — some populations show elevated cortisol, others blunted/low — and dysregulated HPA responses are "not consistently associated with psychopathology" . So the story is dysregulation of the stress axis, not "high cortisol = stress." Never let a client (or yourself) treat a cortisol test as a diagnosis.
  • "Stress" is a genuinely fuzzy construct. The systems (SAM, HPA) are well-characterized; the word "stress" papering over threat, challenge, novelty, and demand is not. Direction of the biology is solid; precise numbers and the neat popular narratives are not.
  • Adrenal fatigue is not a recognized diagnosis. The wellness-industry claim that chronic stress "exhausts your adrenals" and causes a distinct "adrenal fatigue" syndrome is not supported; allostatic load is the evidence-based frame, not adrenal burnout.

Connects to

  • concept-neurobiology-of-trauma (Unit 8) — the memory-and-fear half of the same circuit; this page is its endocrine complement (shared source_units).
  • concept-autonomic-nervous-system — the SAM/fast arm is the sympathetic branch's adrenaline shortcut.
  • concept-counselor-self-care (Unit 8) — recovery as how the body discharges allostatic load; the biological case for self-care as duty.
  • concept-biopsychosocial-model (Unit 5) — chronic stress as a paradigm case of biology, psychology, and social conditions co-producing an outcome.
  • unit11-neuroscience — the hub; the stress-is-adaptive stance.

Sources

Gunnar & Quevedo (Annu. Rev. Psychol.) + stress-neurobiology overview (SAM fast/catecholamines → HPA slow/cortisol; CRH→ACTH→cortisol; negative feedback). Dysregulated-HPA review (PMC4358064) + McEwen allostatic-load literature (allostasis vs. allostatic load; inconsistent cortisol; not consistently tied to psychopathology). Unit 8 concept-neurobiology-of-trauma (amygdala/hippocampus/PFC circuit; the cortisol-is-not-a-clean-biomarker caveat). Full notes in ../research/unit11-neuroscience-sources.md.

pages.title: Substance Use Disorders (the DSM view)
pages.html:
Substance Use Disorders (the DSM view)

This page is deliberately short: the elective module aux-addiction covers addiction at full depth — models, neuroscience, stages of change, relapse, treatment. What belongs here is how substance use disorders sit inside the DSM-5-TR's architecture, because a few structural facts are exactly what exams and intakes require.

One criteria set, eleven criteria, four groups

DSM-5 collapsed DSM-IV's "abuse" vs. "dependence" split into a single substance use disorder per substance class, diagnosed against 11 criteria in four groups :

  1. Impaired control — larger amounts/longer than intended; persistent desire or failed attempts to cut down; great time spent obtaining/using/recovering; craving.
  2. Social impairment — role failure at work/school/home; continued use despite interpersonal problems; important activities given up.
  3. Risky use — use in physically hazardous situations; continued use despite knowing it causes physical/psychological harm.
  4. Pharmacological — tolerance; withdrawal.

Severity is a symptom count — mild (2–3), moderate (4–5), severe (6+) — which makes SUD the manual's most openly dimensional diagnosis, a fact worth noticing for concept-categorical-vs-dimensional. There's a separate SUD per class (alcohol use disorder, opioid use disorder, stimulant use disorder…), plus substance-induced disorders (intoxication, withdrawal, and substance-induced mental disorders — always on the differential for mood, anxiety, and psychotic presentations).

The two distinctions that prevent real harm

  • Physical dependence ≠ addiction. Tolerance and withdrawal that develop under appropriate medical care (prescribed opioids, SSRIs, beta-blockers) do not count toward an SUD diagnosis. A post-surgical patient who needs a taper is not thereby addicted. Full treatment in concept-addiction-models.
  • Behavioral addictions are (almost) not a thing in the DSM. Gambling disorder is the only one in the main text; internet gaming disorder sits in Section III for further study. "Addicted to X" is colloquial, not diagnostic.

Why it matters in this unit

Substance use is the great mimic and the great co-traveler: it can produce depression, anxiety, and psychosis; it co-occurs with nearly every category in this unit (and comorbidity concentrates severity — ); and missing it reroutes the whole treatment plan. The intake habit is simple: always ask about substances, matter-of-factly, whatever the presenting problem. The stance material — meeting use without moralizing, the righting reflex, stages of change — is concept-stages-of-change and concept-treatment-and-recovery in the elective.

Sources

DSM-5-TR SUD criteria via SAMHSA/NCBI NBK565474 (also the aux-addiction module's ). Kessler et al. (2005). Full notes in ../research/unit06-psychopathology-sources.md; full topic treatment in aux-addiction.

pages.title: Suicide Risk Assessment
pages.html:
Suicide Risk Assessment

The single most important reframe in this whole page: you are assessing risk in order to manage it, not to predict who will die. Individual suicide is not reliably predictable — no instrument or risk-factor list forecasts who acts and when — and treating assessment as prophecy leads both to false confidence and to defensive practice . This is the same prediction critique the study-tarasoff reading raised about dangerousness prediction: the tools stratify populations and point you toward the right intervention and disposition, and that is enough to do the job . The goal is a clinical decision — how closely to watch, what to remove, where the person spends tonight — grounded in a direct, humane conversation.

First: ask directly, and don't flinch

The beginner's fear is that naming suicide will "put the idea in someone's head." The evidence is clear that it does not: reviews across community, adolescent, adult, and at-risk samples find no increase in ideation from being asked — and some find that talking about it reduces distress . The real danger is not asking. So ask plainly and non-anxiously:

"Are you thinking about killing yourself?" — or "Sometimes when people feel this bad, they think about ending their life. Are you having thoughts like that?"

Euphemisms ("hurting yourself," "doing something silly") blur the very thing you need to know. Say the word, then be quiet and let the answer land.

Ideation vs. behavior — and the ideation ladder

The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) organizes the assessment around a distinction beginners collapse: suicidal ideation is not suicidal behavior, and each is graded separately .

Ideation runs on a five-point severity ladder of increasing seriousness:

  1. Wish to be dead ("I wish I wouldn't wake up") — passive.
  2. Nonspecific active suicidal thoughts ("I've thought about killing myself") — no method.
  3. Active ideation with methods considered — but no plan or intent.
  4. Active ideation with some intent to act.
  5. Active ideation with a specific plan and intent.

The jump from passive ("I wish I were dead") to active ("I've thought about how") is a meaningful clinical line — but passive ideation is not "safe," it's the start of the conversation. Beyond ideation you assess intensity (frequency, duration, controllability, deterrents, reasons for dying/living) and, separately, behavior: actual attempts, interrupted attempts (stopped by an outside circumstance), aborted/self-interrupted attempts (stopped by the person themselves), and preparatory acts (acquiring means, giving possessions away, writing a note, researching methods) . Preparatory behavior with no "attempt" yet is a serious sign, not a reassurance.

The practical drill (from the syllabus practice rep) is to have a plain sequence you can run without notes: ideation → plan → intent → means/access → preparation → history of past attempts. A past attempt is the single strongest long-term risk factor .

The CASE Approach: how to elicit intent

Shea's Chronological Assessment of Suicide Events (CASE Approach) is a way of organizing the interview so you miss less and uncover more real intent. It walks four chronological regions in order :

  1. Presenting ideation/events — the crisis that brought them in today.
  2. Recent ideation/events — the past ~8 weeks.
  3. Past ideation/events — lifetime history.
  4. Immediate ideation — how they feel about safety right now, and what happens next.

Its central insight is the gap between stated intent (what the client tells you) and reflected intent (how much thinking, planning, and action they describe — which often reveals more than they'll directly admit) and withheld intent (what they're hiding). A person who says "not really" but describes researching methods, giving things away, and writing letters is showing you reflected intent that outweighs the stated denial. Techniques like asking for the behavioral incident (facts and sequence, not opinions — "what did you do next?"), gentle assumption ("what other ways have you thought about?"), and normalization lower the barrier to honest disclosure .

Risk factors vs. warning signs vs. protective factors

This is the confusable trio at the heart of the cluster — and they answer different questions.

What it isTime frameExample
Risk factora standing characteristic that raises baseline, longer-term likelihoodchronic / distalprior attempt, psychiatric disorder, substance use, trauma history, access to firearms, chronic pain, male sex, isolation
Warning signan observable indicator that risk is elevated right nowacute / proximaltalking/writing about death, giving things away, a sudden calm after despair, saying goodbye, seeking means
Protective factora characteristic that lowers likelihoodbufferingreasons for living, children/responsibility, social connectedness, engaged treatment, coping skills, beliefs discouraging suicide

Warning signs are about the near term; risk factors are about the background. A person can carry many chronic risk factors for years at a stable baseline, and it's the acute change — the warning signs, the precipitant — that signals danger in the coming hours to days . The VA/American Association of Suicidology mnemonic for warning signs is IS PATH WARM: Ideation, Substance abuse, Purposelessness, Anxiety/agitation, Trapped, Hopelessness, Withdrawal, Anger, Recklessness, Mood change . Protective factors matter but do not cancel acute risk — a devoted parent in an acute crisis is still in an acute crisis.

Ideation-to-action: why thinking about it and acting on it are different problems

The most useful modern frame is the ideation-to-action framework: the causes of suicidal ideation are distinct from the causes of the progression from ideation to an attempt . This reorganizes the whole assessment.

  • Why people come to think about suicide. In Joiner's Interpersonal Theory, ideation grows from thwarted belongingness ("I'm alone") plus perceived burdensomeness ("they'd be better off without me"). In Klonsky & May's Three-Step Theory (3ST), ideation = psychological pain + hopelessness, and connectedness is what keeps moderate ideation from escalating.
  • Why some act on it. Both theories converge on capability: the move from wanting to doing requires overcoming the powerful, wired-in fear of death and pain. Acquired capability builds through exposure to painful and provocative experiences — prior self-injury, abuse, combat, others' suicides. Practical capability includes access to means.

The clinical payoff: a client with intense ideation but low capability is in a different situation than one who has rehearsed, has access, and has habituated to the fear — and it tells you where to intervene. You can't quickly change someone's pain history, but you can raise connectedness (safety planning, follow-up) and lower practical capability (means reduction) tonight. This is why the two things you do after assessing risk are concept-safety-planning and concept-means-reduction.

From assessment to disposition

Risk is stratified to guide the decision, not to generate a number :

  • Low (ideation without plan/intent, few acute factors, protective factors intact): outpatient care, a collaborative safety plan, means-safety conversation, follow-up.
  • Moderate (active ideation, some intent/planning, mounting warning signs): intensified outpatient or crisis services, increased contact/monitoring, remove means, involve supports.
  • High (persistent ideation with plan and intent, preparatory behavior, acute crisis): do not leave the person alone, immediate means removal, and hospitalization or emergency evaluation.

And this is where Unit 3 becomes non-optional: imminent danger to self is a limit of confidentiality (concept-confidentiality-limits) — you can and must act, including breaking confidentiality to protect life, and you should have told the client this was a limit during informed consent.

The stance traps

  • Freezing / deflecting. The hardest part is staying in the conversation. Changing the subject or rushing to "it'll be okay" abandons the person at the exact moment they risked telling you.
  • False reassurance and premature problem-solving. "You have so much to live for" argues with the pain instead of understanding it. Sit in it first; the connection is an intervention.
  • Treating the screen as the assessment. A PHQ-9 item-9 endorsement or a C-SSRS score is a trip-wire and a structure, not a substitute for the clinical conversation (concept-screening-tools).
  • Assessing to predict. If you catch yourself trying to decide "will they or won't they," reset to "how do I manage this risk and keep them safe." Prediction is the wrong job.

  • concept-confidentiality-limits and concept-duty-to-warn — the ethical/legal authority to act on danger to self or others.
  • study-tarasoff — the prediction critique: assess to manage, not to prophesy.
  • concept-screening-tools — the PHQ-9 item-9 trip-wire and the intake risk screen that hand into this protocol.

This is the same prediction critique the study-tarasoff reading raised about dangerousness prediction: the tools stratify populations and point you toward the right intervention and disposition , and that is enough to do the job S3 . The goal is a clinical decision — how closely to watch, what to remove, where the person spends tonight — grounded in a direct, humane conversation. First: ask directly, and don't flinch The beginner's fear is that naming suicide will "put the idea in someone's head." The evidence is clear that it does not: reviews across community, adolescent, adult, and at-risk samples find no increase in ideation from being asked — and some find that talking about it reduces distress S4 . The real danger is not asking. So ask plainly and non-anxiously: "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" — or "Sometimes when people feel this bad, they think about ending their life. Are you having thoughts like that?" Euphemisms ("hurting yourself," "doing something silly") blur the very thing you need to know. Say the word, then be quiet and let the answer land. Ideation vs. behavior — and the ideation ladder The Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS) organizes the assessment around a distinction beginners collapse: suicidal ideation is not suicidal behavior , and each is graded separately S1 . Ideation runs on a five-point severity ladder of increasing seriousness: Wish to be dead ("I wish I wouldn't wake up") — passive. Nonspecific active suicidal thoughts ("I've thought about killing myself") — no method. Active ideation with methods considered — but no plan or intent. Active ideation with some intent to act. Active ideation with a specific plan and intent. The jump from passive ("I wish I were dead") to active ("I've thought about how") is a meaningful clinical line — but passive ideation is not "safe," it's the start of the conversation. Beyond ideation you assess intensity (frequency, duration, controllability, deterrents, reasons for dying/living) and, separately, behavior : actual attempts, interrupted attempts (stopped by an outside circumstance), aborted/self-interrupted attempts (stopped by the person themselves), and preparatory acts (acquiring means, giving possessions away, writing a note, researching methods) S1 . Preparatory behavior with no "attempt" yet is a serious sign, not a reassurance. The practical drill (from the syllabus practice rep) is to have a plain sequence you can run without notes: ideation → plan → intent → means/access → preparation → history of past attempts. A past attempt is the single strongest long-term risk factor S3 . Past ideation/events — lifetime history. Immediate ideation — how they feel about safety right now , and what happens next. Its central insight is the gap between stated intent (what the client tells you) and reflected intent (how much thinking, planning, and action they describe — which often reveals more than they'll directly admit) and withheld intent (what they're hiding). A person who says "not really" but describes researching methods, giving things away, and writing letters is showing you reflected intent that outweighs the stated denial. Techniques like asking for the behavioral incident (facts and sequence, not opinions — "what did you do next?"), gentle assumption ("what other ways have you thought about?"), and normalization lower the barrier to honest disclosure S2 . pages.title: Supporting the Acutely Bereaved (incl. Death of a Child)
pages.html:
Supporting the Acutely Bereaved — including the Death of a Child

This is the anchor case for the module: someone's child has just died, and you are in the room. The death of a child is one of the most severe losses there is and a top risk factor for prolonged grief (concept-grief-models). The good news for a helper is that being useful here requires no special eloquence — it requires presence, restraint, and follow-through. The bad news is that several things you'll want to say are actively harmful, so the discipline is mostly about what you don't do.

Presence over fixing

The deepest instinct — make this better — is the one to suspend. You cannot make it better and attempts to (silver linings, reframes, reasons) tell the parent you can't bear to stay in it with them. What actually helps: be there, stay, and tolerate the unbearable alongside them. Allow silence; if the parent wants to fill it, they will, and if not, your steady company is itself the help. This is PFA's "Listen" without any pull toward "process" — accompany, don't excavate (concept-pfa-core-actions).

Say the child's name

Bereaved parents overwhelmingly want their child acknowledged — soon after the death and for years after. Use the child's name. Speak about the child. Many people avoid the topic for fear of "reminding" the parent, but the parent has not forgotten; the silence reads as the child being erased. Mentioning the child, sharing a memory of them, is among the most consoling things you can do.

What helps — concretely

  • Do a specific useful thing rather than "let me know if you need anything." A grieving parent cannot project-manage their own support. Bring a meal, take the other kids to school, handle a load of laundry, drive them to an appointment.
  • Follow the parent's lead on whether and how much to talk; let them set the pace and topic.
  • Check in for the long haul — and especially on the hard dates: the birthday, the anniversary of the death, holidays. Support evaporates after the funeral exactly when the acute shock wears off and the absence sets in. Being the person still there at six months matters enormously.
  • Tolerate the oscillation. Per the dual process model, the parent will swing between devastation and functional, even ordinary moments. Don't read a calm or practical hour as "doing great" or as coldness — both modes are normal grief (concept-grief-models).

What harms — phrases to retire

Each of these is common, well-meant, and wounding to a bereaved parent:

  • "Everything happens for a reason." Most bereaved parents do not believe their child died for a reason; this asks them to find meaning in the unbearable on your schedule.
  • "They're in a better place." A grieving parent often cannot imagine a better place for their child than alive, in their arms.
  • "I know how you feel." Unless you have lost a child, you don't — and even then, every loss differs. It pulls focus toward you.
  • "At least…" ("at least you have other children," "at least it was quick"). Any sentence that starts by minimizing the loss lands as minimizing the child.
  • Comparisons and timelines ("you'll feel better in a year," "time heals"). They impose a schedule on something that doesn't keep one.

The throughline: don't explain the death, don't rank it, don't hurry it. Acknowledge it and stay.

Ring Theory: who comforts whom ("comfort in, dump out")

A simple rule for not adding to a grieving person's load. Draw concentric rings: the person at the center of the crisis (here, the bereaved parent), then rings outward for those progressively less central — partner, close family, friends, acquaintances. The rule:

  • Comfort goes IN — toward the center. To anyone closer to the loss than you, you offer support.
  • Complaints/needs go OUT — away from the center. Your own distress about the death ("I can't believe this, I'm devastated") you process with someone further out than you, never dump on the parent.

So you don't tell a bereaved mother how hard her child's death is on you, or ask her to reassure you. If you need to grieve too (and you may), take it to your own outer ring.

When to refer — don't carry clinical risk alone

Acute, even ferocious, grief is normal and not your cue to refer. Escalate to professional help when you see signs beyond ordinary bereavement — and especially:

  • Suicidal ideation or intent, or expressed wish to die/join the child → this is a risk situation; hand off to crisis/clinical care now (see Unit 8 — risk assessment), don't manage it solo.
  • Inability to function in basic ways that persists and isn't oscillating — no movement toward restoration-oriented coping at all over time.
  • Symptoms consistent with Prolonged Grief Disorder past the time threshold (12 months adult / 6 months child), given the elevated PGD risk after a child's death.
  • Substance use escalating to cope; psychosis; self-neglect endangering health.

Referral is not abandonment — "I want to keep showing up and connect you with someone who does this all day" is the model. This is PFA's Linkage action (concept-pfa-core-actions).

Look after yourself, too

Sitting with a parent whose child died has a cost. Helpers absorb some of it (vicarious/secondary stress — a named clinical phenomenon Unit 8 covers). Use your own support (your outer ring per Ring Theory), don't make the bereaved person carry your reaction, and treat your self-care as part of being able to keep showing up — not a luxury. A depleted helper disappears, and disappearing is the thing grieving parents say hurt most.

Connects to

  • concept-death-notification — this page starts after the parent knows; the moment of telling (and answering "where is she?" before it's confirmed) is its own skill.
  • concept-pfa-core-actions — Listen (accompany, don't probe) and Linkage (referral) in action.
  • concept-grief-models — the dual process oscillation and the PGD boundary behind these moves.
  • aux-psychological-first-aid — module hub and stance.
  • Unit 8 — suicide-risk assessment, trauma-informed care, and vicarious-trauma / counselor self-care as an ethical competency.

Sources

Stroebe & Schut dual process (via PMC5033290). PMC9131400 — child loss as PGD predictor. DSM-5-TR — PGD thresholds. Silk & Goldman, Ring Theory (via Psych Central). Nationwide Children's — what to say / not say to a grieving parent. Children's Hospital Colorado — how to help a grieving parent. Full notes in ../research/aux-psychological-first-aid-sources.md.

pages.title: The Therapeutic Alliance (Bordin's Bond/Goal/Task Model)
pages.html:
The Therapeutic Alliance

The "alliance" (or working alliance) is the collaborative relationship between counselor and client. Edward Bordin (1979) gave it the model everyone still uses, and his key move was making it transtheoretical — the same three components describe the working relationship in any orientation, from psychodynamic to CBT.

Bordin's three components

  • Bond — the affective relationship: trust, liking, respect, the sense of being a team. This is what the core conditions and microskills directly build.
  • Goal — agreement on what you're working toward. The client and counselor share the destination rather than the counselor pursuing their own.
  • Task — agreement on the in-session activities and each person's role — what you'll actually do together to get there, and that the client believes it will help.

A useful way to hold it: bond is the relationship, goal is the where, task is the how. A rupture in any of the three weakens the alliance, and they're somewhat independent — you can have warm rapport (bond) while quietly disagreeing about goals or tasks, which stalls therapy.

How Bordin thought it works

Bordin argued the alliance influences outcome not because the relationship is curative on its own, but because it's the ingredient that lets the client accept, follow, and believe in the treatment. The bond makes the work possible; the work does the changing. This is the bridge between "be warm" and "do effective therapy."

The evidence

The alliance is one of the most robust predictors of outcome in all of psychotherapy research: r ≈ .28 across 295 studies and 30,000+ patients (Flückiger et al., 2018), holding across treatment types. Bordin's operationalization is what made it measurable — it spawned the Working Alliance Inventory (WAI) and similar instruments. (See theory-common-factors for the full evidence discussion and the correlation-vs-causation caveat.)

Alliance ruptures and their repair

A rupture is a deterioration in the alliance — and, tellingly, it shows up as a breakdown in exactly Bordin's three parts: a disagreement on goals, a lack of collaboration on tasks, or a strain in the bond. Ruptures are not failures to avoid at all costs; they're routine, and how you handle them is a large part of the work. They come in two markers:

  • Withdrawal ruptures — the client moves away: placating, going quiet, giving minimal answers, intellectualizing, changing the subject. Easy to miss precisely because the surface stays pleasant.
  • Confrontation ruptures — the client moves against: expressing anger or dissatisfaction, complaining about the therapy or the therapist, trying to control the session.

The repair is usually immediacy — gently naming what's happening between you ("I get the sense I pushed us somewhere you didn't want to go — can we check that?") and, when it's your misstep, owning it. The striking finding: Eubanks, Muran & Safran's (2018) meta-analysis links successful rupture repair to better outcomes (r ≈ .29), and rupture-resolution training improves outcomes too. Safran & Muran's earlier work raised the deeper possibility that living through a repaired rupture may help a client more than an alliance that never ruptured — because it models that conflict and disappointment in a relationship can be survived and worked through. Unrepaired ruptures, by contrast, are a leading path to dropout.

Why it matters in the room

Bond/goal/task is a fast diagnostic when a session feels stuck. Ask: is the bond frayed, or do we disagree on the goal, or on the task? Each points to a different repair. Noticing and repairing alliance ruptures — especially the quiet withdrawal kind — is a core competency you'll develop in supervision, and it maps directly onto these three parts.

Connects to

  • concept-core-conditions — UPR/empathy/congruence are how you build the bond.
  • concept-congruence — immediacy is the specific skill for naming and repairing a rupture.
  • concept-microskills-hierarchy — the moment-to-moment behaviors that grow the alliance.
  • concept-attending-and-listening — spotting a quiet withdrawal rupture is an observation skill.
  • theory-attachment (Unit 5) — the developmental theory of the bond: a client's attachment pattern (concept-attachment-styles) shapes how readily they can form and trust the alliance, and Bowlby cast the therapist as a secure base. A frayed bond with a dismissing or preoccupied client is often the old internal working model showing up in the room.
  • theory-common-factors — the alliance is the best-measured of the common factors.
  • theory-yalom-factors and unit10-group (Unit 10) — in group work the alliance has a client-client analog: group cohesion, "the group therapy analog of the relationship in individual therapy." Bordin's bond scales up to a web of member-to-member bonds, and — just like a dyadic alliance — cohesion is built, ruptured (especially in the storming/transition stage), and repaired.
  • concept-informed-consent (Unit 3) — consent done well is an early alliance intervention: Bordin's goal and task agreement is basically structured consent, and honest confidentiality limits (concept-confidentiality-limits) build rather than threaten the bond.
  • Forward link: case conceptualization and treatment planning (Unit 7) operationalize goal and task — the plan is co-authored with the client, which is itself an alliance intervention.

S4 Task — agreement on the in-session activities and each person's role — what you'll actually do together to get there, and that the client believes it will help. S4 A useful way to hold it: bond is the relationship, goal is the where , task is the how . A rupture in any of the three weakens the alliance, and they're somewhat independent — you can have warm rapport (bond) while quietly disagreeing about goals or tasks, which stalls therapy. How Bordin thought it works Bordin argued the alliance influences outcome not because the relationship is curative on its own , but because it's the ingredient that lets the client accept, follow, and believe in the treatment. The bond makes the work possible; the work does the changing. This is the bridge between "be warm" and "do effective therapy." S4 The evidence The alliance is one of the most robust predictors of outcome in all of psychotherapy research: r ≈ .28 across 295 studies and 30,000+ patients (Flückiger et al., 2018), holding across treatment types. S2 Bordin's operationalization is what made it measurable — it spawned the Working Alliance Inventory (WAI) and similar instruments. S4 (See theory-common-factors for the full evidence discussion and the correlation-vs-causation caveat.) Alliance ruptures and their repair A rupture is a deterioration in the alliance — and, tellingly, it shows up as a breakdown in exactly Bordin's three parts: a disagreement on goals , a lack of collaboration on tasks , or a strain in the bond. S15 Ruptures are not failures to avoid at all costs; they're routine, and how you handle them is a large part of the work. They come in two markers: S15 Withdrawal ruptures — the client moves away : placating, going quiet, giving minimal answers, intellectualizing, changing the subject. Easy to miss precisely because the surface stays pleasant. Confrontation ruptures — the client moves against : expressing anger or dissatisfaction, complaining about the therapy or the therapist, trying to control the session. The repair is usually immediacy — gently naming what's happening between you ("I get the sense I pushed us somewhere you didn't want to go — can we check that?") and, when it's your misstep, owning it. The striking finding: Eubanks, Muran & Safran's (2018) meta-analysis links successful rupture repair to better outcomes ( r ≈ .29 ), and rupture-resolution training improves outcomes too. S15 Safran & Muran's earlier work raised the deeper possibility that living through a repaired rupture may help a client more than an alliance that never ruptured — because it models that conflict and disappointment in a relationship can be survived and worked through. Unrepaired ruptures, by contrast, are a leading path to dropout. Why it matters in the room Bond/goal/task is a fast diagnostic when a session feels stuck. Ask: is the bond frayed, or do we disagree on the goal , or on the task ? Each points to a different repair. Noticing and repairing alliance ruptures — especially the quiet withdrawal kind — is a core competency you'll develop in supervision, and it maps directly onto these three parts. Connects to concept-core-conditions — UPR/empathy/congruence are how you build the bond. concept-congruence — immediacy is the specific skill for naming and repairing a rupture. concept-microskills-hierarchy — the moment-to-moment behaviors that grow the alliance. concept-attending-and-listening — spotting a quiet withdrawal rupture is an observation skill. theory-attachment (Unit 5) — the developmental theory of the bond: a client's attachment pattern ( concept-attachment-styles ) shapes how readily they can form and trust the alliance, and Bowlby cast the therapist as a secure base . A frayed bond with a dismissing or preoccupied client is often the old internal working model showing up in the room. theory-common-factors — the alliance is the best-measured of the common factors. theory-yalom-factors and unit10-group (Unit 10) — in group work the alliance has a client- client analog: group cohesion , "the group therapy analog of the relationship in individual therapy." Bordin's bond scales up to a web of member-to-member bonds, and — just like a dyadic alliance — cohesion is built, ruptured (especially in the storming/transition stage), and repaired. concept-informed-consent (Unit 3) — consent done well is an early alliance intervention: Bordin's goal and task agreement is basically structured consent, and honest confidentiality limits ( concept-confidentiality-limits ) build rather than threaten the bond. Forward link: case conceptualization and treatment planning (Unit 7) operationalize goal and task — the plan is co-authored with the client, which is itself an alliance intervention. Sources S2 Flückiger et al. (2018). S4 Therapeutic Alliance and Outcome of Psychotherapy , PMC3198542. S15 Eubanks, Muran & Safran (2018), Alliance Rupture Repair: A Meta-Analysis ; Safran & Muran (2000). Full notes in ../research/unit01-helping-skills-sources.md .
