pages.title: Unit 1 — Basic Helping Skills & the Therapeutic Relationship
pages.html:
Unit 1 — Basic Helping Skills & the Therapeutic Relationship

The one-line version: the relationship is not the warm-up to the therapy — across thousands of studies it is one of the most reliable active ingredients, and the moment-to-moment skills below are how you build it. Almost every beginner's worst habit is jumping to solutions. The unlearning starts here.

This is the literal mechanics of what you do in the first minutes of every session, and the foundation everything else sits on. The pages build in order.

The map

Why the relationship is the work

  1. theory-common-factors — why the relationship matters. The evidence (and the near-century of history, from Rosenzweig's 1936 "dodo bird" to Wampold) that what helps clients is shared across therapies — the bond, the rationale, the client's expectation — more than any one technique. The empirical reason to take the rest of the unit seriously.

The attitudes (Rogers' core conditions)

  1. concept-core-conditions — the overview of Carl Rogers' three conditions, the six-condition model, and the necessary-vs-sufficient debate. It fans out to three deep pages:
    • concept-unconditional-positive-regard — non-contingent worth, and the conditions of worth it reverses.
    • concept-empathy — accurate empathy, the "as if," and Carkhuff's five levels.
    • concept-congruence — genuineness, immediacy, and therapist self-disclosure.
  2. person-carl-rogers — the person and the self-theory the conditions come from (actualizing tendency, organismic valuing, incongruence), plus the honest record (Wisconsin, the Gloria films).

The skills (what you actually do)

  1. concept-attending-and-listening — the foundation skill: SOLER, the three Vs, the use of silence, and observation — plus why attending is not culturally universal.
  2. concept-microskills-hierarchy — Ivey's ladder of teachable skills (attending → observing → questioning → reflecting / paraphrasing / summarizing → influencing) and his five-stage interview. Where the reflection-vs-paraphrase-vs-interpretation distinction lives.
  3. concept-therapeutic-alliance — Bordin's bond + task + goal model, and the rupture & repair skill: a concrete, measurable way to think about the relationship in any orientation.

The stance note (read this twice)

Everyday problem-solving trains one reflex hard: locate the broken thing, fix it, move on. Counseling inverts it. Most of the first session's work is helping a person feel understood — which a solution actively interrupts. The core skill of this unit is reflect the feeling, then stop talking. When you notice yourself reaching for the fix, that noticing is the skill. Several items in this unit's practice set are built specifically to drill that reflex, because it won't come naturally from where you're starting — and that's normal, not a deficit.

What's genuinely contested (so you don't over-learn it)

  • Rogers claimed his conditions were necessary and sufficient — that warmth, empathy, and genuineness are all you need. Most clinicians today accept them as necessary but not sufficient. — see concept-core-conditions.
  • The alliance–outcome link (r ≈ .28, 30,000+ patients) is robust but correlational — a good alliance may partly reflect early improvement, not only cause it. — see concept-therapeutic-alliance.
  • "Relationship over technique" overstates a real finding. The modern view is they work together: technique delivered inside a strong relationship, not instead of it.

Sources

See ../research/unit01-helping-skills-sources.md for full citations –.

S12 The skills (what you actually do) concept-attending-and-listening — the foundation skill: SOLER , the three Vs, the use of silence, and observation — plus why attending is not culturally universal. S5 S14 concept-microskills-hierarchy — Ivey's ladder of teachable skills (attending → observing → questioning → reflecting / paraphrasing / summarizing → influencing) and his five-stage interview. Where the reflection-vs-paraphrase-vs-interpretation distinction lives. S5 S7 concept-therapeutic-alliance — Bordin's bond + task + goal model, and the rupture & repair skill: a concrete, measurable way to think about the relationship in any orientation. S4 S15 The stance note (read this twice) Everyday problem-solving trains one reflex hard: locate the broken thing, fix it, move on. Counseling inverts it. Most of the first session's work is helping a person feel understood — which a solution actively interrupts. The core skill of this unit is reflect the feeling, then stop talking. When you notice yourself reaching for the fix, that noticing is the skill. Several items in this unit's practice set are built specifically to drill that reflex, because it won't come naturally from where you're starting — and that's normal, not a deficit. What's genuinely contested (so you don't over-learn it) Rogers claimed his conditions were necessary and sufficient — that warmth, empathy, and genuineness are all you need. Most clinicians today accept them as necessary but not sufficient. S1 — see concept-core-conditions . The alliance–outcome link (r ≈ .28, 30,000+ patients) is robust but correlational — a good alliance may partly reflect early improvement, not only cause it. S2 — see concept-therapeutic-alliance . "Relationship over technique" overstates a real finding. The modern view is they work together : technique delivered inside a strong relationship, not instead of it. S3 Sources See ../research/unit01-helping-skills-sources.md for full citations S1 – S17 .

pages.title: Unit 2 — Counseling Theories: The Major Schools
pages.html:
Unit 2 — Counseling Theories: The Major Schools

The one-line version: your theory is the lens that tells you what to pay attention to and what to do next. Each major school answers two questions differently — why do people get stuck? and how do they get better? You don't have to commit to one yet. You need a map so you don't feel lost mid-session.

This unit surveys six families of theory. Read each page through one filter — the syllabus's practice rep, which is also the spine of the whole unit:

"This theory says people get stuck because ___, and they get better by ___."

If you can fill in that sentence for all six, you've done the core work of Unit 2.

The map (read in this order; they build on each other historically)

  1. theory-psychodynamic — Freud and his descendants. The unconscious, defenses, and transference. Stuck because of buried, unresolved early conflict; better by making the unconscious conscious (insight). The historical root the others react against.
  2. theory-person-centered — Rogers' humanistic approach. The actualizing tendency and the client as expert. Stuck because the drive to grow got blocked by conditions of worth; better by a relationship offering the core conditions. Builds directly on Unit 1.
  3. theory-existential — not a technique set but a stance on the human condition. Stuck because of how we avoid the givens of existence (death, freedom, isolation, meaning); better by facing them and choosing responsibly.
  4. theory-cbt — Beck and Ellis. Thoughts → feelings → behavior. Stuck because of distorted thinking and learned behavior; better by testing and changing both. The most-researched, most-requested family.
  5. theory-family-systems — Bowen and Minuchin. The problem lives in the relationships, not the person. Stuck because of dysfunctional patterns in the system; better by changing the patterns.
  6. theory-postmodern — solution-focused and narrative. There is no single objective truth; reality is constructed in language. Stuck inside a problem-saturated story; better by re-authoring it. The therapist gives up the expert chair.

The comparison that does the work

The point of the unit is not six isolated summaries — it's being able to tell them apart. This table is the interleaving target (cluster: theory-families):

FamilyStuck because…Better by…Time focusTherapist stance
Psychodynamicunconscious unresolved early conflict; defenses insight — making the unconscious conscious; working through transference pastinterpretive, expert
Person-centeredthe actualizing tendency was blocked by conditions of worth; incongruence a genuine relationship (empathy, UPR, congruence) that frees growth present/futurenon-directive, follows the client
Existentialavoiding the givens of existence; an existential vacuum facing the givens; choosing meaning and taking responsibility present, whole-lifea fellow traveler; philosophical
CBTdistorted thoughts + maladaptive learned behavior identifying/testing thoughts; changing behavior (restructuring, exposure, activation) presentdirective, teaching, collaborative
Family systemsdysfunctional patterns in the relationship system (not the individual) changing the patterns/structure; differentiating self present patterns + multigenerationalactive, sometimes director of enactments
Postmodernbeing trapped in a problem-saturated dominant story; no fixed truth re-authoring the story; building on exceptions and strengths present/futurenon-expert, collaborative, curious

A useful coarse grouping: the first three (psychodynamic, person-centered, existential) are insight/relationship-oriented and grew out of European depth psychology and philosophy; CBT is action/learning-oriented and empirical; family systems moves the unit of analysis from the person to the system; postmodern challenges the idea that the counselor knows the truth at all.

The stance note

Two common traps here:

  • Picking a theory for its elegance, then defending it. Theory is a tool for attention, not an identity. Hold it loosely.
  • Gravitating straight to CBT because it's the most structured. CBT is the most protocol-like and can feel like the most comfortable place to start — which is exactly why you should make yourself understand the relational and meaning-based schools, where the "fix-it" reflex (see unit01-helping-skills) actively backfires. Person-centered and existential therapy work because the counselor resists solving.

Where most counselors actually land: integrative

Very few experienced clinicians use a single pure school. Across large surveys, integrative/eclectic is consistently among the most common self-identified orientations (estimates vary widely by sample — on the order of one in four or more). The mature move is to learn each lens well enough to choose deliberately, then combine them in a principled way — not to grab techniques at random. You are not expected to commit yet; you're expected to be able to think in each one.

What's genuinely contested (so you don't over-learn it)

  • Psychodynamic constructs are hard to falsify. The unconscious and transference are clinically useful but resist clean measurement; the evidence base is solid for depression/anxiety, weaker for OCD/PTSD/psychosis. — see theory-psychodynamic.
  • "Client as expert" can be overstated. Person-centered conditions are widely held to be necessary but not sufficient for many clients (Unit 1). — see theory-person-centered.
  • Differentiation of self (Bowen) is central but its measurement and cross-cultural validity are debated. — see theory-family-systems.
  • "No single truth" (postmodern) is philosophically contested and can sit awkwardly next to evidence-based practice; in practice most clinicians treat it as a stance toward the client's meaning, not a denial of clinical reality.

Connects forward

  • Theory → case conceptualization (Unit 7): the lens you pick here becomes the structure you use to turn intake data into a plan. This is the payoff of Unit 2.
  • CBT here → CBT/MI as practical method (Unit 9): this is the theory; Unit 9 is the toolkit (theory-cbt-practice, theory-motivational-interviewing).
  • Person-centered here → core conditions (Unit 1): same engine, named as a theory.

Sources

See ../research/unit02-theories-sources.md for full citations –.

pages.title: Unit 3 — Ethics, Law & Professional Identity
pages.html:
Unit 3 — Ethics, Law & Professional Identity

This is the one unit where a mistake can end a career or badly harm a client. The syllabus puts it fourth week for a reason: you will face a confidentiality-limit decision early in practicum, and the contours need to be in your head before you're in the chair. The unit has three jobs:

  1. Know the ACA Code — its structure, its principles, and the standards that come up most.
  2. Know confidentiality and its limits cold — including the duty to warn/protect and mandated reporting.
  3. Know who you are professionally — scope of practice, and how counseling differs from psychology, social work, and psychiatry.

CACREP area: Professional Counseling Orientation & Ethical Practice.

The ACA Code of Ethics: structure

The 2014 ACA Code of Ethics (the current edition) contains nine sections, each opening with an aspirational introduction followed by enforceable standards:

§TitleOne-line gist
AThe Counseling Relationshipwelfare, consent, boundaries, termination
BConfidentiality and Privacythe promise and its exceptions
CProfessional Responsibilitycompetence, advertising, public responsibility
DRelationships With Other Professionalscolleagues, teams, consultation
EEvaluation, Assessment, and Interpretationtesting and diagnosis done properly
FSupervision, Training, and Teachingduties of supervisors & educators
GResearch and Publicationresearch ethics with clients/participants
HDistance Counseling, Technology, and Social Medianew in 2014 — telehealth & the digital boundary
IResolving Ethical Issues/what to do about violations, ethics vs. law

Memory scaffold: A and B are where clinical life happens (the relationship and the secret); C–E are your professional conduct; F–G teaching and research; H technology; I meta-rules.

The foundation: five values, six principles

The Code grounds its standards in five professional values (lifespan human development; diversity/multiculturalism; social justice; integrity of the counselor–client relationship; competent, ethical practice) and six ethical principles:

  • Autonomy — fostering the client's right to control the direction of their own life.
  • Nonmaleficence — avoiding actions that cause harm ("first, do no harm").
  • Beneficence — working for the good of the individual and society.
  • Justice — treating individuals equitably; fostering fairness.
  • Fidelity — honoring commitments; keeping the trust the relationship depends on.
  • Veracity — dealing truthfully.

These six are the vocabulary of every ethics discussion you'll have in a program. Real dilemmas are almost always principle vs. principle: breaking confidentiality to stop a suicide is nonmaleficence/beneficence overriding autonomy and fidelity. Notice the trap here: the principles are not a decision procedure you can execute. The Code itself says "no specific ethical decision-making model is always most effective" — you're expected to use a credible, defensible process (identify the problem → consult the Code and the law → consult colleagues → weigh principles → document your reasoning), not to find the one right algorithm.

Legal duty vs. ethical duty (keep these apart)

Two different systems regulate you, and they can disagree:

Ethical dutyLegal duty
Sourceprofessional code (ACA), enforced by association & licensing boardstatute, regulation, case law — enforced by courts & the state
Breach meansethics complaint, sanction, loss of licensecriminal/civil liability, damages
Exampledon't abandon a client (A.12)report suspected child abuse (state statute)

The Code is explicit that breaching it "does not necessarily constitute legal liability" — and the reverse also holds: something can be legal and still unethical (dating a client the day after termination is legal in many states; the Code prohibits it for five years). When ethics and law conflict, Standard I.1.c says: make your commitment to the Code known, try to resolve the conflict, and if it can't be resolved, you may follow the law — acting in the client's best interest. The classic live example is a court order to disclose records: ethically you seek consent or seek to narrow the disclosure (B.2.d), legally you may ultimately have to comply.

A related three-way distinction — privacy vs. confidentiality vs. privilege — is unpacked in concept-confidentiality-limits; privilege is the legal shield (study-tarasoff's cousin case, Jaffee v. Redmond, created the federal version).

The clinical core: consent, confidentiality, and their limits

The working sequence to internalize:

  1. concept-informed-consent — the client's decision to enter counseling must be informed, documented, and ongoing (A.2). The confidentiality limits are disclosed here, up front.
  2. concept-confidentiality-limits — the promise (B.1) and its exceptions (B.2): serious and foreseeable harm, legal requirements, contagious life-threatening disease, court order — with minimal disclosure always the rule.
  3. concept-duty-to-warn — when the exception involves danger to an identifiable other: Tarasoff's duty to warn (1974) → duty to protect (1976), and the state-by-state variation. The case itself: study-tarasoff.
  4. concept-mandated-reporting — the statutory, non-discretionary exception: suspected abuse or neglect of children (all 50 states) and, in most states, vulnerable adults.

This chain is the confidentiality-exceptions cluster — the unit's main interleaving target, because the exceptions are confusable in exactly the way that matters: who triggers them, what discretion you have, and who you tell. Unit 8 (crisis work) will build directly on it.

Boundaries and the professional self

  • concept-dual-relationships — the 2014 Code's two-track approach: a short list of prohibited relationships (sexual/romantic with current clients — absolute; former clients — 5 years; friends/family where objectivity fails) and a longer list of managed boundary questions (attending a client's wedding, the small-town overlap), with documentation required. Includes the crossing-vs-violation distinction.
  • concept-scope-of-practice — practice only within your competence (C.2), grow it properly (education → training → supervised experience), monitor your effectiveness, and stop when impaired.
  • concept-helping-professions-compared — counselor vs. psychologist vs. clinical social worker vs. psychiatrist: training, license, stance, and who prescribes.

The practice rep (from the syllabus)

Write, in plain language, the confidentiality speech you'd give a new client in the first five minutes — including the exceptions. A worked model lives in concept-confidentiality-limits; write yours before reading it, then compare. You will say a version of this for real.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • The law is 50 different laws. Duty to warn/protect, reporting triggers, and privilege all vary by state — mandatory in some, permissive in others, silent in a few. Learn the pattern, then learn your state's statute when you know where you'll practice.
  • Tarasoff assumes prediction that the science doesn't support. Validated tools for predicting dangerousness are lacking; clinical judgment plus consultation and documentation is the actual standard.
  • How much to warn clients up front is debated — exhaustive warnings chill disclosure and aren't retained; the consensus is a clear plain-language summary at intake, revisited when live (consent as process).

Connects to

  • unit01-helping-skills — informed consent and honest limits are alliance builders (concept-therapeutic-alliance): clients trust a counselor who is straight about the rules.
  • Unit 8 (crisis/risk) — the operational side of danger-to-self/others; confidentiality-exceptions is the legal scaffolding under suicide risk assessment. See also aux-psychological-first-aid for the adjacent acute-support skill set.
  • unit04-multicultural — C.2.a makes multicultural competency an ethical requirement, not an elective nicety.

Sources

APA Services, Mandatory reporting. Child Welfare Information Gateway. APA, professions compared. APA Services, prescribing psychologists. UMN open textbook, ch. 1.4. Counseling@Northwestern. Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy. Full notes in ../research/unit03-ethics-law-sources.md.

pages.title: Unit 4 — Multicultural & Social-Justice Competence
pages.html:
Unit 4 — Multicultural & Social-Justice Competence

Empathy without cultural awareness quietly imposes your norms on people. That's the syllabus's one-line case for this unit, and it's worth sitting with: the failure mode isn't hostility, it's a well-meaning counselor reflecting feelings accurately while assuming that talking to a stranger about feelings is a normal thing to do, that eye contact means engagement, that individuating from your family is health, and that the client's hesitancy is "resistance" rather than a reasonable response to a system that has treated their community badly. None of that requires malice — just an unexamined counselor. This unit is the examination.

It is also not optional garnish: the ACA Code makes multicultural competency part of the boundaries of competence themselves (C.2.a — see concept-scope-of-practice), and CACREP gives it its own core area (Social & Cultural Diversity).

The unit has three jobs:

  1. Understand "culture" broadly — race and ethnicity, yes, and also religion, class, ability, gender, sexuality, age, region, language. And the pivot the whole field turns on: the counselor has a culture too. Yours is not the neutral default the others deviate from.
  2. Learn the profession's frameworks — the theory-tripartite-model (1992) and its successor the concept-msjcc (2015), plus the stance that animates both: concept-cultural-humility.
  3. Get concrete — what privilege and power do inside the dyad (concept-privilege-power), what concept-microaggressions look like in session and how to repair them, and how concept-acculturation and help-seeking norms shape who shows up and who stays.

Why this is clinical, not ceremonial

The outcome data first:

  • Among U.S. adults with mental disorders, racial/ethnic minority clients are roughly half as likely as White clients to get treatment, and those who start are more likely to drop out before completing it. Stigma runs higher in several minority communities; barriers include language, cost, provider mistrust, and culturally different understandings of distress.
  • Client-perceived counselor multicultural competence correlates strongly with the therapeutic process (r ≈ .58–.72 with alliance and satisfaction) and moderately with outcomes (r ≈ .29, Tao et al. meta-analysis).
  • Client-perceived counselor cultural humility predicts better outcomes, mediated by the alliance — the mechanism runs straight through Unit 1's concept-therapeutic-alliance.

So the relationship — the thing Unit 1 established as the active ingredient — is exactly what cultural incompetence damages and cultural responsiveness protects. Same engine, harder conditions.

And a humbling measurement result to carry through the unit: the counselor's self-rating is the wrong gauge. Self-reported multicultural competence correlates with social desirability, and once you control for that, it stops predicting actual case-conceptualization ability at all. What predicts outcomes is the client's perception. You do not get to grade your own cultural competence — which is, in itself, the best argument for humility.

FrameworkYearCore structureWhat it added
theory-tripartite-model (Sue, Arredondo & McDavis)1992awareness / knowledge / skillsmade multicultural competence definable and trainable
concept-cultural-humility (Tervalon & Murray-García)1998lifelong self-critique · redress power imbalance · institutional accountabilitythe corrective: competence is not a masterable endpoint
concept-msjcc (Ratts et al.)20154 domains · privileged/marginalized quadrants · AKSA (adds action) · advocacy at 6 socioecological levelsintersectionality, bidirectional privilege, social justice

Read them in that order — each is a response to the previous one. The mc-frameworks cluster exists because programs love asking you to tell them apart.

The concrete layer

  • concept-privilege-power — McIntosh's "invisible knapsack" of unearned assets, why privilege is invisible to its holder, the power asymmetry built into the counseling dyad itself, and broaching (Day-Vines): the skill of raising culture before it becomes the elephant.
  • concept-microaggressions — Sue's taxonomy (microassault / microinsult / microinvalidation), what they do inside a session, how to repair one you committed — and the Lilienfeld critique, because this literature is genuinely contested and you should know both sides.
  • concept-acculturation — Berry's two questions and four strategies (integration / assimilation / separation / marginalization), acculturative stress, worldview, and help-seeking norms — including the client for whom counseling itself is culturally foreign.

The practice rep (from the syllabus)

Write your cultural autobiography: how your background shaped your views on family, emotion, success, authority, and asking for help. The point is to see your own water — this is the tripartite model's awareness dimension and the MSJCC's counselor self-awareness domain done as an exercise, and it is the single assignment nearly every CACREP program will hand you in some form. Notice, while writing it, which sections feel like "just how things are" rather than like a culture. Those are the load-bearing blind spots.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Competence vs. humility is a real framing debate, mostly resolved as complements — competencies name the learnable content, humility names the stance — but know the critique: "competence" implies an endpoint that doesn't exist.
  • The evidence is moderate, not miraculous — r ≈ .29 with outcomes, an evidence base heavy on analogue studies, and self-report measures of dubious validity. Both the importance of the construct and the softness of its measurement are true at once.
  • Microaggression science is disputed in print — taxonomy standard in curricula, critique published in a top journal, Sue conceding several points. Details in concept-microaggressions.
  • How far advocacy extends — the MSJCC's sixth-level ambitions (public policy, global) raise live questions about the counselor's role boundaries.

Connects to

  • unit01-helping-skills — the alliance is the mechanism through which cultural humility works (concept-therapeutic-alliance); empathy (concept-empathy) is necessary but not culturally self-executing.
  • unit03-ethics-law — C.2.a makes this unit an ethical requirement, not an elective (concept-scope-of-practice); informed consent must be culturally and developmentally appropriate (A.2.c, concept-informed-consent).
  • unit02-theories — every theory family carries cultural assumptions (individuation, self-actualization, direct emotional disclosure); the postmodern family (theory-postmodern) is the most explicitly culture-aware.
  • unit07-assessment — culture-fair assessment (norms, standardization, and the limits of a validity coefficient outside its population) and the culture-bound limits of diagnosis pick this thread up clinically.

(2015) meta-analysis. Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy review. Lilienfeld (2017). Wikipedia (orientation). NIMHD + PMC disparities data. ACA Code C.2.a. pages.title: Unit 5 — Human Development Across the Lifespan
pages.html:
Unit 5 — Human Development Across the Lifespan

The syllabus gives this unit its one-line justification: you can't tell what's wrong if you don't know what's normal for the age. A 3-year-old who doesn't grasp that others see the world differently is on schedule; a 30-year-old who can't is not. A toddler with separation anxiety is developing well; the same protest in a specific context tells you something else. Development is the baseline against which "clinical concern" is even a meaningful phrase — so this unit builds the baseline, and then teaches the one framework that will show up in your consulting room more than any other: attachment.

This is a Tier 2 clinical-foundations unit. It maps to CACREP's Human Growth & Development core area, and it hands forward directly to unit06-psychopathology (you diagnose against a developmental norm) and back to unit01-helping-skills (attachment is the theory of how your client will relate to you).

The four frameworks, and why attachment leads

FrameworkWhoWhat it explainsThe one-line version
theory-attachmentBowlby & Ainsworthhow early caregiving builds a template for all later closenessthe single most clinically useful developmental idea
theory-eriksons-stagesErik Eriksonthe psychosocial task the person is wrestling with at each life phase"which crisis is this client stuck in?"
theory-piagetJean Piagethow thinking itself is reorganized from infancy to adolescence"what kind of reasoning can this person actually do?"
concept-biopsychosocial-modelGeorge Engelthe frame that keeps all three (plus biology and context) in one picture"the person suffers as a whole, not as isolated organs"

The syllabus and course-map both flag attachment as the single most clinically useful developmental idea, and this unit takes that seriously: attachment gets a full theory page (theory-attachment), a dedicated four-styles page built for discrimination (concept-attachment-styles), and the people who built it (person-bowlby-ainsworth). The reason is unit01-helping-skills: attachment patterns show up constantly in how clients relate to you and to others. The client who needs constant reassurance and merges with you, the client who stays cool and keeps the alliance at arm's length, the client whose closeness and fear fire at once — those are attachment patterns walking into the room, and Bowlby explicitly called the therapist an attachment figure.

The thread that runs through everything: risk, not destiny

The hardest thing to hold correctly in this unit — and the place the "fix-it" reflex does the most damage — is that developmental frameworks describe probabilities, not verdicts. Insecure attachment is a risk factor for later problems only if development continues in the context of other risks; many insecurely attached children turn out fine, and later relationships (including therapy) can revise the template. Erikson's "crises" are not pass/fail exams — you can carry an unresolved one forward and still rework it later. A client is never their attachment "type," their stuck Erikson stage, or their Piaget ceiling. Two technical names for why:

  • Equifinality — many different developmental paths can lead to the same outcome (depression has many roads in).
  • Multifinality — the same starting point (say, an insecure infancy) can lead to many different outcomes.

Both are just formal ways of saying: a developmental history is a hypothesis about a client, not a diagnosis of one. Use it to understand, not to file them.

Distinguishing typical development from clinical concern

This is a stated objective, and it has a concrete clinical shape. Clinicians who work with children practice developmental surveillance — a longitudinal habit of eliciting concerns, taking a milestone history, observing, and applying judgment — using age-dependent milestone norms to calibrate how concerned to be when something is missing. The same logic scales to any age: know the normal range first, treat deviations as questions rather than answers, and remember that most variation is normal variation. Over-pathologizing ordinary developmental turbulence (adolescent identity churn, a toddler's defiance, an older adult's life review) is the mirror-image error to missing a real delay — and both are failures of knowing the baseline.

The practice rep (from the syllabus)

Sketch your own attachment history and your Erikson stages. Where do you land on the four attachment styles (concept-attachment-styles) — and can you see it in how you do closeness now? Which Erikson crisis are you actually working on (theory-eriksons-stages)? Self-application is what makes these frameworks stick, and it previews the countertransference work of the whole program: your own attachment pattern will shape how you sit with a clinging client or a distant one.

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • "Sensitive parenting → secure baby" is not a clean law. The sensitivity–security correlation is only modest (r ≈ .24), and the "transmission gap" means a parent's own state of mind predicts the baby's attachment beyond what observed sensitivity explains. Temperament is a live rival account.
  • The Strange Situation may be an "imposed ethic." Secure is the most common style in every culture studied, but the procedure was built on US norms and its behaviors can mean different things elsewhere.
  • Erikson and Piaget are heuristics, not measured facts. The stage ages are approximate and culture-bound; Piaget under-credited infants, over-credited adolescents, and skipped culture (Vygotsky's critique).
  • The biopsychosocial model is both indispensable and vague. It's the field's default case-formulation frame and is criticized as a "slogan" that licenses everything and specifies nothing. Hold it as a checklist you must make specific to this client.

Connects to

  • unit01-helping-skills — attachment is the theory of how the client relates to you; the concept-therapeutic-alliance is, in part, an attachment relationship, and a secure-base therapist is doing concept-core-conditions with a developmental rationale.
  • unit02-theories — theory-psychodynamic shares attachment's roots (early relationships shape the adult); theory-family-systems and the biopsychosocial model share a systems logic.
  • unit06-psychopathology — diagnosis is read against a developmental norm; attachment disruption is a transdiagnostic risk factor.
  • The elective concept-grief-models (PFA module) picks up the lifespan's end — aging, loss, and grief — clinically; this unit's Erikson stage 8 (integrity vs. despair) is its developmental frame.

Sources

StatPearls — Erikson. StatPearls — Cognitive Development (Piaget). Jones et al. (2015), Development and Psychopathology attachment review. Bolton & Gillett (2019), biopsychosocial model. van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg (1988). Main & Solomon (1990) + disorganized-risk meta-analyses. Simply Psychology — Ainsworth. AAP developmental surveillance. Full notes in ../research/unit05-development-sources.md.

pages.title: Unit 6 — Psychopathology & the DSM-5-TR
pages.html:
Unit 6 — Psychopathology & the DSM-5-TR

This unit teaches the language of diagnosis — the major categories of mental disorder and the manual that organizes them — while holding onto the syllabus's framing sentence: diagnosis is a shorthand, not a verdict. You will be expected to formulate diagnostic impressions in practicum, and knowing the criteria cold is also the best protection against the opposite error: calling ordinary distress a disorder. Roughly a quarter of U.S. adults meet criteria for some DSM disorder in a given year (26.2% twelve-month prevalence), and nearly half will at some point in their lives — numbers that read either as "mental illness is common" or as "the categories are drawn too wide," and that tension is itself part of the curriculum.

This is a Tier 2 clinical-foundations unit. It feeds CACREP's Assessment & Diagnosis territory, sits on the developmental baseline from unit05-development (you can't call something abnormal without knowing what's normal for the age), and hands forward to Unit 7 (turning diagnosis into assessment and case conceptualization) and Unit 8 (risk). The cultural competence of unit04-multicultural is load-bearing here: misdiagnosis is what cultural incompetence looks like when it holds a pen.

The map of the unit

Two kinds of pages. First, the manual itself and its limits:

  • concept-dsm-structure — how the DSM-5-TR is organized, what changed and why, culture in diagnosis, and how diagnosis meets insurance in the real world.
  • concept-categorical-vs-dimensional — the live scientific fight over whether disorders are categories at all: comorbidity, HiTOP, the p factor, RDoC, and diagnostic inflation.

Second, the major categories a counselor must recognize — each page built around what distinguishes this from its neighbors, because differential discrimination is the actual clinical skill:

PageCategoryThe discrimination that matters most
concept-mood-disordersdepressive & bipolar disordersdepression vs. grief; unipolar vs. bipolar
concept-anxiety-disordersGAD, panic, phobias, social anxietywhat the fear is about; expected vs. unexpected panic
concept-trauma-stressor-disordersPTSD, acute stress, adjustment, prolonged griefwhich stressor + which clock
concept-ocdOCD & relatedobsession/compulsion vs. worry; OCD vs. OCPD
concept-psychotic-disordersschizophrenia spectrumduration lines; psychosis vs. mood-with-psychosis
concept-personality-disordersthe ten PDs in three clusterstrait pattern vs. episode; cluster A/B/C
concept-substance-use-disordersSUDs (bridge to the addiction elective)use vs. disorder; dependence vs. addiction
concept-neurodevelopmental-disordersADHD, autism spectrumdevelopmental onset vs. adult-onset lookalikes
concept-eating-disordersanorexia, bulimia, binge-eatingthe weight criterion; compensation or not

What is a "disorder" in the first place?

The DSM's working answer has three recurring ingredients, and they show up in almost every criteria set in this unit: a clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion, or behavior; that reflects a dysfunction rather than an expectable response to a stressor or a culturally sanctioned pattern; and that causes distress or impairment in functioning. The "distress or impairment" clause is the one beginners under-weight: symptoms alone are not a diagnosis. Plenty of people hear a voice occasionally, check the stove twice, or feel wrecked for weeks after a loss — the criteria are written (imperfectly) to keep those people out of the manual. The clause is also your daily protection against over-pathologizing: when impairment is absent, the diagnosis usually is too.

And a person is never the diagnosis. The style rule — "a client with schizophrenia," never "a schizophrenic" — is not politeness theater; labels that fuse person and disorder measurably feed stigma and biased assumptions, which is why person-first language is the professional standard. The map is not the territory: a diagnosis compresses a person into a billing-ready noun so clinicians can communicate, research can aggregate, and treatment can be planned. Compression loses information. Unit 7's case conceptualization is where the information comes back.

Comorbidity: the norm, not the exception

Memorize one set of numbers: of people meeting criteria for any disorder in a year, 55% have one diagnosis, 22% have two, and 23% have three or more — and severity concentrates dramatically in the highly comorbid few. Anxiety plus depression is the everyday example; substance use disorders co-travel with nearly everything. Clinically this means: never stop looking after the first criteria set fits. Scientifically it means something more uncomfortable — categories that co-occur this much may not be distinct things (see concept-categorical-vs-dimensional).

Culture, insurance, and the other real-world facts

Diagnosis happens inside institutions. Three facts to carry:

  • Culture first. "Behavior that is aberrant in one culture can be standard in another" ; the DSM's own Cultural Formulation Interview exists because criteria applied without context misdiagnose. Details on concept-dsm-structure; foundation in unit04-multicultural.
  • Insurance runs on diagnosis. In U.S. practice, reimbursement generally requires a covered diagnosis code, which quietly pressures clinicians toward diagnosing — one of the counseling profession's standing complaints about the medical model it must operate inside.
  • Diagnosis is shared turf. Counselors diagnose in most settings (check your state's scope rules — concept-scope-of-practice); psychiatrists prescribe (concept-helping-professions-compared). You'll coordinate across that line constantly.

The practice rep (from the syllabus)

Pick the big three — major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, PTSD — and learn their criteria well enough to explain each to a layperson in two minutes: what it is, what it isn't, and what would make a clinician think of it. The two-minute constraint is the point; it forces criteria out of list form and into understanding. (Each has a production item in the item bank.)

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • Whether the categories are real. Poor field-trial reliability for many diagnoses, massive comorbidity, and within-diagnosis heterogeneity power serious dimensional alternatives (HiTOP, p factor, RDoC) — none of which is ready to run a clinic.
  • Where normal ends. Frances's "diagnostic inflation" case (ADHD tripled, childhood bipolar up forty-fold) vs. the access argument that lowered thresholds catch treatable suffering earlier.
  • Grief. The bereavement exclusion is gone (DSM-5) and prolonged grief disorder is in (DSM-5-TR) — evidence-based moves that still might medicalize mourning. The PFA elective's concept-grief-models carries the same tension from the support side.
  • The criteria you'll memorize here are paraphrases. This unit's numbers come from peer-reviewed secondary references, not the (paywalled) manual itself; before you lean on a criterion with a real client, read it in the DSM-5-TR. [Sources file, note 4]

  • aux-addiction — the elective module is this unit's substance-use chapter at full depth.

pages.text: Unit 6 — Psychopathology & the DSM-5-TR This unit teaches the language of diagnosis — the major categories of mental disorder and the manual that organizes them — while holding onto the syllabus's framing sentence: diagnosis is a shorthand, not a verdict. You will be expected to formulate diagnostic impressions in practicum, and knowing the criteria cold is also the best protection against the opposite error: calling ordinary distress a disorder. Roughly a quarter of U.S. adults meet criteria for some DSM disorder in a given year (26.2% twelve-month prevalence), and nearly half will at some point in their lives S17 S1 — numbers that read either as "mental illness is common" or as "the categories are drawn too wide," and that tension is itself part of the curriculum. This is a Tier 2 clinical-foundations unit. It feeds CACREP's Assessment & Diagnosis territory, sits on the developmental baseline from unit05-development (you can't call something abnormal without knowing what's normal for the age), and hands forward to Unit 7 (turning diagnosis into assessment and case conceptualization ) and Unit 8 (risk). The cultural competence of unit04-multicultural is load-bearing here: misdiagnosis is what cultural incompetence looks like when it holds a pen. The map of the unit Two kinds of pages. First, the manual itself and its limits: concept-dsm-structure — how the DSM-5-TR is organized, what changed and why, culture in diagnosis, and how diagnosis meets insurance in the real world. concept-categorical-vs-dimensional — the live scientific fight over whether disorders are categories at all: comorbidity, HiTOP, the p factor, RDoC, and diagnostic inflation. Second, the major categories a counselor must recognize — each page built around what distinguishes this from its neighbors , because differential discrimination is the actual clinical skill: Page Category The discrimination that matters most concept-mood-disorders depressive & bipolar disorders depression vs. grief; unipolar vs. bipolar concept-anxiety-disorders GAD, panic, phobias, social anxiety what the fear is about; expected vs. unexpected panic concept-trauma-stressor-disorders PTSD, acute stress, adjustment, prolonged grief which stressor + which clock concept-ocd OCD & related obsession/compulsion vs. worry; OCD vs. OCPD concept-psychotic-disorders schizophrenia spectrum duration lines; psychosis vs. mood-with-psychosis concept-personality-disorders the ten PDs in three clusters trait pattern vs. episode; cluster A/B/C concept-substance-use-disorders SUDs (bridge to the addiction elective) use vs. disorder; dependence vs. addiction concept-neurodevelopmental-disorders ADHD, autism spectrum developmental onset vs. adult-onset lookalikes concept-eating-disorders anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating the weight criterion; compensation or not What is a "disorder" in the first place? The DSM's working answer has three recurring ingredients, and they show up in almost every criteria set in this unit: a clinically significant disturbance in cognition, emotion, or behavior; that reflects a dysfunction rather than an expectable response to a stressor or a culturally sanctioned pattern; and that causes distress or impairment in functioning. S1 S23 The "distress or impairment" clause is the one beginners under-weight: symptoms alone are not a diagnosis. Plenty of people hear a voice occasionally, check the stove twice, or feel wrecked for weeks after a loss — the criteria are written (imperfectly) to keep those people out of the manual. The clause is also your daily protection against over-pathologizing: when impairment is absent, the diagnosis usually is too. And a person is never the diagnosis. The style rule — "a client with schizophrenia," never "a schizophrenic" — is not politeness theater; labels that fuse person and disorder measurably feed stigma and biased assumptions, which is why person-first language is the professional standard. S1 The map is not the territory: a diagnosis compresses a person into a billing-ready noun so clinicians can communicate, research can aggregate, and treatment can be planned. Compression loses information. Unit 7's case conceptualization is where the information comes back. Comorbidity: the norm, not the exception Memorize one set of numbers: of people meeting criteria for any disorder in a year, 55% have one diagnosis, 22% have two, and 23% have three or more — and severity concentrates dramatically in the highly comorbid few. S17 Anxiety plus depression is the everyday example; substance use disorders co-travel with nearly everything. Clinically this means: never stop looking after the first criteria set fits. Scientifically it means something more uncomfortable — categories that co-occur this much may not be distinct things (see concept-categorical-vs-dimensional ). Culture, insurance, and the other real-world facts Diagnosis happens inside institutions. Three facts to carry: Culture first. "Behavior that is aberrant in one culture can be standard in another" S23 ; the DSM's own Cultural Formulation Interview exists because criteria applied without context misdiagnose. Details on concept-dsm-structure ; foundation in unit04-multicultural . Insurance runs on diagnosis. In U.S. practice, reimbursement generally requires a covered diagnosis code, which quietly pressures clinicians toward diagnosing — one of the counseling profession's standing complaints about the medical model it must operate inside. S3 Diagnosis is shared turf. Counselors diagnose in most settings (check your state's scope rules — concept-scope-of-practice ); psychiatrists prescribe ( concept-helping-professions-compared ). You'll coordinate across that line constantly. The practice rep (from the syllabus) Pick the big three — major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, PTSD — and learn their criteria well enough to explain each to a layperson in two minutes : what it is, what it isn't, and what would make a clinician think of it. The two-minute constraint is the point; it forces criteria out of list form and into understanding. (Each has a production item in the item bank.) What's contested (don't over-learn it) Whether the categories are real. Poor field-trial reliability for many diagnoses, massive comorbidity, and within-diagnosis heterogeneity power serious dimensional alternatives (HiTOP, p factor, RDoC) — none of which is ready to run a clinic. S18 S19 S20 Where normal ends. Frances's "diagnostic inflation" case (ADHD tripled, childhood bipolar up forty-fold) vs. the access argument that lowered thresholds catch treatable suffering earlier. S21 Grief. The bereavement exclusion is gone (DSM-5) and prolonged grief disorder is in (DSM-5-TR) — evidence-based moves that still might medicalize mourning. S22 S2 The PFA elective's concept-grief-models carries the same tension from the support side. The criteria you'll memorize here are paraphrases. pages.title: Unit 7 — Assessment, Diagnosis & Case Conceptualization
pages.html:
Unit 7 — Assessment, Diagnosis & Case Conceptualization

Unit 6 gave you the diagnostic categories. This unit is the machinery that turns a real person in a chair into one of them — and then past it. The syllabus's framing sentence is the one to hold: case conceptualization is "the skill that separates having a nice chat from doing therapy." The intake is your first full session with nearly every client ; everything downstream — the plan, the referral, the risk decision, the note the insurer reads — is built from what you gather and how you organize it.

This is a Tier 2 clinical-foundations unit feeding CACREP's Assessment & Testing area. It sits on three earlier units and hands to a fourth:

  • ← Unit 2 (theory as lens). Case conceptualization is theory doing work: your orientation decides what counts as the cause and what counts as the fix (unit02-theories).
  • ← Unit 6 (diagnosis). The DSM label is an input to the formulation, not the endpoint of thinking (concept-dsm-structure).
  • ← Unit 5 (the normal baseline) and Unit 4 (culture). You can't read a mental status exam or a screening score without knowing what's developmentally normal (unit05-development) and without the humility not to misread a cultural difference as pathology (unit04-multicultural).
  • → Unit 8 (risk). The risk screen embedded in every intake is where this unit and crisis work overlap — built out there in full.

The map of the unit

The unit moves in the order a case actually moves: gather → describe → measure → judge the tools → explain → plan.

PageThe job it doesThe one idea
concept-intake-interviewthe first session — gathering the raw materialpresenting problem + biopsychosocial history + current functioning, on a relational frame
concept-mental-status-examdescribing current state in a shared vocabularya snapshot, not a diagnosis; describe what you see, don't interpret
concept-screening-toolsmeasuring severity and tracking changePHQ-9 / GAD-7 flag a domain, they don't diagnose; measure at every visit
concept-reliability-validityknowing when to trust a numberreliable ≠ valid; a screen is tuned to not miss, so it over-flags
concept-case-conceptualizationexplaining how it got this waythe Five Ps; diagnosis says what, formulation says why + what maintains it
concept-treatment-planningturning the story into a shared planmeasurable goals, the golden thread — measure to serve the work

Assessment is not a phase — it's the whole relationship, thinly

The beginner's picture is a pipeline: assess first, then treat. The reality is that assessment and intervention run together. The intake interview is already an intervention — being carefully listened to is the first dose of the common factors from unit01-helping-skills — and every later session re-assesses (Is the plan working? Has risk changed?). Sommers-Flanagan's frame is that the clinical interview is the foundational assessment tool and that rapport and information-gathering are not a trade-off: the relationship is part of the data, and a client who feels judged will hand you a worse history . This is the same stance caution that runs through the whole curriculum — the reflex to collect all the data efficiently serves the helper; the client is served by being met.

Four things a counselor assesses (and where each lives)

Sommers-Flanagan names four assessment-interview types ; this unit covers three, and the fourth is Unit 8:

  1. Intake interview — the most common; gathers the initial picture. → concept-intake-interview
  2. Mental status examination — a semi-structured description of current state. → concept-mental-status-exam
  3. Psychodiagnostic interview — pins a DSM impression to guide treatment. → Unit 6 supplies the categories; concept-case-conceptualization is where the impression becomes a plan.
  4. Suicide / risk assessment — the highest-stakes interview. → Unit 8 (previewed by item 9 of the PHQ-9 and the intake risk screen).

The through-line: measure, but don't be captured by the measure

This unit hands the technically-minded student a genuine strength — structured instruments, scoring rules, reliability coefficients — and a matching trap. Measurement-based care works: routinely giving a PHQ-9 or GAD-7 at each visit catches non-response and deterioration earlier than clinical impression alone, and the effect is strongest for the patients who would otherwise quietly not improve . And a screen is calibrated to over-flag on purpose (high sensitivity), a validity coefficient is meaningless outside the norming population , and a treatment plan built only from what a scale can score can shrink a person to a number and import the billing incentives flagged in concept-dsm-structure. The discipline the unit teaches: let the numbers sharpen the clinical picture, never replace it. A positive screen is a question, not an answer.

The practice rep (from the syllabus)

Take a character from a novel or show and write a one-page conceptualization: presenting problem, relevant history, your hypothesis about what maintains the problem (the perpetuating factors — this is the load-bearing part), and two measurable goals. The "what maintains it" line is where conceptualization lives; anyone can list symptoms. (Built as a production item in the bank.)

What's contested (don't over-learn it)

  • A screen is not a diagnosis, and the cut-point is not a law. ≥10 on the PHQ-9/GAD-7 is a flag calibrated for a population, not a threshold of truth (≥8 is optimal in some samples) .
  • Reliability ≠ validity, and neither licenses use. A consistent test can be consistently wrong, and a valid one misfires outside its norms — the culture-fair-assessment worry from unit04-multicultural lands squarely here .
  • The MSE is subjective. It's a snapshot that varies between clinicians and only supports a diagnosis; over-reading one MSE is a classic beginner error .
  • "Measurable" can crowd out "meaningful." SMART goals and outcome monitoring catch real problems the eye misses — and can also reduce the work to what a form can score .

Connects to

  • unit02-theories — the lens that turns a formulation into a plan; conceptualization is theory applied.
  • unit06-psychopathology — supplies the categories; concept-dsm-structure's "diagnosis as hypothesis to revisit" is this unit's starting line.
  • unit05-development — the normal baseline the MSE and screens are read against; concept-biopsychosocial-model is the natural formulation frame.
  • unit04-multicultural — culture-fair assessment; a screen or MSE read context-blind misdiagnoses.
  • unit01-helping-skills — the intake is the microskills doing assessment work.
  • Unit 8 (crisis/risk) — the risk screen hands forward to it (built); and Unit 12 (progress monitoring ↔ outcome measurement, built) — measurement-based care hands forward to it.

Sources

StatPearls, Mental Status Examination. Spitzer et al. (2006), GAD-7. IOM, Overview of Psychological Testing. Sommers-Flanagan, The Clinical Interview as an Assessment Tool. Rutter & Brown (2017), GAD-7 psychometrics. Research Methods in Psychology (OER). Fortney et al. (2017), measurement-based care. Doran (1981), SMART. Full notes in ../research/unit07-assessment-sources.md.

pages.title: Unit 8 — Crisis, Risk Assessment & Trauma-Informed Care
pages.html:
Unit 8 — Crisis, Risk Assessment & Trauma-Informed Care

This is the unit the syllabus says carries the most weight for keeping a client and you safe from day one: "A client may disclose suicidal thoughts in your first week of practicum. Freezing is not an option. This unit is where preparation directly protects a life." Two skills sit at its center, and they pull in opposite directions in a way worth naming up front. One is leaning in without flinching — asking a frightened, shut-down, or actively suicidal person the direct questions most people are trained by ordinary life to avoid. The other is restraint — resisting the beginner's urge to excavate a trauma history "to understand," because with trauma the reflex to dig is itself a way to do harm. Crisis work is where the fix-it stance is most dangerous in both directions: doing too little (freezing, changing the subject, false reassurance) and doing too much (probing, over-controlling, rescuing).

This is a Tier 2 clinical-foundations unit and, per the syllabus, one of the three you'd do even if you had only a month (Units 1, 3, 8). It ties into CACREP's Helping Relationships and its crisis-and-trauma competencies. It rests on two earlier units and hands to a later one:

  • ← Unit 3 (the rules). A suicidal or homicidal disclosure is exactly where confidentiality reaches its limits — danger to self, danger to others (concept-confidentiality-limits, concept-duty-to-warn). You cannot do crisis work without the ethical map from Unit 3, and the prediction critique from study-tarasoff lands here too: we assess risk to manage it, not to prophesy who will act.
  • ← Unit 7 (the risk screen). Every intake carries a risk screen, and item 9 of the PHQ-9 is a trip-wire that lands you here (concept-screening-tools, concept-intake-interview). Unit 7 flags risk; Unit 8 is what you do about a positive flag.
  • → Unit 11 (the brain). The neurobiology of trauma is a working-level preview of the stress-response and nervous-system material that Unit 11 develops in full.

It also borders the aux-psychological-first-aid elective (acute crisis support and grief) and the aux-addiction elective (overdose, means, and crisis in substance use) — both were written pointing forward to this unit, and are now wired into it.

The map of the unit

The unit runs in two arcs. Danger (screen it, plan around it, reduce the means, talk a crisis down) and trauma (how it works in the brain, the stance that avoids re-harm, and the cost the work exacts on the counselor).

PageThe job it doesThe one idea
concept-suicide-risk-assessmentscreening and assessing suicide riskask directly; separate ideation from behavior; assess to manage, not to predict
concept-safety-planningwhat you build with an at-risk clienta collaborative, prioritized plan — not a no-suicide contract
concept-means-reductionputting time and distance between crisis and methodcrises are brief and method-lethality varies enormously; reducing access saves lives
concept-de-escalationthe crisis-intervention and verbal de-escalation modelssafety is the through-line; one calm voice, choices not threats
concept-neurobiology-of-traumaa working model of the traumatized brainamygdala up, hippocampus/PFC down; the body reacts before the story arrives
concept-trauma-informed-carethe universal stance that avoids re-traumatizingtrauma-informed (avoid harm) ≠ trauma treatment (reduce symptoms); don't dig
concept-vicarious-traumawhat the work does to the helperempathic exposure reshapes the counselor's own schemas — a cost of caring, not a weakness
concept-counselor-self-carewhy looking after yourself is an ethical dutyACA C.2.g: an impaired counselor must not keep working; prevention is organizational, not only personal

The stance: lean in on danger, hold back on trauma

Both halves of this unit correct a fear-driven reflex, and they correct it in opposite directions.

On danger, the reflex is avoidance. Beginners fear that asking about suicide directly will "plant the idea," so they soften it, talk around it, or don't ask. The evidence is unambiguous: asking about suicide does not increase risk and may reduce distress . The move is to ask plainly and non-anxiously — "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" — and then tolerate the answer. Freezing, changing the subject, or rushing to reassure ("I'm sure it'll be fine") are the failures, not the question.

On trauma, the reflex is excavation. The technically-minded helper wants the whole history "to understand the problem." But trauma-informed care does not require the client to disclose or process the trauma ; pushing for the narrative before safety and trust exist is a classic way helpers re-traumatize. The move is to assume any client may be a survivor, create safety, and let the story come — or not — at the client's pace. This is the same don't-probe restraint the aux-psychological-first-aid elective teaches for acute crisis.

Both halves share one non-negotiable: safety first, and safety continuously. In the crisis models it is the thread through every step, not a box you check once .

What's contested (hold these carefully)

  • You can assess risk; you cannot predict the individual. Instruments and risk-factor lists identify elevated-risk populations and guide disposition — they do not forecast who dies or when. This is the study-tarasoff prediction critique in a new setting: assess to manage risk, not to prophesy .
  • No-suicide contracts don't work. A client's promise not to self-harm has no evidence of reducing suicide, can create false reassurance, and gives the client nothing to do. Collaborative safety planning replaced it .
  • Trauma neurobiology: trust the direction, not the decimals. The amygdala-up / hippocampus-and-PFC-down picture is well supported in direction; cortisol findings are inconsistent, and the window of tolerance and polyvagal theory are useful heuristics, not settled brain states. van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score is popular-press — good for framing, corroborate the mechanics elsewhere .
  • Trauma-informed ≠ trauma-focused. The universal stance (avoid re-traumatization) is not the specialized treatment (PE, CPT, TF-CBT, EMDR). Conflating them is what makes a beginner dig .
  • Self-care is ethics, not indulgence. Unaddressed vicarious trauma impairs judgment and boundaries; ACA C.2.g makes practicing while impaired a breach .

A note on the weight of this material

This unit is emotionally heavy, and the syllabus says so plainly: if any of it touches something personal rather than purely professional, that's worth bringing to your own therapy or a trusted person. The material here is kept clinical and precise on purpose. The counselor-cost pages (concept-vicarious-trauma, concept-counselor-self-care) are not an afterthought — they're the unit acknowledging that doing this work well and doing it for a long time are the same problem.

Connects to

  • unit03-ethics-law — confidentiality limits, duty to warn/protect, and the prediction critique are the legal-ethical frame for every risk decision here.
  • unit07-assessment — the intake risk screen and PHQ-9 item 9 hand forward to this unit's assessment protocol.
  • aux-psychological-first-aid — acute crisis support and grief; the don't-probe stance is shared.
  • aux-addiction — overdose, naloxone, and means safety in substance-use crises.
  • Unit 6 (concept-trauma-stressor-disorders) — PTSD/ASD as diagnoses; this unit adds the neurobiology, the informed-care stance, and treatment pointers those pages deferred here.

pages.text: Unit 8 — Crisis, Risk Assessment & Trauma-Informed Care This is the unit the syllabus says carries the most weight for keeping a client and you safe from day one: "A client may disclose suicidal thoughts in your first week of practicum. Freezing is not an option. This unit is where preparation directly protects a life." Two skills sit at its center, and they pull in opposite directions in a way worth naming up front. One is leaning in without flinching — asking a frightened, shut-down, or actively suicidal person the direct questions most people are trained by ordinary life to avoid. The other is restraint — resisting the beginner's urge to excavate a trauma history "to understand," because with trauma the reflex to dig is itself a way to do harm. Crisis work is where the fix-it stance is most dangerous in both directions: doing too little (freezing, changing the subject, false reassurance) and doing too much (probing, over-controlling, rescuing). This is a Tier 2 clinical-foundations unit and, per the syllabus, one of the three you'd do even if you had only a month (Units 1, 3, 8). It ties into CACREP's Helping Relationships and its crisis-and-trauma competencies. It rests on two earlier units and hands to a later one: ← Unit 3 (the rules). A suicidal or homicidal disclosure is exactly where confidentiality reaches its limits — danger to self, danger to others ( concept-confidentiality-limits , concept-duty-to-warn ). You cannot do crisis work without the ethical map from Unit 3, and the prediction critique from study-tarasoff lands here too: we assess risk to manage it, not to prophesy who will act. ← Unit 7 (the risk screen). Every intake carries a risk screen, and item 9 of the PHQ-9 is a trip-wire that lands you here ( concept-screening-tools , concept-intake-interview ). Unit 7 flags risk; Unit 8 is what you do about a positive flag. → Unit 11 (the brain). The neurobiology of trauma is a working-level preview of the stress-response and nervous-system material that Unit 11 develops in full. It also borders the aux-psychological-first-aid elective (acute crisis support and grief) and the aux-addiction elective (overdose, means, and crisis in substance use) — both were written pointing forward to this unit, and are now wired into it. The map of the unit The unit runs in two arcs. Danger (screen it, plan around it, reduce the means, talk a crisis down) and trauma (how it works in the brain, the stance that avoids re-harm, and the cost the work exacts on the counselor). Page The job it does The one idea concept-suicide-risk-assessment screening and assessing suicide risk ask directly; separate ideation from behavior; assess to manage , not to predict concept-safety-planning what you build with an at-risk client a collaborative, prioritized plan — not a no-suicide contract concept-means-reduction putting time and distance between crisis and method crises are brief and method-lethality varies enormously; reducing access saves lives concept-de-escalation the crisis-intervention and verbal de-escalation models safety is the through-line; one calm voice, choices not threats concept-neurobiology-of-trauma a working model of the traumatized brain amygdala up, hippocampus/PFC down; the body reacts before the story arrives concept-trauma-informed-care the universal stance that avoids re-traumatizing trauma- informed (avoid harm) ≠ trauma treatment (reduce symptoms); don't dig concept-vicarious-trauma what the work does to the helper empathic exposure reshapes the counselor's own schemas — a cost of caring, not a weakness concept-counselor-self-care why looking after yourself is an ethical duty ACA C.2.g: an impaired counselor must not keep working; prevention is organizational, not only personal The stance: lean in on danger, hold back on trauma Both halves of this unit correct a fear-driven reflex, and they correct it in opposite directions. On danger, the reflex is avoidance. Beginners fear that asking about suicide directly will "plant the idea," so they soften it, talk around it, or don't ask. The evidence is unambiguous: asking about suicide does not increase risk and may reduce distress S4 . The move is to ask plainly and non-anxiously — "Are you thinking about killing yourself?" — and then tolerate the answer. Freezing, changing the subject, or rushing to reassure ("I'm sure it'll be fine") are the failures, not the question. On trauma, the reflex is excavation. The technically-minded helper wants the whole history "to understand the problem." But trauma-informed care does not require the client to disclose or process the trauma S12 ; pushing for the narrative before safety and trust exist is a classic way helpers re-traumatize. The move is to assume any client may be a survivor, create safety, and let the story come — or not — at the client's pace. This is the same don't-probe restraint the aux-psychological-first-aid elective teaches for acute crisis. Both halves share one non-negotiable: safety first, and safety continuously . In the crisis models it is the thread through every step, not a box you check once S9 . What's contested (hold these carefully) You can assess risk; you cannot predict the individual. Instruments and risk-factor lists identify elevated-risk populations and guide disposition — they do not forecast who dies or when. This is the study-tarasoff prediction critique in a new setting: assess to manage risk, not to prophesy S1 S3 S5 . No-suicide contracts don't work. A client's promise not to self-harm has no evidence of reducing suicide, can create false reassurance, and gives the client nothing to do . Collaborative safety planning replaced it S6 S7 . Trauma neurobiology: trust the direction, not the decimals. The amygdala-up / hippocampus-and-PFC-down picture is well supported in direction ; cortisol findings are inconsistent, and the window of tolerance and polyvagal theory are useful heuristics , not settled brain states. van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score is popular-press — good for framing, corroborate the mechanics elsewhere S14 S15 S17 . Trauma-informed ≠ trauma-focused. The universal stance (avoid re-traumatization) is not the specialized treatment (PE, CPT, TF-CBT, EMDR). Conflating them is what makes a beginner dig S12 S13 . Self-care is ethics, not indulgence. Unaddressed vicarious trauma impairs judgment and boundaries; ACA C.2.g makes practicing while impaired a breach S19 S21 . A note on the weight of this material This unit is emotionally heavy, and the syllabus says so plainly: if any of it touches something personal rather than purely professional, that's worth bringing to your own therapy or a trusted person. The material here is kept clinical and precise on purpose. The counselor-cost pages ( concept-vicarious-trauma , concept-counselor-self-care ) are not an afterthought — they're the unit acknowledging that doing this work well and doing it for a long time are the same problem. Connects to unit03-ethics-law — confidentiality limits, duty to warn/protect, and the prediction critique are the legal-ethical frame for every risk decision here. unit07-assessment — the intake risk screen and PHQ-9 item 9 hand forward to this unit's assessment protocol. aux-psychological-first-aid — acute crisis support and grief; the don't-probe stance is shared. aux-addiction — overdose, naloxone, and means safety in substance-use crises. Unit 6 ( concept-trauma-stressor-disorders ) — PTSD/ASD as diagnoses ; this unit adds the neurobiology , the informed-care stance , and treatment pointers those pages deferred here. pages.title: Unit 9 — Evidence-Based Modalities (a practical toolkit)
pages.html:
Unit 9 — Evidence-Based Modalities (a practical toolkit)

Units 1–8 built the room: the relationship (Unit 1), the map of theories (Unit 2), the rules (Unit 3), the cultural lens (Unit 4), what's normal (Unit 5), what goes wrong (Unit 6), how to assess it (Unit 7), and how to handle danger (Unit 8). This unit hands you the tools you actually reach for once you're in the chair with a real person and a real problem. It is deliberately concrete: the syllabus frames it as "hands-on familiarity with a few methods you'll likely use directly." These are the structured, protocol-like interventions — the part of the work most legible to a technically-minded helper — which is exactly why the unit opens and closes with the same warning: a technique is only ever as good as the relationship it runs on (theory-common-factors).

This is a Tier 3 "rounding out" unit that ties into CACREP's Counseling & Helping Relationships area. It leans on two earlier units and repays a few electives:

  • ← Unit 1 (the relational engine). Motivational Interviewing's OARS (concept-oars) is the microskills set from concept-microskills-hierarchy, pointed at ambivalence. Name that link every time — you already know the engine.
  • ← Unit 2 (the theory). CBT's theory lives in theory-cbt; this unit is its practice (theory-cbt-practice, concept-cognitive-triangle, concept-behavioral-activation). Solution-focused worldview lives in theory-postmodern; here you get its toolkit (theory-solution-focused).
  • → the electives. The aux-addiction module applies MI and CBT to substance use specifically; the change-stages map (concept-stages-of-change) is the terrain MI moves a client across. This unit is the general-tools home those modules pointed forward to.

What "evidence-based" actually means here

The unit's title is a small trap. Evidence-based practice (EBP) is not "run the manual with the biggest effect size." The APA definition is the integration of three things: (1) the best available research, (2) clinical expertise, and (3) the client's characteristics, culture, and preferences . A method with strong research support that the client won't engage, or that ignores their culture (Unit 4) or their stage of readiness (Unit 8's crisis stance, the electives' concept-stages-of-change), is not "evidence-based practice" for this person. You are assembling a toolkit and choosing from it, not ranking techniques and always grabbing #1.

And the humbling backdrop from Unit 1: across bona-fide therapies, specific-technique differences are usually small, and the alliance carries a large share of the outcome — the "dodo-bird" finding . This does not make technique pointless; it means technique works through the relationship, not instead of it. Every "which modality fits this client?" item in this unit sits under that caveat.

The six tools, and the three "waves"

CBT-family therapies are often described in three historical waves , which is the cleanest way to organize the unit:

WaveTargetsThis unit's tools
1st — behavioralobservable behavior; conditioning, reinforcement, avoidanceBehavioral Activation (concept-behavioral-activation)
2nd — cognitivethe content of thought; is it accurate?CBT / cognitive restructuring (theory-cbt-practice, concept-cognitive-triangle)
3rd — contextualyour relationship to thought; acceptance over controlACT (concept-act) and DBT (concept-dbt-skills)

Two more tools sit outside the wave scheme because they're styles / stances rather than content models:

  • Motivational Interviewing (theory-motivational-interviewing, concept-oars) — not a treatment so much as a way of talking that resolves ambivalence. It's what you use before any of the above will land, when the client isn't sure they want to change.
  • Solution-Focused Brief Therapy (theory-solution-focused) — a postmodern toolkit that ignores the problem's origins and builds on exceptions and a described future.
ToolThe one ideaReach for it when…
theory-cbt-practice / concept-cognitive-triangleevents don't cause feelings — interpretations do; test the thoughtdistorted thinking maintains distress (depression, anxiety, panic)
concept-behavioral-activationact your way into feeling, not feel your way into actingdepression, withdrawal, avoidance — even without touching thoughts
theory-motivational-interviewing / concept-oarslet the client voice the arguments for changeambivalence: substance use, behavior change, "I know I should, but…"
theory-solution-focusedbuild the solution, don't excavate the problembrief work, strengths, clients tired of problem-talk
concept-actstop fighting inner experience; move toward valueschronic pain/anxiety, rumination, "control agenda" has failed
concept-dbt-skillshold acceptance and change together; teach skillsemotion dysregulation, self-harm, BPD, crisis-prone clients

The stance thread runs straight through this unit

This whole curriculum keeps flagging the beginner's urge to "fix." Unit 9 is where that urge is most tempting — these are the fixing tools — and, remarkably, where two of the methods make resisting the fix their central technique:

  • Motivational Interviewing names the trap by its name. The righting reflex — your impulse to jump in, warn, and correct the client toward health — reliably makes the client defend the status quo . MI's entire method is to hold that reflex and let the client argue for their own change. This is the Unit 1 stance shift, formalized into a technique.
  • The third-wave therapies invert "fix" into "accept." ACT and DBT stop trying to change or eliminate difficult thoughts and feelings and instead change the client's relationship to them (acceptance, defusion, distress tolerance) . The paradox — you change by stopping the struggle to change — is the opposite of the debugging reflex.

Even the two most protocol-like tools carry the caution: CBT is collaborative empiricism (you test thoughts with the client, you don't correct them) , and behavioral activation is done with a depressed client's buy-in, not prescribed at them.

What's contested (hold these carefully)

  • "Evidence-based" ≠ "best." The alliance and other common factors account for much of the outcome; between bona-fide therapies, technique differences are typically small . Choosing a modality matters most for fit and engagement, less as a horse race.
  • The cognitive part of CBT may not be the active ingredient. Jacobson's dismantling trial found behavioral activation alone worked as well as full CBT with cognitive restructuring added ; Dimidjian 2006 found BA matched medication and beat cognitive therapy for severe depression . This genuinely complicates the intuitive "you must fix the thoughts" story.
  • Third-wave ≠ proven-superior. ACT and DBT are evidence-based, but they have not been shown to outperform standard CBT for most conditions; "third wave" is a family and a philosophy, not a ranking .
  • Allegiance and publication bias inflate the numbers, especially in the SFBT literature — the largest reported effect sizes come from proponent sources; the peer-reviewed meta-analytic estimate is more modest .

Connects to

  • theory-common-factors (Unit 1) — the dodo-bird / alliance caveat that frames the whole unit.
  • concept-microskills-hierarchy and concept-oars (Unit 1 ↔ Unit 9) — the shared relational engine; OARS is microskills aimed at ambivalence.
  • theory-cbt and theory-postmodern (Unit 2) — the theory whose practice this unit teaches.
  • concept-case-conceptualization and concept-treatment-planning (Unit 7) — conceptualization picks the tool; the tool fills the treatment plan's "interventions."
  • aux-addiction and concept-stages-of-change — MI/CBT applied to addiction; the readiness map MI works across.

Franklin et al. (2024) SFBT meta-analysis. ACBS, six core processes of ACT. Linehan, DBT Skills Training Manual. Hayes & Hofmann (2017), "third wave." APA (2006), Evidence-Based Practice in Psychology. Unit 1 theory-common-factors (dodo-bird / alliance). Full notes in ../research/unit09-modalities-sources.md.
