pages.title: Unit 10 — Group Counseling
pages.html:
Unit 10 — Group Counseling

Everything up to here has assumed a room with two people in it. This unit changes the arithmetic. In a group, the counselor is no longer the only — or even the main — agent of change: the members heal each other, and the counselor's job shifts from providing help to cultivating the conditions under which members provide it to one another. That shift is the whole unit. The syllabus objective is deliberately narrow and deliberately deep: understand why groups heal differently than individual work. Not "additionally," not "more cheaply" — differently, through mechanisms that one-on-one therapy structurally cannot supply.

This is a Tier 3 "rounding out" unit that maps directly onto CACREP's Group Counseling and Group Work core area — a required competency and one of the most common practicum placements, because so much of community mental health, addiction treatment, and inpatient care is delivered in groups. It leans hardest on Unit 1.

  • ← Unit 1 (the relational engine, multiplied). The single most important therapeutic factor, group cohesiveness, is the group analog of the therapeutic alliance (concept-therapeutic-alliance) — "a client-client equivalent to the client-therapist alliance" . So the Unit 1 lesson holds and is amplified: the relationship (now a web of relationships) carries much of the outcome, and technique runs through it (theory-common-factors). The leader's moment-to-moment moves — reflection, immediacy, observation — are the Unit 1 microskills (concept-microskills-hierarchy) redeployed to shape what happens between members.
  • ↔ the rest of the curriculum. Group stages rhyme with development (theory-eriksons-stages); the social microcosm is attachment and interpersonal patterns (concept-attachment-styles) enacted live; screening and confidentiality are Unit 3 ethics (concept-confidentiality-limits, concept-informed-consent) with a group-shaped twist; and specific methods (DBT skills groups, concept-dbt-skills; MI in groups, theory-motivational-interviewing) are Unit 9 tools delivered in this format.

Why a group heals differently

Irvin Yalom, whose Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy is the field's defining text , catalogued the change mechanisms as therapeutic factors (theory-yalom-factors). Several of them cannot exist in individual therapy at all:

  • Universality — "I'm not the only one." You can tell a client in individual therapy that others struggle too; only a group lets them witness it. This alone dissolves a great deal of shame and isolation.
  • Altruism — being useful to someone else. A depressed client who has felt like a burden for months discovers they have something to give. Individual therapy makes the client a permanent recipient; a group makes them a helper.
  • Interpersonal learning in a social microcosm — the deepest one. Given time, members recreate their habitual interpersonal world inside the group : the person who feels chronically rejected starts to provoke rejection; the caretaker exhausts themselves tending everyone. The group becomes a live, low-stakes replica of the member's outside relationships — and, unlike the outside world, it will tell them what it's like to be on the other end of them. That honest feedback, delivered inside a caring group, is a corrective emotional experience you cannot manufacture in a dyad.

The counselor's leverage is therefore indirect. The beginner's trap — covered below — is to run individual therapy in front of an audience, taking turns doing one-on-one work while everyone else watches. That wastes the entire apparatus. The skill is to activate the group as the therapist.

The map of the unit

PageThe one idea
theory-yalom-factorsthe eleven therapeutic factors — why groups work; cohesiveness and interpersonal learning above all
concept-group-development-stagesgroups develop over time (forming → storming → norming → performing; Corey's initial/transition/working/final) — read the stage, don't fight it
concept-group-leadershipthe leader's role: the four functions, the here-and-now focus, and the finding that too much "stimulation" harms
concept-group-typesthe ASGW four types — task, psychoeducational, counseling, psychotherapy — matched by depth of aim
concept-difficult-group-membersthe monopolist, the silent member, the help-rejecting complainer — problems to work with, not eliminate
concept-group-ethics-and-formationscreening, preparation, and the confidentiality limit unique to groups (you cannot guarantee it)

The stance shift for this unit

The "resist the urge to fix" thread that runs through the whole curriculum takes a specific form in group work: decenter yourself and trust the group.

  • Trust the members. The instinct to be the one who responds to every disclosure is the individual-therapy reflex. In a group it starves the members of the chance to help each other — killing universality, altruism, and interpersonal learning in one move. When a member shares, the higher-skill response is often to turn to the group ("Does anyone else know that feeling?") rather than to answer yourself.
  • Here-and-now over there-and-then. The pull is to help members solve the problems they bring from outside (the "there-and-then"). The power is in what's happening in the room, right now — how members are relating to each other and to you . Process beats content.
  • A difficult member is an opportunity, not an obstacle. The monopolist and the help-rejecting complainer are enacting, live, the very patterns that hurt them outside. The reflex is to manage them so the group runs smoothly; the work is to make their pattern examinable — for their benefit and the group's (concept-difficult-group-members).
  • Groups can harm. The encounter-group research found real casualties, concentrated under aggressive, over-stimulating leaders . This is why screening, preparation, and leadership balance (concept-group-leadership) are ethical duties, not style preferences.

What's contested (hold these carefully)

  • The therapeutic factors are clinically derived, not a validated factor structure. Yalom's eleven are an enormously useful clinical map, but their relative importance shifts by group type, member, and study, and members and leaders rank them differently . Treat them as a vocabulary for what's happening, not a measured mechanism.
  • Cohesion is central clinically but its efficacy evidence is thinner than its billing. It's called "the core mechanism of action" , yet the harder empirical support in group research attaches to interpersonal feedback and the alliance more than to cohesion or emotional climate . Hold "cohesion is everything" as a strong clinical heuristic, not a settled finding.
  • "Group is the budget option" is wrong on the evidence. Burlingame's meta-analysis of 46 RCTs found zero outcome difference between group and individual therapy across disorders when treatment, patients, and dose are matched . Group is equivalent and cheaper, not cheaper and worse — and it is badly underused relative to that evidence.

pages.text: Unit 10 — Group Counseling Everything up to here has assumed a room with two people in it. This unit changes the arithmetic. In a group, the counselor is no longer the only — or even the main — agent of change: the members heal each other , and the counselor's job shifts from providing help to cultivating the conditions under which members provide it to one another. That shift is the whole unit. The syllabus objective is deliberately narrow and deliberately deep: understand why groups heal differently than individual work. Not "additionally," not "more cheaply" — differently , through mechanisms that one-on-one therapy structurally cannot supply. This is a Tier 3 "rounding out" unit that maps directly onto CACREP's Group Counseling and Group Work core area — a required competency and one of the most common practicum placements, because so much of community mental health, addiction treatment, and inpatient care is delivered in groups. It leans hardest on Unit 1. ← Unit 1 (the relational engine, multiplied). The single most important therapeutic factor, group cohesiveness , is the group analog of the therapeutic alliance ( concept-therapeutic-alliance ) — "a client-client equivalent to the client-therapist alliance" S1 . So the Unit 1 lesson holds and is amplified: the relationship (now a web of relationships) carries much of the outcome, and technique runs through it ( theory-common-factors ). The leader's moment-to-moment moves — reflection, immediacy, observation — are the Unit 1 microskills ( concept-microskills-hierarchy ) redeployed to shape what happens between members . ↔ the rest of the curriculum. Group stages rhyme with development ( theory-eriksons-stages ); the social microcosm is attachment and interpersonal patterns ( concept-attachment-styles ) enacted live; screening and confidentiality are Unit 3 ethics ( concept-confidentiality-limits , concept-informed-consent ) with a group-shaped twist; and specific methods ( DBT skills groups , concept-dbt-skills ; MI in groups, theory-motivational-interviewing ) are Unit 9 tools delivered in this format. Why a group heals differently Irvin Yalom , whose Theory and Practice of Group Psychotherapy is the field's defining text S2 , catalogued the change mechanisms as therapeutic factors ( theory-yalom-factors ). Several of them cannot exist in individual therapy at all : Universality — "I'm not the only one." You can tell a client in individual therapy that others struggle too; only a group lets them witness it. This alone dissolves a great deal of shame and isolation. Altruism — being useful to someone else. A depressed client who has felt like a burden for months discovers they have something to give. Individual therapy makes the client a permanent recipient; a group makes them a helper. Interpersonal learning in a social microcosm — the deepest one. Given time, members recreate their habitual interpersonal world inside the group S2 S3 : the person who feels chronically rejected starts to provoke rejection; the caretaker exhausts themselves tending everyone. The group becomes a live, low-stakes replica of the member's outside relationships — and, unlike the outside world, it will tell them what it's like to be on the other end of them . That honest feedback, delivered inside a caring group, is a corrective emotional experience you cannot manufacture in a dyad. The counselor's leverage is therefore indirect. The beginner's trap — covered below — is to run individual therapy in front of an audience , taking turns doing one-on-one work while everyone else watches. That wastes the entire apparatus. The skill is to activate the group as the therapist. The map of the unit Page The one idea theory-yalom-factors the eleven therapeutic factors — why groups work; cohesiveness and interpersonal learning above all concept-group-development-stages groups develop over time (forming → storming → norming → performing; Corey's initial/transition/working/final) — read the stage, don't fight it concept-group-leadership the leader's role : the four functions, the here-and-now focus, and the finding that too much "stimulation" harms concept-group-types the ASGW four types — task, psychoeducational, counseling, psychotherapy — matched by depth of aim concept-difficult-group-members the monopolist, the silent member, the help-rejecting complainer — problems to work with , not eliminate concept-group-ethics-and-formation screening, preparation, and the confidentiality limit unique to groups (you cannot guarantee it) The stance shift for this unit The "resist the urge to fix" thread that runs through the whole curriculum takes a specific form in group work: decenter yourself and trust the group. Trust the members. The instinct to be the one who responds to every disclosure is the individual-therapy reflex. In a group it starves the members of the chance to help each other — killing universality, altruism, and interpersonal learning in one move. When a member shares, the higher-skill response is often to turn to the group ("Does anyone else know that feeling?") rather than to answer yourself. Here-and-now over there-and-then. The pull is to help members solve the problems they bring from outside (the "there-and-then"). The power is in what's happening in the room, right now — how members are relating to each other and to you S2 . Process beats content. A difficult member is an opportunity, not an obstacle. The monopolist and the help-rejecting complainer are enacting, live, the very patterns that hurt them outside. The reflex is to manage them so the group runs smoothly; the work is to make their pattern examinable — for their benefit and the group's ( concept-difficult-group-members ). Groups can harm. The encounter-group research found real casualties , concentrated under aggressive, over-stimulating leaders S5 . This is why screening, preparation, and leadership balance ( concept-group-leadership ) are ethical duties, not style preferences. What's contested (hold these carefully) The therapeutic factors are clinically derived, not a validated factor structure. Yalom's eleven are an enormously useful clinical map, but their relative importance shifts by group type, member, and study , and members and leaders rank them differently S1 S2 . Treat them as a vocabulary for what's happening, not a measured mechanism. Cohesion is central clinically but its efficacy evidence is thinner than its billing. It's called "the core mechanism of action" S1 , yet the harder empirical support in group research attaches to interpersonal feedback and the alliance more than to cohesion or emotional climate S1 . Hold "cohesion is everything" as a strong clinical heuristic, not a settled finding. "Group is the budget option" is wrong on the evidence. Burlingame's meta-analysis of 46 RCTs found zero outcome difference between group and individual therapy across disorders when treatment, patients, and dose are matched S4 . Group is equivalent and cheaper , not cheaper and worse — and it is badly underused relative to that evidence. pages.title: Unit 11 — Neuroscience & Biological Bases of Behavior
pages.html:
Unit 11 — Neuroscience & Biological Bases of Behavior

You are not going to be a neuroscientist, and you will never prescribe a medication. So why does a counselor need the brain? Because clients ask. "What's actually wrong with my brain?" "Is this a chemical imbalance?" "Should I go on medication — and if I do, will I be on it forever?" "My psychiatrist put me on an SSRI; what does that even do?" A counselor who can answer these responsibly — accurately, without overclaiming, and knowing exactly where their scope ends and a prescriber's begins — is doing real clinical work. A counselor who can't either goes silent or, worse, improvises medical advice they aren't licensed to give. The syllabus objective is deliberately modest and deliberately practical: build a working mental model of the brain and body in mental health. Enough to explain, to coordinate, and to refer. Not enough to play doctor.

This is a Tier 3 "rounding out" unit that maps onto the biological bases strand of CACREP's Human Growth & Development core area, and onto its psychopharmacology requirement — counselors are trained in the "classifications, indications, and contraindications of commonly prescribed psychopharmacological medications for appropriate medical referrals and consultation" . Note the last clause: the competency is for referral and consultation, never prescribing. It depends most on Units 6 and 8.

  • ← Unit 8 (this is where the trauma brain gets its full body). Unit 8's concept-neurobiology-of-trauma gave a working-level preview — the amygdala/hippocampus/PFC circuit, the HPA axis, the window of tolerance — flagged source_units: [8, 11] because this unit is its full home. Here the concept-stress-response gets the complete two-system story (fast SAM + slow HPA), and the concept-autonomic-nervous-system explains the fight/flight/freeze machinery underneath it.
  • ← Unit 6 (this is the medication depth those disorder pages deferred). concept-mood-disorders, concept-psychotic-disorders, and concept-personality-disorders repeatedly pointed forward to "meds — Unit 11." concept-psychotropic-classes is that page: what each class does, and the counselor's non-prescribing role around it.
  • ↔ Unit 5, Unit 9. Biology is one leg of Unit 5's concept-biopsychosocial-model — this unit fills in that leg without letting it swallow the other two. And Unit 9's claim that "therapy works" gets its mechanism here: concept-neuroplasticity-therapy shows that psychotherapy is itself a biological treatment that changes the brain.

The map of the unit

PageThe one idea
concept-neuron-neurotransmissionthe substrate: neurons talk across synapses using neurotransmitters (glutamate/GABA, dopamine, serotonin, norepinephrine, ACh); drugs act by agonism, antagonism, or reuptake blockade
concept-autonomic-nervous-systemthe body's automatic balance: sympathetic (fight/flight) vs. parasympathetic (rest/digest), plus the freeze shutdown — the machinery of arousal you watch in the room
concept-stress-responsethe two-speed stress cascade: fast SAM/adrenaline (seconds) + slow HPA/cortisol (minutes); adaptive acutely, allostatic load chronically
concept-psychotropic-classesthe five med classes (antidepressants, anti-anxiety, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, stimulants) — what they do, and the counselor's coordinate-and-refer, never-prescribe role
concept-neuroplasticity-therapythe brain rewires with experience (Hebb; "fire together, wire together") — so psychotherapy changes the brain, and biology is a lever for therapy, not a verdict against it

The stance shift for this unit

The "resist the urge to fix" thread takes a specific and slightly paradoxical shape here. This is the unit most likely to tempt you toward the fix reflex — because biology feels like the level where the real machinery lives, the "actual" cause under the messy human story. The discipline is to hold the biology as one lens among three, not the master lens.

  • Biology is a leg of the stool, not the floor it stands on. The biopsychosocial model is not "biology, plus some soft stuff." Genes, neurotransmitters, meaning, relationships, and social conditions are co-causes, and the biological one is not automatically the most fundamental. Collapsing a person into their neurochemistry ("it's just a chemical imbalance") is neuro-reductionism, and it's usually both wrong (see below) and clinically deflating — it tells a client their problem is a broken part, not a life to be understood and changed.
  • You don't prescribe — you translate, coordinate, and refer. The whole medication skill set for a counselor is: recognize the classes, know roughly what they do and their common side effects, educate the client enough to have an informed conversation with their prescriber, consult with that prescriber, and refer . What you never do is start, stop, change, or second-guess a medication — including telling a client who feels better that they can quit. That's practicing medicine without a license and, with some drugs, dangerous (see concept-psychotropic-classes).
  • Neuroscience destigmatizes both directions. Used well, biology reduces shame: naming the freeze response as an automatic brainstem reflex frees a survivor from "why didn't I fight back," and knowing that therapy itself changes the brain (concept-neuroplasticity-therapy) dissolves the false hierarchy that puts "real" (medical) treatment above "just talking." Talking is biological.

What's contested — hold these carefully

This is an area where the popular story runs well ahead of the settled science, exactly as Unit 8 warned. Read the direction of the findings as solid and the confident narratives as suspect.

  • The "chemical imbalance" theory of depression is not supported. A 2022 umbrella review found no consistent evidence that depression is caused by low serotonin — across metabolites, receptors, the transporter, tryptophan-depletion, and gene studies . Antidepressants still help many people (Cipriani's network meta-analysis: all 21 beat placebo, though by modest margins ) — but not, it seems, by correcting a known deficiency; the leading account is now downstream neuroplasticity . Hold the tension: "chemical imbalance" is a myth; medication can still be genuinely useful. (The review is itself contested — teach it both-sides.)
  • The dopamine hypothesis of schizophrenia is real but partial. The modern version is elevated presynaptic striatal dopamine driving aberrant salience, not "too much dopamine, everywhere" — and glutamate, GABA, and others are also involved . Antipsychotics block D2 and dampen positive symptoms; they don't "cure a dopamine excess."
  • Neuroplasticity is real but overhyped. The brain genuinely rewires with experience , and therapy leverages that . But "neuroplasticity" has become a marketing word for a great deal of unfounded "rewire your brain" content — and the link from a specific therapy move to a specific brain change is largely inferential; neural correlates are not mechanism .
  • Polyvagal theory, "amygdala hijack," and left-brain/right-brain are clinically popular metaphors whose strong neurophysiological claims are contested or oversimplified . Use them as bridges to clients, not as established fact (carried over from Unit 8).

Connects to

  • concept-neurobiology-of-trauma (Unit 8) — the trauma-specific application; this unit is its full neuroscience home (source_units: [8, 11]).
  • concept-biopsychosocial-model (Unit 5) — biology as one of three co-equal domains; this unit fills the biological leg without letting it dominate.
  • concept-mood-disorders, concept-psychotic-disorders, concept-personality-disorders (Unit 6) — the disorders whose medications live on concept-psychotropic-classes.
  • theory-cbt-practice and concept-behavioral-activation (Unit 9) — "therapy works" gets its neuroplastic mechanism here.
  • concept-scope-of-practice and concept-helping-professions-compared (Unit 3) — who prescribes, and the counselor's coordinate-and-refer boundary.
  • concept-neuroscience-of-addiction (addiction elective) — the dopamine/reward-circuit story applied to substances.

Sources

StatPearls, Physiology, Neurotransmitters. StatPearls, Physiology, Autonomic Nervous System. Gunnar & Quevedo (Annu. Rev. Psychol.) + McEwen allostatic-load literature. NIMH, Mental Health Medications. Moncrieff et al. (2022), Molecular Psychiatry (serotonin umbrella review; contested — reply flagged). SSRI-to-neuroplasticity literature (PMC5624993). Howes & Kapur, dopamine hypothesis v.III / aberrant salience. Hebb + open neuroplasticity text. Kandel (1998), Am. J. Psychiatry. Baxter et al. (1992) + imaging review. Cozolino, The Neuroscience of Psychotherapy (anchor; offline, corroborated). CACREP 2016 standards + TPC (counselor psychopharmacology scope). Cross-unit anchors (Unit 8 trauma neurobiology; polyvagal caveat). Full notes in ../research/unit11-neuroscience-sources.md.

pages.title: Unit 12 — Research Methods & Program Evaluation
pages.html:
Unit 12 — Research Methods & Program Evaluation

You will spend far more of your career reading research than doing it — and that reading is not optional. "Evidence-based practice" is written into the ACA Code, into insurance requirements, into your program's accreditation, and into the expectation that you can tell a client's family why you chose the approach you did. The field you are entering is also crowded with confident claims that do not survive scrutiny: brand-name therapies promising outsized effects, "brain-based" workshops, screening gadgets, and a steady stream of headlines. The skill this unit builds is discernment — the ability to look at a study, a statistic, or a marketing claim and ask the right questions: What kind of study is this? Can it support the causal claim being made? How big is the effect, and does the size matter for a real person? Who could this generalize to? Was it done ethically? The syllabus objective is deliberately practical, and the course-map is explicit about the altitude: quiz choosing the method, not executing it. You are not being trained to be a statistician; you are being trained to be a critical consumer and, for your own caseload and program, a competent evaluator.

This is the final unit of the twelve-unit spine and a Tier 3 "rounding out" unit. It maps directly onto CACREP's core area Research and Program Evaluation (§2.F.8), whose framing is exactly the consumer-and-evaluator posture above: critique research to inform practice, identify evidence-based practices, run needs assessments and outcome measures, and do all of it ethically and with cultural humility . It depends most on Unit 7.

  • ← Unit 7 (this is where outcome measurement gets its methods). Unit 7's concept-reliability-validity carries source_units: [7, 12] because the psychometrics it introduced (reliability, validity, sensitivity/specificity) are research-methods content doing clinical work; and concept-screening-tools and concept-treatment-planning pointed forward to "the outcome-monitoring thread Unit 12 picks up." Here that thread gets its engine: concept-single-case-design and the reliable-change idea on concept-effect-size are what turn a repeated PHQ-9 into evidence that this client is actually getting better.
  • ↔ Unit 9 (this is the definition Unit 9 was already using). unit09-modalities's hub defined evidence-based practice as APA's three-legged integration and warned that "evidence-based" is not a horse race; concept-evidence-based-practice is the full account of that definition, the evidence hierarchy underneath it, and the empirically-supported-treatment tiers. The allegiance-bias caution that down-weighted SFBT's largest effect sizes is a Unit 12 concept meeting you early.
  • ↔ Unit 10, Unit 3. Unit 10's claim that group ≈ individual therapy (Burlingame's 46-RCT equivalence) — and that groups can harm — are effect-size and evidence-appraisal claims; and the research-ethics half of this unit is the study-world analog of Unit 3's clinical ethics: concept-irb-research-ethics is to a research participant what concept-informed-consent and concept-confidentiality-limits are to a client.

The map of the unit

PageThe one idea
concept-experimental-vs-correlationalonly an experiment (manipulation + random assignment + control) licenses a causal claim; correlational studies show association, and the directionality/third-variable problems are why "correlation ≠ causation"; quasi-experiments sit in between
concept-validity-threatsfour questions of a study — statistical-conclusion, internal, construct, external validity — and the classic threats (history, maturation, selection, regression to the mean, attrition…); the internal↔external tradeoff
concept-effect-sizea p-value tells you whether, an effect size tells you how big, and clinical significance tells you whether it matters to a person; what a p-value does and does not mean; confidence intervals; the reliable change index
concept-evidence-based-practiceEBP = integrating best research + clinical expertise + client values (not "research wins"); the evidence hierarchy; empirically-supported-treatment tiers; and the replication crisis / allegiance & publication bias that keep you humble
concept-single-case-designyou can run a rigorous experiment on one person — ABAB (reversal) and multiple-baseline designs, read by visual inspection; the clinical cousin is progress monitoring (good enough to guide care, not to prove causation)
concept-program-evaluationjudging a program or service (not seeking generalizable knowledge): needs assessment → formative → process → summative → outcome; steering the ship vs. judging the trip
concept-irb-research-ethicsthe Belmont three principles (respect for persons / beneficence / justice) → consent, risk-benefit, fair selection; the IRB; the abuses (Nuremberg, Tuskegee) behind the rules; ACA Section G

The stance shift for this unit

The Unit-wide "resist the urge to fix" caution takes a quieter but important form here: the number is not the person. Research literacy is a tool for good clinical judgment, not a replacement for it — and the two failure modes are opposite and equally bad.

  • Don't worship the evidence, and don't dismiss it. A statistically significant result from a randomized trial is a real, valuable thing — and it is a statement about a group average, generated under study conditions, that may or may not describe the individual in your office (the nomothetic–idiographic gap). EBP is integration: the research is one leg of a three-legged stool, standing alongside your clinical expertise and this client's values and culture . Treating "the manual says" as a trump card is as much a failure of the stance as ignoring the evidence altogether.
  • A finding is a claim, not a verdict — hold it at the right confidence. The field's most famous results include ones that did not replicate . The discipline is calibration: strong designs and replicated effects earn more confidence; single studies, tiny effects, and developer-run trials earn less. Being a discerning consumer means resisting both credulity ("new study proves…") and cynicism ("it's all garbage") — the same both-sides posture Units 4, 6, 9, and 11 asked you to hold about contested claims.
  • Measurement serves the work, not the reverse. The reason to track outcomes (concept-single-case-design, measurement-based care) is that it catches the client who is quietly not getting better — the one your clinical intuition is most likely to miss . That is measurement in service of the relationship, exactly the opposite of reducing a person to a score. "Measurable" is not the same as "meaningful" (the Unit 7 caution), and the RCI exists precisely to ask whether a numeric change is real and meaningful for this person .
  • Research ethics is clinical ethics, one step removed. Consent, confidentiality, non-exploitation, honesty — Section G is the same duty of care you already met in Unit 3, applied to the person who agrees to be studied instead of the person who agrees to be helped .

What's contested — hold these carefully

  • The replication crisis is real, and its scope is debated. The 2015 Open Science Collaboration replicated only ~36% of 100 studies at significance, with effect sizes halving — a genuine, field-shaking result. But how bad the crisis is, and how much questionable research practices vs. ordinary sampling variability drive it, is itself contested. Teach the direction as solid (the field over-published fragile, over-flexible findings; reforms like preregistration followed) without overclaiming that "most of psychology is false."
  • The evidence hierarchy ranks designs, not quality. The pyramid puts systematic reviews and RCTs on top — a good heuristic — but a poorly conducted meta-analysis is not automatically better than a well-conducted cohort study, RCTs can have poor external validity, and manualized-treatment research can miss what a naturalistic study captures. The hierarchy is a starting question, not the final answer; appraise execution, don't just read the label.
  • "Empirically supported" ≠ "best," and allegiance inflates the record. The empirically-supported-treatment list is a floor (this treatment has been shown to work for this problem), not a ranking that makes unlisted approaches worthless — and the common-factors / dodo-bird finding (Unit 9) shows technique differences are often small. Allegiance and publication bias systematically make the developer's own trials look best (the SFBT-effect-size caution from Unit 9; the group-therapy claims of Unit 10) .
  • Group averages under-describe individuals (nomothetic vs. idiographic). Everything the significance-testing machinery produces is about populations; a clinician treats a person. A large average effect leaves some clients unchanged or worse, which is exactly why single-client outcome monitoring exists alongside group research . This is the unit's central humility and the reason the stance section leads with "the number is not the person."

  • unit09-modalities and theory-solution-focused (Unit 9) — the EBP three legs and the allegiance-bias caution, given their full account here.
  • theory-yalom-factors (Unit 10) — "group ≈ individual" and "groups can harm" as effect-size / evidence-appraisal claims.
  • unit03-ethics-law, concept-informed-consent, concept-dual-relationships (Unit 3) — the clinical ethics that research ethics mirrors.

Sources

Cohen (1988) + Sullivan & Feinn (2012), effect size. p-value education + the ASA statement. Jacobson & Truax (1991), clinical significance / RCI. APA (2006), evidence-based practice in psychology. Chambless & Hollon (1998), empirically supported therapies. evidence-hierarchy library guides. Open Science Collaboration (2015) + Simmons et al. (2011), the replication crisis. Fortney et al. (2017), measurement-based care. program-evaluation toolkits + Astramovich & Coker. the Belmont Report. Nuremberg/Tuskegee/Common Rule. ACA Code, Section G. CACREP 2016 §2.F.8. pages.text: Unit 12 — Research Methods & Program Evaluation You will spend far more of your career reading research than doing it — and that reading is not optional. "Evidence-based practice" is written into the ACA Code, into insurance requirements, into your program's accreditation, and into the expectation that you can tell a client's family why you chose the approach you did. The field you are entering is also crowded with confident claims that do not survive scrutiny: brand-name therapies promising outsized effects, "brain-based" workshops, screening gadgets, and a steady stream of headlines. The skill this unit builds is discernment — the ability to look at a study, a statistic, or a marketing claim and ask the right questions: What kind of study is this? Can it support the causal claim being made? How big is the effect, and does the size matter for a real person? Who could this generalize to? Was it done ethically? The syllabus objective is deliberately practical, and the course-map is explicit about the altitude: quiz choosing the method, not executing it. You are not being trained to be a statistician; you are being trained to be a critical consumer and, for your own caseload and program, a competent evaluator . This is the final unit of the twelve-unit spine and a Tier 3 "rounding out" unit. It maps directly onto CACREP's core area Research and Program Evaluation (§2.F.8), whose framing is exactly the consumer-and-evaluator posture above: critique research to inform practice, identify evidence-based practices, run needs assessments and outcome measures, and do all of it ethically and with cultural humility S21 . It depends most on Unit 7. ← Unit 7 (this is where outcome measurement gets its methods). pages.title: Sources — Elective module: Understanding & Changing Addictive Behavior
pages.html:
Sources — Elective module: Understanding & Changing Addictive Behavior

Evidence base for ../wiki/aux-addiction.md and its concept pages. Each entry has a one-line authority note. This is an elective/ad-hoc module (off the 12-unit syllabus spine; aux- namespace); it borders Unit 6 (Psychopathology / substance use disorders) and Unit 9 (Evidence-Based Modalities). Clinically loaded topic — claims are kept precise, tied to federal health agencies (NIDA, SAMHSA, HHS), diagnostic authority (DSM-5-TR), and peer-reviewed / Cochrane work, not recovery-industry marketing. "What works" in addiction is partly contested and the disease-vs-choice framing is an active debate — both are flagged rather than smoothed over.

What addiction is: definition, diagnosis, models

  • National Institute on Drug Abuse (NIDA). Drugs, Brains, and Behavior: The Science of Addiction — "Drug Misuse and Addiction." <https://nida.nih.gov/publications/drugs-brains-behavior-science-addiction/drug-misuse-addiction> — The U.S. federal research agency's flagship public-science text. Source for the standard definition — addiction as a "chronic, relapsing disorder characterized by compulsive drug seeking and use despite adverse consequences," a brain disorder because of functional changes to reward/stress/self-control circuits — and for "no single factor determines whether a person will become addicted."
  • NIDA. Drugs, Brains, and Behavior — "Treatment and Recovery." <https://nida.nih.gov/publications/drugs-brains-behavior-science-addiction/treatment-recovery> — Source for the 40–60% relapse rate, its comparison to relapse in other chronic diseases (diabetes 30–50%, hypertension & asthma 50–70%), the framing that relapse signals treatment needs resuming/adjusting, not failure, and the principle that addiction is treatable but not simply "curable."
  • NIDA. Understanding Drug Use and Addiction (DrugFacts). <https://nida.nih.gov/publications/drugfacts/understanding-drug-use-addiction> — Concise .gov reference: drugs flood the reward circuit with dopamine; the brain adapts (tolerance), and cue-driven wanting persists; risk is multi-factorial (genes ~40–60% of risk, environment, development).
  • DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022) — Substance Use Disorders, via SAMHSA/NCBI Bookshelf (TIP / Substance Use Screening, Risk Assessment, and Use Disorder Diagnosis in Adults, Table 3). <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK565474/table/table-3/> — Diagnostic authority. The 11 SUD criteria in four groups — impaired control (1–4), social impairment (5–7), risky use (8–9), pharmacological (10–11: tolerance, withdrawal) — and the severity thresholds: mild 2–3, moderate 4–5, severe 6+. Also the rule that tolerance and withdrawal don't count toward diagnosis when the drug is taken as prescribed under medical supervision.
  • American Psychiatric Association — "What Is a Substance Use Disorder?" and "Internet Gaming." <https://www.psychiatry.org/patients-families/addiction-substance-use-disorders/what-is-a-substance-use-disorder> · <https://www.psychiatry.org/patients-families/internet-gaming> — Patient-facing but from the DSM's publisher. Confirms SUD as a treatable brain-affecting disorder and that Internet Gaming Disorder sits in DSM-5 Section III ("conditions for further study"), not as a formal diagnosis.
  • Yau YHC & Potenza MN (2015). "Gambling Disorder and Other Behavioral Addictions: Recognition and Treatment." Harvard Review of Psychiatry (PMC4458066). <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4458066/> — Peer-reviewed. Gambling disorder is the only behavioral (non-substance) addiction recognized in DSM-5-TR, moved beside substance disorders on the basis of shared symptoms, neurobiology (reward circuitry, "near-miss" effects), and treatment response; internet gaming remains provisional.

The neurobiology

  • Koob GF & Volkow ND (2016). "Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis." The Lancet Psychiatry 3(8):760–773. (Framework also summarized in the open review "The neurobiology of addiction," PMC6767400: <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6767400/>) — The canonical three-stage addiction cycle: (1) binge/intoxication — reward & incentive-salience circuitry in the basal ganglia; (2) withdrawal/negative affect — loss of reward + recruited stress systems in the extended amygdala; (3) preoccupation/anticipation — impaired executive control & craving in the prefrontal cortex. Also the shift from positive reinforcement (early, chasing the high) to negative reinforcement (later, escaping the low).

How change happens: readiness, motivation, relapse

  • Prochaska JO & DiClemente CC — the Transtheoretical Model / Stages of Change. Overview: Boston University School of Public Health, Behavioral Change Models <https://sphweb.bumc.bu.edu/otlt/mph-modules/sb/behavioralchangetheories/behavioralchangetheories6.html> · corroborated by Simply Psychology <https://www.simplypsychology.org/transtheoretical-model.html> — Foundational stage model: precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (with relapse/recycling as an expected event). Change is spiral, not linear; matching the intervention to the person's stage is the point. Decisional balance shifts as the person moves.
  • Larimer ME, Palmer RS & Marlatt GA (1999). "Relapse Prevention: An Overview of Marlatt's Cognitive-Behavioral Model." Alcohol Research & Health (NIAAA), PMC6760427. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6760427/> — Peer-reviewed (federal alcohol institute) exposition of Relapse Prevention (RP): immediate determinants (high-risk situations, coping skills, outcome expectancies, the abstinence violation effect) and covert antecedents (lifestyle, urges/cravings). Coping success raises self-efficacy and cuts relapse risk. Distinguishes a lapse (a single slip) from a relapse (return to prior pattern), and the AVE — the guilt/"I've blown it" spiral that turns one into the other.
  • SAMHSA — TIP 35: Enhancing Motivation for Change in Substance Use Disorder Treatment (Ch. 3, Motivational Interviewing), NCBI Bookshelf NBK571068. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK571068/> — Federal treatment-improvement protocol built on Miller & Rollnick's Motivational Interviewing (MI). Source for ambivalence as the target, evoking change talk vs. reinforcing sustain talk, "rolling with resistance," resisting the righting reflex (the urge to fix/argue), and the RULE heuristic (Resist the righting reflex, Understand motivations, Listen, Empower).

What treatment actually is (the evidence)

  • NIDA — "Medications for Opioid Use Disorder" (research topic) + SAMHSA MOUD guidance. <https://nida.nih.gov/research-topics/medications-opioid-use-disorder> — Three FDA-approved medications for OUD — methadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist), naltrexone (antagonist, ER injection). Methadone and buprenorphine — not naltrexone — are proven to reduce overdose and all-cause mortality (roughly halving fatal-overdose risk). MOUD stabilizes brain chemistry, cuts cravings, and enables engagement in the rest of treatment. Withholding it in favor of "medication-free" recovery is not evidence-based for OUD.
  • Kelly JF, Humphreys K & Ferri M (2020). Cochrane systematic review — "Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder"; clinician distillation in Alcohol and Alcoholism (PMC8060988). <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8060988/> · review: <https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD012880.pub2/full> — Gold-standard review: manualized AA/Twelve-Step Facilitation is more effective than other established treatments (e.g., CBT) for continuous abstinence and at least as good on other outcomes, at substantially lower cost — largely by linking people to a free, durable recovery network. A meaningful reversal of the long-standing "no evidence for AA" claim.
  • Contingency Management (CM) for stimulant use disorder — Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy; Khazanov GK et al. (2024), Addiction. <https://societyforpsychotherapy.org/contingency-management-for-stimulant-addiction-the-most-effective-evidence-based-treatment-youve-never-used/> · <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/add.16497> — CM (tangible rewards/vouchers contingent on verified abstinence) is described as the most effective, "gold-standard" treatment for stimulant use disorder — the class (cocaine, methamphetamine) with no FDA-approved medication. Note the live tension between abstinence-only CM and harm-reduction (reduced-use) goals.
  • SMART Recovery (Self-Management and Recovery Training) — organizational overview (SMART Recovery / American Addiction Centers). <https://americanaddictioncenters.org/therapy-treatment/smart-recovery> · <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMART_Recovery> — The main secular, self-empowerment alternative to 12-step mutual-help (founded 1994). A 4-Point Program (build motivation; cope with urges; manage thoughts/feelings/behaviors; live a balanced life) built on CBT/REBT and MI — no higher power, no lifelong label. Orientation source; evidence base is thinner than AA's.

The framing debate (contested — surface, don't smooth)

  • Heilig M, Kalivas P, et al. / Lewis M — the brain-disease-vs.-learning debate. "Q: Is Addiction a Brain Disease or a Moral Failing? A: Neither" (PMC5486515) <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486515/> · Lewis critique via Neuroethics (PMC5486510) <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5486510/> — The active academic dispute. The dominant brain-disease model (BDM) (NIDA/Volkow) is challenged by Marc Lewis and others who argue addiction is a learned, developmental pattern of a normally-functioning plastic brain, not a disease — and by "disorder of choice" theorists. A middle position holds it is "neither a brain disease nor a moral failing" but a disorder shaped by biology, learning, and environment. The BDM's clinical value (reduces blame, supports treatment access) is real; so is the worry that it can imply helplessness. Keep the vocabulary of all three models; don't teach any single one as settled fact.
  • U.S. Surgeon General (HHS, 2016). Facing Addiction in America: The Surgeon General's Report on Alcohol, Drugs, and Health. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK424857/> — The federal consensus report. Corroborates the chronic-condition framing, the enormous treatment gap (most people with SUD never receive specialty care), and the shift toward a public-health, continuum-of-care model. Used here for orientation/consensus, not for specific statistics beyond that framing.

The neurobiology S4 Koob GF & Volkow ND (2016). "Neurobiology of addiction: a neurocircuitry analysis." The Lancet Psychiatry 3(8):760–773. (Framework also summarized in the open review "The neurobiology of addiction," PMC6767400: <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6767400/>) — The canonical three-stage addiction cycle : (1) binge/intoxication — reward & incentive-salience circuitry in the basal ganglia ; (2) withdrawal/negative affect — loss of reward + recruited stress systems in the extended amygdala ; (3) preoccupation/anticipation — impaired executive control & craving in the prefrontal cortex. Also the shift from positive reinforcement (early, chasing the high) to negative reinforcement (later, escaping the low). How change happens: readiness, motivation, relapse S6 Prochaska JO & DiClemente CC — the Transtheoretical Model / Stages of Change. Overview: Boston University School of Public Health, Behavioral Change Models <https://sphweb.bumc.bu.edu/otlt/mph-modules/sb/behavioralchangetheories/behavioralchangetheories6.html> · corroborated by Simply Psychology <https://www.simplypsychology.org/transtheoretical-model.html> — Foundational stage model: precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (with relapse/recycling as an expected event). Change is spiral, not linear ; matching the intervention to the person's stage is the point. Decisional balance shifts as the person moves. S7 Larimer ME, Palmer RS & Marlatt GA (1999). "Relapse Prevention: An Overview of Marlatt's Cognitive-Behavioral Model." Alcohol Research & Health (NIAAA), PMC6760427. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6760427/> — Peer-reviewed (federal alcohol institute) exposition of Relapse Prevention (RP) : immediate determinants ( high-risk situations , coping skills, outcome expectancies , the abstinence violation effect ) and covert antecedents (lifestyle, urges/cravings). Coping success raises self-efficacy and cuts relapse risk. Distinguishes a lapse (a single slip) from a relapse (return to prior pattern), and the AVE — the guilt/"I've blown it" spiral that turns one into the other. S8 SAMHSA — TIP 35: Enhancing Motivation for Change in Substance Use Disorder Treatment (Ch. 3, Motivational Interviewing), NCBI Bookshelf NBK571068. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK571068/> — Federal treatment-improvement protocol built on Miller & Rollnick's Motivational Interviewing (MI) . Source for ambivalence as the target, evoking change talk vs. reinforcing sustain talk , "rolling with resistance," resisting the righting reflex (the urge to fix/argue), and the RULE heuristic (Resist the righting reflex, Understand motivations, Listen, Empower). What treatment actually is (the evidence) S9 NIDA — "Medications for Opioid Use Disorder" (research topic) + SAMHSA MOUD guidance. <https://nida.nih.gov/research-topics/medications-opioid-use-disorder> — Three FDA-approved medications for OUD — methadone (full agonist), buprenorphine (partial agonist), naltrexone (antagonist, ER injection). Methadone and buprenorphine — not naltrexone — are proven to reduce overdose and all-cause mortality (roughly halving fatal-overdose risk). MOUD stabilizes brain chemistry, cuts cravings, and enables engagement in the rest of treatment. Withholding it in favor of "medication-free" recovery is not evidence-based for OUD. S10 Kelly JF, Humphreys K & Ferri M (2020). Cochrane systematic review — "Alcoholics Anonymous and other 12-step programs for alcohol use disorder"; clinician distillation in Alcohol and Alcoholism (PMC8060988). <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8060988/> · review: <https://www.cochranelibrary.com/cdsr/doi/10.1002/14651858.CD012880.pub2/full> — Gold-standard review: manualized AA/Twelve-Step Facilitation is more effective than other established treatments (e.g., CBT) for continuous abstinence and at least as good on other outcomes, at substantially lower cost — largely by linking people to a free, durable recovery network. A meaningful reversal of the long-standing "no evidence for AA" claim. S11 Contingency Management (CM) for stimulant use disorder — Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy; Khazanov GK et al. (2024), Addiction . <https://societyforpsychotherapy.org/contingency-management-for-stimulant-addiction-the-most-effective-evidence-based-treatment-youve-never-used/> · <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/add.16497> — CM (tangible rewards/vouchers contingent on verified abstinence) is described as the most effective, "gold-standard" treatment for stimulant use disorder — the class (cocaine, methamphetamine) with no FDA-approved medication. Note the live tension between abstinence-only CM and harm-reduction (reduced-use) goals. S14 SMART Recovery (Self-Management and Recovery Training) — organizational overview (SMART Recovery / American Addiction Centers). <https://americanaddictioncenters.org/therapy-treatment/smart-recovery> · <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMART_Recovery> — The main secular, self-empowerment alternative to 12-step mutual-help (founded 1994). A 4-Point Program (build motivation; cope with urges; manage thoughts/feelings/behaviors; live a balanced life) built on CBT/REBT and MI — no higher power, no lifelong label. Orientation source; evidence base is thinner than AA's. The framing debate (contested — surface, don't smooth) S13 Heilig M, Kalivas P, et al. / Lewis M — the brain-disease-vs.-learning debate. "Q: Is Addiction a Brain Disease or a Moral Failing? A: Neither" (PMC5486515) <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5486515/> · Lewis critique via Neuroethics (PMC5486510) <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5486510/> — The active academic dispute. The dominant brain-disease model (BDM) (NIDA/Volkow) is challenged by Marc Lewis and others who argue addiction is a learned, developmental pattern of a normally-functioning plastic brain , not a disease — and by " disorder of choice " theorists. A middle position holds it is "neither a brain disease nor a moral failing" but a disorder shaped by biology, learning, and environment. The BDM's clinical value (reduces blame, supports treatment access) is real; so is the worry that it can imply helplessness. Keep the vocabulary of all three models; don't teach any single one as settled fact. S15 U.S. Surgeon General (HHS, 2016). Facing Addiction in America: The Surgeon General's Report on Alcohol, Drugs, and Health. <https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK424857/> — The federal consensus report. Corroborates the chronic-condition framing , the enormous treatment gap (most people with SUD never receive specialty care), and the shift toward a public-health, continuum-of-care model. Used here for orientation/consensus, not for specific statistics beyond that framing.

pages.title: Sources — Elective module: Psychological First Aid & Acute Grief Support
pages.html:
Sources — Elective module: Psychological First Aid & Acute Grief Support

Evidence base for ../wiki/aux-psychological-first-aid.md and its concept pages. Each entry has a one-line authority note. This is an elective/ad-hoc module (off the 12-unit syllabus spine); it leans on the same triangulation rules as any unit. Clinically heavy topic — claims are kept precise and tied to professional bodies and peer-reviewed work, not SEO grief blogs.

Psychological First Aid frameworks

  • WHO, War Trauma Foundation & World Vision International (2011). Psychological First Aid: Guide for Field Workers. Geneva: World Health Organization. WHO IRIS: <https://iris.who.int/server/api/core/bitstreams/e7e129fb-b306-496d-84a5-67bb70abc130/content> — The global consensus PFA guide; endorsed by 24+ international humanitarian agencies. Source for the Look / Listen / Link action principles and the "humane, supportive, practical help" framing.
  • National Child Traumatic Stress Network (NCTSN) & National Center for PTSD (2006). Psychological First Aid: Field Operations Guide, 2nd ed. <https://www.nctsn.org/resources/psychological-first-aid-pfa-field-operations-guide-2nd-edition> — The U.S. evidence-informed standard, co-developed by the two leading American trauma bodies. Source for the eight Core Actions.
  • U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, National Center for PTSD — Psychological First Aid (provider page). <https://www.ptsd.va.gov/disaster_events/for_providers/psychological_first_aid.asp> — .gov clinical reference. Confirms the 8 Core Actions and the objective "to reduce initial distress and foster short- and long-term adaptive functioning," and that PFA does not require survivors to talk about their experience.

Why PFA is not debriefing (the evidence that reshaped acute response)

  • Rose S, Bisson J, Churchill R, Wessely S. Psychological debriefing for preventing post traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. <https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD000560_psychological-debriefing-preventing-post-traumatic-stress-disorder-ptsd> — Gold-standard systematic review. Single-session individual psychological debriefing is not useful for preventing PTSD and may increase risk of PTSD/depression in some.
  • National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) — PTSD guideline (NG116). — UK national clinical guideline: do not offer psychologically-focused debriefing for the prevention or treatment of PTSD. (Cited via and NICE summaries; corroborates the Cochrane conclusion at guideline level.)

Grief and bereavement models

  • "Understanding grief and bereavement." PMC / NIH (PMC5033290). <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5033290/> — Peer-reviewed overview surveying Kübler-Ross, Freud's grief work, the dual process model, resilience/meaning-making, and complicated-grief features.
  • Stroebe M & Schut H (1999). The Dual Process Model of coping with bereavement. — Foundational peer-reviewed model: oscillation between loss-oriented and restoration-oriented coping. (Described in detail in and .)
  • Worden JW. Grief Counseling and Grief Therapy. — Standard clinical text; source for the Four Tasks of Mourning (accept the reality of the loss; process the pain; adjust to a world without the deceased; find an enduring connection while moving forward).
  • Stroebe M et al. / "Stages of Grief Portrayed on the Internet: A Systematic Analysis and Critical Appraisal." Frontiers in Psychology (PMC8675126). <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8675126/> — Peer-reviewed critical appraisal of the Kübler-Ross stage model: built from interviews with dying patients, not the bereaved; grief does not follow a fixed order; popular misuse can make people feel they are "grieving wrong."

Prolonged grief disorder (the clinical boundary)

  • Prigerson HG et al. (2021). Validation of the new DSM-5-TR criteria for prolonged grief disorder and the PG-13-Revised scale. World Psychiatry. <https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20823> — Peer-reviewed validation of the PGD criteria.
  • "Prolonged grief disorder in DSM-5-TR: early predictors." PMC9131400. <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9131400/> — Peer-reviewed: loss of a child and loss to unnatural/violent causes are among the strongest predictors of PGD; unpreparedness for the death raises risk.
  • DSM-5-TR (American Psychiatric Association, 2022) — Prolonged Grief Disorder. — Diagnostic authority: the 12-month (adult) / 6-month (child/adolescent) threshold and the core symptoms (intense yearning/preoccupation). Cited via and APA materials.

Practical support of the bereaved (incl. death of a child)

  • Susan Silk & Barry Goldman (2013), "How not to say the wrong thing," Los Angeles Times; explainer via Psych Central. <https://psychcentral.com/health/circle-of-grief-ring-theory> — Origin of Ring Theory ("comfort IN, dump OUT"): support flows toward the center of the crisis, complaints flow outward. Widely adopted clinical heuristic.
  • Nationwide Children's Hospital — "What to Say and What Not to Say to a Grieving Parent" (700 Children's, clinically reviewed). <https://www.nationwidechildrens.org/family-resources-education/700childrens/2023/07/grieving-a-child> — Pediatric-hospital patient-education: acknowledge the child, say the child's name, follow the parent's lead, check in over the long haul; avoid "they're in a better place," "everything happens for a reason," "I know how you feel."
  • Children's Hospital Colorado — "How to Help a Grieving Parent." <https://www.childrenscolorado.org/doctors-and-departments/departments/grief-and-loss/how-to-help-a-grieving-parent/> — Corroborating hospital grief-program guidance: presence over fixing, tolerate silence, mark anniversaries/birthdays, offer concrete help rather than "let me know if you need anything."

Death notification (added 2026-07-08)

  • Hobgood C, Harward D, Newton K, Davis W (2005). "The educational intervention 'GRIEV_ING' improves the death notification skills of residents." Academic Emergency Medicine 12(4):296–301. <https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15805319/> — Peer-reviewed origin of the GRIEV_ING death-notification protocol; a defined training built on it measurably improved resident physicians' confidence and competence.
  • American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP) — _Delivering the News with Compassion: The GRIEV_ING Death Notification Protocol_ (trainer's manual). <https://www.acep.org/siteassets/uploads/uploaded-files/acep/clinical-and-practice-management/resources/academics/deathnotificationtrainersmanual.pdf> — Professional-body training standard; full expansion of the mnemonic (Gather, Resources, Identify, Educate, Verify with the words "died"/"dead", space, Inquire, Nuts-and-bolts, Give), incl. the explicit instruction to avoid euphemisms.
  • MADD (Mothers Against Drunk Driving), adopted by the U.S. DOJ Office for Victims of Crime — Death Notification: Breaking the Bad News with Concern for the Professional and Compassion for the Survivor (training curriculum). Described in: <https://www.officer.com/home/article/10249064/death-notification-breaking-the-bad-news> — The de-facto law-enforcement standard, source of the five principles: in person, in time, in pairs, in plain language, with compassion — including "don't be afraid of the D-words; 'expired,' 'passed on,' 'lost' are words of denial."
  • Chapple A, Ziebland S (2010). "Viewing the body after bereavement due to a traumatic death: qualitative study in the UK." BMJ 340:c2032. <https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2862150/> — Peer-reviewed qualitative study (n=80 bereaved by suicide/traumatic death): of 49 who viewed, 35 said it was right, 2 regretted it (both with badly damaged bodies and no real choice); some non-viewers later wished they had. Conclusion: offer a prepared, genuine choice — "clinicians should not assume that relatives will be harmed by seeing a bruised or damaged body."
  • McCarroll JE et al. (2024). "Notification, viewing the body, and social and cultural considerations after traumatic death: a systematic literature review." Disaster Medicine and Public Health Preparedness. <https://doi.org/10.1017/dmp.2024.209> (Cambridge Core; paywalled) — Recent systematic review confirming notification + viewing-the-body as an evidence topic; abstract-level orientation only (full text not consulted).
  • [S2 — additional use] The NCTSN/NCPTSD PFA Field Operations Guide (see above) contains the acute-response sections this page leans on: when a family member is missing (accurate information, no premature reassurance), when a death occurs, support for death notification, and support for body identification (Core Action 2, Safety and Comfort).

pages.title: Unit 1 sources — Helping Skills & the Therapeutic Relationship
pages.html:
Unit 1 sources — Helping Skills & the Therapeutic Relationship

Evidence base for Unit 1 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S3].

Researched 2026-06-27. Triangulated across professional bodies, peer-reviewed/open-access work, NCBI/StatPearls, and a university course page. Lower-tier counselling-training sites used for orientation/wording only and labeled as such.

Tier: peer-reviewed / professional reference (lean on these)

  • StatPearls — Person-Centered Therapy (Rogerian Therapy), NCBI Bookshelf. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK589708/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI). Authority: high. Key points: Three core conditions — accurate empathy ("the therapist conveys an accurate understanding of the patient's private world"), congruence (therapist transparently conveys feelings/thoughts to genuinely relate), unconditional positive regard (a warm environment conveying clients are accepted unconditionally). Rogers proposed six necessary-and-sufficient conditions for change (incl. psychological contact, client incongruence, and the client's perception of the therapist's empathy/UPR). Pioneered early 1940s; tied to the Human Potential Movement. Client problem = incongruence between self-image and experienced reality. Limitations noted: critics say the principles are "too vague," there's "a lack of controlled research on the efficacy," and it may be less suited to clients who struggle to talk about themselves. Evidence mixed: not inferior to CBT at 6 months for depression, possibly inferior at 12 months; comparable for trauma with fewer dropouts.
  • Flückiger, Del Re, Wampold & Horvath (2018), The Alliance in Adult Psychotherapy: A Meta-Analytic Synthesis, Psychotherapy. (Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy copy.) https://societyforpsychotherapy.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/Fluckiger-et-al-2018.pdf Definitive alliance meta-analysis. Authority: high (peer-reviewed). Headline: alliance–outcome r = .278 (95% CI [.256, .299]), k = 295 independent studies, >30,000 patients (1978–2017), face-to-face and internet-based. One of the most robust and replicated predictors in psychotherapy research. (Association is correlational; direction/causation debated — alliance and improvement likely reinforce each other.) Cross-check: PMC summary confirms d ≈ 0.57 / r ≈ .28 figure across >30,000 clients.
  • Wampold (2015), How important are the common factors in psychotherapy? An update, World Psychiatry 14(3). https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/wps.20238/full Leading common-factors statement. Authority: high (peer-reviewed). NOTE: full text was paywalled on fetch (HTTP 402); claims below corroborated via search abstracts + secondary summaries — verify exact effect sizes against the primary before quoting numerically. Contextual Model: a treatment works when it has (a) a cogent rationale the client accepts, (b) is delivered by a clinician with whom the client has a therapeutic relationship, and (c) involves actions the client expects to help. Argues common factors (alliance, empathy, expectations, goal consensus) carry much of psychotherapy's effect — the relationship "seemingly outstripping" technique, though contemporary view is relationship and technique work together, not in opposition.
  • Therapeutic Alliance and Outcome of Psychotherapy: Historical Excursus, Measurements, and Prospects, PMC3198542. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3198542/ Open-access review. Authority: high. Bordin (1979) reformulated alliance as transtheoretical, three components: bond (the affective relationship), task (agreement on the in-session activities/techniques), goal (agreement on the desired outcomes). Bordin held the alliance influences outcome not by being curative itself but as the ingredient that lets the client accept/follow/believe in the treatment. Led to measures: Working Alliance Inventory (WAI), Penn Helping Alliance Questionnaire. Since 2002 APA recognizes alliance as an empirically validated common factor.

Tier: university / institutional (good for structure)

  • Penn State World Campus, RHS 301 — Counseling Microskills. https://courses.worldcampus.psu.edu/welcome/rhs301/001/content/01_lesson/06_page.html University course page. Authority: medium-high (.edu, teaching material). Ivey microskills hierarchy (pyramid, base → top): foundation = Rogerian conditions (genuineness, empathy, UPR) + ethics + multicultural competence → attending behavior (eye contact, vocal quality, verbal tracking, body language) → observation skills (verbal/nonverbal mismatches) → open & closed questions → reflecting/encouraging/paraphrasing/summarizing & reflection of feeling → (higher) the five-stage interview → influencing skills (self-disclosure, confrontation, interpretation). Master lower skills before higher.
  • iResearchNet — Allen Ivey (History of Counseling). https://psychology.iresearchnet.com/counseling-psychology/history-of-counseling/allen-ivey/ Reference encyclopedia. Authority: medium. Ivey developed microcounseling/microskills (~1967–1971) to isolate teachable units of helping behavior. Approach validated by 450+/600+ data-based studies per the publisher's claims (treat the exact count as marketing — directionally well-supported).
  • counseling.education — Reflecting & Listening Skills. https://counseling.education/counseling/skills/reflecting.html Counselor-educator teaching site. Authority: medium (orientation/wording). Reflecting content (paraphrase): repeating back a version of what the client said (shows listening; weaker alone). Reflecting feeling: names the client's emotion, requires a wide feeling vocabulary matched to intensity. Summarizing: broadest — condenses several paraphrases/reflections, used at session start/end. Interpretation: going beyond what the client said — adding the counselor's read of meaning/needs (an influencing skill, higher up the hierarchy, more risk).
  • Duan, Wei & others / A Comparison of Empathy and Sympathy Between Counselors-in-Training and Their Non-Counseling Academic Peers, The Professional Counselor (NBCC journal). https://tpcjournal.nbcc.org/a-comparison-of-empathy-and-sympathy-between-counselors-in-training-and-their-non-counseling-academic-peers/ Peer-reviewed counseling journal (National Board for Certified Counselors). Authority: high for the empathy/sympathy distinction specifically. Empathy has affective + cognitive components — experiencing and comprehending another's emotional state (Vossen, Piotrowski & Valkenburg, 2015). Sympathy "like empathy, involves an understanding of another's emotion and includes an emotional response, but it consists of feelings of sorrow or concern for the distressed or needy other rather than merely feeling the same emotion" (Eisenberg et al., 2010). Clinical stakes: Clark (2010) warns that "the misapplication of sympathetic responses as empathic responses can interfere in the counseling relationship" — clients need empathic, not sympathetic, responses.

Tier: orientation only (wording/teaching gloss — NOT load-bearing for claims)

  • CounsellingTutor — Rogers' core conditions / reflecting & paraphrasing. https://counsellingtutor.com/counselling-approaches/person-centred-approach-to-counselling/carl-rogers-core-conditions/ Training site. Authority: low. Orientation/phrasing only; corroborate any claim against S1/S4.
  • SimplyPsychology — Client-Centred Therapy. https://www.simplypsychology.org/client-centred-therapy.html Popular education site. Authority: low. Orientation only.

In-depth upgrade additions (researched 2026-07-19)

Sources added when Unit 1 was upgraded concise → in-depth. Same triangulation/authority rules. Two anchor books (Carkhuff 1969; Egan 1975) are offline — corroborated via reputable secondary summaries + the primary publication record, and flagged inline.

Tier: peer-reviewed / professional reference

  • Eubanks, Muran & Safran (2018), Alliance Rupture Repair: A Meta-Analysis, Psychotherapy 55(4), 508–519. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30335462/ Peer-reviewed meta-analysis (Div. 29 task force). Authority: high. A rupture = a deterioration in the alliance — disagreement on goals, lack of collaboration on tasks, or a strain in the bond (note: maps onto Bordin's three components). Two markers: withdrawal ruptures (client moves away — placating, denying, going silent, changing subject) and confrontation ruptures (client moves against — anger, complaints, pressure/control). Meta-analysis of rupture-repair vs. outcome: r = .29 (k = 11, N = 1,314), a moderate positive relation; rupture-resolution training also improved outcomes. Foundational work: Safran & Muran (2000), Negotiating the Therapeutic Alliance — repairing a rupture may benefit the client more than an alliance with no ruptures.
  • Common-factors history — primary/secondary composite. Rosenzweig (1936), Some Implicit Common Factors in Diverse Methods of Psychotherapy, Am. J. Orthopsychiatry — coined "common factors" and invoked the Dodo bird ("Everybody has won, and all must have prizes"). Frank & Frank (1961/1991), Persuasion and Healing — clients arrive demoralized; four shared healing components (an emotionally charged confiding relationship, a healing setting, a rationale/myth, and a ritual/procedure) + the expectation of help. Assay & Lambert (1999) — the widely-reproduced "pie": ~40% client/extratherapeutic, ~30% relationship, ~15% expectancy/placebo, ~15% technique. Wampold & Imel (2015), The Great Psychotherapy Debate (2nd ed.) — the modern Contextual-Model statement. Corroboration: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_factors_theory; simplypsychology.org dodo-bird page. Authority: high for the primary claims (classic, heavily cited). Caveat: the Lambert percentages are an illustrative heuristic, not a formal variance decomposition — cite as "roughly," not as measured partition.
  • Montgomery et al. (2024), The shifting sound of silence: A constructivist grounded theory, Counselling and Psychotherapy Research (Wiley). https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/capr.12654 Peer-reviewed. Authority: high (for silence typology). Therapeutic silence falls into productive, neutral, and obstructive categories; productive silences give the client space to access emotion, find expression, or reflect. Silence is part of attending; it is most useful after a strong alliance and when a client is processing intense feeling. Cross-check: positivepsychology.com/silence-in-therapy; counselingschools.com. Tier: institutional / teaching (structure & wording; classics corroborated across ≥2)

  • Carkhuff's five-level empathy scale (Carkhuff, 1969, Helping and Human Relations; from Truax & Carkhuff, 1967). Offline book → corroborated across: counsellingcentral.com/understanding-empathy-a-deep-dive-into-robert-carkhuffs-empathy-scale/; CounsellingTutor "Carkhuff Rating Scales Explained" (PDF); sites.google.com empathy-training-lit-review (Carkhuff 1969). L3 interchangeable — accurately reflects the client's expressed content and feeling, no more, no less; the minimally facilitative baseline for effective helping. Authority: medium-high. 1902–1987. Method arc: non-directive (1942) → client-centered (1951, Client-Centered Therapy — the 19 propositions / self-theory of personality; the phenomenological field) → person-centered (extended to education, groups, conflict). Actualizing tendency (innate growth drive — "violets through concrete"). 1957 "necessary and sufficient conditions" paper. 1982 APA survey: ranked #1 most influential psychotherapist in America. Later peace/cross-cultural work (Belfast, South Africa, Soviet Union; Rust workshop); widely reported to have been nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize (1987). Criticisms: vagueness/oversimplification; the "organismic trusting" / "if it feels right it is right" objection; reflection reduced to parody; Western individualism. (1967), The Therapeutic Relationship and Its Impact: A Study of Psychotherapy with Schizophrenics — long read as a disappointment (the conditions did not produce dramatic gains with hospitalized patients, and the project was marred by an internal data dispute), though it showed modest positive outcomes, especially when patients were more "in contact." Authority: medium (orientation); the concepts trace to Rogers (1959), "A Theory of Therapy, Personality, and Interpersonal Relationships." Organismic valuing process = an innate internal compass rating experience by whether it serves actualization. Conditions of worth = when significant others give conditional positive regard, the child internalizes their standards and starts valuing experience by others' criteria — creating incongruence between the self-concept and organismic experience (the engine of distress that UPR is meant to reverse).
  • Egan's Skilled Helper & SOLER. Gerard Egan, The Skilled Helper (1975), Loyola Univ. Chicago — offline book → corroborated across counsellingtutor.com (Egan/SOLER + Skilled-Helper approach) and counsellingcentral.com/the-egan-model-and-soler/ and the Life Charity SOLER handout. Authority: medium-high (a standard counselor-training text). SOLER operationalizes attending as observable behaviors: Squarely face the client, Open posture, Lean slightly in, Eye contact (without staring), Relax. The Skilled Helper three-stage map: Stage 1 Current Picture (what's going on?), Stage 2 Preferred Picture (what do I want instead?), Stage 3 The Way Forward (how do I get there?). Caveat: SOLER's norms (direct eye contact, square facing) are culturally specific — to be used flexibly, not as a rigid rule (see unit04-multicultural); Egan himself framed it as a guide.

Open threads / where sources disagree or hedge

  • "Necessary and sufficient" (Rogers, 1957): the strong claim that the six conditions are all that's needed is contested — most integrative clinicians treat the conditions as necessary but not sufficient. Flag in the reading.
  • Alliance causation: the r≈.28 association is robust but correlational; whether a strong alliance causes improvement or partly reflects early improvement is debated. Don't overclaim.
  • Person-centered efficacy: evidence is mixed vs. CBT (S1); good rapport ≠ proven superiority.
  • Microskills study counts (450–600 studies): publisher figures; cite as "extensively studied," not a hard number.
  • Lambert's percentages (40/30/15/15): a memorable heuristic, not a formal variance decomposition — repeatedly reproduced but methodologically contested. Present as "roughly," and note the debate about whether common factors can even be cleanly separated from technique (S16).
  • Carkhuff / Egan anchors offline: the empathy-scale (S11) and SOLER/Skilled-Helper (S14) primary books weren't fetchable; both are classics corroborated across ≥2 independent teaching sources, but exact level-wording and stage-wording should be verified against the primary before clinical use.
  • SOLER is culturally loaded: direct eye contact / square facing read as respectful in dominant US-white norms but intrusive elsewhere — the Unit 4 material complicates it; the reading flags it.
  • Rogers Nobel nomination (1987): widely reported but nomination records are sealed 50 years — stated as "reportedly nominated," not as verified fact.
  • Wisconsin project: honest read is "landmark that tempered the sufficient claim" — modest, not null, results; don't caricature it as a clean failure or inflate it as a success (S12).
