pages.title: Unit 2 sources — Counseling Theories: The Major Schools
pages.html:
Unit 2 sources — Counseling Theories: The Major Schools

Evidence base for Unit 2 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S5].

Researched 2026-06-27. Triangulated across NCBI/StatPearls peer-reviewed clinical references, an open textbook (OpenStax), peer-reviewed journal articles (PMC), an academic book chapter, and encyclopedic references. Lower-tier training/blog sites used for orientation/wording only and labeled as such. Anchor text (not online): Corey, Theory and Practice of Counseling and Psychotherapy — the standard survey; used as the structural backbone, corroborated online.

Tier: peer-reviewed / professional reference (lean on these)

  • StatPearls — Psychodynamic Therapy, NCBI Bookshelf (NBK606117). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK606117/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI). Authority: high. Key points: psychodynamic theory holds that "unconscious thoughts, desires, and memories significantly impact behavior"; the unconscious is "a vast reservoir of often repressed or forgotten material that continues to influence behaviors and emotions, even if people are unaware of its influence." Emphasizes unresolved conflicts from early childhood. Defense mechanisms = "unconscious psychological strategies that individuals use to cope with anxiety"; Anna Freud distinguished adaptive vs. maladaptive. Transference = "unconscious redirection of feelings, expectations, and relational patterns from past relationships—especially early ones—onto the therapist"; countertransference = the clinician's unconscious reactions to the patient. Change mechanisms: insight, affect (emotional processing), and the therapeutic alliance. Lineage: Freud (1890s) → Anna Freud / ego psychology → object relations. Limitations: effective for depression/anxiety but "limited or less robust" evidence for OCD, PTSD, psychosis; criticized for difficulty of empirical validation and cost/length.
  • StatPearls — Defense Mechanisms, NCBI Bookshelf (NBK559106). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559106/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI). Authority: high. Defense mechanisms as unconscious anxiety-management; named exemplars: repression, denial, projection, displacement, sublimation, rationalization, reaction formation. Used for the defense-mechanism examples in the psychodynamic page.
  • StatPearls — Person-Centered Therapy (Rogerian Therapy), NCBI Bookshelf (NBK589708). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK589708/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI). Authority: high. (Shared with Unit 1.) Pioneered by Rogers (early 1940s); grounded in the idea people are "inherently motivated toward achieving positive psychological functioning" (the actualizing tendency). Client is the expert in their own life and leads the direction; therapist is non-directive. Three core conditions: empathy, congruence, unconditional positive regard. Client problem = incongruence between self-image and experienced reality. Limitations: principles can be "too vague," efficacy evidence mixed (not inferior to CBT for depression at 6 months, possibly inferior at 12).
  • StatPearls — Cognitive Behavior Therapy, NCBI Bookshelf (NBK470241). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK470241/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI). Authority: high. CBT links thoughts, emotions, behaviors; "dysfunctional automatic thoughts that are exaggerated, distorted, mistaken, or unrealistic … play a significant role in psychopathology." Three levels: automatic thoughts (immediate interpretations), cognitive distortions (dichotomous thinking, overgeneralization, catastrophizing, mind reading, personalization), underlying beliefs (intermediate conditional rules; core beliefs like "I am inadequate"). Beck developed CT in the 1960s after observing depressed patients' cognitive distortions, reframing depression as fundamentally a cognitive disorder. Typical course ≈ 8–12 weekly sessions; often combined with medication. Extensively researched; effective for depression, anxiety, eating disorders, substance abuse, personality disorders, and as an adjunct for bipolar/schizophrenia.
  • A Historical and Theoretical Review of Cognitive Behavioral Therapies, PMC6208646. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6208646/ Peer-reviewed (open access). Authority: high. REBT (Ellis, 1950s) and Cognitive Therapy (Beck, 1960s) are the two earliest CBTs. Ellis's ABC model: emotional disturbance is caused not by events (A) but by beliefs/evaluations (B) about them, producing consequences (C); REBT is "the original form and one of the main pillars" of CBT. Ellis emphasized the rational/irrational distinction and a more confrontational disputation style; Beck more collaborative, treating automatic thoughts as hypotheses to test (collaborative empiricism) rather than errors to argue away. Used for the Ellis-vs-Beck distinction.
  • Yalom, Existential Psychotherapy (1980) — the four ultimate concerns. Corroborated via: Wikipedia summary https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_Psychotherapy_(book) and Yalom's own site https://www.yalom.com/existential-psychotherapy Primary framework (Yalom 1980). Authority: high as a primary source; accessed here via reputable secondary summaries — verify exact wording against the book before quoting verbatim. Yalom argues psychological distress stems from confrontation with four ultimate concerns / givens of existence: (1) death — the inevitable, ultimate limitation; (2) freedom — we are the sole authors of our lives and therefore responsible, which is groundless and anxiety-provoking; (3) isolation — our ultimate aloneness (born and die alone); (4) meaninglessness — no given meaning, so we must create our own. Each confrontation generates an "existential dynamic conflict."
  • Existential isolation review, PMC5553124. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5553124/ Peer-reviewed (open access). Authority: high (for the isolation typology). Distinguishes existential isolation (the unbridgeable gap between self and others) from interpersonal isolation (being apart from other people) and intrapersonal isolation (disconnection from parts of oneself). Used to keep the three senses of "isolation" straight.
  • Differentiation of self: A scoping review of Bowen Family Systems Theory's core construct, ScienceDirect (2021). https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0272735821001446 Peer-reviewed scoping review. Authority: high (for differentiation). Differentiation of self — the cornerstone of Bowen's model — is the capacity to maintain a clear sense of self and make values-based decisions while managing emotional reactivity yet remaining emotionally connected to others. Links to the multigenerational transmission process (people partner at similar differentiation levels; levels can decline across generations).
  • Brown (2024), Bowen family systems theory and practice: Illustration and critique revisited, Australian & New Zealand Journal of Family Therapy. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/anzf.1589 Peer-reviewed. Authority: high (for the critique). Revisits Bowen theory's strengths and limitations (e.g., debates over empirical operationalization of differentiation, cultural/gender critiques of the differentiation ideal). Used to flag what is contested in family-systems theory.

Tier: open textbook / institutional (good for structure & corroboration)

  • OpenStax, Psychology 2e, §16.2 Types of Treatment. https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/16-2-types-of-treatment Open textbook (peer-reviewed, Rice University). Authority: high. Crisp orientation contrasts used in the hub page: • Psychoanalysis/psychodynamic — "most of our psychological problems are the result of repressed impulses and trauma experienced in childhood"; past-oriented; directive; uses free association, dream analysis, transference. Modern version "less intensive than Freud's original." • CBT — "how you think determines how you feel and act"; targets cognitive distortions + self-defeating behaviors; present-oriented; directive; ABC model. Behavioral subtype: maladaptive responses learned via classical/operant conditioning, changed via counterconditioning, exposure, systematic desensitization, token economies. • Humanistic/Rogerian — client-centered, non-directive ("does not give advice or provide interpretations"); focuses on conscious thoughts and the present/future; uses active listening, UPR, genuineness, empathy; problem = incongruence between real and ideal self. (Note: this OpenStax section does not cover family-systems or postmodern therapies — those are sourced from S10–S14.)
  • LibreTexts (Kelland), Personality Theory in a Cultural Context — Viktor Frankl and Logotherapy. https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Psychology/Culture_and_Community/Personality_Theory_in_a_Cultural_Context_(Kelland)/09%3A_Viktor_Frankl_Rollo_May_and_Existential_Psychology/9.03%3A_Viktor_Frankl_and_Logotherapy Open textbook. Authority: medium-high. Frankl's will-to-meaning (vs. Freud's will-to-pleasure, Adler's will-to-power). Three sources of meaning: (1) creating/achieving through work or a deed; (2) experiencing something or encountering someone (esp. love); (3) the attitude one takes toward unavoidable suffering — "the last of the human freedoms." Failure to find meaning → existential vacuum and noogenic neurosis. Techniques: paradoxical intention (deliberately intensify the feared symptom to gain distance) and dereflection (redirect attention away from anxious self-monitoring).
  • EBSCO Research Starters — Family systems theory. https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/health-and-medicine/family-systems-theory Curated encyclopedic reference. Authority: medium-high. The family is an emotional unit / system; the individual's symptom is understood in the context of relationships, not in isolation. Bowen contributed differentiation and triangulation (a two-person tension recruits a third to stabilize). Minuchin's structural family therapy focuses on family structure, subsystems, and boundaries as enacted in the session. Source of the "problem lives in the relationship system" framing and the Bowen-vs-Minuchin contrast.
  • Tarragona (2008), Postmodern/Poststructuralist Therapies (academic book chapter). https://is.muni.cz/el/fss/jaro2012/PST450/um/Tarragona_2008_Postmodern_Therapies.pdf Academic book chapter (course-hosted PDF). Authority: medium-high. Social constructionism: no single objective truth; reality is constructed through language and relationship; meaning emerges in dialogue. Therapist adopts a non-expert, collaborative stance. SFBT (de Shazer & Berg): future-oriented, resource-focused — miracle question, exception questions, scaling. Narrative (White & Epston): "the person is not the problem"; externalizing the problem; dominant (problem-saturated) story vs. alternative story; unique outcomes; re-authoring a preferred narrative.
  • SAGE Encyclopedia of Theory in Counseling and Psychotherapy — Solution-Focused Brief Therapy. https://sk.sagepub.com/ency/edvol/the-sage-encyclopedia-of-theory-in-counseling-and-psychotherapy/chpt/solutionfocused-brief-therapy Reference encyclopedia (peer-reviewed editorial). Authority: high. SFBT as a postmodern, constructivist, future-oriented, anti-deterministic approach; clients are assumed able to change quickly and to construct "problem-free" language toward a new reality; cofounded by Steve de Shazer and Insoo Kim Berg; arose alongside early family therapy.

Tier: orientation only (wording/teaching gloss — NOT load-bearing for claims)

  • Survey data on theoretical orientation (integrative/eclectic prevalence). Aggregated via ScienceDirect topic page and a teaching summary of APA Division 12 (2010) data. https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/psychology/theoretical-orientation Authority: medium; treat figures as approximate. Across large therapist surveys, integrative/eclectic is consistently among the most common self-identified orientations; estimates vary widely by sample (one survey: only ~15% used a single orientation; APA Div. 12 2010: cognitive ≈ 31%, eclectic ≈ 22%; range commonly cited ~13–42%). Used only for the "most counselors end up integrative" claim, stated with a hedge.
  • SimplyPsychology — Logotherapy / Humanistic Psychology. https://www.simplypsychology.org/logotherapy.html Popular education site. Authority: low. Orientation/phrasing only; corroborate against S6/S7.
  • GoodTherapy — Family Systems Therapy. https://www.goodtherapy.org/learn-about-therapy/types/family-systems-therapy Consumer therapy directory. Authority: low. Orientation only; corroborate against S10–S12.

Open threads / where sources disagree or hedge

  • Psychodynamic evidence base: supportive for depression/anxiety but weaker/contested for OCD, PTSD, psychosis; long-standing critique that core constructs (the unconscious, transference) are hard to operationalize and falsify . Flag in the reading.
  • Person-centered "sufficiency": Rogers held the core conditions are necessary and sufficient; mainstream view is necessary-but-not-sufficient (see Unit 1 concept-core-conditions) .
  • Differentiation of self: central to Bowen but its measurement and cross-cultural validity are debated; the "differentiation" ideal has drawn gender/cultural critique .
  • Integrative/eclectic prevalence : directionally well-supported (it's common), but exact percentages vary widely by survey, profession, and year — cite as "most" / "among the most common," not a hard number.
  • Yalom's four givens : a clinically influential framework, not an experimentally tested taxonomy — present it as an organizing lens, not a measured fact.

pages.title: Unit 3 sources — Ethics, Law & Professional Identity
pages.html:
Unit 3 sources — Ethics, Law & Professional Identity

Evidence base for Unit 3 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1].

Researched 2026-07-06. Anchored on the primary document itself — the 2014 ACA Code of Ethics (full text extracted and quoted verbatim) — triangulated with peer-reviewed clinical references (NCBI/StatPearls, PMC), primary case law (Cornell LII), professional bodies (APA, ACA), a federal clearinghouse (.gov), and university/.edu pages. Lower-tier practice-blog sources used for orientation/wording only and labeled as such. Anchor text (not online): Remley & Herlihy, Ethical, Legal, and Professional Issues in Counseling — used as the structural model for how counseling programs teach this material; every substantive claim here is corroborated online.

Tier: primary documents & case law (the ground truth)

  • American Counseling Association — 2014 ACA Code of Ethics (official PDF, counseling.org). https://www.counseling.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/ethics/2014-aca-code-of-ethics.pdf The primary document — the profession's own code, approved by the ACA Governing Council. Authority: highest (it IS the object of study). Full text extracted; all standard numbers and quotes below are verbatim. Key content used: Preamble — five core professional values (human development across the lifespan; diversity/multiculturalism; social justice; integrity of the counselor–client relationship; competent and ethical practice) and six ethical principles: autonomy ("fostering the right to control the direction of one's life"), nonmaleficence ("avoiding actions that cause harm"), beneficence ("working for the good of the individual and society"), justice ("treating individuals equitably and fostering fairness and equality"), fidelity ("honoring commitments and keeping promises"), veracity ("dealing truthfully"). Purpose section: nine sections A–I; "No specific ethical decision-making model is always most effective"; "A breach of the standards and principles provided herein does not necessarily constitute legal liability or violation of the law." A.2.a informed consent as ongoing process, reviewed "in writing and verbally"; A.2.b types of information needed (purposes, goals, techniques, risks/benefits, qualifications, continuation of services, role of technology). A.4.a avoiding harm. A.5.a sexual/romantic relationships with current clients, their partners, or family members prohibited (in-person and electronic); A.5.c former clients — prohibited for 5 years after last professional contact, and even then requires documented forethought that it isn't exploitive; A.5.d friends/family prohibited where objectivity is impaired; A.5.e personal virtual relationships with current clients prohibited. A.6.a–e managing boundaries: previous relationships, extending boundaries (weddings, hospital visits, purchasing a client's product), documenting boundary extensions prior to the interaction when feasible, role changes require fresh informed consent, avoiding harmful nonprofessional relationships. B.1.b respect for privacy; B.1.c "Counselors disclose information only with appropriate consent or with sound legal or ethical justification"; B.1.d explanation of limitations "at initiation and throughout." B.2.a the general confidentiality requirement "does not apply when disclosure is required to protect clients or identified others from serious and foreseeable harm or when legal requirements demand"; consult when in doubt. B.2.b end-of-life exception (option to maintain confidentiality); B.2.c contagious life-threatening diseases (may disclose to identifiable third parties at serious/foreseeable risk, after assessing client's intent to inform; follow state law); B.2.d court-ordered disclosure (seek client consent or seek to limit/prohibit disclosure); B.2.e minimal disclosure ("only essential information is revealed"). C.2.a boundaries of competence ("education, training, supervised experience, state and national professional credentials, and appropriate professional experience"; multicultural competency required across all specialties); C.2.b new specialty areas only after education/training/supervised experience; C.2.d monitor effectiveness; C.2.f continuing education; C.2.g impairment (refrain from providing services when impaired). I.1.c conflicts between ethics and laws: make known commitment to the Code, try to resolve; if unresolvable, "may adhere to the requirements of the law."
  • Jaffee v. Redmond, 518 U.S. 1 (1996) — opinion text, Cornell Law School LII. https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/95-266.ZO.html Primary case law (U.S. Supreme Court), hosted by Cornell's Legal Information Institute. Authority: highest for what the case held. 7–2 decision (Stevens): recognized a psychotherapist–patient privilege under Federal Rule of Evidence 501 — protecting confidential communications from compelled disclosure in federal court. Reasoning: effective psychotherapy "depends upon an atmosphere of confidence and trust"; "the mere possibility of disclosure may impede development of the confidential relationship necessary for successful treatment." Privilege explicitly extended to licensed social workers (the therapist in the case was a clinical social worker). Used for the privacy/confidentiality/privilege distinction.

Tier: peer-reviewed / professional reference (lean on these)

  • StatPearls — Duty to Warn, NCBI Bookshelf (NBK542236). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542236/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI). Authority: high. Tarasoff case facts (Poddar/Tarasoff, 1968–69; therapist Dr. Lawrence Moore alerted campus police; Poddar released; clinical notes ordered destroyed; Tarasoff killed October 1969). Tarasoff I (1974) = duty to warn the potential victim; Tarasoff II (1976) = broader duty to protect ("take reasonable precautions to protect these third parties"). Justice Tobriner: "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." Reasonable protective steps menu: increase appointment frequency, arrange removal of weapons, adjust/initiate medication, voluntary/involuntary hospitalization, involve family, notify victim or police. State variation (as of the article's 2012-based count): 23 states mandatory by statute, 10 common-law duty, 11 permissive, 6 no guidance (incl. e.g. Arkansas, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota). Post-Tarasoff cases: Jablonski v. United States (must review prior records), Ewing v. Goldstein (threats communicated by family members count, in CA). APA (1987) threat criteria: specific identifiable victim + intent and ability + imminence. Candid about limits: "guidelines on accurately predicting and assessing dangerousness are lacking."
  • Darby, W. C., & Weinstock, R. (2018). The Limits of Confidentiality: Informed Consent and Psychotherapy. Focus (Am Psychiatr Publ), via PMC (PMC6493245). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6493245/ Peer-reviewed journal article (PMC open access). Authority: high. Standard mandated exceptions (danger to self/others, child and elder abuse; state-specific additions). Notes there is often "no specific legal obligation to inform patients of the limits of confidentiality," but ethical duties require it; exhaustive up-front warnings would be "time prohibitive and unnecessarily frightening for rare scenarios"; patients show poor retention of consent information weeks later — supports treating informed consent as an ongoing process, not a one-time signature.
  • APA Services — Mandatory reporting (patient confidentiality series). https://www.apaservices.org/practice/legal/patient-confidentiality/mandatory-reporting Professional body (American Psychological Association practice arm). Authority: high. Categories: child abuse/neglect, elder & vulnerable-adult abuse/neglect, duty to warn/protect. Trigger = suspicion, not proof; timing "typically require[s] immediate action." "All states and the District of Columbia provide some form of immunity from liability for good faith reporting." Failure to report: criminal charges (misdemeanor→felony), fines/jail, plus civil liability. Emphasizes knowing your jurisdiction's specific law.
  • Child Welfare Information Gateway — Mandatory Reporters of Child Abuse and Neglect (State Statutes Series). https://www.childwelfare.gov/topics/systemwide/laws-policies/statutes/manda/ Federal clearinghouse (.gov, U.S. Children's Bureau). Authority: high. The page indexes the full state-by-state statute compilation. Covers which professional groups are mandated reporters, standards for making a report, privileged-communication carve-outs, reporter-identity confidentiality. Used as the pointer for "check your state's statute."
  • APA — What Is the Difference Between Psychologists, Psychiatrists and Social Workers? (apa.org, PTSD guideline patient pages). https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/patients-and-families/psychotherapy-professionals Professional body (APA). Authority: high. Training paths: psychiatrists = MD/DO + psychiatry residency (3–4 yrs), prescribe, biologically focused; psychologists = doctoral degree (PhD/PsyD/EdD), 4–6 yrs + supervised practice + licensure; social workers = MSW → LCSW after supervised clinical work; counselors = master's → licensure (LPC).
  • APA Services — About prescribing psychologists (RxP). https://www.apaservices.org/advocacy/issues/prescriptive-authority/prescribing-psychologists Professional body (APA practice arm). Authority: high — but dated: lists the first five RxP states. New Mexico (2002, first), Louisiana (2004), Illinois (2014), Iowa (2016), Idaho (2017); also DoD, U.S. Public Health Service, Indian Health Service. Requires postdoctoral MS in clinical psychopharmacology + supervised hours + national psychopharmacology exam. Note: later reporting (Cato Institute 2024; Behavioral Health Business 2025) adds Colorado (2023) and Utah (2024) — treat "how many states" as a moving target (~7 as of 2024–25).

Tier: university / open-textbook (solid orientation)

  • Open textbook — Ethical Practice in Co-Occurring Substance Use Disorder and Mental Health Counseling, ch. 1.4 "Ethical Codes and Standards" (Univ. of Minnesota open library). https://open.lib.umn.edu/ethicalpractice/chapter/1-4-ethical-codes-and-standards/ Open textbook, University of Minnesota. Authority: moderate-high. Corroborates the nine-section structure of the 2014 ACA Code and the six ethical principles as the foundation for the standards.
  • Northwestern University (Counseling@Northwestern) — Understanding the ACA Code of Ethics. https://counseling.northwestern.edu/blog/aca-code-of-ethics/ University counseling-program page (.edu blog). Authority: moderate — orientation; consistent with . Plain-language definitions of the six principles; sections each open with an aspirational introduction.

Tier: practitioner / orientation only (wording and examples; not load-bearing)

  • Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy — Boundaries and Multiple Relationships in Psychotherapy: Recommendations for Ethical Practice. https://societyforpsychotherapy.org/boundaries-and-multiple-relationships-in-psychotherapy-recommendations-for-ethical-practice/ APA Division 29's practitioner outlet. Authority: moderate. Boundary crossing = nonpejorative departure from common practice that may even help (shaking an extended hand; extending a session in crisis) vs. boundary violation = departure that is harmful/exploitative and places the client or the work at serious risk (e.g., romantic relationship). Multiple relationships become problems when they impair judgment, exploit, or raise risk of harm.
  • Zur Institute (Ofer Zur) — Dual Relationships, Multiple Relationships, Boundaries, Boundary Crossings & Boundary Violations. https://www.zurinstitute.com/boundaries-dual-relationships/ Practitioner CE site by a boundaries specialist. Authority: moderate/orientation — used for the rural/small-community unavoidability point and terminology mapping (ACA says "nonprofessional relationships"; APA says "multiple relationships"), cross-checked against /.

Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings)

  1. "Duty to warn" is a misnomer in most places. The 1976 ruling replaced warn with the broader protect, and state law varies enormously (mandatory / permissive / silent). Any flat statement "therapists must warn" is wrong as law in many states.
  2. Prediction is shaky. StatPearls is explicit that validated tools for predicting dangerousness are lacking — the legal duty assumes a predictive ability the science doesn't cleanly support. This is the field's own critique of Tarasoff.
  3. How much to disclose up front is genuinely debated: exhaustive confidentiality warnings may chill disclosure and aren't retained anyway; the ethical consensus is a clear, plain-language summary at intake plus revisiting as situations arise (consent as process).
  4. RxP state count is a moving target — sources disagree (5 vs 7) because the APA page is dated; flagged in the reading.
  5. State variation pervades everything legal in this unit (reporting triggers, privilege statutes, duty-to-protect specifics). The readings teach the pattern and repeatedly point to "check your state's statute."

Anchored on the primary document itself — the 2014 ACA Code of Ethics (full text extracted and quoted verbatim) — triangulated with peer-reviewed clinical references (NCBI/StatPearls, PMC), primary case law (Cornell LII), professional bodies (APA, ACA), a federal clearinghouse (.gov), and university/.edu pages. Lower-tier practice-blog sources used for orientation/wording only and labeled as such. Anchor text (not online): Remley & Herlihy, Ethical, Legal, and Professional Issues in Counseling — used as the structural model for how counseling programs teach this material; every substantive claim here is corroborated online. Tier: primary documents & case law (the ground truth) S1 American Counseling Association — 2014 ACA Code of Ethics (official PDF, counseling.org). https://www.counseling.org/docs/default-source/default-document-library/ethics/2014-aca-code-of-ethics.pdf The primary document — the profession's own code, approved by the ACA Governing Council. Authority: highest (it IS the object of study). Full text extracted; all standard numbers and quotes below are verbatim. Key content used: Preamble — five core professional values (human development across the lifespan; diversity/multiculturalism; social justice; integrity of the counselor–client relationship; competent and ethical practice) and six ethical principles : autonomy ("fostering the right to control the direction of one's life"), nonmaleficence ("avoiding actions that cause harm"), beneficence ("working for the good of the individual and society"), justice ("treating individuals equitably and fostering fairness and equality"), fidelity ("honoring commitments and keeping promises"), veracity ("dealing truthfully"). Purpose section: nine sections A–I; "No specific ethical decision-making model is always most effective"; "A breach of the standards and principles provided herein does not necessarily constitute legal liability or violation of the law." A.2.a informed consent as ongoing process, reviewed "in writing and verbally"; A.2.b types of information needed (purposes, goals, techniques, risks/benefits, qualifications, continuation of services, role of technology). A.4.a avoiding harm. A.5.a sexual/romantic relationships with current clients, their partners, or family members prohibited (in-person and electronic); A.5.c former clients — prohibited for 5 years after last professional contact, and even then requires documented forethought that it isn't exploitive; A.5.d friends/family prohibited where objectivity is impaired; A.5.e personal virtual relationships with current clients prohibited. A.6.a–e managing boundaries: previous relationships, extending boundaries (weddings, hospital visits, purchasing a client's product), documenting boundary extensions prior to the interaction when feasible, role changes require fresh informed consent, avoiding harmful nonprofessional relationships. B.1.b respect for privacy; B.1.c "Counselors disclose information only with appropriate consent or with sound legal or ethical justification"; B.1.d explanation of limitations "at initiation and throughout." B.2.a the general confidentiality requirement "does not apply when disclosure is required to protect clients or identified others from serious and foreseeable harm or when legal requirements demand"; consult when in doubt. B.2.b end-of-life exception (option to maintain confidentiality); B.2.c contagious life-threatening diseases (may disclose to identifiable third parties at serious/foreseeable risk, after assessing client's intent to inform; follow state law); B.2.d court-ordered disclosure (seek client consent or seek to limit/prohibit disclosure); B.2.e minimal disclosure ("only essential information is revealed"). C.2.a boundaries of competence ("education, training, supervised experience, state and national professional credentials, and appropriate professional experience"; multicultural competency required across all specialties); C.2.b new specialty areas only after education/training/supervised experience; C.2.d monitor effectiveness; C.2.f continuing education; C.2.g impairment (refrain from providing services when impaired). I.1.c conflicts between ethics and laws: make known commitment to the Code, try to resolve; if unresolvable, "may adhere to the requirements of the law." S2 Jaffee v. Redmond, 518 U.S. 1 (1996) — opinion text, Cornell Law School LII. https://www.law.cornell.edu/supct/html/95-266.ZO.html Primary case law (U.S. Supreme Court), hosted by Cornell's Legal Information Institute. Authority: highest for what the case held. 7–2 decision (Stevens): recognized a psychotherapist–patient privilege under Federal Rule of Evidence 501 — protecting confidential communications from compelled disclosure in federal court . Reasoning: effective psychotherapy "depends upon an atmosphere of confidence and trust"; "the mere possibility of disclosure may impede development of the confidential relationship necessary for successful treatment." Privilege explicitly extended to licensed social workers (the therapist in the case was a clinical social worker). Used for the privacy/confidentiality/privilege distinction. Tier: peer-reviewed / professional reference (lean on these) S3 StatPearls — Duty to Warn , NCBI Bookshelf (NBK542236). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK542236/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI). Authority: high. Tarasoff case facts (Poddar/Tarasoff, 1968–69; therapist Dr. Lawrence Moore alerted campus police; Poddar released; clinical notes ordered destroyed; Tarasoff killed October 1969). Tarasoff I (1974) = duty to warn the potential victim; Tarasoff II (1976) = broader duty to protect ("take reasonable precautions to protect these third parties"). Justice Tobriner: "The protective privilege ends where the public peril begins." Reasonable protective steps menu: increase appointment frequency, arrange removal of weapons, adjust/initiate medication, voluntary/involuntary hospitalization, involve family, notify victim or police. State variation (as of the article's 2012-based count): 23 states mandatory by statute, 10 common-law duty, 11 permissive, 6 no guidance (incl. e.g. Arkansas, Kansas, Maine, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota). Post-Tarasoff cases: Jablonski v. United States (must review prior records), Ewing v. Goldstein (threats communicated by family members count, in CA). APA (1987) threat criteria: specific identifiable victim + intent and ability + imminence. Candid about limits: "guidelines on accurately predicting and assessing dangerousness are lacking." S4 Darby, W. C., & Weinstock, R. (2018). The Limits of Confidentiality: Informed Consent and Psychotherapy. Focus (Am Psychiatr Publ), via PMC (PMC6493245). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6493245/ Peer-reviewed journal article (PMC open access). Authority: high. Standard mandated exceptions (danger to self/others, child and elder abuse; state-specific additions). Notes there is often "no specific legal obligation to inform patients of the limits of confidentiality," but ethical duties require it; exhaustive up-front warnings would be "time prohibitive and unnecessarily frightening for rare scenarios"; patients show poor retention of consent information weeks later — supports treating informed consent as an ongoing process , not a one-time signature. S5 APA Services — Mandatory reporting (patient confidentiality series). https://www.apaservices.org/practice/legal/patient-confidentiality/mandatory-reporting Professional body (American Psychological Association practice arm). Authority: high. Categories: child abuse/neglect, elder & vulnerable-adult abuse/neglect, duty to warn/protect. Trigger = suspicion , not proof; timing "typically require[s] immediate action." "All states and the District of Columbia provide some form of immunity from liability for good faith reporting." Failure to report: criminal charges (misdemeanor→felony), fines/jail, plus civil liability. Emphasizes knowing your jurisdiction's specific law. S6 Child Welfare Information Gateway — Mandatory Reporters of Child Abuse and Neglect (State Statutes Series). https://www.childwelfare.gov/topics/systemwide/laws-policies/statutes/manda/ Federal clearinghouse (.gov, U.S. Children's Bureau). Authority: high. The page indexes the full state-by-state statute compilation. Covers which professional groups are mandated reporters, standards for making a report, privileged-communication carve-outs, reporter-identity confidentiality. Used as the pointer for "check your state's statute." S7 APA — What Is the Difference Between Psychologists, Psychiatrists and Social Workers? (apa.org, PTSD guideline patient pages). https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline/patients-and-families/psychotherapy-professionals Professional body (APA). Authority: high. Training paths: psychiatrists = MD/DO + psychiatry residency (3–4 yrs), prescribe, biologically focused; psychologists = doctoral degree (PhD/PsyD/EdD), 4–6 yrs + supervised practice + licensure; social workers = MSW → LCSW after supervised clinical work; counselors = master's → licensure (LPC). S8 APA Services — About prescribing psychologists (RxP). https://www.apaservices.org/advocacy/issues/prescriptive-authority/prescribing-psychologists Professional body (APA practice arm). Authority: high — but dated : lists the first five RxP states. New Mexico (2002, first), Louisiana (2004), Illinois (2014), Iowa (2016), Idaho (2017); also DoD, U.S. Public Health Service, Indian Health Service. Requires postdoctoral MS in clinical psychopharmacology + supervised hours + national psychopharmacology exam. Note: later reporting (Cato Institute 2024; Behavioral Health Business 2025) adds Colorado (2023) and Utah (2024) — treat "how many states" as a moving target (~7 as of 2024–25). pages.title: Unit 4 sources — Multicultural & Social-Justice Competence
pages.html:
Unit 4 sources — Multicultural & Social-Justice Competence

Evidence base for Unit 4 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1].

Researched 2026-07-06. Anchored on the profession's two framework documents — the 1992 multicultural counseling competencies (Sue, Arredondo & McDavis) and their 2015 successor, the MSJCC (official ACA-endorsed PDF + ACA's own companion article) — triangulated with the primary articles behind each core concept (Tervalon & Murray-García 1998; Berry 1997; Sue et al. 2007; McIntosh 1989; Day-Vines et al. 2007), peer-reviewed outcome research (Hook 2013; Tao 2015 meta-analysis), and the published critiques (Lilienfeld 2017; the MCC-measurement literature). Anchor text (not online): Sue, Sue, Neville & Smith, Counseling the Culturally Diverse — used as the structural model for how programs teach this unit; every substantive claim here is corroborated online.

Tier: primary framework documents (the ground truth)

  • Ratts, Singh, Nassar-McMillan, Butler & McCullough (2015) — Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies (official PDF, counseling.org). https://www.counseling.org/docs/default-source/competencies/multicultural-and-social-justice-counseling-competencies.pdf The primary document — endorsed by AMCD (June 29, 2015) and ACA (July 20, 2015). Authority: highest (it IS the object of study). Structure: four developmental domains — (1) counselor self-awareness, (2) client worldview, (3) counseling relationship, (4) counseling and advocacy interventions; the first three each carry aspirational competencies AKSA — attitudes & beliefs, knowledge, skills, action (the addition to the 1992 triad). Four quadrants crossing counselor × client privileged/marginalized statuses: I privileged counselor–marginalized client; II privileged–privileged; III marginalized counselor–privileged client; IV marginalized–marginalized — identities are fluid and intersectional, so counselor and client each hold both privileged and marginalized statuses at once. Advocacy domain is organized on a socioecological model with six levels: intrapersonal → interpersonal → institutional → community → public policy → international/global.
  • Ratts, Singh, Butler, Nassar-McMillan & McCullough — Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies: Practical applications in counseling (Counseling Today / counseling.org). https://www.counseling.org/publications/counseling-today-magazine/article-archive/article/legacy/multicultural-and-social-justice-counseling-competencies-practical-applications-in-counseling The authors' own plain-language companion in ACA's magazine. Authority: high (same authors, ACA outlet). Quadrant wording ("reflect the fluidity of identities and how dynamics of power, privilege and oppression impact the counseling relationship"); worked advocacy examples (school counselor gets a wheelchair-accessible route fixed; connecting clients to identity-affirming community organizations); explicit framing of MSJCC as an update of the 1992 competencies that moves beyond "majority counselor / minority client" to bidirectional, intersectional privilege dynamics.
  • Sue, Arredondo & McDavis (1992). Multicultural Counseling Competencies and Standards: A Call to the Profession. Journal of Counseling & Development, 70(4), 477–486. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/j.1556-6676.1992.tb01642.x The founding document of the tripartite model (paywalled; abstract + heavy secondary corroboration via ). Authority: highest for what the 1992 model says. Defines multicultural counseling competence as three characteristics: (1) awareness of the counselor's own values, biases, and worldview; (2) knowledge of the client's worldview, customs, and sociopolitical context; (3) culturally appropriate intervention skills — each crossed with beliefs/attitudes, knowledge, and skills dimensions. Operationalized into 31 competencies by Arredondo et al. (1996). The most widely used and researched MCC model in the literature.
  • Tervalon, M., & Murray-García, J. (1998). Cultural Humility Versus Cultural Competence: A Critical Distinction in Defining Physician Training Outcomes in Multicultural Education. J Health Care Poor Underserved, 9(2), 117–125. https://melanietervalon.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/08/CulturalHumility_Tervalon-and-Murray-Garcia-Article.pdf (mirror: https://med.umn.edu/sites/med.umn.edu/files/cultural_humility_versus_cultural_competence.jhealthpoorunderserved.1998.pdf) The primary article that coined "cultural humility" (author-hosted + UMN-hosted PDFs; content corroborated via and secondary summaries). Authority: highest for the concept. Cited in 1,500+ peer-reviewed articles by 2019. Cultural humility = "a lifelong commitment to self-evaluation and self-critique, to redressing the power imbalances … and to developing mutually beneficial and non-paternalistic … partnerships with communities." Three commitments: (1) lifelong self-evaluation & self-critique, (2) redressing power imbalances in the clinician–client dyad, (3) institutional accountability / non-paternalistic partnership. Core critique of "competence": it implies a masterable endpoint — a finite body of knowledge one can complete — which misrepresents culture and invites false confidence.
  • McIntosh, P. (1989). White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack. Peace and Freedom Magazine. https://med.umn.edu/sites/med.umn.edu/files/2022-12/White-Privilege_McIntosh-1989.pdf The primary essay (UMN-hosted PDF; also hosted by the National SEED Project, which McIntosh founded). Authority: highest for the concept; the standard teaching text on privilege. Privilege as "an invisible package of unearned assets" — the knapsack metaphor; ~50 concrete everyday examples; the key move is that privilege is unearned and invisible to its holder ("invisible systems conferring dominance"), which is why counselor self-awareness work is required rather than optional.

Tier: peer-reviewed primary research (lean on these)

  • Sue, D. W., Capodilupo, Torino, Bucceri, Holder, Nadal & Esquilin (2007). Racial Microaggressions in Everyday Life: Implications for Clinical Practice. American Psychologist, 62(4), 271–286. https://www.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/default/files/event/263076/media/slspublic/Sue-RadicalMicroagressionsInEverydayLife.pdf (PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17516773/) Peer-reviewed (American Psychologist); the taxonomy's primary source. Authority: high. Microaggressions = "brief and commonplace daily verbal, behavioral, or environmental indignities, whether intentional or unintentional, that communicate hostile, derogatory, or negative racial slights and insults." Taxonomy: microassault (explicit, usually conscious derogation — name-calling, deliberate exclusion), microinsult (rude/demeaning slights, often unconscious — "you're so articulate"), microinvalidation (negating the person's experiential reality — "I don't see color," "anyone can succeed if they work hard"). Clinical relevance: they occur in therapy and rupture the alliance.
  • Berry, J. W. (1997). Immigration, Acculturation, and Adaptation. Applied Psychology: An International Review, 46(1), 5–34. https://iaap-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1464-0597.1997.tb01087.x The canonical acculturation framework (paywalled; abstract + corroboration via ); cited 16,000+ times. Authority: highest for the model. Two independent dimensions: (1) maintain heritage culture/identity? (2) seek contact/participation with the larger society? Crossing them yields four strategies: integration (yes/yes), assimilation (no/yes), separation (yes/no), marginalization (no/no — originally "deculturation"). Acculturative stress; integration consistently predicts the best psychological and sociocultural adaptation, marginalization the worst.
  • Hook, Davis, Owen, Worthington & Utsey (2013). Cultural Humility: Measuring Openness to Culturally Diverse Clients. Journal of Counseling Psychology, 60(3), 353–366. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25602610/ (correction notice; original 2013 JCP) Peer-reviewed; the empirical operationalization of cultural humility in therapy. Authority: high. Defines cultural humility as an other-oriented (rather than self-focused) interpersonal stance, marked by respect and lack of superiority toward the client's cultural background. Client-rated therapist cultural humility → stronger working alliance → better therapy outcomes (alliance mediates). Notable: it is the client's perception that carries the effect.
  • Tao, Owen, Pace & Imel (2015). A Meta-Analysis of Multicultural Competencies and Psychotherapy Process and Outcome. Journal of Counseling Psychology, 62(3), 337–350. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26167650/ Peer-reviewed meta-analysis (20 independent samples). Authority: high — the best single summary of whether MCC "works." Client-perceived therapist MCC correlates strongly with process variables (r ≈ .58–.72 with alliance, satisfaction) and moderately with outcomes (r ≈ .29). Key caveat: effects are for client perceptions; therapist self-reported MCC is a much weaker predictor.
  • Day-Vines, N. L., et al. (2007). Broaching the Subjects of Race, Ethnicity, and Culture During the Counseling Process. Journal of Counseling & Development, 85(4), 401–409. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ775546 Peer-reviewed (JCD); the standard framework for raising culture in session. Authority: high. Broaching = the counselor's ability to consider and raise how sociopolitical factors (race, ethnicity, culture) influence the client's concerns. Continuum of five styles: avoidant → isolating → continuing/incongruent (awkward, mechanical) → integrated/congruent (meaningful, substantive) → infusing (extends beyond sessions into the counselor's life). Broaching done well strengthens the alliance and outcomes; a 2021 JCD update (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jcad.12380) adds concrete strategies.

Tier: critiques & the state of the evidence (surface, don't smooth over)

  • Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy — The State of Multicultural Counseling Competencies Research. https://www.societyforpsychotherapy.org/the-state-of-multicultural-counseling-competencies-research/ APA Division 29's practitioner-research outlet. Authority: moderate-high; a candid literature review. Measurement problems: self-report MCC instruments (MCI, MAKSS, CCCI-R) correlate with social desirability, and after controlling for it, self-reported MCC showed no association with actual multicultural case-conceptualization ability (Constantine & Ladany, 2000). Heavy reliance on analogue studies and pseudo-clients; "surprisingly little empirical research" with real clients. Client-perceived competence ≠ therapist self-rated competence.
  • Lilienfeld, S. O. (2017). Microaggressions: Strong Claims, Inadequate Evidence. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 12(1), 138–169. https://scottlilienfeld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/lilienfeld2017-3.pdf Peer-reviewed critique (author-hosted PDF). Authority: high — the standard scientific counterweight. The microaggression research program's five premises (clear operationalization; uniformly negative interpretation by minority group members; implicitly aggressive motives; valid assessment via subjective report alone; adverse mental-health impact) are each under-supported; definitions are elastic; proposes "perceived racial slight" as a more neutral term; recommends abandoning the "aggression" implication pending better evidence. Sue's rejoinder conceded many points while defending the lived-experience research tradition. Both sides continue: Williams (2019, Perspect Psychol Sci) answers Lilienfeld point-by-point.

Tier: professional bodies & disparities data (context)

  • Wikipedia — Cultural humility (used as a corroborated index to the primary literature, not as an authority). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_humility Tertiary; every claim taken from it is anchored to /. Authority: orientation only. Confirms the Tervalon & Murray-García definition/dimensions and the competence-as-endpoint critique; notes 1,500+ citations by 2019.
  • Simply Psychology — What Is Acculturation and Why It Happens + Maricopa open textbook, Berry's Model of Acculturation. https://www.simplypsychology.org/acculturation-definition.html · https://open.maricopa.edu/culturepsychology/chapter/berrys-model-of-acculturation/ Tertiary teaching summaries (one SEO-tier, one open textbook). Authority: orientation only; used to corroborate the standard reading of , not for load-bearing claims. Standard presentation of the two dimensions, four strategies, and the integration-best/marginalization-worst adaptation gradient.
  • NIMHD Research Spotlight — Examining Why Mental Health Service Use and Dropout Rates Vary Across Racial/Ethnic Groups (+ PMC: mental-illness stigma in Black, Latina/o, and Asian Americans). https://www.nimhd.nih.gov/news-events/research-spotlight/examining-why-mental-health-service-use-and-dropout-rates-vary · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5568160/ Federal research institute (.gov) + peer-reviewed (PMC). Authority: high. Among U.S. adults with mental disorders, racial/ethnic minority clients are roughly half as likely as White clients to receive treatment and more likely to drop out before completing it; stigma runs higher in several minority communities and predicts treatment avoidance; barriers include language access, cost, mistrust of providers, and culturally shaped understandings of distress and help-seeking. This is the outcome data that makes the unit clinical, not decorative.
  • American Counseling Association (2014). ACA Code of Ethics, Standard C.2.a. (see Unit 3 sources file, there) Already on file from Unit 3. Multicultural competency is an ethical requirement across all specialties — boundaries of competence explicitly include "multicultural competency" — which is the formal bridge from Unit 3 to this unit.

Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings)

  1. "Competence" vs. "humility" is a live framing debate. Tervalon & Murray-García's critique — competence implies a masterable endpoint — is widely accepted in training programs, yet the field's official frameworks (MSJCC) still use "competencies." Most current writers treat them as complements (humility is the stance, competencies the learnable content), but the tension is real and worth knowing by name.
  2. Self-reported multicultural competence is a weak, possibly invalid signal. It correlates with social desirability, and controlling for that erases its association with actual case-conceptualization ability. What predicts outcomes is the client's perception of the counselor's competence/humility — a humbling result that is itself an argument for humility.
  3. The MCC→outcome effect is moderate, not overwhelming (r ≈ .29 in Tao et al.), and the evidence base leans on analogue studies and pseudo-clients. Strong claims in either direction outrun the data.
  4. Microaggression research is genuinely contested. Sue's taxonomy is standard curriculum AND Lilienfeld's critique (elastic definitions, subjective-report-only assessment, unproven causal mental-health claims) is published in a top journal — with Sue conceding several points. Learn both; a program will expect the taxonomy, a good program will also expect the critique.
  5. Berry's four boxes are tidier than reality. Widely taught, but later work criticizes the categories as static and context-blind (people integrate at work and separate at home; the "choice" of strategy is constrained by the receiving society's openness). Berry himself pairs each individual strategy with a society-level condition (multiculturalism, melting pot, segregation, exclusion).
  6. MSJCC's advocacy mandate has boundary questions. How far "counseling and advocacy interventions" should extend (in-office empowerment vs. public-policy activism) is debated within the profession; the framework itself brackets advocacy "with, and on behalf of" clients at six socioecological levels but leaves scope judgments to the counselor.
pages.text: Unit 4 sources — Multicultural & Social-Justice Competence Evidence base for Unit 4 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1] . Researched 2026-07-06. Anchored on the profession's two framework documents — the 1992 multicultural counseling competencies (Sue, Arredondo & McDavis) and their 2015 successor, the MSJCC (official ACA-endorsed PDF + ACA's own companion article) — triangulated with the primary articles behind each core concept (Tervalon & Murray-García 1998; Berry 1997; Sue et al. 2007; McIntosh 1989; Day-Vines et al. 2007), peer-reviewed outcome research (Hook 2013; Tao 2015 meta-analysis), and the published critiques (Lilienfeld 2017; the MCC-measurement literature). Anchor text (not online): Sue, Sue, Neville & Smith, Counseling the Culturally Diverse — used as the structural model for how programs teach this unit; every substantive claim here is corroborated online. Tier: primary framework documents (the ground truth) S1 Ratts, Singh, Nassar-McMillan, Butler & McCullough (2015) — Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies (official PDF, counseling.org). https://www.counseling.org/docs/default-source/competencies/multicultural-and-social-justice-counseling-competencies.pdf The primary document — endorsed by AMCD (June 29, 2015) and ACA (July 20, 2015). Authority: highest (it IS the object of study). Structure: four developmental domains — (1) counselor self-awareness, (2) client worldview, (3) counseling relationship, (4) counseling and advocacy interventions; the first three each carry aspirational competencies AKSA — attitudes & beliefs, knowledge, skills, action (the addition to the 1992 triad). Four quadrants crossing counselor × client privileged/marginalized statuses: I privileged counselor–marginalized client; II privileged–privileged; III marginalized counselor–privileged client; IV marginalized–marginalized — identities are fluid and intersectional, so counselor and client each hold both privileged and marginalized statuses at once. Advocacy domain is organized on a socioecological model with six levels: intrapersonal → interpersonal → institutional → community → public policy → international/global. S2 Ratts, Singh, Butler, Nassar-McMillan & McCullough — Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies: Practical applications in counseling (Counseling Today / counseling.org). https://www.counseling.org/publications/counseling-today-magazine/article-archive/article/legacy/multicultural-and-social-justice-counseling-competencies-practical-applications-in-counseling The authors' own plain-language companion in ACA's magazine. Authority: high (same authors, ACA outlet). Quadrant wording ("reflect the fluidity of identities and how dynamics of power, privilege and oppression impact the counseling relationship"); worked advocacy examples (school counselor gets a wheelchair-accessible route fixed; connecting clients to identity-affirming community organizations); explicit framing of MSJCC as an update of the 1992 competencies that moves beyond "majority counselor / minority client" to bidirectional, intersectional privilege dynamics. S3 Sue, Arredondo & McDavis (1992). Multicultural Counseling Competencies and Standards: A Call to the Profession. Journal of Counseling & Development, 70(4), 477–486. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/j.1556-6676.1992.tb01642.x The founding document of the tripartite model (paywalled; abstract + heavy secondary corroboration via S2 S11 S12 ). Authority: highest for what the 1992 model says. Defines multicultural counseling competence as three characteristics: (1) awareness of the counselor's own values, biases, and worldview; (2) knowledge of the client's worldview, customs, and sociopolitical context; (3) culturally appropriate intervention skills — each crossed with beliefs/attitudes, knowledge, and skills dimensions. Operationalized into 31 competencies by Arredondo et al. (1996). The most widely used and researched MCC model in the literature. S11 S12 S4 Tervalon, M., & Murray-García, J. (1998). Cultural Humility Versus Cultural Competence: A Critical Distinction in Defining Physician Training Outcomes in Multicultural Education. J Health Care Poor Underserved, 9(2), 117–125. https://melanietervalon.com/wp-content/uploads/2013/08/CulturalHumility_Tervalon-and-Murray-Garcia-Article.pdf (mirror: https://med.umn.edu/sites/med.umn.edu/files/cultural_humility_versus_cultural_competence.jhealthpoorunderserved.1998.pdf) The primary article that coined "cultural humility" (author-hosted + UMN-hosted PDFs; content corroborated via S13 and secondary summaries). Authority: highest for the concept. Cited in 1,500+ peer-reviewed articles by 2019. Cultural humility = "a lifelong commitment to self-evaluation and self-critique, to redressing the power imbalances … and to developing mutually beneficial and non-paternalistic … partnerships with communities." Three commitments: (1) lifelong self-evaluation & self-critique, (2) redressing power imbalances in the clinician–client dyad, (3) institutional accountability / non-paternalistic partnership. Core critique of "competence": it implies a masterable endpoint — a finite body of knowledge one can complete — which misrepresents culture and invites false confidence. S5 McIntosh, P. (1989). White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack. Peace and Freedom Magazine. https://med.umn.edu/sites/med.umn.edu/files/2022-12/White-Privilege_McIntosh-1989.pdf The primary essay (UMN-hosted PDF; also hosted by the National SEED Project, which McIntosh founded). Authority: highest for the concept; the standard teaching text on privilege. Privilege as "an invisible package of unearned assets" — the knapsack metaphor; ~50 concrete everyday examples; the key move is that privilege is unearned and invisible to its holder ("invisible systems conferring dominance"), which is why counselor self-awareness work is required rather than optional. Tier: peer-reviewed primary research (lean on these) S6 Sue, D. W., Capodilupo, Torino, Bucceri, Holder, Nadal & Esquilin (2007). Racial Microaggressions in Everyday Life: Implications for Clinical Practice. American Psychologist, 62(4), 271–286. https://www.law.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/default/files/event/263076/media/slspublic/Sue-RadicalMicroagressionsInEverydayLife.pdf (PubMed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17516773/) Peer-reviewed (American Psychologist); the taxonomy's primary source. Authority: high. Microaggressions = "brief and commonplace daily verbal, behavioral, or environmental indignities, whether intentional or unintentional, that communicate hostile, derogatory, or negative racial slights and insults." Taxonomy: microassault (explicit, usually conscious derogation — name-calling, deliberate exclusion), microinsult (rude/demeaning slights, often unconscious — "you're so articulate"), microinvalidation (negating the person's experiential reality — "I don't see color," "anyone can succeed if they work hard"). Clinical relevance: they occur in therapy and rupture the alliance. S7 Berry, J. W. (1997). Immigration, Acculturation, and Adaptation. Applied Psychology: An International Review, 46(1), 5–34. https://iaap-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1464-0597.1997.tb01087.x The canonical acculturation framework (paywalled; abstract + corroboration via S14 ); cited 16,000+ times. Authority: highest for the model. Two independent dimensions: (1) maintain heritage culture/identity? (2) seek contact/participation with the larger society? Crossing them yields four strategies: integration (yes/yes), assimilation (no/yes), separation (yes/no), marginalization (no/no — originally "deculturation"). Acculturative stress; integration consistently predicts the best psychological and sociocultural adaptation, marginalization the worst. S8 Hook, Davis, Owen, Worthington & Utsey (2013). Cultural Humility: Measuring Openness to Culturally Diverse Clients. Journal of Counseling Psychology, 60(3), 353–366. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25602610/ (correction notice; original 2013 JCP) Peer-reviewed; the empirical operationalization of cultural humility in therapy. Authority: high. Defines cultural humility as an other-oriented (rather than self-focused) interpersonal stance , marked by respect and lack of superiority toward the client's cultural background. Client-rated therapist cultural humility → stronger working alliance → better therapy outcomes (alliance mediates). Notable: it is the client's perception that carries the effect. S9 Tao, Owen, Pace & Imel (2015). A Meta-Analysis of Multicultural Competencies and Psychotherapy Process and Outcome. Journal of Counseling Psychology, 62(3), 337–350. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26167650/ Peer-reviewed meta-analysis (20 independent samples). Authority: high — the best single summary of whether MCC "works." Client-perceived therapist MCC correlates strongly with process variables (r ≈ .58–.72 with alliance, satisfaction) and moderately with outcomes (r ≈ .29) . Key caveat: effects are for client perceptions ; therapist self-reported MCC is a much weaker predictor. S10 Day-Vines, N. L., et al. (2007). Broaching the Subjects of Race, Ethnicity, and Culture During the Counseling Process. Journal of Counseling & Development, 85(4), 401–409. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ775546 Peer-reviewed (JCD); the standard framework for raising culture in session. Authority: high. Broaching = the counselor's ability to consider and raise how sociopolitical factors (race, ethnicity, culture) influence the client's concerns. Continuum of five styles: avoidant → isolating → continuing/incongruent (awkward, mechanical) → integrated/congruent (meaningful, substantive) → infusing (extends beyond sessions into the counselor's life). Broaching done well strengthens the alliance and outcomes; a 2021 JCD update (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jcad.12380) adds concrete strategies. Tier: critiques & the state of the evidence (surface, don't smooth over) S11 Society for the Advancement of Psychotherapy — The State of Multicultural Counseling Competencies Research . https://www.societyforpsychotherapy.org/the-state-of-multicultural-counseling-competencies-research/ APA Division 29's practitioner-research outlet. Authority: moderate-high; a candid literature review. Measurement problems: self-report MCC instruments (MCI, MAKSS, CCCI-R) correlate with social desirability , and after controlling for it, self-reported MCC showed no association with actual multicultural case-conceptualization ability (Constantine & Ladany, 2000). Heavy reliance on analogue studies and pseudo-clients; "surprisingly little empirical research" with real clients. Client-perceived competence ≠ therapist self-rated competence. S12 Lilienfeld, S. O. (2017). Microaggressions: Strong Claims, Inadequate Evidence. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 12(1), 138–169. https://scottlilienfeld.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/lilienfeld2017-3.pdf Peer-reviewed critique (author-hosted PDF). Authority: high — the standard scientific counterweight. The microaggression research program's five premises (clear operationalization; uniformly negative interpretation by minority group members; implicitly aggressive motives; valid assessment via subjective report alone; adverse mental-health impact) are each under-supported; definitions are elastic; proposes "perceived racial slight" as a more neutral term; recommends abandoning the "aggression" implication pending better evidence. Sue's rejoinder conceded many points while defending the lived-experience research tradition. Both sides continue: Williams (2019, Perspect Psychol Sci ) answers Lilienfeld point-by-point. Tier: professional bodies & disparities data (context) S13 Wikipedia — Cultural humility (used as a corroborated index to the primary literature, not as an authority). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_humility Tertiary; every claim taken from it is anchored to S4 / S8 . Authority: orientation only. Confirms the Tervalon & Murray-García definition/dimensions and the competence-as-endpoint critique; notes 1,500+ citations by 2019. S14 Simply Psychology — What Is Acculturation and Why It Happens + Maricopa open textbook, Berry's Model of Acculturation . https://www.simplypsychology.org/acculturation-definition.html · https://open.maricopa.edu/culturepsychology/chapter/berrys-model-of-acculturation/ Tertiary teaching summaries (one SEO-tier, one open textbook). Authority: orientation only; used to corroborate the standard reading of S7 , not for load-bearing claims. Standard presentation of the two dimensions, four strategies, and the integration-best/marginalization-worst adaptation gradient. S15 NIMHD Research Spotlight — Examining Why Mental Health Service Use and Dropout Rates Vary Across Racial/Ethnic Groups (+ PMC: mental-illness stigma in Black, Latina/o, and Asian Americans). https://www.nimhd.nih.gov/news-events/research-spotlight/examining-why-mental-health-service-use-and-dropout-rates-vary · https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5568160/ Federal research institute (.gov) + peer-reviewed (PMC). Authority: high. Among U.S. adults with mental disorders, racial/ethnic minority clients are roughly half as likely as White clients to receive treatment and more likely to drop out before completing it; stigma runs higher in several minority communities and predicts treatment avoidance; barriers include language access, cost, mistrust of providers, and culturally shaped understandings of distress and help-seeking. This is the outcome data that makes the unit clinical, not decorative. S16 American Counseling Association (2014). ACA Code of Ethics , Standard C.2.a. (see Unit 3 sources file, S1 there) Already on file from Unit 3. Multicultural competency is an ethical requirement across all specialties — boundaries of competence explicitly include "multicultural competency" — which is the formal bridge from Unit 3 to this unit. Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings) "Competence" vs. "humility" is a live framing debate. Tervalon & Murray-García's critique — competence implies a masterable endpoint — is widely accepted in training programs, yet the field's official frameworks (MSJCC) still use "competencies." Most current writers treat them as complements (humility is the stance , competencies the learnable content ), but the tension is real and worth knowing by name. S4 S1 S13 Self-reported multicultural competence is a weak, possibly invalid signal. It correlates with social desirability, and controlling for that erases its association with actual case-conceptualization ability. What predicts outcomes is the client's perception of the counselor's competence/humility — a humbling result that is itself an argument for humility. S11 S9 S8 The MCC→outcome effect is moderate, not overwhelming (r ≈ .29 in Tao et al.), and the evidence base leans on analogue studies and pseudo-clients. Strong claims in either direction outrun the data. S9 S11 Microaggression research is genuinely contested. Sue's taxonomy is standard curriculum AND Lilienfeld's critique (elastic definitions, subjective-report-only assessment, unproven causal mental-health claims) is published in a top journal — with Sue conceding several points. Learn both; a program will expect the taxonomy, a good program will also expect the critique. S6 S12 Berry's four boxes are tidier than reality. Widely taught, but later work criticizes the categories as static and context-blind (people integrate at work and separate at home; the "choice" of strategy is constrained by the receiving society's openness). Berry himself pairs each individual strategy with a society-level condition (multiculturalism, melting pot, segregation, exclusion). S7 S14 MSJCC's advocacy mandate has boundary questions. How far "counseling and advocacy interventions" should extend (in-office empowerment vs. public-policy activism) is debated within the profession; the framework itself brackets advocacy "with, and on behalf of" clients at six socioecological levels but leaves scope judgments to the counselor. S1 S2
