pages.title: Unit 5 sources — Human Development Across the Lifespan
pages.html:
Unit 5 sources — Human Development Across the Lifespan

Evidence base for Unit 5 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1].

Researched 2026-07-17. Anchored on peer-reviewed clinical references (NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls for Erikson and Piaget; a Development and Psychopathology framework review for attachment; the open-access Biopsychosocial Model of Health and Disease volume for Engel), triangulated with the primary methodological papers (van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg's cross-cultural meta-analysis; Main & Solomon's disorganized category; Bartholomew & Horowitz / Hazan & Shaver / the AAI for adult attachment) and professional-body guidance (AAP developmental surveillance). Orientation-tier teaching summaries (Simply Psychology, LibreTexts) are used only to corroborate the standard reading of the primaries, and flagged as such. Anchor text (not online): Broderick & Blewitt, The Life Span (written for helping professions) — used as the structural model for how this material is taught to counselors; every substantive claim here is corroborated online.

Tier: peer-reviewed clinical references & primary theory (ground truth)

  • Orenstein, G. A., & Lewis, L. (updated 2022). Erikson's Stages of Psychosocial Development. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK556096. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556096/ (table: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556096/table/article-21284.table0/) Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI Bookshelf). Authority: high for the model as taught clinically. Eight sequential psychosocial stages across the lifespan, each a tension between a positive (syntonic) and negative (dystonic) tendency; navigating the two yields an ego virtue/strength. Built on Freud's psychosexual stages but adds social dynamics and extends into adulthood. Table (stage → conflict → virtue): Infancy Trust vs. Mistrust → Hope; Early Childhood Autonomy vs. Shame/Doubt → Will; Play Age Initiative vs. Guilt → Purpose; School Age Industry vs. Inferiority → Competence; Adolescence Identity vs. Role/Identity Confusion → Fidelity; Young Adulthood Intimacy vs. Isolation → Love; Adulthood Generativity vs. Stagnation → Care; Old Age Integrity vs. Despair → Wisdom. Resolution of a stage is not required to move to the next; the later stages partly repeat earlier ones (development is "ever-evolving," not rigid). Joan Erikson later added a tentative ninth stage (very old age).
  • Malik, F., & Marwaha, R. (updated 2022). Cognitive Development. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK537095. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537095/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI Bookshelf). Authority: high for Piaget as taught clinically. Piaget's engine: schema (mental structure), assimilation (fitting new information into an existing schema) and accommodation (revising the schema when it doesn't fit), driven toward equilibration. Four stages: Sensorimotor (0–2; knowledge through sensory/motor action; object permanence emerges ~6 months = objects exist when out of sight); Pre-operational (2–7; symbols and language, but egocentrism — inability to perceive that others think differently — and no conservation); Concrete operational (7–11; logical operations on concrete material, conservation, reversibility, inductive logic); Formal operational (12+; abstract and hypothetical-deductive reasoning — theories, "love," "justice"). Stated limitations: underestimates infants and overestimates adolescents; theory of mind is mastered by ~4–5 years, earlier than Piaget's egocentrism timeline; stages are "poorly generalizable" and conservation overlaps stages; Piaget neglected social and cultural contributions (the Vygotsky critique).
  • Jones-Mason, Cassidy, et al. (2015). Contributions of Attachment Theory and Research: A Framework for Future Research, Translation, and Policy. Development and Psychopathology, 25(4pt2). PMC4085672. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4085672/ Peer-reviewed review by senior attachment researchers. Authority: high — the load-bearing source for the clinical/developmental claims. Attachment = "an organized system of behaviors that has a predictable outcome (i.e., proximity) and serves an identifiable biological function (i.e., protection)." The secure base (a base to explore from) and safe haven (a haven to return to in distress) are "the heart of attachment theory." Early experience builds internal working models / a secure base script ("when I am hurt, I go to my mother and receive comfort"); secure people hold coherent narratives, insecure people show gaps/distortions. Risk, not destiny: following Waddington's developmental-pathways model, early attachment is "not expected to be perfectly predictive of later outcomes"; insecurity "is thought to be a risk factor for later psychopathology if subsequent development occurs in the context of other risk factors." Intergenerational transmission: a parent's AAI state of mind predicts the infant's attachment pattern, but the "transmission gap" — maternal sensitive behavior does not fully explain that link — is one of the field's central unsolved problems. Bowlby characterized the therapist as an attachment figure in long-term psychotherapy.
  • Bolton, D., & Gillett, G. (2019). The Biopsychosocial Model 40 Years On. In* The Biopsychosocial Model of Health and Disease *(open access). NCBI Bookshelf, NBK552030. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK552030/ Open-access scholarly monograph chapter. Authority: high — a careful, criticism-aware treatment. Engel's model rejected the biomedical model's reductionism (complex illness reduced to one physical primary principle), physicalism, and mind–body dualism; it drew on general systems theory — nested, interacting biological/psychological/social domains that reciprocally influence health. Legitimized psychosocial intervention alongside medication and multidisciplinary care. Criticisms: Ghaemi — it "gives mental health professionals permission to do everything but no specific guidance," ideology masquerading as theory; Kendler — "never … a scientific model … It was a slogan," though useful as a teaching tool; the "equal in all cases" reading contradicts cases where biology alone explains outcomes. Revival: locate the model in specific conditions and stages (social factors may dominate aetiology, biology the acute treatment) and treat its job as theorizing the interactions between domains, not asserting equal weight everywhere.
  • Engel, G. L. (1977). The Need for a New Medical Model: A Challenge for Biomedicine. Science, 196(4286), 129–136. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/847460/ The primary paper that introduced the term (paywalled full text; content corroborated via ). Authority: highest for what Engel actually proposed. Argued the dominant biomedical model was reductionist and dualist and left "no room within its framework for the social, psychological, and behavioral dimensions of illness"; proposed a systems-based model spanning biological, psychological, and social levels.

Tier: primary attachment-methodology papers (lean on these)

  • van IJzendoorn, M. H., & Kroonenberg, P. M. (1988). Cross-Cultural Patterns of Attachment: A Meta-Analysis of the Strange Situation. Child Development, 59(1), 147–156. https://www.scirp.org/reference/referencespapers?referenceid=3437369 (corroborated: https://www.simplypsychology.org/culture-attachment.html) The canonical cross-cultural meta-analysis (32 studies, 8 countries, ~2,000 classifications). Authority: high. Secure was the most common classification in every country sampled (roughly 50–75%); intra-cultural variation was ~1.5× the inter-cultural variation — differences within a country exceeded differences between countries. Caveats that puncture over-strong universality claims: 18 of 32 studies were US samples and only a handful were in collectivist cultures; the Strange Situation may be an "imposed etic" — behaviors can look identical across cultures yet mean different things (e.g., German independence read as avoidance; Japanese distress at separation read as resistance because infants are rarely left alone).
  • Main, M., & Solomon, J. (1990). Procedures for identifying infants as disorganized/disoriented during the Ainsworth Strange Situation. In Greenberg et al. (Eds.), Attachment in the Preschool Years. (+ disorganized-as-risk meta-analyses, Development and Psychopathology.) https://www.child-encyclopedia.com/attachment/according-experts/disorganization-attachment-strategies-infancy-and-childhood (corroboration/orientation) The primary source for the fourth (D) category (1980s conference work, 1990 chapter); disorganized-risk claims corroborated via peer-reviewed meta-analyses. Authority: high for the D category; risk claims held probabilistically. Added the disorganized/disoriented (D) classification for infants who show contradictory, incomplete, or fearful behavior on reunion (freezing, approaching then backing away, dazed/ trance-like states) — a breakdown of an organized strategy, typically where the caregiver is both the source of and the solution to alarm ("fright without solution"; associated with frightening/frightened parenting, abuse, or unresolved parental loss/trauma). Disorganization is the classification most robustly linked to later problems — a broad, transdiagnostic relational risk factor for internalizing and (especially) externalizing problems, dissociation, and later borderline features — but the link is probabilistic and moderated by later context, not deterministic.
  • Adult attachment — Hazan & Shaver (1987); Bartholomew & Horowitz (1991); George, Kaplan & Main (Adult Attachment Interview). https://openbooks.library.baylor.edu/lifespanhumandevelopment/chapter/chapter-17-2-attachment-in-adulthood/ · https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/foc.8.1.foc127 Open textbook + a peer-reviewed clinical review (Focus/APA) on adult attachment and psychotherapy. Authority: high for the adult framework. Hazan & Shaver (1987): first self-report of adult romantic attachment, translating Ainsworth's three infant patterns into three adult styles. Bartholomew & Horowitz (1991): four-category model built on two dimensions — anxiety (about abandonment/self-worth) and avoidance (of intimacy/dependence): secure (low/low), preoccupied (high anxiety/low avoidance), dismissing (low anxiety/high avoidance), fearful (high/high). AAI (George, Kaplan & Main): assesses an adult's state of mind with respect to attachment — secure/autonomous, dismissing, preoccupied, unresolved/disorganized — from narrative coherence, not romantic self-report. Clinical: a client's pattern shows up in the alliance (preoccupied clients may seek reassurance and merge; dismissing clients may minimize and keep distance); the relationship can be a corrective attachment experience.

Tier: professional-body & orientation-tier corroboration (context)

  • Simply Psychology — Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation (and Cultural Variations in Attachment). https://www.simplypsychology.org/mary-ainsworth.html Orientation-tier teaching summary; every load-bearing claim anchored to . Authority: orientation only. Standard presentation of the eight 3-minute episodes, the five scored behaviors (proximity/ contact seeking, contact maintaining, avoidance, resistance, search), and the original-sample proportions (~70% secure, 15% avoidant, 15% resistant, from a small US middle-class Baltimore sample). Caregiver correlates: sensitive, consistent responsiveness → secure; consistently unresponsive/rejecting-of-distress → avoidant; inconsistent (sometimes responsive, sometimes not) → resistant/ambivalent. Criticisms of the sensitivity hypothesis: De Wolff & van IJzendoorn (1997) found only a modest sensitivity–security correlation (r ≈ .24); temperament accounts (Kagan) argue inborn temperament drives the classification; interactionist accounts (Belsky & Rovine) say temperament × caregiving; plus the cross-cultural bias in .
  • Simply Psychology / LibreTexts — John Bowlby (four phases; monotropy; internal working model; maternal deprivation). https://www.simplypsychology.org/stages-of-attachment-identified-by-john-bowlby-and-schaffer-emerson-1964.html · https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Courses/Pittsburg_State_University/The_Developing_Child/13:_Social_and_Emotional_Development_in_Infancy_and_Toddlerhood/13.05:_Attachment Orientation-tier; anchored to . Authority: orientation only. Bowlby's four phases of attachment development: pre-attachment (birth–~6 wks; signals to any adult) → attachment-in-the-making (~6 wks–6–8 mo; prefers familiar people) → clear-cut attachment (~7–24 mo; specific primary figure, separation anxiety peaks) → reciprocal / goal-corrected partnership (24 mo+; understands the caregiver has separate goals). Attachment as an evolved survival system; monotropy (a bias toward one principal attachment figure), a sensitive/critical period, and the internal working model as the template early attachment leaves for later relationships.
  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Developmental Surveillance and Screening + Zubler et al. (2022), Evidence-Informed Milestones for Developmental Surveillance Tools, Pediatrics. https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/ · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/149/3/e2021052138/184748/ Professional-body guidance + peer-reviewed milestone update. Authority: high for the typical-vs-clinical framing. Developmental surveillance is the longitudinal process of eliciting concerns, taking a milestone history, observing the child, and applying clinical judgment across well-child visits; milestones define age-dependent population norms so that failure to attain one calibrates the level of concern. Basis for distinguishing normal-range variation from a red flag that warrants screening/referral — the counselor's version of "you can't tell what's wrong if you don't know what's normal for the age."

Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings)

  1. Maternal sensitivity is real but not the whole story. Ainsworth's sensitivity hypothesis is supported only at a modest effect size (De Wolff & van IJzendoorn r ≈ .24), and the "transmission gap" means parental state of mind (AAI) predicts infant attachment beyond what observed sensitivity explains. Temperament (Kagan) and interactionist accounts (Belsky & Rovine) are live alternatives. Don't teach "sensitive parenting → secure baby" as a clean causal law.
  2. The Strange Situation may be an imposed etic. Secure is modal everywhere and within-culture variation exceeds between-culture variation , but the procedure was built on US norms and its behaviors can mean different things across cultures (German "avoidance," Japanese "resistance"). Attachment security may be universal in function while its behavioral markers are culture-bound.
  3. Attachment is a risk factor, not a diagnosis or destiny. Insecure and even disorganized attachment raise the probability of later problems only in the context of continuing risk; many insecurely attached children do fine, and later relationships (including therapy) can revise the internal working model. Resist typing a client by an attachment "category."
  4. Erikson's stages are a clinical heuristic, not measured fact. Ages are approximate and culture-bound (adolescent "identity" and the very existence of an extended adolescence are partly Western/modern), stages need not be resolved in order, and the theory is hard to falsify. Useful as a "where is this person stuck?" lens, not as a developmental law.
  5. Piaget under-credited infants and over-credited adolescents, and skipped culture. Object permanence and theory of mind arrive earlier than he claimed; many adults don't reliably use formal-operational reasoning; and Vygotsky's sociocultural critique (development is scaffolded by social interaction and language, the "zone of proximal development") names what Piaget's solo-scientist child leaves out. Stages describe a real sequence better than they fix real ages.
  6. The biopsychosocial model is widely used and widely criticized at once. It is the field's default case-formulation frame, yet critics (Ghaemi, Kendler) call it a vague "slogan" that licenses anything and specifies nothing. Hold it as an organizing checklist that must be made specific to this client — not as an explanation by itself.
pages.text: Unit 5 sources — Human Development Across the Lifespan Evidence base for Unit 5 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1] . Researched 2026-07-17. Anchored on peer-reviewed clinical references (NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls for Erikson and Piaget; a Development and Psychopathology framework review for attachment; the open-access Biopsychosocial Model of Health and Disease volume for Engel), triangulated with the primary methodological papers (van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg's cross-cultural meta-analysis; Main & Solomon's disorganized category; Bartholomew & Horowitz / Hazan & Shaver / the AAI for adult attachment) and professional-body guidance (AAP developmental surveillance). Orientation-tier teaching summaries (Simply Psychology, LibreTexts) are used only to corroborate the standard reading of the primaries, and flagged as such. Anchor text (not online): Broderick & Blewitt, The Life Span (written for helping professions) — used as the structural model for how this material is taught to counselors; every substantive claim here is corroborated online. Tier: peer-reviewed clinical references & primary theory (ground truth) S1 Orenstein, G. A., & Lewis, L. (updated 2022). Erikson's Stages of Psychosocial Development. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK556096. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556096/ (table: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556096/table/article-21284.table0/) Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI Bookshelf). Authority: high for the model as taught clinically. Eight sequential psychosocial stages across the lifespan, each a tension between a positive ( syntonic ) and negative ( dystonic ) tendency; navigating the two yields an ego virtue/strength . Built on Freud's psychosexual stages but adds social dynamics and extends into adulthood. Table (stage → conflict → virtue): Infancy Trust vs. Mistrust → Hope ; Early Childhood Autonomy vs. Shame/Doubt → Will ; Play Age Initiative vs. Guilt → Purpose ; School Age Industry vs. Inferiority → Competence ; Adolescence Identity vs. Role/Identity Confusion → Fidelity ; Young Adulthood Intimacy vs. Isolation → Love ; Adulthood Generativity vs. Stagnation → Care ; Old Age Integrity vs. Despair → Wisdom . Resolution of a stage is not required to move to the next ; the later stages partly repeat earlier ones (development is "ever-evolving," not rigid). Joan Erikson later added a tentative ninth stage (very old age). S2 Malik, F., & Marwaha, R. (updated 2022). Cognitive Development. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK537095. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537095/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference (NCBI Bookshelf). Authority: high for Piaget as taught clinically. Piaget's engine: schema (mental structure), assimilation (fitting new information into an existing schema) and accommodation (revising the schema when it doesn't fit), driven toward equilibration . Four stages: Sensorimotor (0–2; knowledge through sensory/motor action; object permanence emerges ~6 months = objects exist when out of sight); Pre-operational (2–7; symbols and language, but egocentrism — inability to perceive that others think differently — and no conservation); Concrete operational (7–11; logical operations on concrete material, conservation , reversibility, inductive logic); Formal operational (12+; abstract and hypothetical-deductive reasoning — theories, "love," "justice"). Stated limitations: underestimates infants and overestimates adolescents ; theory of mind is mastered by ~4–5 years , earlier than Piaget's egocentrism timeline; stages are "poorly generalizable" and conservation overlaps stages; Piaget neglected social and cultural contributions (the Vygotsky critique). S3 Jones-Mason, Cassidy, et al. (2015). Contributions of Attachment Theory and Research: A Framework for Future Research, Translation, and Policy. Development and Psychopathology, 25(4pt2). PMC4085672. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4085672/ Peer-reviewed review by senior attachment researchers. Authority: high — the load-bearing source for the clinical/developmental claims. Attachment = "an organized system of behaviors that has a predictable outcome (i.e., proximity) and serves an identifiable biological function (i.e., protection)." The secure base (a base to explore from) and safe haven (a haven to return to in distress) are "the heart of attachment theory." Early experience builds internal working models / a secure base script ("when I am hurt, I go to my mother and receive comfort"); secure people hold coherent narratives, insecure people show gaps/distortions. Risk, not destiny: following Waddington's developmental-pathways model, early attachment is "not expected to be perfectly predictive of later outcomes"; insecurity "is thought to be a risk factor for later psychopathology if subsequent development occurs in the context of other risk factors." Intergenerational transmission: a parent's AAI state of mind predicts the infant's attachment pattern, but the "transmission gap" — maternal sensitive behavior does not fully explain that link — is one of the field's central unsolved problems. Bowlby characterized the therapist as an attachment figure in long-term psychotherapy. S4 Bolton, D., & Gillett, G. (2019). The Biopsychosocial Model 40 Years On. In* The Biopsychosocial Model of Health and Disease *(open access). NCBI Bookshelf, NBK552030. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK552030/ Open-access scholarly monograph chapter. Authority: high — a careful, criticism-aware treatment. Engel's model rejected the biomedical model's reductionism (complex illness reduced to one physical primary principle), physicalism , and mind–body dualism ; it drew on general systems theory — nested, interacting biological/psychological/social domains that reciprocally influence health. Legitimized psychosocial intervention alongside medication and multidisciplinary care. Criticisms: Ghaemi — it "gives mental health professionals permission to do everything but no specific guidance," ideology masquerading as theory; Kendler — "never … a scientific model … It was a slogan," though useful as a teaching tool; the "equal in all cases" reading contradicts cases where biology alone explains outcomes. Revival: locate the model in specific conditions and stages (social factors may dominate aetiology, biology the acute treatment) and treat its job as theorizing the interactions between domains, not asserting equal weight everywhere. S5 Engel, G. L. (1977). The Need for a New Medical Model: A Challenge for Biomedicine. Science, 196(4286), 129–136. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/847460/ The primary paper that introduced the term (paywalled full text; content corroborated via S4 ). Authority: highest for what Engel actually proposed. Argued the dominant biomedical model was reductionist and dualist and left "no room within its framework for the social, psychological, and behavioral dimensions of illness"; proposed a systems-based model spanning biological, psychological, and social levels. Tier: primary attachment-methodology papers (lean on these) S6 van IJzendoorn, M. H., & Kroonenberg, P. M. (1988). Cross-Cultural Patterns of Attachment: A Meta-Analysis of the Strange Situation. Child Development, 59(1), 147–156. https://www.scirp.org/reference/referencespapers?referenceid=3437369 (corroborated: https://www.simplypsychology.org/culture-attachment.html) The canonical cross-cultural meta-analysis (32 studies, 8 countries, ~2,000 classifications). Authority: high. Secure was the most common classification in every country sampled (roughly 50–75%); intra-cultural variation was ~1.5× the inter-cultural variation — differences within a country exceeded differences between countries. Caveats that puncture over-strong universality claims: 18 of 32 studies were US samples and only a handful were in collectivist cultures; the Strange Situation may be an "imposed etic" — behaviors can look identical across cultures yet mean different things (e.g., German independence read as avoidance; Japanese distress at separation read as resistance because infants are rarely left alone). S7 Main, M., & Solomon, J. (1990). Procedures for identifying infants as disorganized/disoriented during the Ainsworth Strange Situation. In Greenberg et al. (Eds.), Attachment in the Preschool Years. (+ disorganized-as-risk meta-analyses, Development and Psychopathology.) https://www.child-encyclopedia.com/attachment/according-experts/disorganization-attachment-strategies-infancy-and-childhood (corroboration/orientation) The primary source for the fourth (D) category (1980s conference work, 1990 chapter); disorganized-risk claims corroborated via peer-reviewed meta-analyses. Authority: high for the D category; risk claims held probabilistically. Added the disorganized/disoriented (D) classification for infants who show contradictory, incomplete, or fearful behavior on reunion (freezing, approaching then backing away, dazed/ trance-like states) — a breakdown of an organized strategy , typically where the caregiver is both the source of and the solution to alarm ("fright without solution"; associated with frightening/frightened parenting, abuse, or unresolved parental loss/trauma). Disorganization is the classification most robustly linked to later problems — a broad, transdiagnostic relational risk factor for internalizing and (especially) externalizing problems, dissociation, and later borderline features — but the link is probabilistic and moderated by later context , not deterministic. S8 Adult attachment — Hazan & Shaver (1987); Bartholomew & Horowitz (1991); George, Kaplan & Main (Adult Attachment Interview). https://openbooks.library.baylor.edu/lifespanhumandevelopment/chapter/chapter-17-2-attachment-in-adulthood/ · https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/foc.8.1.foc127 Open textbook + a peer-reviewed clinical review (Focus/APA) on adult attachment and psychotherapy. Authority: high for the adult framework. Hazan & Shaver (1987): first self-report of adult romantic attachment, translating Ainsworth's three infant patterns into three adult styles. Bartholomew & Horowitz (1991): four-category model built on two dimensions — anxiety (about abandonment/self-worth) and avoidance (of intimacy/dependence): secure (low/low), preoccupied (high anxiety/low avoidance), dismissing (low anxiety/high avoidance), fearful (high/high). AAI (George, Kaplan & Main): assesses an adult's state of mind with respect to attachment — secure/autonomous, dismissing, preoccupied, unresolved/disorganized — from narrative coherence, not romantic self-report. Clinical: a client's pattern shows up in the alliance (preoccupied clients may seek reassurance and merge; dismissing clients may minimize and keep distance); the relationship can be a corrective attachment experience. Tier: professional-body & orientation-tier corroboration (context) S9 Simply Psychology — Mary Ainsworth's Strange Situation (and Cultural Variations in Attachment ). https://www.simplypsychology.org/mary-ainsworth.html Orientation-tier teaching summary; every load-bearing claim anchored to S3 S6 S7 . Authority: orientation only. Standard presentation of the eight 3-minute episodes , the five scored behaviors (proximity/ contact seeking, contact maintaining, avoidance, resistance, search), and the original-sample proportions (~ 70% secure, 15% avoidant, 15% resistant , from a small US middle-class Baltimore sample). Caregiver correlates: sensitive, consistent responsiveness → secure; consistently unresponsive/rejecting-of-distress → avoidant; inconsistent (sometimes responsive, sometimes not) → resistant/ambivalent. Criticisms of the sensitivity hypothesis: De Wolff & van IJzendoorn (1997) found only a modest sensitivity–security correlation (r ≈ .24) ; temperament accounts (Kagan) argue inborn temperament drives the classification; interactionist accounts (Belsky & Rovine) say temperament × caregiving; plus the cross-cultural bias in S6 . S10 Simply Psychology / LibreTexts — John Bowlby (four phases; monotropy; internal working model; maternal deprivation). https://www.simplypsychology.org/stages-of-attachment-identified-by-john-bowlby-and-schaffer-emerson-1964.html · https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Courses/Pittsburg_State_University/The_Developing_Child/13:_Social_and_Emotional_Development_in_Infancy_and_Toddlerhood/13.05:_Attachment Orientation-tier; anchored to S3 . Authority: orientation only. Bowlby's four phases of attachment development : pre-attachment (birth–~6 wks; signals to any adult) → attachment-in-the-making (~6 wks–6–8 mo; prefers familiar people) → clear-cut attachment (~7–24 mo; specific primary figure, separation anxiety peaks) → reciprocal / goal-corrected partnership (24 mo+; understands the caregiver has separate goals). Attachment as an evolved survival system; monotropy (a bias toward one principal attachment figure), a sensitive/critical period , and the internal working model as the template early attachment leaves for later relationships. S11 American Academy of Pediatrics — Developmental Surveillance and Screening + Zubler et al. (2022), Evidence-Informed Milestones for Developmental Surveillance Tools, Pediatrics. https://www.aap.org/en/patient-care/developmental-surveillance-and-screening-patient-care/ · https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/149/3/e2021052138/184748/ Professional-body guidance + peer-reviewed milestone update. Authority: high for the typical-vs-clinical framing. Developmental surveillance is the longitudinal process of eliciting concerns, taking a milestone history, observing the child, and applying clinical judgment across well-child visits; milestones define age-dependent population norms so that failure to attain one calibrates the level of concern . Basis for distinguishing normal-range variation from a red flag that warrants screening/referral — the counselor's version of "you can't tell what's wrong if you don't know what's normal for the age." Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings) Maternal sensitivity is real but not the whole story. Ainsworth's sensitivity hypothesis is supported only at a modest effect size (De Wolff & van IJzendoorn r ≈ .24), and the "transmission gap" means parental state of mind (AAI) predicts infant attachment beyond what observed sensitivity explains. Temperament (Kagan) and interactionist accounts (Belsky & Rovine) are live alternatives. Don't teach "sensitive parenting → secure baby" as a clean causal law. S3 S9 The Strange Situation may be an imposed etic. Secure is modal everywhere and within-culture variation exceeds between-culture variation S6 , but the procedure was built on US norms and its behaviors can mean different things across cultures (German "avoidance," Japanese "resistance"). Attachment security may be universal in function while its behavioral markers are culture-bound. S6 S9 Attachment is a risk factor, not a diagnosis or destiny. Insecure and even disorganized attachment raise the probability of later problems only in the context of continuing risk; many insecurely attached children do fine, and later relationships (including therapy) can revise the internal working model. Resist typing a client by an attachment "category." S3 S7 Erikson's stages are a clinical heuristic, not measured fact. Ages are approximate and culture-bound (adolescent "identity" and the very existence of an extended adolescence are partly Western/modern), stages need not be resolved in order, and the theory is hard to falsify. Useful as a "where is this person stuck?" lens, not as a developmental law. S1 Piaget under-credited infants and over-credited adolescents, and skipped culture. Object permanence and theory of mind arrive earlier than he claimed; many adults don't reliably use formal-operational reasoning; and Vygotsky's sociocultural critique (development is scaffolded by social interaction and language, the "zone of proximal development") names what Piaget's solo-scientist child leaves out. Stages describe a real sequence better than they fix real ages . S2 The biopsychosocial model is widely used and widely criticized at once. It is the field's default case-formulation frame, yet critics (Ghaemi, Kendler) call it a vague "slogan" that licenses anything and specifies nothing. Hold it as an organizing checklist that must be made specific to this client — not as an explanation by itself. S4 S5

pages.html:
Unit 6 sources — Psychopathology & the DSM-5-TR

Evidence base for Unit 6 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1].

Researched 2026-07-17. Anchored on peer-reviewed clinical references (NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls for every major disorder category; the World Psychiatry DSM-5-TR overview by First et al. — the manual's own editors), triangulated with epidemiology primaries (Kessler's NCS-R), the dimensional-critique literature (HiTOP, the p factor, RDoC, Frances), and counseling-profession sources (The Professional Counselor / NBCC on the multiaxial removal and what diagnosis means for counselors). The DSM-5-TR itself is the anchor text (not freely online); criteria summarized here are taken from peer-reviewed secondary clinical references (StatPearls), which is the standard teaching practice — quote the manual itself before relying on any criterion in a real clinical or exam context. The APA's own dsm5.org/psychiatry.org pages block automated access (403) and are cited only via the First et al. overview .

Tier: the manual — structure, history, and what the TR changed

  • OpenStax Psychology 2e, §15.2 Diagnosing and Classifying Psychological Disorders (open textbook). https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/15-2-diagnosing-and-classifying-psychological-disorders Peer-reviewed open textbook. Authority: high for orientation-level DSM history and the standard criticisms. DSM-I (1952) had 106 diagnoses in 130 pages, organized on a format the U.S. Army developed in WWII; DSM-III (1980) had 265 diagnoses in 886 pages; DSM-5 (2013) contains 237 disorders. Each entry gives diagnostic features, diagnostic criteria, prevalence, and risk factors; comorbidity rates are documented (e.g., "41% of people with OCD also meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder"). Homosexuality removed as a diagnosis in 1973; the bereavement exclusion removed in DSM-5. Worldwide "the ICD is more frequently used for clinical diagnosis, whereas the DSM is more valued for research." Standing criticisms: the DSM "overpathologize[s] the human condition by turning common human problems into mental illnesses"; "nearly half of all Americans will meet the criteria for a DSM disorder at some point in their life." Anti-labeling stance: don't say "schizophrenics"/"depressives" — such labels "objectify people"; "a psychological disorder is not what a person is; it is something that a person has."
  • First, M. B., et al. (2022). DSM-5-TR: overview of what's new and what's changed. World Psychiatry, 21(2). PMC9077590. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9077590/ Peer-reviewed overview by the DSM-5-TR's own editors. Authority: highest available online for what the TR is. A text revision updates descriptive text from literature review, but DSM-5-TR went further: prolonged grief disorder added (intense yearning/preoccupation with the deceased ≥12 months after the death, with impairing grief symptoms — see the PFA module's grief pages), plus unspecified mood disorder and stimulant-induced mild neurocognitive disorder; free-standing symptom codes for suicidal behavior and nonsuicidal self-injury (recordable without any diagnosis); criteria/specifier changes to 70+ disorders; terminology updates ("experienced gender," "individual assigned male/female at birth") and a full-text review by an Ethnoracial Equity and Inclusion Work Group.
  • Kress, V. E., et al. (2014). The Removal of the Multiaxial System in the DSM-5: Implications and Practice Suggestions for Counselors. The Professional Counselor (NBCC). https://tpcjournal.nbcc.org/the-removal-of-the-multiaxial-system-in-the-dsm-5-implications-and-practice-suggestions-for-counselors/ Peer-reviewed counseling journal. Authority: high for the counseling-profession angle. DSM-IV's five axes: I clinical disorders; II personality disorders & intellectual disability; III relevant medical conditions; IV psychosocial/environmental stressors; V Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF, 0–100). DSM-5 dropped all five for nonaxial documentation (all disorders listed together by clinical priority), WHODAS 2.0 replacing the GAF, and expanded V/Z codes for psychosocial context (housing, abuse, relational problems). Counselor implications: the shift reinforces a neurobiological/medical model while counselors emphasize "strength-based and developmentally, culturally and contextually sensitive approaches" — contextual factors must now be documented deliberately, without structural prompts. Catalogs the profession's standing critiques: the DSM has historically "marginalized, stigmatized and harmed those who are different," lacks cross-cultural validity, encourages reductionism, and reflects political as well as scientific processes.
  • SAMHSA (NCBI Bookshelf). DSM-IV to DSM-5 Changes: Overview. NBK519711. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519711/ Government clinical reference. Authority: high for the mechanics of the DSM-IV→5 transition. Details the axis system and its removal; the GAF was eliminated for "conceptual lack of clarity (i.e., including symptoms, suicide risk, and disabilities in the descriptors) and questionable psychometric properties." DSM-5 eliminated the "disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence" chapter, redistributing those disorders through a lifespan-ordered manual (neurodevelopmental disorders first, neurocognitive disorders last).

Tier: disorder-category clinical references (criteria-level ground truth)

  • Bains, N., & Abdijadid, S. (updated 2023). Major Depressive Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK559078. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559078/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. MDD: 5 of 9 symptoms for ≥2 weeks, at least one being depressed mood or anhedonia, causing functional impairment; the nine: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt/worthlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, appetite/weight change, psychomotor retardation or agitation, sleep disturbance, suicidal thoughts. A manic/hypomanic episode must be excluded (that's bipolar). Children may show irritable rather than sad mood. Lifetime prevalence ~12% (range 5–17%), roughly double in women. Untreated episodes last 6–12 months; recurrence ~50% after one episode, 70% after two, 90% after three. Differentials include dysthymia, bereavement, adjustment disorder with depressed mood, bipolar disorders, substance/medical causes.
  • Marzani, G., & Neff, A. P. (updated 2023). Bipolar Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK558998. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK558998/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Manic episode: elevated or irritable mood with increased activity/energy ≥7 days (or any duration if hospitalization required), with 3+ symptoms (4+ if mood only irritable): grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured talkativeness, flight of ideas/racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity/agitation, high-risk behavior (spending sprees, sexual indiscretion). Hypomania: same symptom picture but ≥4 days, no marked impairment, no hospitalization, no psychosis. Bipolar I = at least one manic episode (depression not required); Bipolar II = at least one hypomanic episode + at least one major depressive episode, never mania; cyclothymia = 2+ years of subthreshold hypomanic and depressive symptoms. Bipolar-spectrum lifetime prevalence ~2.4%; correct diagnosis typically lags first contact by ~6–10 years; 20–30% of "MDD" patients transition to bipolar within 3 years; suicide rate ~20–30× the general population.
  • Munir, S., & Takov, V. (updated 2022). Generalized Anxiety Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK441870. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441870/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. GAD: excessive anxiety and worry, more days than not, ≥6 months, about multiple domains; difficulty controlling the worry; 3+ of 6 associated symptoms (restlessness, easy fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance); distress/ impairment; not attributable to a substance or medical cause (rule out hyperthyroidism, caffeine, stimulants). Women ~2× men; up to ~20% of adults have an anxiety disorder in a given year; course chronic and relapsing.
  • Cackovic, C., Nazir, S., & Marwaha, R. (updated 2023). Panic Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK430973. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430973/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Panic attack: "an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort" peaking within minutes, with 4+ of 13 physical/cognitive symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control or "going crazy," fear of dying). Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks plus ≥1 month of worry about further attacks and/or maladaptive behavior change (avoidance). Key discrimination: in other anxiety disorders, attacks are cued/expected (e.g., panic at public speaking in social anxiety disorder); medical mimics (hyperthyroid, cardiac, vestibular) must be excluded.
  • Mann, S. K., & Marwaha, R. (updated 2023). Posttraumatic Stress Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK559129. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559129/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Criterion A gate: exposure to "actual or threatened death, injury, or sexual violence" — directly experienced, witnessed in person, learned of happening to a close relative/friend, or repeated indirect professional exposure (first responders). Then four clusters: B intrusion (1+) (intrusive memories, nightmares, flashbacks, cued distress/reactivity); C avoidance (1+) (of internal reminders and/or external cues); D negative alterations in cognition/mood (2+) (amnesia for aspects, "I am bad," blame, persistent fear/guilt/shame, detachment, diminished interest, no positive emotion); E arousal/reactivity (2+) (irritability, recklessness, hypervigilance, startle, concentration, sleep). Duration >1 month + impairment. Specifiers: dissociative (depersonalization/derealization) and delayed expression (full criteria ≥6 months post-trauma). Lifetime prevalence ~6.1–9.2% (US). Differentials: acute stress disorder (same family, symptoms 3 days–1 month), adjustment disorder (stressor of any severity, not necessarily Criterion-A trauma; onset within 3 months).
  • Hany, M., et al. (updated 2024). Schizophrenia. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK539864. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539864/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. 2+ of 5 symptom domains for a significant portion of one month — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms (at least one must be delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech) — with continuous signs ≥6 months including ≥1 month of active-phase symptoms and functional decline. Positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization) respond to antipsychotics better than negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition). Spectrum by duration: brief psychotic disorder (1 day–<1 month), schizophreniform (<6 months), schizophrenia (≥6 months); schizoaffective = mood episodes concurrent with active-phase symptoms (plus ≥2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms); delusional disorder = delusions without the other characteristic symptoms. Lifetime risk ~1%; men ~1.7× incidence, earlier onset, more negative symptoms. Complete recovery in only ~13.5%; life expectancy ~15 years shorter; suicide the most common cause of premature death. Dopamine hypothesis: mesolimbic dysregulation → "misattribution of importance to irrelevant objects or events" (aberrant salience).
  • Fariba, K. A., et al. (updated 2023). Personality Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK556058. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556058/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. General definition: "an enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates significantly from the norms and expectations of the surrounding culture" — pervasive, inflexible, onset by adolescence/early adulthood, stable, causing distress or impairment. Cluster A (odd/eccentric): paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal. Cluster B (dramatic/emotional/erratic): antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C (anxious/fearful): avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive (OCPD). Prevalence ~6.1% (WHO); much higher in clinical and incarcerated populations. "With the exception of borderline personality disorder, there are no high-quality, evidence-based psychotherapies for personality disorders" — DBT is the established borderline treatment. The DSM-5-TR also carries the Alternative Model (AMPD): a hybrid dimensional-categorical system rating impairment in personality functioning plus pathological traits. Countertransference management is a core clinical challenge.
  • Brock, H., et al. (updated 2024). Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK553162. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553162/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Obsessions: "recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are … intrusive and unwanted." Compulsions: "repetitive behaviors or mental acts that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly." Diagnosis: obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (≥1 hr/day) or cause marked distress/impairment. DSM-5 moved OCD out of the anxiety chapter into Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders (with body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania, excoriation disorder) on shared phenomenology/neurobiology. Most patients have insight (only 2–4% lack it) — symptoms are ego-dystonic (recognized as irrational, unwanted). Contrast OCPD: "a chronic pattern of perfectionism and rigid control" experienced as rational and ego-syntonic, with no true obsessions/compulsions.
  • Moore, C. A., & Bokor, B. R. (updated 2023). Anorexia Nervosa. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK459148. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459148/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high (AN); BN/BED facts corroborated in-page. AN: restriction of intake → significantly low body weight + intense fear of gaining weight + distorted body image; restricting vs. binge-eating/purging subtypes. The weight criterion is the line against bulimia nervosa, where weight is normal or above. Lifetime prevalence 0.3–1%, mostly female, onset late adolescence/early adulthood. Among the deadliest psychiatric conditions: elevated all-cause mortality via medical complications and suicide (~25% of AN deaths); ~three-fourths of outpatients remit within 5 years.
  • Magnus, W., et al. (updated 2023). Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK441838. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441838/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. ADHD: 6+ of 9 inattentive and/or 6+ of 9 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms in children (5+ at 17+), onset before age 12, present in 2+ settings, impairing. Three presentations: predominantly inattentive, predominantly hyperactive/impulsive, combined. Adult prevalence ~3–6%; roughly half of childhood cases attenuate substantially by adulthood. Overlapping inattention/concentration symptoms make ADHD, anxiety, and depression mutual misdiagnosis risks.
  • Mughal, S., et al. (updated 2022). Autism Spectrum Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK525976. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK525976/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. ASD: persistent deficits in all three social-communication areas (social-emotional reciprocity; nonverbal communication; developing/maintaining relationships) plus 2+ of 4 restricted/repetitive behavior types (stereotyped movements/speech; insistence on sameness/routines; highly restricted fixated interests; sensory hyper-/hyporeactivity), with onset in the early developmental period. DSM-5 merged autistic disorder, Asperger syndrome, and PDD-NOS into the single spectrum. CDC 2020: ~1 in 36 8-year-olds; 74% have ≥1 comorbidity.
  • DSM-5-TR Substance Use Disorder criteria, via SAMHSA / NCBI Bookshelf NBK565474 (table 3). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK565474/table/table-3/ Diagnostic authority (same source anchors the aux-addiction module's ). Authority: high. The 11 SUD criteria in four groups — impaired control, social impairment, risky use, pharmacological (tolerance/withdrawal) — with severity mild (2–3), moderate (4–5), severe (6+); one SUD per substance class; tolerance/withdrawal under prescribed medical care don't count toward a diagnosis. Full treatment in the elective module (aux-addiction).

Tier: epidemiology, comorbidity & the dimensional debate

  • Kessler, R. C., et al. (2005). Prevalence, Severity, and Comorbidity of 12-Month DSM-IV Disorders in the National Comorbidity Survey Replication. Arch Gen Psychiatry, 62(6). PMC2847357. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2847357/ The canonical US psychiatric-epidemiology survey. Authority: high (DSM-IV-era numbers). 12-month prevalence: any disorder 26.2% — anxiety 18.1%, mood 9.5%, impulse-control 8.9%, substance 3.8%. Of 12-month cases, 55% carry one diagnosis, 22% two, 23% three or more — comorbidity is routine, not exotic. Severity: 22.3% serious, 37.3% moderate, 40.4% mild — and seriousness concentrates in the highly comorbid few (classes covering ~7% of the sample hold 43.6% of serious cases). (Companion lifetime paper: ~46% lifetime prevalence — the "nearly half" figure in .)
  • Ruggero, C. J., Kotov, R., et al. (2019). Integrating the Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) into Clinical Practice. J Consult Clin Psychol. PMC6859953. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6859953/ Peer-reviewed statement by the HiTOP consortium. Authority: high for the dimensional critique/model. Four problems with categorical diagnosis: reliability ("~40% of diagnoses examined in the DSM-5 field trials showed poor inter-rater agreement"); comorbidity (excessive co-occurrence questions the categories' distinctness); heterogeneity ("individuals with the same diagnosis can have distinct, even non-overlapping sets of symptoms"); continuity ("most psychopathology falls along a continuum with normality"). HiTOP: a six-level hierarchy — general (p) factor → six spectra (internalizing, antagonistic externalizing, disinhibited externalizing, thought disorder, detachment, somatoform) → subfactors → syndromes → symptom components/traits. Honest limit: "no direct evidence yet that implementation of HiTOP diagnoses in clinical settings will improve treatment outcomes."
  • Caspi, A., & Moffitt, T. E. (2014). The p Factor: One General Psychopathology Factor in the Structure of Psychiatric Disorders? Clin Psychol Sci, 2(2). PMC4209412. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4209412/ Primary paper, Dunedin cohort (n≈1,000, ages 18–38). Authority: high. Psychiatric disorders' co-occurrence fits a hierarchical model: three spectra (internalizing, externalizing, thought disorder) under one general p factor, analogous to g in intelligence. Higher p → "more life impairment, greater familiality, worse developmental histories, and more compromised early-life brain function." The p factor "explains why it is challenging to find causes, consequences, biomarkers, and treatments with specificity to individual mental disorders."
  • NIMH. About RDoC (Research Domain Criteria). https://www.nimh.nih.gov/research/research-funded-by-nimh/rdoc/about-rdoc The funder's own framework page. Authority: high for what RDoC is and isn't. RDoC = "a set of research principles for investigating mental disorders" organized around six functional domains studied from genes to behavior across the normal-to-abnormal range — built because symptom-defined categories are heterogeneous and comorbid. Explicit limit: "RDoC is not meant to serve as a diagnostic guide, nor is it intended to replace current diagnostic systems."
  • Frances, A. (2013). The past, present and future of psychiatric diagnosis. World Psychiatry, 12(2). PMC3683254. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3683254/ Commentary by the chair of the DSM-IV task force — the loudest credentialed critic of DSM-5. Authority: high as a position piece, not as settled fact. "Diagnostic inflation": ADHD diagnoses tripled in twenty years, childhood bipolar up forty-fold, autism up twenty-fold; a prospective cohort (Great Smoky Mountains Study) found a cumulative 83% rate of mental disorder by age 21. Drivers include drug-company marketing that "sell[s] psychiatric diagnoses by convincing potential patients and prescribers that expectable life problems were really mental disorders." Diagnosis should "ensure reliable and accurate diagnosis and effective, safe, and necessary treatment" — not sweep in people likely to recover on their own.
  • Pies, R. W. (2014). The Bereavement Exclusion and DSM-5: An Update and Commentary. Innov Clin Neurosci, 11(7–8). PMC4204469. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4204469/ Peer-reviewed commentary by a participant in the debate (pro-removal side; counter-arguments summarized in-text). Authority: high for the shape of the debate. DSM-IV barred an MDD diagnosis in the first two months after bereavement absent override features (psychosis, suicidality). DSM-5 removed the exclusion because bereavement-triggered depression doesn't demonstrably "differ in nature, course, or outcome from depression of equal severity in any other context," and because depression is "a potentially lethal disorder" — while critics warned the change medicalizes ordinary grief. Clinically usable qualitative differences: grief preserves self-esteem, comes in waves that include positive memories, and is consolable; major depression trends toward pervasive misery, worthlessness/self-loathing, and inconsolability.
  • SAMHSA (NCBI Bookshelf). Cultural Formulation in Diagnosis and Cultural Concepts of Distress. In: Improving Cultural Competence (TIP 59), NBK248426. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK248426/ Government treatment-improvement protocol. Authority: high. DSM-5 retired "culture-bound syndrome" for three concepts: cultural syndromes (recognized symptom clusters, e.g., ataque de nervios, susto), cultural idioms of distress (culturally shared ways of expressing distress), and cultural explanations (causal attributions, e.g., susto as soul loss after a fright). The Outline for Cultural Formulation covers five domains (identity; explanations of illness; psychosocial environment; the client–clinician relationship; overall assessment); the 16-question Cultural Formulation Interview operationalizes it. "Behavior that is aberrant in one culture can be standard in another" — e.g., apparent paranoia can be normative in migrants from oppressive contexts.

Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings)

  1. The categories themselves are the contested object. DSM-5 field trials showed poor inter-rater agreement for a large share of tested diagnoses; comorbidity is the norm (45% of 12-month cases carry 2+ diagnoses); same-diagnosis patients can share almost no symptoms; and no common disorder has been shown to be a true natural category. HiTOP, the p factor, and RDoC are serious empirical alternatives — but none is ready to replace the DSM in the clinic, and HiTOP's own authors concede there's no outcome evidence yet for using it clinically.
  2. Diagnostic inflation is a real fight, not a fringe complaint. Frances (who chaired DSM-IV) argues the boundaries of disorder have expanded into normal life, pushed partly by pharmaceutical marketing; defenders answer that lowered thresholds catch treatable suffering earlier. Both dynamics are documented. Hold diagnosis as a tool with false-positive and false-negative costs.
  3. Grief vs. depression is the emblem case. Removing the bereavement exclusion (DSM-5) and adding prolonged grief disorder (DSM-5-TR) are defensible on the evidence and legitimately feared as pathologizing love and loss — the PFA module's grief pages carry the same tension. The qualitative markers (self-esteem preserved, waves, consolability) are the working discrimination.
  4. Criteria summarized secondhand. The DSM-5-TR text itself is paywalled; criteria here come from peer-reviewed secondary references (StatPearls et al.). Counts and durations were cross-checked across sources, but quote the manual before relying on a criterion clinically. Prevalence figures vary by survey and era (NCS-R is DSM-IV-based); treat them as order-of-magnitude. [S5–S17]
  5. Culture cuts through everything. The same behavior can be normative or symptomatic depending on context; the DSM's own cultural tools (CFI, cultural concepts of distress) exist because unexamined criteria misdiagnose — this is Unit 4's tripartite/humility material applied to diagnosis.
pages.text: Unit 6 sources — Psychopathology & the DSM-5-TR Evidence base for Unit 6 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1] . Researched 2026-07-17. Anchored on peer-reviewed clinical references (NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls for every major disorder category; the World Psychiatry DSM-5-TR overview by First et al. — the manual's own editors), triangulated with epidemiology primaries (Kessler's NCS-R), the dimensional-critique literature (HiTOP, the p factor, RDoC, Frances), and counseling-profession sources (The Professional Counselor / NBCC on the multiaxial removal and what diagnosis means for counselors). The DSM-5-TR itself is the anchor text (not freely online); criteria summarized here are taken from peer-reviewed secondary clinical references (StatPearls), which is the standard teaching practice — quote the manual itself before relying on any criterion in a real clinical or exam context. The APA's own dsm5.org/psychiatry.org pages block automated access (403) and are cited only via the First et al. overview S2 . Tier: the manual — structure, history, and what the TR changed S1 OpenStax Psychology 2e, §15.2 Diagnosing and Classifying Psychological Disorders (open textbook). https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/15-2-diagnosing-and-classifying-psychological-disorders Peer-reviewed open textbook. Authority: high for orientation-level DSM history and the standard criticisms. DSM-I (1952) had 106 diagnoses in 130 pages, organized on a format the U.S. Army developed in WWII; DSM-III (1980) had 265 diagnoses in 886 pages; DSM-5 (2013) contains 237 disorders. Each entry gives diagnostic features, diagnostic criteria, prevalence, and risk factors; comorbidity rates are documented (e.g., "41% of people with OCD also meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder"). Homosexuality removed as a diagnosis in 1973; the bereavement exclusion removed in DSM-5. Worldwide "the ICD is more frequently used for clinical diagnosis, whereas the DSM is more valued for research." Standing criticisms: the DSM "overpathologize[s] the human condition by turning common human problems into mental illnesses"; "nearly half of all Americans will meet the criteria for a DSM disorder at some point in their life." Anti-labeling stance: don't say "schizophrenics"/"depressives" — such labels "objectify people"; "a psychological disorder is not what a person is; it is something that a person has." S2 First, M. B., et al. (2022). DSM-5-TR: overview of what's new and what's changed. World Psychiatry, 21(2). PMC9077590. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9077590/ Peer-reviewed overview by the DSM-5-TR's own editors. Authority: highest available online for what the TR is. A text revision updates descriptive text from literature review, but DSM-5-TR went further: prolonged grief disorder added (intense yearning/preoccupation with the deceased ≥12 months after the death, with impairing grief symptoms — see the PFA module's grief pages), plus unspecified mood disorder and stimulant-induced mild neurocognitive disorder; free-standing symptom codes for suicidal behavior and nonsuicidal self-injury (recordable without any diagnosis); criteria/specifier changes to 70+ disorders ; terminology updates ("experienced gender," "individual assigned male/female at birth") and a full-text review by an Ethnoracial Equity and Inclusion Work Group . S3 Kress, V. E., et al. (2014). The Removal of the Multiaxial System in the DSM-5: Implications and Practice Suggestions for Counselors. The Professional Counselor (NBCC). https://tpcjournal.nbcc.org/the-removal-of-the-multiaxial-system-in-the-dsm-5-implications-and-practice-suggestions-for-counselors/ Peer-reviewed counseling journal. Authority: high for the counseling-profession angle. DSM-IV's five axes: I clinical disorders; II personality disorders & intellectual disability; III relevant medical conditions; IV psychosocial/environmental stressors; V Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF, 0–100). DSM-5 dropped all five for nonaxial documentation (all disorders listed together by clinical priority), WHODAS 2.0 replacing the GAF, and expanded V/Z codes for psychosocial context (housing, abuse, relational problems). Counselor implications: the shift reinforces a neurobiological/medical model while counselors emphasize "strength-based and developmentally, culturally and contextually sensitive approaches" — contextual factors must now be documented deliberately, without structural prompts. Catalogs the profession's standing critiques: the DSM has historically "marginalized, stigmatized and harmed those who are different," lacks cross-cultural validity, encourages reductionism, and reflects political as well as scientific processes. S4 SAMHSA (NCBI Bookshelf). DSM-IV to DSM-5 Changes: Overview. NBK519711. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519711/ Government clinical reference. Authority: high for the mechanics of the DSM-IV→5 transition. Details the axis system and its removal; the GAF was eliminated for "conceptual lack of clarity (i.e., including symptoms, suicide risk, and disabilities in the descriptors) and questionable psychometric properties." DSM-5 eliminated the "disorders usually first diagnosed in infancy, childhood, or adolescence" chapter, redistributing those disorders through a lifespan-ordered manual (neurodevelopmental disorders first, neurocognitive disorders last). Tier: disorder-category clinical references (criteria-level ground truth) S5 Bains, N., & Abdijadid, S. (updated 2023). Major Depressive Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK559078. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559078/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. MDD: 5 of 9 symptoms for ≥2 weeks, at least one being depressed mood or anhedonia , causing functional impairment; the nine: depressed mood, anhedonia, guilt/worthlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, appetite/weight change, psychomotor retardation or agitation, sleep disturbance, suicidal thoughts. A manic/hypomanic episode must be excluded (that's bipolar). Children may show irritable rather than sad mood. Lifetime prevalence ~12% (range 5–17%), roughly double in women . Untreated episodes last 6–12 months; recurrence ~50% after one episode, 70% after two, 90% after three. Differentials include dysthymia, bereavement, adjustment disorder with depressed mood, bipolar disorders, substance/medical causes. S6 Marzani, G., & Neff, A. P. (updated 2023). Bipolar Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK558998. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK558998/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Manic episode: elevated or irritable mood with increased activity/energy ≥7 days (or any duration if hospitalization required), with 3+ symptoms (4+ if mood only irritable): grandiosity, decreased need for sleep, pressured talkativeness, flight of ideas/racing thoughts, distractibility, increased goal-directed activity/agitation, high-risk behavior (spending sprees, sexual indiscretion). Hypomania: same symptom picture but ≥4 days, no marked impairment, no hospitalization, no psychosis . Bipolar I = at least one manic episode (depression not required); Bipolar II = at least one hypomanic episode + at least one major depressive episode, never mania; cyclothymia = 2+ years of subthreshold hypomanic and depressive symptoms. Bipolar-spectrum lifetime prevalence ~2.4%; correct diagnosis typically lags first contact by ~6–10 years; 20–30% of "MDD" patients transition to bipolar within 3 years ; suicide rate ~20–30× the general population. S7 Munir, S., & Takov, V. (updated 2022). Generalized Anxiety Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK441870. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK441870/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. GAD: excessive anxiety and worry, more days than not, ≥6 months , about multiple domains; difficulty controlling the worry ; 3+ of 6 associated symptoms (restlessness, easy fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance); distress/ impairment; not attributable to a substance or medical cause (rule out hyperthyroidism, caffeine, stimulants). Women ~2× men; up to ~20% of adults have an anxiety disorder in a given year; course chronic and relapsing. S8 Cackovic, C., Nazir, S., & Marwaha, R. (updated 2023). Panic Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK430973. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430973/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Panic attack: "an abrupt surge of intense fear or discomfort" peaking within minutes, with 4+ of 13 physical/cognitive symptoms (palpitations, sweating, trembling, dyspnea, chest pain, nausea, dizziness, chills/heat, paresthesias, derealization/depersonalization, fear of losing control or "going crazy," fear of dying). Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks plus ≥1 month of worry about further attacks and/or maladaptive behavior change (avoidance). Key discrimination: in other anxiety disorders, attacks are cued/expected (e.g., panic at public speaking in social anxiety disorder); medical mimics (hyperthyroid, cardiac, vestibular) must be excluded. S9 Mann, S. K., & Marwaha, R. (updated 2023). Posttraumatic Stress Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK559129. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559129/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Criterion A gate: exposure to "actual or threatened death, injury, or sexual violence" — directly experienced, witnessed in person, learned of happening to a close relative/friend, or repeated indirect professional exposure (first responders). Then four clusters: B intrusion (1+) (intrusive memories, nightmares, flashbacks, cued distress/reactivity); C avoidance (1+) (of internal reminders and/or external cues); D negative alterations in cognition/mood (2+) (amnesia for aspects, "I am bad," blame, persistent fear/guilt/shame, detachment, diminished interest, no positive emotion); E arousal/reactivity (2+) (irritability, recklessness, hypervigilance, startle, concentration, sleep). Duration >1 month + impairment. Specifiers: dissociative (depersonalization/derealization) and delayed expression (full criteria ≥6 months post-trauma). Lifetime prevalence ~6.1–9.2% (US). Differentials: acute stress disorder (same family, symptoms 3 days–1 month), adjustment disorder (stressor of any severity, not necessarily Criterion-A trauma; onset within 3 months). S10 Hany, M., et al. (updated 2024). Schizophrenia. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK539864. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK539864/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. 2+ of 5 symptom domains for a significant portion of one month — delusions, hallucinations, disorganized speech, grossly disorganized/catatonic behavior, negative symptoms (at least one must be delusions, hallucinations, or disorganized speech) — with continuous signs ≥6 months including ≥1 month of active-phase symptoms and functional decline. Positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization) respond to antipsychotics better than negative symptoms (flat affect, avolition). Spectrum by duration: brief psychotic disorder (1 day–<1 month), schizophreniform (<6 months), schizophrenia (≥6 months); schizoaffective = mood episodes concurrent with active-phase symptoms (plus ≥2 weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms); delusional disorder = delusions without the other characteristic symptoms. Lifetime risk ~1%; men ~1.7× incidence, earlier onset, more negative symptoms. Complete recovery in only ~13.5%; life expectancy ~15 years shorter; suicide the most common cause of premature death. Dopamine hypothesis: mesolimbic dysregulation → "misattribution of importance to irrelevant objects or events" (aberrant salience). S11 Fariba, K. A., et al. (updated 2023). Personality Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK556058. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK556058/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. General definition: "an enduring pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates significantly from the norms and expectations of the surrounding culture" — pervasive, inflexible, onset by adolescence/early adulthood, stable, causing distress or impairment. Cluster A (odd/eccentric): paranoid, schizoid, schizotypal. Cluster B (dramatic/emotional/erratic): antisocial, borderline, histrionic, narcissistic. Cluster C (anxious/fearful): avoidant, dependent, obsessive-compulsive (OCPD). Prevalence ~6.1% (WHO); much higher in clinical and incarcerated populations. "With the exception of borderline personality disorder, there are no high-quality, evidence-based psychotherapies for personality disorders" — DBT is the established borderline treatment. The DSM-5-TR also carries the Alternative Model (AMPD) : a hybrid dimensional-categorical system rating impairment in personality functioning plus pathological traits. Countertransference management is a core clinical challenge. S12 Brock, H., et al. (updated 2024). Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK553162. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK553162/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Obsessions: "recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are … intrusive and unwanted." Compulsions: "repetitive behaviors or mental acts that the person feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rules that must be applied rigidly." Diagnosis: obsessions and/or compulsions that are time-consuming (≥1 hr/day) or cause marked distress/impairment. DSM-5 moved OCD out of the anxiety chapter into Obsessive-Compulsive and Related Disorders (with body dysmorphic disorder, hoarding disorder, trichotillomania, excoriation disorder) on shared phenomenology/neurobiology. Most patients have insight (only 2–4% lack it) — symptoms are ego-dystonic (recognized as irrational, unwanted). Contrast OCPD : "a chronic pattern of perfectionism and rigid control" experienced as rational and ego-syntonic, with no true obsessions/compulsions. S13 Moore, C. A., & Bokor, B. R. (updated 2023). Anorexia Nervosa. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK459148. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459148/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high (AN); BN/BED facts corroborated in-page. Among the deadliest psychiatric conditions: elevated all-cause mortality via medical complications and suicide (~25% of AN deaths) ; ~three-fourths of outpatients remit within 5 years. Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings) The categories themselves are the contested object. DSM-5 field trials showed poor inter-rater agreement for a large share of tested diagnoses; comorbidity is the norm (45% of 12-month cases carry 2+ diagnoses); same-diagnosis patients can share almost no symptoms; and no common disorder has been shown to be a true natural category. HiTOP, the p factor, and RDoC are serious empirical alternatives — but none is ready to replace the DSM in the clinic, and HiTOP's own authors concede there's no outcome evidence yet for using it clinically. S17 S18 S19 S20 Diagnostic inflation is a real fight, not a fringe complaint. Frances (who chaired DSM-IV) argues the boundaries of disorder have expanded into normal life, pushed partly by pharmaceutical marketing; defenders answer that lowered thresholds catch treatable suffering earlier. Both dynamics are documented. Hold diagnosis as a tool with false-positive and false-negative costs. S21 S1 Grief vs. depression is the emblem case. Removing the bereavement exclusion (DSM-5) and adding prolonged grief disorder (DSM-5-TR) are defensible on the evidence and legitimately feared as pathologizing love and loss — the PFA module's grief pages carry the same tension. The qualitative markers (self-esteem preserved, waves, consolability) are the working discrimination. S22 S2 Criteria summarized secondhand. The DSM-5-TR text itself is paywalled; criteria here come from peer-reviewed secondary references (StatPearls et al.). Counts and durations were cross-checked across sources, but quote the manual before relying on a criterion clinically . Prevalence figures vary by survey and era (NCS-R is DSM-IV-based); treat them as order-of-magnitude. [S5–S17] Culture cuts through everything. The same behavior can be normative or symptomatic depending on context; the DSM's own cultural tools (CFI, cultural concepts of distress) exist because unexamined criteria misdiagnose — this is Unit 4's tripartite/humility material applied to diagnosis. S23 S3
