pages.html:
Unit 7 sources — Assessment, Diagnosis & Case Conceptualization

Evidence base for Unit 7 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1].

Researched 2026-07-17. Anchored on peer-reviewed clinical references (NCBI Bookshelf StatPearls for the mental status examination and for sensitivity/specificity; the NCBI Bookshelf IOM report on psychological testing for reliability/validity/standardization), the instrument-validation primaries (Kroenke et al. 2001 for the PHQ-9; Spitzer et al. 2006 for the GAD-7, corroborated by a peer-reviewed psychometric replication), the anchor text's author (Sommers-Flanagan on the clinical interview), a peer-reviewed counseling journal (The Professional Counselor) for the Five Ps case-formulation framework, and a peer-reviewed Psychiatric Services statement on measurement-based care. Screening-instrument details were cross-checked against the APA's public assessment page. Some measurement-based-care and treatment-planning specifics come from sources whose full text 403'd to automated access (Psychiatric Services PDF, the OER reliability chapter) and are cited via their abstracts / search-indexed text plus a corroborating source — flagged where used. Documentation conventions like the "golden thread" are practice/compliance norms, not scientific findings, and are cited to a practitioner reference at orientation level and labeled as such.

Tier: the clinical interview and the mental status exam

  • Voss, R. M., & M Das, J. (updated 2023). Mental Status Examination. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK546682. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK546682/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high for MSE domains and their definitions. The MSE covers appearance, behavior, motor activity, speech, mood, affect, thought process, thought content, perceptions, cognition (alertness/orientation/attention/memory/abstract reasoning), insight, and judgment. Key distinctions the page draws explicitly: mood is the patient's subjective, self-reported emotional state (documented in their own words) while affect is the clinician's observed emotional expression (euthymic, flat, labile, congruent/ incongruent); thought process is the form/organization of thinking (circumstantial, tangential, flight of ideas, loose associations, perseveration, blocking) while thought content is what is thought about (delusions, obsessions, suicidal/homicidal ideation); insight is the patient's understanding of their illness while judgment is their capacity to make sound decisions — and the two dissociate (poor insight can coexist with fair judgment). The MSE is a cross-sectional snapshot of current state, "a subjective assessment … which may vary significantly between clinicians," and it does not by itself constitute a diagnosis — it aids diagnosis only combined with history, substance/medical history, and collateral/objective data.
  • Sommers-Flanagan, J. (2019). The Clinical Interview as an Assessment Tool (blog essay drawn from Clinical Interviewing, Sommers-Flanagan & Sommers-Flanagan). johnsommersflanagan.com. https://johnsommersflanagan.com/2019/06/29/the-clinical-interview-as-an-assessment-tool/ The Unit's anchor author. Authority: high for interview structure and stance (the standard counseling text). The clinical interview is the foundational assessment method — it organizes, assesses, and communicates information about a client's current state, and (for risk) is "the gold standard." Four assessment-interview types: (1) the intake interview (the most common; gathers initial information), (2) the psychodiagnostic interview (establishes a diagnosis to guide treatment), (3) the mental status examination (a semi-structured protocol across ~nine domains), and (4) suicide assessment (see Unit 8). The intake addresses three core areas: the presenting problem, the psychosocial (biopsychosocial) history, and current functioning. Structure ranges from unstructured → semi-structured → highly structured, and skilled clinicians blend structured elements into a relational frame — rapport and information-gathering are not opposed; the relationship is itself part of the assessment (ties back to unit01-helping-skills).

Tier: screening instruments (validation primaries + corroboration)

  • Kroenke, K., Spitzer, R. L., & Williams, J. B. W. (2001). The PHQ-9: Validity of a Brief Depression Severity Measure. Journal of General Internal Medicine, 16(9), 606–613. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1046/j.1525-1497.2001.016009606.x The PHQ-9 validation primary. Authority: high (the definitive source for the instrument). The PHQ-9 is a 9-item self-report scoring each of the DSM major-depression symptoms 0–3 ("not at all" → "nearly every day") over the last two weeks; total 0–27. Severity anchors: 5 / 10 / 15 / 20 = mild / moderate / moderately severe / severe (0–4 minimal). At a cut-point of ≥10, sensitivity and specificity for major depression are both 88%. Internal consistency Cronbach's α = 0.86–0.89; strong test-retest. Item 9 screens passive/active thoughts of death or self-harm — a positive answer obligates a direct risk follow-up (Unit 8). The instrument maps one item to each of the nine MDD criteria, so it doubles as a criteria refresher.
  • Spitzer, R. L., Kroenke, K., Williams, J. B. W., & Löwe, B. (2006). A Brief Measure for Assessing Generalized Anxiety Disorder: The GAD-7. Archives of Internal Medicine, 166(10), 1092–1097. https://ctc-ri.org/sites/default/files/uploads/gad7_ref.pdf The GAD-7 validation primary. Authority: high. The GAD-7 is a 7-item self-report (0–3 each), total 0–21; cut-points 5 / 10 / 15 = mild / moderate / severe. At ≥10: sensitivity 89%, specificity 82% for GAD. Internal consistency α ≈ 0.92; good test-retest and convergent validity. Though built for GAD, it also performs as a screen for panic disorder (sens ~74%), social anxiety disorder (~72%), and PTSD (~66%) — a reminder that a positive screen names a domain of distress, not a diagnosis.
  • American Psychological Association. Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9 & PHQ-2). APA assessment-tools resource. https://www.apa.org/pi/about/publications/caregivers/practice-settings/assessment/tools/patient-health Professional-body summary. Authority: high for practical use and access. Confirms PHQ-9 structure/scoring and that scores ≥10 carry a 7–13.6× increased likelihood of a depression diagnosis while ≤4 drops it below ~1-in-25. The PHQ-2 (first two items — depressed mood + anhedonia) is an ultra-brief pre-screen; a positive PHQ-2 prompts the full PHQ-9. The PHQ family is free to use and available in 30+ languages (a real reason for its ubiquity).
  • Rutter, L. A., & Brown, T. A. (2017). Psychometric Properties of the GAD-7 in a Heterogeneous Psychiatric Sample. Frontiers in Psychology / J Psychopathol Behav Assess. PMC6691128. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6691128/ Peer-reviewed psychometric replication. Authority: high for reliability/validity numbers beyond primary-care samples. In a heterogeneous clinical sample the GAD-7 was unidimensional (one-factor), α = 0.83–0.93, with strong convergent validity (BAI r = 0.69; SCL-90 anxiety r = 0.76) and sensitivity to treatment change (Cohen's d ≈ 0.5). Suggests a slightly lower optimal cut (≥8: sens 0.92, spec 0.70) in some populations — illustrating that cut-points are population-dependent, not universal constants.

Tier: reliability, validity, and screening statistics

  • Institute of Medicine (US) Committee. Overview of Psychological Testing. In: Psychological Testing in the Service of Disability Determination. NCBI Bookshelf, NBK305233 (2015). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK305233/ National Academies / IOM consensus report. Authority: high for measurement theory. Reliability = the stability/consistency of scores: test-retest (across time), inter-rater (across scorers), parallel/alternate forms, and internal consistency (item homogeneity — Cronbach's α). Validity = "the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses" — and critically, validity attaches to the interpretation/use, not to the test itself. Evidence types: content, criterion-related (predictive/concurrent), and construct. The report states plainly that reliable scores do not guarantee validity. Standardization = fixed administration procedures plus a representative normative sample; applying a test outside its norming population risks misinterpretation. Trustworthy testing needs reliability + validity evidence + standardized administration + representative norms + qualified administration + fairness across groups — psychometrics alone don't license clinical use.
  • Price, P. C., Jhangiani, R., Chiang, I. A., et al. Reliability and Validity of Measurement. In: Research Methods in Psychology (2nd Canadian Ed.), open textbook (opentextbc.ca / KPU Pressbooks). https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/reliability-and-validity-of-measurement/ Peer-reviewed open educational resource. Authority: high for orientation-level psychometrics (full text 403'd to automated fetch; content via search-indexed summary + corroboration by S5). Reliability kinds — test-retest (same test, two times), internal consistency (split-half; Cronbach's α, ~0.70+ acceptable), inter-rater (agreement across judges). Validity kinds — face (looks right), content (covers the whole construct), criterion (concurrent vs. predictive), construct (fits the theoretical network; convergent + discriminant). The load-bearing relationship: a measure can be reliable but not valid (consistently measuring the wrong thing), and reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity — "you can't be valid without being reliable, but you can be reliable without being valid."
  • Shreffler, J., & Huecker, M. R. (updated 2023). Diagnostic Testing Accuracy: Sensitivity, Specificity, Predictive Values and Likelihood Ratios. StatPearls / NCBI Bookshelf, NBK557491. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557491/ Peer-reviewed clinical reference. Authority: high. Sensitivity = true positives ÷ all who have the condition (a sensitive test, when negative, helps rule OUT — "SnNOut"); specificity = true negatives ÷ all who don't (a specific test, when positive, helps rule IN — "SpPin"). The two trade off: pushing a cut-point to catch more cases raises sensitivity and lowers specificity. PPV/NPV (how much a positive/negative result means) depend on prevalence — the same test yields a lower PPV in a low-prevalence population. Screening instruments are deliberately tuned toward high sensitivity (miss few cases, accept false positives); a positive screen is a flag to assess further, not a diagnosis.

Tier: case conceptualization and treatment planning

  • Kramer, G. A., & Rogers, J. R. (2023, exemplar). Case Formulation and Intervention: Application of the Five Ps Framework in Substance Use Counseling. The Professional Counselor (NBCC). https://tpcjournal.nbcc.org/case-formulation-and-intervention-application-of-the-five-ps-framework-in-substance-use-counseling/ Peer-reviewed counseling journal. Authority: high for the counseling case-conceptualization angle. Case formulation (a.k.a. conceptualization) builds a multidimensional, idiographic picture of the client that "allows clinicians to target specific areas of concern" — Macneil et al. (2012) argued diagnosis alone is insufficient; you must add causal, lifestyle, and personal factors. The Five Ps: Presenting problem; Predisposing factors (biological/environmental/personality vulnerabilities that raise risk); Precipitating factors (proximal triggers of the current episode); Perpetuating factors (what sustains/reinforces the problem); Protective factors (strengths, relationships, resources that buffer). The framework "permits counselors to both assess and intervene essentially simultaneously" and — unlike CBT-bound formulation models — "does not adhere to any particular theoretical orientation," so the counselor's theory (Unit 2) still chooses the intervention.
  • PsychDB. Biopsychosocial Model and Case Formulation. psychdb.com (teaching reference). https://www.psychdb.com/teaching/biopsychosocial-case-formulation Clinician-teaching reference (orientation-tier). Authority: moderate — corroborates S4's Ps and crosses them with the biopsychosocial grid. Presents the 4 Ps × biopsychosocial grid: each P (predisposing / precipitating / perpetuating / protective) is asked across the biological, psychological, and social domains (e.g., predisposing biological = genetics/temperament; predisposing social = early adversity; perpetuating psychological = maladaptive coping; protective social = supportive relationships). Frames formulation as the explanatory counterpart to diagnosis: "what is wrong, how it got that way, and what can be done about it," attributing the biopsychosocial frame to Engel (1977/1980) and its systematization to Weerasekera (1993). (See concept-biopsychosocial-model from Unit 5.)
  • Fortney, J. C., Unützer, J., Wrenn, G., et al. (2017). A Tipping Point for Measurement-Based Care. Psychiatric Services, 68(2), 179–188. https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.201500439 Peer-reviewed policy/evidence statement. Authority: high (full PDF 403'd; core claims via the journal's abstract/indexed text). Measurement-based care (MBC) = the routine administration of validated symptom scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7, PCL, AUDIT-C) at each visit, with the scores fed back to guide treatment decisions. MBC improves outcomes — effects are strongest for patients who would otherwise not improve — because it detects non-response and deterioration earlier than clinical impression alone (clinicians relying on unaided judgment routinely fail to notice worsening). It operationalizes the screening→monitoring loop: the same instrument that flags a problem at intake tracks whether treatment is working. Underused despite the evidence — the "tipping point" argument.
  • Doran, G. T. (1981). There's a S.M.A.R.T. Way to Write Management's Goals and Objectives. Management Review, 70(11), 35–36. (History via the SMART-criteria overview.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMART_criteria Origin citation for the SMART acronym. Authority: high for provenance; the clinical adaptation is convention. SMART originated in management, not clinical work — Doran's original words were Specific, Measurable, Assignable, Realistic, Time-related; the counseling adaptation reads Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. It is a format for writing objectives, not a therapy — its value in treatment planning is forcing vague aims ("feel less anxious") into reviewable ones ("reduce GAD-7 from 16 to ≤7 within 12 weeks").
  • ICANotes / SonderMind. Golden Thread Documentation for Behavioral Health. (practitioner/compliance references.) https://www.icanotes.com/2025/10/20/golden-thread-documentation-mental-health/ Practitioner/vendor references (orientation-tier). Authority: low-moderate — a documentation/compliance convention, not a scientific claim; cited as such. The "golden thread" is the auditable chain assessment/diagnosis → treatment-plan goal → measurable objective → session interventions → progress notes → review: any note should trace backward to the goal it serves and the diagnosis that makes it medically necessary. Payers reimburse for impairment, not symptoms, so the plan must tie the diagnosis to functional limitations and measurable targets. Distinguishes goals (broad clinical outcomes) from objectives (small, measurable steps toward them).

Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings)

  1. A screen is not a diagnosis — and cut-points are not laws. The PHQ-9 and GAD-7 are tuned for high sensitivity to avoid missing cases, which means false positives are expected; a positive screen mandates a clinical interview, never a diagnosis by number. And the "≥10" cut-point is population-dependent (≥8 optimal in some psychiatric samples) — treat cut-scores as calibrated flags, not thresholds of truth.
  2. Reliability ≠ validity, and neither licenses use. A test can be perfectly consistent and consistently wrong; validity attaches to the interpretation for a purpose, and even a valid, reliable test misinterprets when applied outside its normative population — the culture-fair- assessment worry from unit04-multicultural lands here.
  3. Diagnosis vs. formulation is the unit's spine. Diagnosis (Unit 6) names what; case conceptualization explains how it got this way and what maintains it and points to what to do — filtered through the counselor's theory (Unit 2). The DSM label is an input to the formulation, not a substitute for it.
  4. The MSE is a snapshot, and a subjective one. It captures current state, varies between clinicians, and only supports (never makes) a diagnosis — over-reading a single MSE, or confusing mood with affect / process with content / insight with judgment, is the common beginner error.
  5. "Measurable" can crowd out "meaningful." SMART goals and MBC genuinely catch non-response earlier and satisfy payers — but a plan built only from what a scale can score risks reducing the person to a number and importing the medical model's incentives (the same billing pressure flagged in concept-dsm-structure). Measure to serve the work, not the reverse.
  6. Provenance caveats. PHQ-9/GAD-7 primaries and the StatPearls/IOM references were read directly; the Psychiatric Services MBC full text and the OER reliability chapter 403'd to automated access and are cited via abstract/indexed summaries plus a corroborating source. The golden-thread material is a documentation convention from practitioner references, labeled orientation-tier.

Biopsychosocial Model and Case Formulation. psychdb.com (teaching reference). https://www.psychdb.com/teaching/biopsychosocial-case-formulation Clinician-teaching reference (orientation-tier). Authority: moderate — corroborates S4's Ps and crosses them with the biopsychosocial grid. Presents the 4 Ps × biopsychosocial grid : each P (predisposing / precipitating / perpetuating / protective) is asked across the biological, psychological, and social domains (e.g., predisposing biological = genetics/temperament; predisposing social = early adversity; perpetuating psychological = maladaptive coping; protective social = supportive relationships). Frames formulation as the explanatory counterpart to diagnosis: "what is wrong, how it got that way, and what can be done about it," attributing the biopsychosocial frame to Engel (1977/1980) and its systematization to Weerasekera (1993) . (See concept-biopsychosocial-model from Unit 5.) S12 Fortney, J. C., Unützer, J., Wrenn, G., et al. (2017). A Tipping Point for Measurement-Based Care. Psychiatric Services, 68(2), 179–188. https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.201500439 Peer-reviewed policy/evidence statement. Authority: high (full PDF 403'd; core claims via the journal's abstract/indexed text). Measurement-based care (MBC) = the routine administration of validated symptom scales (PHQ-9, GAD-7, PCL, AUDIT-C) at each visit, with the scores fed back to guide treatment decisions. MBC improves outcomes — effects are strongest for patients who would otherwise not improve — because it detects non-response and deterioration earlier than clinical impression alone (clinicians relying on unaided judgment routinely fail to notice worsening). It operationalizes the screening→monitoring loop: the same instrument that flags a problem at intake tracks whether treatment is working. Underused despite the evidence — the "tipping point" argument. S13 Doran, G. T. (1981). There's a S.M.A.R.T. Way to Write Management's Goals and Objectives. Management Review, 70(11), 35–36. (History via the SMART-criteria overview.) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SMART_criteria Origin citation for the SMART acronym. Authority: high for provenance; the clinical adaptation is convention. SMART originated in management , not clinical work — Doran's original words were Specific, Measurable, Assignable, Realistic, Time-related ; the counseling adaptation reads Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound. It is a format for writing objectives , not a therapy — its value in treatment planning is forcing vague aims ("feel less anxious") into reviewable ones ("reduce GAD-7 from 16 to ≤7 within 12 weeks"). S14 ICANotes / SonderMind. Golden Thread Documentation for Behavioral Health. (practitioner/compliance references.) https://www.icanotes.com/2025/10/20/golden-thread-documentation-mental-health/ Practitioner/vendor references (orientation-tier). Authority: low-moderate — a documentation/compliance convention, not a scientific claim; cited as such. The "golden thread" is the auditable chain assessment/diagnosis → treatment-plan goal → measurable objective → session interventions → progress notes → review : any note should trace backward to the goal it serves and the diagnosis that makes it medically necessary. Payers reimburse for impairment , not symptoms, so the plan must tie the diagnosis to functional limitations and measurable targets. Distinguishes goals (broad clinical outcomes) from objectives (small, measurable steps toward them). Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings) A screen is not a diagnosis — and cut-points are not laws. The PHQ-9 and GAD-7 are tuned for high sensitivity to avoid missing cases, which means false positives are expected; a positive screen mandates a clinical interview, never a diagnosis by number. And the "≥10" cut-point is population-dependent (≥8 optimal in some psychiatric samples) — treat cut-scores as calibrated flags, not thresholds of truth. S2 S3 S9 S10 Reliability ≠ validity, and neither licenses use. A test can be perfectly consistent and consistently wrong; validity attaches to the interpretation for a purpose , and even a valid, reliable test misinterprets when applied outside its normative population — the culture-fair- assessment worry from unit04-multicultural lands here. S5 S11 Diagnosis vs. formulation is the unit's spine. Diagnosis (Unit 6) names what ; case conceptualization explains how it got this way and what maintains it and points to what to do — filtered through the counselor's theory (Unit 2). The DSM label is an input to the formulation, not a substitute for it. S4 S8 The MSE is a snapshot, and a subjective one. It captures current state, varies between clinicians, and only supports (never makes) a diagnosis — over-reading a single MSE, or confusing mood with affect / process with content / insight with judgment, is the common beginner error. S1 "Measurable" can crowd out "meaningful." SMART goals and MBC genuinely catch non-response earlier and satisfy payers — but a plan built only from what a scale can score risks reducing the person to a number and importing the medical model's incentives (the same billing pressure flagged in concept-dsm-structure ). Measure to serve the work, not the reverse. S12 S13 S14 Provenance caveats. PHQ-9/GAD-7 primaries and the StatPearls/IOM references were read directly; the Psychiatric Services MBC full text and the OER reliability chapter 403'd to automated access and are cited via abstract/indexed summaries plus a corroborating source. The golden-thread material is a documentation convention from practitioner references, labeled orientation-tier.
