pages.title: Unit 8 sources — Crisis, Risk Assessment & Trauma-Informed Care
pages.html:
Unit 8 sources — Crisis, Risk Assessment & Trauma-Informed Care

Evidence base for Unit 8 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1].

Researched 2026-07-18. This is the syllabus's highest-stakes unit ("preparation directly protects a life") and an emotionally heavy one — material is kept clinical and precise, no sensationalism (per CLAUDE.md). Anchored where possible on primary instruments and validation studies (the Columbia C-SSRS; Stanley & Brown's Safety Planning Intervention and its RCT; the Project BETA de-escalation consensus), government/professional bodies (SAMHSA's trauma-informed framework; the VA suicide-risk guide; Harvard's Means Matter program), and peer-reviewed clinical/counseling literature (a peer-reviewed HPA-axis review read in full via pypdf; the Trippany/Kress Journal of Counseling & Development vicarious-trauma article read in full via pypdf). Two anchor books (James & Gilliland; Herman) are offline and cited via reputable secondary sources, flagged. Per the course-map's explicit caution, van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score is popular-press: its neurobiology claims are corroborated against peer-reviewed sources and the popular/contested pieces (the memory-as-storage metaphor, polyvagal theory) are flagged as such in the readings.

Tier: suicide risk assessment (instruments, interviewing, frameworks)

  • Columbia Lighthouse Project. Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). Columbia University Department of Psychiatry / The Columbia Lighthouse Project. (Validation: Posner, K., et al. (2011). The Columbia–Suicide Severity Rating Scale: Initial Validity and Internal Consistency Findings From Three Multisite Studies With Adolescents and Adults. American Journal of Psychiatry, 168(12), 1266–1277.) https://www.columbiapsychiatry.org/research-labs/columbia-suicide-severity-rating-scale-c-ssrs · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22193671/ Widely adopted, validated risk-screening instrument. Authority: high for the ideation/behavior distinction and the severity ladder. The C-SSRS separates suicidal ideation from suicidal behavior and grades each. Ideation is rated on a five-point severity ladder of increasing seriousness: (1) wish to be dead; (2) nonspecific active suicidal thoughts; (3) active ideation with methods considered (no plan); (4) active ideation with some intent to act; (5) active ideation with a specific plan and intent. Intensity items capture frequency, duration, controllability, deterrents, and reasons. The behavior subscale records actual attempts, interrupted attempts (stopped by an outside circumstance), aborted/self-interrupted attempts (stopped by the person), preparatory acts (assembling means, giving things away, writing a note), and non-suicidal self-injury. Plain language; requires no mental-health training to administer; endorsed across clinical, research, and institutional settings.
  • Shea, S. C. The Chronological Assessment of Suicide Events (the CASE Approach). Training Institute for Suicide Assessment and Clinical Interviewing (TISA); SPRC Best Practices Registry. (Shea, S. C. (2009). Suicide Assessment Part 2: Uncovering Suicidal Intent Using the CASE Approach. Psychiatric Times.) https://suicideassessment.com/the-case-approach/ · https://www.psychiatrist.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/11584_chronological-assessment-suicide-events-practical.pdf Widely taught interviewing strategy (SPRC-registered). Authority: high for the interviewing method and the stated/reflected/withheld-intent distinction. The CASE Approach is an interviewing strategy for eliciting suicidal ideation, planning, behavior, and intent with higher validity. It sequences the interview through four chronological regions: (1) presenting ideation/events (the crisis that brought them in), (2) recent ideation/events (past ~8 weeks), (3) past ideation/events (lifetime), and (4) immediate ideation (how they feel about safety right now and their disposition). The delineation keeps the clinician "on task" and reduces errors of omission. Shea distinguishes stated intent (what the client reports), reflected intent (the extent of thinking/planning/action the client describes, which may reveal more than the stated intent), and withheld intent — the interview's job is to maximize reflected intent and minimize what's withheld. Validity-enhancing techniques (e.g., behavioral incident — asking for fact/sequence rather than opinion; gentle assumption; normalization; denial of the specific) reduce the tendency to under-report.
  • U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs / VA National Center for Patient Safety. Suicide Risk Assessment Guide — Reference Manual. mentalhealth.va.gov. https://www.mentalhealth.va.gov/docs/suicide_risk_assessment_reference_guide.pdf Government clinical reference. Authority: high for the warning-signs mnemonic, the acute/chronic distinction, and risk stratification. Distinguishes chronic/distal risk factors (long-standing background vulnerabilities: prior attempts — the single strongest predictor — psychiatric disorder, substance use, chronic pain/ illness, trauma/abuse history, family history, access to means, male sex, social isolation) from acute/proximal risk factors and warning signs (recent events and states that raise risk in the near term). Warning signs via the IS PATH WARM mnemonic (American Association of Suicidology): Ideation, Substance abuse, Purposelessness, Anxiety/agitation, Trapped, Hopelessness, Withdrawal, Anger, Recklessness, Mood change. Protective factors: reasons for living, social connectedness, responsibility to family/children, engaged treatment, coping skills, cultural/religious beliefs discouraging suicide. Direct inquiry does not increase risk. Ask about ideation → plan → intent → means/access → preparatory behavior. Risk stratification guides disposition: low (outpatient + safety plan + follow-up), moderate (intensified outpatient / crisis services / increased monitoring / remove means), high (hospitalization / do not leave alone / immediate means removal).
  • Dazzi, T., Gribble, R., Wessely, S., & Fear, N. T. (2014). Does Asking About Suicide and Related Behaviours Induce Suicidal Ideation? What Is the Evidence? Psychological Medicine, 44(16), 3361–3363. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/psychological-medicine/article/does-asking-about-suicide-and-related-behaviours-induce-suicidal-ideation-what-is-the-evidence/ Peer-reviewed evidence synthesis. Authority: high for the "asking doesn't plant the idea" claim. Reviewing studies across community, adult, adolescent, and at-risk samples, found no evidence that asking about suicide induces or increases suicidal ideation; several studies found acknowledging and talking about suicide may reduce rather than increase ideation. Refutes the common clinician fear that direct questioning is dangerous — the far greater risk is not asking.
  • Klonsky, E. D., & May, A. M. (2015). The Three-Step Theory (3ST): A New Theory of Suicide Rooted in the "Ideation-to-Action" Framework. International Journal of Cognitive Therapy, 8(2), 114–129. (Framework origin: Joiner, T. (2005). Why People Die by Suicide, the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide.) https://www2.psych.ubc.ca/~klonsky/publications/3ST.pdf Peer-reviewed theory. Authority: high for the ideation-to-action framework and its clinical implications. The ideation-to-action framework holds that the development of suicidal ideation and the progression from ideation to an attempt are distinct processes with distinct causes — so factors that explain who thinks about suicide differ from factors that explain who acts. Joiner's Interpersonal Theory (IPTS): ideation arises from thwarted belongingness + perceived burdensomeness; the leap to an attempt requires acquired capability (habituation to pain, fear, and death through exposure — prior self-injury, abuse, others' suicide, etc.). Klonsky & May's 3ST: ideation = pain (usually psychological) + hopelessness; connectedness is the key factor that keeps moderate ideation from escalating; the move to attempt is governed by capacity for suicide (dispositional, acquired, practical). Clinical upshot: a person with strong ideation but low capability, or a client whose connectedness is intact, is at a different kind of risk than one who has acquired capability — and means access is a practical contributor to capacity.

Tier: safety planning and means reduction

  • Stanley, B., & Brown, G. K. (2012). Safety Planning Intervention: A Brief Intervention to Mitigate Suicide Risk. Cognitive and Behavioral Practice, 19(2), 256–264. (Template + clinician guidance: Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention, suicidesafetyplan.com; National Jewish Health clinician guide.) https://suicidesafetyplan.com/ · https://www.nationaljewish.org/suicide-awareness/suicidal-patients-next-steps/safety-plan-with-a-patient The intervention's primary source + official template. Authority: high for the six steps and the collaborative stance. The Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) is a brief, collaborative, clinician-assisted tool: a prioritized, written list of coping strategies and supports for a suicidal crisis. Six steps, in order of escalating external reliance: (1) Warning signs (personal thoughts/images/moods/ behaviors that a crisis is building) → (2) Internal coping strategies the client can do alone to distract without contacting anyone (walk, music, exercise) → (3) Social contacts and settings that provide distraction (people/places, without disclosing the crisis) → (4) People to ask for help (family/friends the client will tell) → (5) Professionals and agencies to contact in crisis (clinician, local ED, 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) → (6) Making the environment safe (reducing access to lethal means — the means-restriction step). The ordering matters: it moves from self-reliance toward external help so the earliest steps are things the client can always do. It is built with the client, not handed to them, and is a living document to revisit. Explicitly not a "no-suicide contract" (see S7).
  • Stanley, B., et al. (2018). Comparison of the Safety Planning Intervention With Follow-up vs Usual Care of Suicidal Patients Treated in the Emergency Department. JAMA Psychiatry, 75(9), 894–900. (No-suicide-contract critique: Rudd, M. D., Mandrusiak, M., & Joiner, T. E. (2006). The Case Against No-Suicide Contracts. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 62(2), 243–251.) https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/2687370 Peer-reviewed effectiveness study + peer-reviewed critique. Authority: high for the evidence base and the contract contrast. In a cohort study of ED patients, the SPI plus structured telephone follow-up was associated with ~45% fewer suicidal behaviors over six months versus usual care, and with greater treatment engagement. Safety planning is endorsed by the Joint Commission, the VA/DoD guideline, and the Zero Suicide framework. By contrast, the "no-suicide contract" / "no-harm contract" (a client's promise not to self-harm) is not evidence-based: no study shows it reduces suicide or attempts, it can create false reassurance for the clinician, it shifts toward defensive rather than therapeutic practice, and it offers the client nothing to do in a crisis. A commitment-to-safety or safety plan (what the client will do, and how to get help) has replaced it.
  • Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Means Matter program. Lethal Means Counseling and Means Matter research summaries. https://hsph.harvard.edu/research/means-matter/lethal-means-counseling/ · https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/lethal-means-safety-counseling Public-health program at a leading school. Authority: high for means-restriction rationale and the counseling method. Means reduction / lethal-means safety counseling = collaboratively reducing a suicidal person's access to highly lethal methods until the crisis passes. Rationale: (1) case fatality varies enormously by method — roughly 85–90% of firearm attempts are fatal, versus a few percent for overdose/cutting — so the method a person reaches for in a crisis heavily determines whether they live; (2) suicidal crises are often brief and impulsive — the interval between deciding and acting is frequently minutes to an hour; (3) method substitution is incomplete — many people do not simply switch to an equally lethal method, and (4) most attempt survivors do not go on to die by suicide (roughly 9 in 10). The counseling targets firearms (best: temporary off-site storage with a trusted person or facility; otherwise locked, unloaded, ammunition stored separately) and medications (limit quantities, lock up, dispose of excess). It is collaborative and time-limited ("while things are hard"), not confiscation. Despite the evidence it is underused — one survey found ~78% of EDs assess access to means but only ~35% provide means counseling.

Tier: crisis intervention and de-escalation models

  • James, R. K., & Gilliland, B. E. Crisis Intervention Strategies (anchor text; latest eds.). Six-step model summarized via clinician references (ICANotes; university crisis-intervention course materials). https://www.icanotes.com/2022/04/19/6-step-crisis-intervention-model-explained/ The unit's anchor text (offline); six-step model corroborated via reputable secondary references. Authority: high for the model's content, secondary for exact wording. Defines a crisis as a perception of an event or situation as an intolerable difficulty that exceeds the person's current resources and coping (Caplan's tradition) — crisis is in the perception/response, not the event. The six-step model blends listening (steps 1–3) and acting (steps 4–6): (1) Define the problem from the client's viewpoint; (2) Ensure client safety — the continuous first priority; (3) Provide support (unconditional, present); (4) Examine alternatives (mobilize situational supports, coping mechanisms, positive thinking); (5) Make plans (concrete, collaborative, doable steps that restore some control); (6) Obtain commitment to the plan. Safety is not one step but the thread running through all six.
  • Roberts, A. R. (2005). Bridging the Past and Present to the Future of Crisis Intervention and Crisis Management. In Crisis Intervention Handbook: Assessment, Treatment, and Research (3rd ed.). Roberts' Seven-Stage Crisis Intervention Model (R-SSCIM). (Summarized via crisis-intervention teaching references.) https://umsystem.pressbooks.pub/aswbprep/chapter/crisis-intervention-theories/ Established crisis-intervention model. Authority: high for the seven stages (secondary summary). Roberts' seven stages: (1) plan and conduct a biopsychosocial and lethality/risk assessment; (2) establish rapport and a collaborative relationship; (3) identify the major problems (including the "last straw"/precipitant); (4) deal with feelings and emotions (active listening, validation); (5) generate and explore alternatives; (6) develop and formulate an action plan; (7) follow-up plan and agreement. Shares the assessment-first, rapport, alternatives, plan, and follow-up spine with the James & Gilliland model — different granularity, same logic.
  • Richmond, J. S., Berlin, J. S., Fishkind, A. B., et al. (2012). Verbal De-escalation of the Agitated Patient: Consensus Statement of the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry Project BETA De-escalation Workgroup. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine, 13(1), 17–25. PMC3298202. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3298202/ Professional consensus statement. Authority: high for verbal de-escalation technique. Project BETA (Best practices in Evaluation and Treatment of Agitation). De-escalation goal in three moves: verbally engage the patient → establish a collaborative relationship → verbally de-escalate them out of agitation. The ten domains: (1) respect personal space (≥ two arms' lengths; keep exits clear for both); (2) do not be provocative (calm posture, hands visible, no challenge); (3) establish verbal contact — only one person speaks to the patient; (4) be concise (short sentences, simple words — agitated people process language poorly); (5) identify wants and feelings; (6) listen closely (active listening; "Miller's law" — assume what they say is true from their view; restate it back); (7) agree or agree to disagree (find common ground); (8) set clear limits matter-of-factly, without threats; (9) offer choices and optimism (alternatives to violence, realistic hope); (10) debrief the patient and staff afterward. Coercion/restraint is a last resort — it can reinforce that violence resolves conflict and is associated with worse outcomes; successful verbal de-escalation preserves dignity and the therapeutic relationship.

Tier: trauma neurobiology, trauma-informed care, and trauma treatment

  • Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA). (2014). SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach. HHS Publication No. (SMA) 14-4884. Rockville, MD. https://library.samhsa.gov/product/samhsas-concept-trauma-and-guidance-trauma-informed-approach/sma14-4884 (definition/4Rs/6 principles confirmed via the National Coalition for Homeless Veterans research brief and OpenTextBC peer-support curriculum) The field's foundational trauma-informed-care framework. Authority: high (primary framework document; specifics corroborated across two secondary summaries). Definition — the "three E's": trauma results from an Event (or series of events) that is Experienced by the person as harmful or life-threatening and that has lasting adverse Effects on functioning and mental, physical, social, emotional, or spiritual well-being. The subjective experience is what makes an event traumatic — the same event traumatizes one person and not another. A trauma-informed approach — the "four R's": an organization/program (1) Realizes the widespread impact of trauma and paths to recovery; (2) Recognizes the signs and symptoms of trauma in clients, staff, and others; (3) Responds by integrating knowledge of trauma into policies, procedures, and practices; and (4) actively resists re-traumatization. Six key principles: (i) Safety; (ii) Trustworthiness and transparency; (iii) Peer support; (iv) Collaboration and mutuality; (v) Empowerment, voice, and choice; (vi) Cultural, historical, and gender issues. Crucially, SAMHSA distinguishes a trauma-informed approach (a universal, organization-wide stance that assumes any client may be a trauma survivor and aims above all to avoid re-traumatizing) from trauma-specific interventions/services (treatments that directly address trauma symptoms and the traumatic event). The primary goal of the approach is to avoid re-traumatization; it does not require the client to disclose or process the trauma.
  • American Psychological Association (2017), Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of PTSD, and U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs / Department of Defense (2023), VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of PTSD. (First-line trauma-focused psychotherapies.) https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline · https://www.healthquality.va.gov/guidelines/MH/ptsd/ Professional-body evidence guidelines. Authority: high for what counts as trauma treatment. Both guidelines identify trauma-focused psychotherapies as first-line for PTSD: Prolonged Exposure (PE), Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT), Trauma-Focused CBT (TF-CBT — the standard for children/adolescents), and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR). These are trauma treatments — structured, symptom-reducing, delivered by clinicians trained in the specific protocol — and are categorically different from trauma-informed care, which is a stance any counselor adopts to create safety and avoid harm regardless of setting or specialty. (EMDR's mechanism — whether the bilateral eye movements add anything beyond the exposure component — remains debated even though the package works; flagged in the reading.)
  • Sheffler, J. L., et al. / peer-reviewed synthesis: Childhood Trauma, the HPA Axis and Psychiatric Illnesses: A Targeted Literature Synthesis. Frontiers in Psychiatry / PMC9120425 (2022). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9120425/ Peer-reviewed review (read in full via pypdf). Authority: high for the HPA axis and limbic/prefrontal stress circuitry. The HPA axis: the hypothalamus releases CRH → the pituitary releases ACTH → the adrenal cortex releases cortisol; the system is normally reined in by negative feedback (cortisol and hippocampal output inhibit further CRH). Trauma/early-life stress dysregulates it — findings are inconsistent (some show elevated baseline cortisol, others reduced morning cortisol/blunted reactivity), and "dysregulated responses are not consistently associated with psychopathology," a caution against over-reading cortisol as a trauma biomarker. Circuitry: the amygdala assigns emotional/threat valence and is excitatory to the HPA axis (enlarged/hyperactive after early stress); the hippocampus contextualizes memory and is inhibitory to the axis (reduced volume is a common trauma/MDD finding); the medial prefrontal cortex provides top-down regulation (reduced volume after childhood maltreatment). McEwen's allostatic load frames chronic stress as a lasting shift in the body's set-point.
  • Guy-Evans, O. / Simply Psychology. The Neurobiology of Trauma: How Traumatic Experiences Change the Brain. simplypsychology.com. (Orientation-tier synthesis; corroborated against S14.) https://www.simplypsychology.com/articles/neurobiology-of-trauma Educational secondary source. Authority: moderate (orientation-level; used for the working-model framing and corroborated by peer-reviewed S14). Working model: in trauma/PTSD the amygdala is hyperactive (exaggerated, over-generalized fear), the hippocampus shows reduced volume (8–26% in some combat-veteran samples) and fails to time-stamp the memory as past (so it intrudes as if present), and the prefrontal cortex shows reduced regulatory activity — a "regulatory failure" where fear can't be dampened. Distinguishes explicit memory (hippocampus-dependent, verbal, narrative, contextualized) from implicit memory (amygdala-dependent, non-verbal, sensory/emotional/bodily) — trauma disrupts explicit encoding while strengthening implicit, so a survivor may have somatic/emotional reactions and fragmentary sensory images without a coherent narrative ("the body remembers before the mind"). The fight/flight/freeze cascade includes freeze/tonic immobility — an involuntary shutdown, not a choice, which matters for how survivors judge their own "why didn't I fight back" reactions.
  • Siegel, D. J. (1999). The Developing Mind. — the "window of tolerance." (Summarized via clinical trauma-education references; PA DHS trauma-informed-care tip sheet.) https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/dhs/documents/trauma-informed-care/tip-sheets/2024-09-september-final-tts.pdf Widely used clinical heuristic. Authority: moderate (a useful teaching model, not a validated neurobiological construct — flagged as such). The window of tolerance is the arousal band within which a person can process experience and stay regulated (think clearly, stay present, feel without being overwhelmed). Above it = hyperarousal (fight/flight: panic, rage, racing thoughts, hypervigilance); below it = hypoarousal (freeze/ shutdown: numbness, dissociation, flatness, collapse). Trauma narrows and destabilizes the window, so small triggers push a survivor out of it. Clinical use: notice which side the client is on and help them back into the window (grounding for hyperarousal; re-engagement/orienting for hypoarousal) before doing any content work — a concrete operationalization of trauma-informed pacing. A heuristic, not a measured brain state.
  • van der Kolk, B. (2014). The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma. Viking. (Popular-press — flagged per course-map.) Best-selling trade book; clinically influential but not peer-reviewed. Authority: low-moderate — used only for framing already corroborated by S14/S15; contested claims labeled. Popularized the ideas that trauma is registered in the body and nervous system (not just as narrative memory), that traumatic memory is stored differently from ordinary memory, and that body-based and regulation-focused approaches matter. Corroborated: the explicit/implicit memory split and limbic hyperarousal (S14, S15). Flagged as contested/overstated: the strong "the body stores trauma" metaphor, sweeping claims about repressed/recovered traumatic memory (the memory-as-videotape view is rejected by memory science — trauma memory is reconstructive and suggestible), and reliance on polyvagal theory (Porges), whose specific neurophysiological claims are scientifically contested. Use the book for orientation and metaphor, corroborate the mechanisms elsewhere.

Tier: counselor cost of the work (vicarious trauma, self-care)

  • McCann, I. L., & Pearlman, L. A. (1990). Vicarious Traumatization: A Framework for Understanding the Psychological Effects of Working With Victims. Journal of Traumatic Stress, 3(1), 131–149. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00975140 The construct's origin paper. Authority: high for the definition and the Constructivist Self-Development Theory (CSDT) frame. Coined "vicarious traumatization" (VT). VT is the transformation of the counselor's inner experience — disruptions to their cognitive schemas (beliefs about self and world in the areas of safety, trust, esteem, intimacy, and control) — resulting from empathic engagement with clients' trauma material. It is framed by Constructivist Self-Development Theory (CSDT): people construct reality through schemas, and repeated exposure to others' trauma reshapes the helper's schemas. VT is cumulative (each traumatized client reinforces the change) and potentially permanent if unaddressed — and it is a normal, expectable cost of caring, not a weakness.
  • Trippany, R. L., Kress, V. E. W., & Wilcoxon, S. A. (2004). Preventing Vicarious Trauma: What Counselors Should Know When Working With Trauma Survivors. Journal of Counseling & Development, 82(1), 31–37. https://ovc.ojp.gov/sites/g/files/xyckuh226/files/media/document/vt_summary_and_a_new_theory-508.pdf Peer-reviewed counseling journal (read in full via pypdf). Authority: high for the VT/burnout/countertransference distinctions and prevention. Draws the key distinctions: VT is a reaction to specific client trauma material, occurs only in those working with trauma survivors, has a sudden/abrupt onset, involves schema disruptions (safety/trust/esteem/intimacy/control) and intrusive imagery, and is pervasive (spills into all of life) and cumulative. Burnout is general emotional exhaustion/overload from difficult or high-volume caseloads, occurs in any profession, has a gradual onset, and lacks the schema/imagery changes. Countertransference is the counselor's reaction rooted in their own past experiences and is session-bound, whereas VT transcends the session. The paper stresses that unaddressed VT is an ethical problem (boundary lapses, clinical error, misdiagnosis, "rescuing," reduced quality of care) and lays out prevention as shared responsibility: caseload management (limit trauma clients per week), peer supervision/consultation (85% of trauma counselors' most-used coping method; also an ethical way to debrief given confidentiality limits), agency responsibility (supervision, training, benefits, caseload limits — VT prevention is organizational, not just personal), traumatology training, work/play/rest balance, social support, and meaning/spirituality.
  • Figley, C. R. (1995). Compassion Fatigue: Coping With Secondary Traumatic Stress Disorder in Those Who Treat the Traumatized. + Stamm, B. H. Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL). proqol.org. https://proqol.org/ Foundational construct + the standard measure. Authority: high for the STS/compassion-fatigue terms and the ProQOL. Secondary traumatic stress (STS) = PTSD-like symptoms (intrusion, avoidance, arousal) arising from indirect exposure to another's trauma; onset can be rapid (even a single exposure). Compassion fatigue is Figley's umbrella term often taken to combine STS + burnout — the cumulative cost of caring. The ProQOL (Stamm) measures professional quality of life on three scales: compassion satisfaction (the positive — the reward of helping), burnout, and secondary traumatic stress — capturing that the work has both a fulfilling and a depleting side. (Terms overlap in the literature; the readings treat VT, STS, compassion fatigue, burnout, and countertransference as a confusable cluster and quiz the discriminations.)
  • American Counseling Association. (2014). ACA Code of Ethics. — C.2.g (Impairment) and the professional-responsibility sections. (Also cited in Unit 3.) https://www.counseling.org/resources/aca-code-of-ethics.pdf The profession's binding ethics code. Authority: high for the self-care-as-ethical-duty claim. Standard C.2.g (Impairment): counselors monitor themselves for signs of impairment from their own physical, mental, or emotional problems, refrain from offering or providing services when impaired, seek assistance, and — if necessary — limit, suspend, or terminate their professional responsibilities until it is safe to resume. This is the code hook that makes self-care an ethical competency, not a personal luxury: an impaired counselor (including one impaired by unaddressed VT/ STS) who keeps seeing clients is committing an ethical breach. (See concept-scope-of-practice from Unit 3.)

Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings)

  1. We cannot reliably predict individual suicide. Risk factors and instruments (C-SSRS, IS PATH WARM) identify populations at elevated risk and guide intervention and disposition; they do not forecast who will die and when — actuarial prediction of individual suicide is poor. This is the same prediction critique raised against Tarasoff-style dangerousness prediction in Unit 3 (study-tarasoff). Assess to intervene and manage risk, not to prophesy.
  2. Asking about suicide does not plant the idea. The clinician's fear of "putting the thought in their head" is not supported; direct, plain questioning is safe and may reduce distress. The real danger is avoidance.
  3. No-suicide contracts are not evidence-based and can create false reassurance and defensive practice; collaborative safety planning (with means reduction) has replaced them.
  4. Means restriction works at the population level despite the substitution objection. Critics argue people substitute methods; the evidence is that substitution is incomplete, crises are often transient/impulsive, and case fatality differs so much by method that reducing access to the most lethal means saves lives.
  5. Trauma neurobiology: read the direction, not the details. The amygdala-up / hippocampus-and-PFC- down picture and the explicit/implicit memory split are well supported in direction, but cortisol findings are inconsistent and not a clean biomarker, and the window of tolerance and polyvagal theory are clinically useful heuristics, not validated brain states. van der Kolk's Body Keeps the Score is popular-press — corroborate its mechanisms (done here against S14/ S15) and treat the strong "trauma stored in the body" and recovered-memory claims as contested.
  6. Trauma-informed ≠ trauma treatment. A trauma-informed approach (SAMHSA's 4 Rs / 6 principles) is a universal stance to avoid re-traumatization that any counselor adopts and that does not require the client to disclose or process the trauma; trauma treatment (PE, CPT, TF-CBT, EMDR) is a specific, trained modality that reduces symptoms. Conflating them leads beginners to "dig for the trauma story," which is exactly what trauma-informed care restrains (ties to the don't-probe stance from aux-psychological-first-aid and concept-intake-interview).
  7. The cost-of-the-work terms overlap. VT (schema disruption from empathic exposure), STS (PTSD-like symptoms from indirect exposure), compassion fatigue (STS + burnout), burnout (general overload), and countertransference (from the counselor's own history) are distinct constructs with fuzzy edges in the literature; the unit teaches the discriminations while noting the overlap. Self-care is an ethical duty (ACA C.2.g), and prevention is organizational, not only personal.
  8. Provenance caveats. James & Gilliland and Herman are offline (books) and cited via reputable secondary summaries; the SAMHSA framework's exact wording was confirmed across two secondary summaries plus the primary publication record; the HPA-axis review (S14) and the Trippany/Kress counseling article (S19) were read in full via pypdf. Firearm case-fatality and crisis-duration figures are order-of-magnitude public-health estimates from Means Matter, not precise constants.
pages.text: Unit 8 sources — Crisis, Risk Assessment & Trauma-Informed Care Evidence base for Unit 8 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1] . Researched 2026-07-18. This is the syllabus's highest-stakes unit ("preparation directly protects a life") and an emotionally heavy one — material is kept clinical and precise, no sensationalism (per CLAUDE.md). Anchored where possible on primary instruments and validation studies (the Columbia C-SSRS; Stanley & Brown's Safety Planning Intervention and its RCT; the Project BETA de-escalation consensus), government/professional bodies (SAMHSA's trauma-informed framework; the VA suicide-risk guide; Harvard's Means Matter program), and peer-reviewed clinical/counseling literature (a peer-reviewed HPA-axis review read in full via pypdf; the Trippany/Kress Journal of Counseling & Development vicarious-trauma article read in full via pypdf). Two anchor books (James & Gilliland; Herman) are offline and cited via reputable secondary sources, flagged. Per the course-map's explicit caution, van der Kolk's The Body Keeps the Score is popular-press : its neurobiology claims are corroborated against peer-reviewed sources and the popular/contested pieces (the memory-as-storage metaphor, polyvagal theory) are flagged as such in the readings. Tier: suicide risk assessment (instruments, interviewing, frameworks) S1 Columbia Lighthouse Project. Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (C-SSRS). Columbia University Department of Psychiatry / The Columbia Lighthouse Project. (Validation: Posner, K., et al. (2011). The Columbia–Suicide Severity Rating Scale: Initial Validity and Internal Consistency Findings From Three Multisite Studies With Adolescents and Adults. American Journal of Psychiatry, 168(12), 1266–1277.) https://www.columbiapsychiatry.org/research-labs/columbia-suicide-severity-rating-scale-c-ssrs · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22193671/ Widely adopted, validated risk-screening instrument. Authority: high for the ideation/behavior distinction and the severity ladder. The C-SSRS separates suicidal ideation from suicidal behavior and grades each. Ideation is rated on a five-point severity ladder of increasing seriousness: (1) wish to be dead ; (2) nonspecific active suicidal thoughts ; (3) active ideation with methods considered (no plan); (4) active ideation with some intent to act; (5) active ideation with a specific plan and intent . Intensity items capture frequency, duration, controllability, deterrents, and reasons. The behavior subscale records actual attempts, interrupted attempts (stopped by an outside circumstance), aborted/self-interrupted attempts (stopped by the person), preparatory acts (assembling means, giving things away, writing a note), and non-suicidal self-injury. Plain language; requires no mental-health training to administer; endorsed across clinical, research, and institutional settings. S2 Shea, S. C. The Chronological Assessment of Suicide Events (the CASE Approach). Training Institute for Suicide Assessment and Clinical Interviewing (TISA); SPRC Best Practices Registry. (Shea, S. C. (2009). Suicide Assessment Part 2: Uncovering Suicidal Intent Using the CASE Approach. Psychiatric Times.) https://suicideassessment.com/the-case-approach/ · https://www.psychiatrist.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/02/11584_chronological-assessment-suicide-events-practical.pdf Widely taught interviewing strategy (SPRC-registered). Authority: high for the interviewing method and the stated/reflected/withheld-intent distinction. The CASE Approach is an interviewing strategy for eliciting suicidal ideation, planning, behavior, and intent with higher validity. It sequences the interview through four chronological regions : (1) presenting ideation/events (the crisis that brought them in), (2) recent ideation/events (past ~8 weeks), (3) past ideation/events (lifetime), and (4) immediate ideation (how they feel about safety right now and their disposition). The delineation keeps the clinician "on task" and reduces errors of omission . Shea distinguishes stated intent (what the client reports), reflected intent (the extent of thinking/planning/action the client describes, which may reveal more than the stated intent), and withheld intent — the interview's job is to maximize reflected intent and minimize what's withheld. Validity-enhancing techniques (e.g., behavioral incident — asking for fact/sequence rather than opinion; gentle assumption ; normalization ; denial of the specific ) reduce the tendency to under-report. S3 U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs / VA National Center for Patient Safety. Suicide Risk Assessment Guide — Reference Manual. mentalhealth.va.gov. https://www.mentalhealth.va.gov/docs/suicide_risk_assessment_reference_guide.pdf Government clinical reference. Authority: high for the warning-signs mnemonic, the acute/chronic distinction, and risk stratification. Distinguishes chronic/distal risk factors (long-standing background vulnerabilities: prior attempts — the single strongest predictor — psychiatric disorder, substance use, chronic pain/ illness, trauma/abuse history, family history, access to means, male sex, social isolation) from acute/proximal risk factors and warning signs (recent events and states that raise risk in the near term). Warning signs via the IS PATH WARM mnemonic (American Association of Suicidology): I deation, S ubstance abuse, P urposelessness, A nxiety/agitation, T rapped, H opelessness, W ithdrawal, A nger, R ecklessness, M ood change. Protective factors : reasons for living, social connectedness, responsibility to family/children, engaged treatment, coping skills, cultural/religious beliefs discouraging suicide. Direct inquiry does not increase risk. Ask about ideation → plan → intent → means/access → preparatory behavior . Risk stratification guides disposition: low (outpatient + safety plan + follow-up), moderate (intensified outpatient / crisis services / increased monitoring / remove means), high (hospitalization / do not leave alone / immediate means removal). S4 Dazzi, T., Gribble, R., Wessely, S., & Fear, N. T. (2014). Does Asking About Suicide and Related Behaviours Induce Suicidal Ideation? What Is the Evidence? Psychological Medicine, 44(16), 3361–3363. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/psychological-medicine/article/does-asking-about-suicide-and-related-behaviours-induce-suicidal-ideation-what-is-the-evidence/ Peer-reviewed evidence synthesis. Authority: high for the "asking doesn't plant the idea" claim. Reviewing studies across community, adult, adolescent, and at-risk samples, found no evidence that asking about suicide induces or increases suicidal ideation ; several studies found acknowledging and talking about suicide may reduce rather than increase ideation. Refutes the common clinician fear that direct questioning is dangerous — the far greater risk is not asking. S5 Klonsky, E. D., & May, A. M. (2015). The Three-Step Theory (3ST): A New Theory of Suicide Rooted in the "Ideation-to-Action" Framework. International Journal of Cognitive Therapy, 8(2), 114–129. (Framework origin: Joiner, T. (2005). Why People Die by Suicide , the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide.) https://www2.psych.ubc.ca/~klonsky/publications/3ST.pdf Peer-reviewed theory. Authority: high for the ideation-to-action framework and its clinical implications. The ideation-to-action framework holds that the development of suicidal ideation and the progression from ideation to an attempt are distinct processes with distinct causes — so factors that explain who thinks about suicide differ from factors that explain who acts. Joiner's Interpersonal Theory (IPTS): ideation arises from thwarted belongingness + perceived burdensomeness ; the leap to an attempt requires acquired capability (habituation to pain, fear, and death through exposure — prior self-injury, abuse, others' suicide, etc.). Klonsky & May's 3ST: ideation = pain (usually psychological) + hopelessness ; connectedness is the key factor that keeps moderate ideation from escalating; the move to attempt is governed by capacity for suicide (dispositional, acquired, practical). Clinical upshot: a person with strong ideation but low capability, or a client whose connectedness is intact, is at a different kind of risk than one who has acquired capability — and means access is a practical contributor to capacity. Tier: safety planning and means reduction S6 Stanley, B., & Brown, G. K. (2012). Safety Planning Intervention: A Brief Intervention to Mitigate Suicide Risk. Cognitive and Behavioral Practice, 19(2), 256–264. (Template + clinician guidance: Stanley-Brown Safety Planning Intervention, suicidesafetyplan.com; National Jewish Health clinician guide.) https://suicidesafetyplan.com/ · https://www.nationaljewish.org/suicide-awareness/suicidal-patients-next-steps/safety-plan-with-a-patient The intervention's primary source + official template. Authority: high for the six steps and the collaborative stance. The Safety Planning Intervention (SPI) is a brief, collaborative, clinician-assisted tool: a prioritized, written list of coping strategies and supports for a suicidal crisis. Six steps, in order of escalating external reliance: (1) Warning signs (personal thoughts/images/moods/ behaviors that a crisis is building) → (2) Internal coping strategies the client can do alone to distract without contacting anyone (walk, music, exercise) → (3) Social contacts and settings that provide distraction (people/places, without disclosing the crisis) → (4) People to ask for help (family/friends the client will tell) → (5) Professionals and agencies to contact in crisis (clinician, local ED, 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline ) → (6) Making the environment safe (reducing access to lethal means — the means-restriction step). The ordering matters: it moves from self-reliance toward external help so the earliest steps are things the client can always do. It is built with the client, not handed to them , and is a living document to revisit. Explicitly not a "no-suicide contract" (see S7). S7 Stanley, B., et al. (2018). Comparison of the Safety Planning Intervention With Follow-up vs Usual Care of Suicidal Patients Treated in the Emergency Department. JAMA Psychiatry, 75(9), 894–900. (No-suicide-contract critique: Rudd, M. D., Mandrusiak, M., & Joiner, T. E. (2006). The Case Against No-Suicide Contracts. Journal of Clinical Psychology, 62(2), 243–251.) https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/2687370 Peer-reviewed effectiveness study + peer-reviewed critique. Authority: high for the evidence base and the contract contrast. In a cohort study of ED patients, the SPI plus structured telephone follow-up was associated with ~45% fewer suicidal behaviors over six months versus usual care, and with greater treatment engagement. Safety planning is endorsed by the Joint Commission, the VA/DoD guideline, and the Zero Suicide framework . By contrast, the "no-suicide contract" / "no-harm contract" (a client's promise not to self-harm) is not evidence-based : no study shows it reduces suicide or attempts, it can create false reassurance for the clinician, it shifts toward defensive rather than therapeutic practice, and it offers the client nothing to do in a crisis. A commitment-to-safety or safety plan (what the client will do, and how to get help) has replaced it. S8 Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, Means Matter program. Lethal Means Counseling and Means Matter research summaries. https://hsph.harvard.edu/research/means-matter/lethal-means-counseling/ · https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/lethal-means-safety-counseling Public-health program at a leading school. Authority: high for means-restriction rationale and the counseling method. Means reduction / lethal-means safety counseling = collaboratively reducing a suicidal person's access to highly lethal methods until the crisis passes. Rationale: (1) case fatality varies enormously by method — roughly 85–90% of firearm attempts are fatal , versus a few percent for overdose/cutting — so the method a person reaches for in a crisis heavily determines whether they live; (2) suicidal crises are often brief and impulsive — the interval between deciding and acting is frequently minutes to an hour ; (3) method substitution is incomplete — many people do not simply switch to an equally lethal method, and (4) most attempt survivors do not go on to die by suicide (roughly 9 in 10 ). The counseling targets firearms (best: temporary off-site storage with a trusted person or facility; otherwise locked, unloaded, ammunition stored separately) and medications (limit quantities, lock up, dispose of excess). It is collaborative and time-limited ("while things are hard"), not confiscation. Despite the evidence it is underused — one survey found ~78% of EDs assess access to means but only ~35% provide means counseling. Tier: crisis intervention and de-escalation models S9 James, R. K., & Gilliland, B. E. Crisis Intervention Strategies (anchor text; latest eds.). Six-step model summarized via clinician references (ICANotes; university crisis-intervention course materials). https://www.icanotes.com/2022/04/19/6-step-crisis-intervention-model-explained/ The unit's anchor text (offline); six-step model corroborated via reputable secondary references. Authority: high for the model's content, secondary for exact wording. Defines a crisis as a perception of an event or situation as an intolerable difficulty that exceeds the person's current resources and coping (Caplan's tradition) — crisis is in the perception/response , not the event. The six-step model blends listening (steps 1–3) and acting (steps 4–6): (1) Define the problem from the client's viewpoint; (2) Ensure client safety — the continuous first priority; (3) Provide support (unconditional, present); (4) Examine alternatives (mobilize situational supports, coping mechanisms, positive thinking); (5) Make plans (concrete, collaborative, doable steps that restore some control); (6) Obtain commitment to the plan. Safety is not one step but the thread running through all six. S10 Roberts, A. R. (2005). Bridging the Past and Present to the Future of Crisis Intervention and Crisis Management. In Crisis Intervention Handbook: Assessment, Treatment, and Research (3rd ed.). Roberts' Seven-Stage Crisis Intervention Model (R-SSCIM). (Summarized via crisis-intervention teaching references.) https://umsystem.pressbooks.pub/aswbprep/chapter/crisis-intervention-theories/ Established crisis-intervention model. Authority: high for the seven stages (secondary summary). Roberts' seven stages : (1) plan and conduct a biopsychosocial and lethality/risk assessment ; (2) establish rapport and a collaborative relationship ; (3) identify the major problems (including the "last straw"/precipitant); (4) deal with feelings and emotions (active listening, validation); (5) generate and explore alternatives ; (6) develop and formulate an action plan ; (7) follow-up plan and agreement . Shares the assessment-first, rapport, alternatives, plan, and follow-up spine with the James & Gilliland model — different granularity, same logic. S11 Richmond, J. S., Berlin, J. S., Fishkind, A. B., et al. (2012). Verbal De-escalation of the Agitated Patient: Consensus Statement of the American Association for Emergency Psychiatry Project BETA De-escalation Workgroup. Western Journal of Emergency Medicine, 13(1), 17–25. PMC3298202. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3298202/ Professional consensus statement. Authority: high for verbal de-escalation technique. Project BETA (Best practices in Evaluation and Treatment of Agitation). De-escalation goal in three moves: verbally engage the patient → establish a collaborative relationship → verbally de-escalate them out of agitation. The ten domains : (1) respect personal space (≥ two arms' lengths; keep exits clear for both); (2) do not be provocative (calm posture, hands visible, no challenge); (3) establish verbal contact — only one person speaks to the patient; (4) be concise (short sentences, simple words — agitated people process language poorly); (5) identify wants and feelings ; (6) listen closely (active listening; "Miller's law" — assume what they say is true from their view; restate it back); (7) agree or agree to disagree (find common ground); (8) set clear limits matter-of-factly, without threats; (9) offer choices and optimism (alternatives to violence, realistic hope); (10) debrief the patient and staff afterward. Coercion/restraint is a last resort — it can reinforce that violence resolves conflict and is associated with worse outcomes; successful verbal de-escalation preserves dignity and the therapeutic relationship. Tier: trauma neurobiology, trauma-informed care, and trauma treatment S12 Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA). (2014). SAMHSA's Concept of Trauma and Guidance for a Trauma-Informed Approach. HHS Publication No. (SMA) 14-4884. Rockville, MD. https://library.samhsa.gov/product/samhsas-concept-trauma-and-guidance-trauma-informed-approach/sma14-4884 (definition/4Rs/6 principles confirmed via the National Coalition for Homeless Veterans research brief and OpenTextBC peer-support curriculum) The field's foundational trauma-informed-care framework. Authority: high (primary framework document; specifics corroborated across two secondary summaries). Definition — the "three E's": trauma results from an Event (or series of events) that is Experienced by the person as harmful or life-threatening and that has lasting adverse Effects on functioning and mental, physical, social, emotional, or spiritual well-being. The subjective experience is what makes an event traumatic — the same event traumatizes one person and not another. A trauma-informed approach — the "four R's": an organization/program (1) Realizes the widespread impact of trauma and paths to recovery; (2) Recognizes the signs and symptoms of trauma in clients, staff, and others; (3) Responds by integrating knowledge of trauma into policies, procedures, and practices; and (4) actively resists re-traumatization . Six key principles: (i) Safety ; (ii) Trustworthiness and transparency ; (iii) Peer support ; (iv) Collaboration and mutuality ; (v) Empowerment, voice, and choice ; (vi) Cultural, historical, and gender issues . Crucially, SAMHSA distinguishes a trauma-informed approach (a universal, organization-wide stance that assumes any client may be a trauma survivor and aims above all to avoid re-traumatizing ) from trauma-specific interventions/services (treatments that directly address trauma symptoms and the traumatic event). The primary goal of the approach is to avoid re-traumatization ; it does not require the client to disclose or process the trauma. S13 American Psychological Association (2017), Clinical Practice Guideline for the Treatment of PTSD , and U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs / Department of Defense (2023), VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of PTSD. (First-line trauma-focused psychotherapies.) https://www.apa.org/ptsd-guideline · https://www.healthquality.va.gov/guidelines/MH/ptsd/ Professional-body evidence guidelines. Authority: high for what counts as trauma treatment. Both guidelines identify trauma-focused psychotherapies as first-line for PTSD: Prolonged Exposure (PE) , Cognitive Processing Therapy (CPT) , Trauma-Focused CBT (TF-CBT — the standard for children/adolescents ) , and Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) . These are trauma treatments — structured, symptom-reducing, delivered by clinicians trained in the specific protocol — and are categorically different from trauma- informed care , which is a stance any counselor adopts to create safety and avoid harm regardless of setting or specialty. (EMDR's mechanism — whether the bilateral eye movements add anything beyond the exposure component — remains debated even though the package works; flagged in the reading.) S14 Sheffler, J. L., et al. / peer-reviewed synthesis: Childhood Trauma, the HPA Axis and Psychiatric Illnesses: A Targeted Literature Synthesis. Frontiers in Psychiatry / PMC9120425 (2022). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9120425/ Peer-reviewed review (read in full via pypdf). Authority: high for the HPA axis and limbic/prefrontal stress circuitry. The HPA axis : the hypothalamus releases CRH → the pituitary releases ACTH → the adrenal cortex releases cortisol ; the system is normally reined in by negative feedback (cortisol and hippocampal output inhibit further CRH). Trauma/early-life stress dysregulates it — findings are inconsistent (some show elevated baseline cortisol, others reduced morning cortisol/blunted reactivity), and "dysregulated responses are not consistently associated with psychopathology ," a caution against over-reading cortisol as a trauma biomarker. Circuitry: the amygdala assigns emotional/threat valence and is excitatory to the HPA axis (enlarged/hyperactive after early stress); the hippocampus contextualizes memory and is inhibitory to the axis (reduced volume is a common trauma/MDD finding); the medial prefrontal cortex provides top-down regulation (reduced volume after childhood maltreatment). McEwen's allostatic load frames chronic stress as a lasting shift in the body's set-point. S15 Guy-Evans, O. / Simply Psychology. The Neurobiology of Trauma: How Traumatic Experiences Change the Brain. simplypsychology.com. (Orientation-tier synthesis; corroborated against S14.) https://www.simplypsychology.com/articles/neurobiology-of-trauma Educational secondary source. Authority: moderate (orientation-level; used for the working-model framing and corroborated by peer-reviewed S14). Working model: in trauma/PTSD the amygdala is hyperactive (exaggerated, over-generalized fear), the hippocampus shows reduced volume (8–26% in some combat-veteran samples) and fails to time-stamp the memory as past (so it intrudes as if present), and the prefrontal cortex shows reduced regulatory activity — a "regulatory failure" where fear can't be dampened. Distinguishes explicit memory (hippocampus-dependent, verbal, narrative, contextualized) from implicit memory (amygdala-dependent, non-verbal, sensory/emotional/bodily) — trauma disrupts explicit encoding while strengthening implicit, so a survivor may have somatic/emotional reactions and fragmentary sensory images without a coherent narrative ("the body remembers before the mind"). The fight/flight/freeze cascade includes freeze/tonic immobility — an involuntary shutdown, not a choice, which matters for how survivors judge their own "why didn't I fight back" reactions. S16 Siegel, D. J. (1999). The Developing Mind. — the "window of tolerance." (Summarized via clinical trauma-education references; PA DHS trauma-informed-care tip sheet.) https://www.pa.gov/content/dam/copapwp-pagov/en/dhs/documents/trauma-informed-care/tip-sheets/2024-09-september-final-tts.pdf Widely used clinical heuristic. Authority: moderate (a useful teaching model, not a validated neurobiological construct — flagged as such). The window of tolerance is the arousal band within which a person can process experience and stay regulated (think clearly, stay present, feel without being overwhelmed). Above it = hyperarousal (fight/flight: panic, rage, racing thoughts, hypervigilance); below it = hypoarousal (freeze/ shutdown: numbness, dissociation, flatness, collapse). Trauma narrows and destabilizes the window, so small triggers push a survivor out of it. Clinical use: notice which side the client is on and help them back into the window (grounding for hyperarousal; re-engagement/orienting for hypoarousal) before doing any content work — a concrete operationalization of trauma-informed pacing. A heuristic , not a measured brain state. S17 van der Kolk, B. (2014). The Body Keeps the Score: Brain, Mind, and Body in the Healing of Trauma. Viking. (Popular-press — flagged per course-map.) Best-selling trade book; clinically influential but not peer-reviewed . Authority: low-moderate — used only for framing already corroborated by S14/S15; contested claims labeled. Popularized the ideas that trauma is registered in the body and nervous system (not just as narrative memory), that traumatic memory is stored differently from ordinary memory, and that body-based and regulation-focused approaches matter. Corroborated : the explicit/implicit memory split and limbic hyperarousal (S14, S15). Flagged as contested/overstated : the strong "the body stores trauma" metaphor, sweeping claims about repressed/recovered traumatic memory (the memory-as-videotape view is rejected by memory science — trauma memory is reconstructive and suggestible), and reliance on polyvagal theory (Porges), whose specific neurophysiological claims are scientifically contested . Use the book for orientation and metaphor, corroborate the mechanisms elsewhere. Tier: counselor cost of the work (vicarious trauma, self-care) S18 McCann, I. L., & Pearlman, L. A. (1990). Vicarious Traumatization: A Framework for Understanding the Psychological Effects of Working With Victims. Journal of Traumatic Stress, 3(1), 131–149. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00975140 The construct's origin paper. Authority: high for the definition and the Constructivist Self-Development Theory (CSDT) frame. Coined "vicarious traumatization" (VT). VT is the transformation of the counselor's inner experience — disruptions to their cognitive schemas (beliefs about self and world in the areas of safety, trust, esteem, intimacy, and control ) — resulting from empathic engagement with clients' trauma material. It is framed by Constructivist Self-Development Theory (CSDT) : people construct reality through schemas, and repeated exposure to others' trauma reshapes the helper's schemas. VT is cumulative (each traumatized client reinforces the change) and potentially permanent if unaddressed — and it is a normal, expectable cost of caring , not a weakness. S19 Trippany, R. L., Kress, V. E. W., & Wilcoxon, S. A. (2004). Preventing Vicarious Trauma: What Counselors Should Know When Working With Trauma Survivors. Journal of Counseling & Development, 82(1), 31–37. https://ovc.ojp.gov/sites/g/files/xyckuh226/files/media/document/vt_summary_and_a_new_theory-508.pdf Peer-reviewed counseling journal (read in full via pypdf). Authority: high for the VT/burnout/countertransference distinctions and prevention. Draws the key distinctions : VT is a reaction to specific client trauma material , occurs only in those working with trauma survivors, has a sudden/abrupt onset , involves schema disruptions (safety/trust/esteem/intimacy/control) and intrusive imagery , and is pervasive (spills into all of life) and cumulative . Burnout is general emotional exhaustion/overload from difficult or high-volume caseloads, occurs in any profession, has a gradual onset, and lacks the schema/imagery changes. Countertransference is the counselor's reaction rooted in their own past experiences and is session-bound , whereas VT transcends the session. The paper stresses that unaddressed VT is an ethical problem (boundary lapses, clinical error, misdiagnosis, "rescuing," reduced quality of care) and lays out prevention as shared responsibility : caseload management (limit trauma clients per week), peer supervision/consultation (85% of trauma counselors' most-used coping method; also an ethical way to debrief given confidentiality limits), agency responsibility (supervision, training, benefits, caseload limits — VT prevention is organizational, not just personal ), traumatology training , work/play/rest balance , social support, and meaning/spirituality . S20 Figley, C. R. (1995). Compassion Fatigue: Coping With Secondary Traumatic Stress Disorder in Those Who Treat the Traumatized. + Stamm, B. H. Professional Quality of Life Scale (ProQOL). proqol.org. https://proqol.org/ Foundational construct + the standard measure. Authority: high for the STS/compassion-fatigue terms and the ProQOL. Secondary traumatic stress (STS) = PTSD-like symptoms (intrusion, avoidance, arousal) arising from indirect exposure to another's trauma; onset can be rapid (even a single exposure). Compassion fatigue is Figley's umbrella term often taken to combine STS + burnout — the cumulative cost of caring . The ProQOL (Stamm) measures professional quality of life on three scales: compassion satisfaction (the positive — the reward of helping), burnout , and secondary traumatic stress — capturing that the work has both a fulfilling and a depleting side. (Terms overlap in the literature; the readings treat VT, STS, compassion fatigue, burnout, and countertransference as a confusable cluster and quiz the discriminations.) S21 American Counseling Association. (2014). ACA Code of Ethics. — C.2.g (Impairment) and the professional-responsibility sections. (Also cited in Unit 3.) https://www.counseling.org/resources/aca-code-of-ethics.pdf The profession's binding ethics code. Authority: high for the self-care-as-ethical-duty claim. Standard C.2.g (Impairment) : counselors monitor themselves for signs of impairment from their own physical, mental, or emotional problems, refrain from offering or providing services when impaired , seek assistance, and — if necessary — limit, suspend, or terminate their professional responsibilities until it is safe to resume. This is the code hook that makes self-care an ethical competency, not a personal luxury : an impaired counselor (including one impaired by unaddressed VT/ STS) who keeps seeing clients is committing an ethical breach. (See concept-scope-of-practice from Unit 3.) Points of disagreement / uncertainty found (surfaced in readings) We cannot reliably predict individual suicide. Risk factors and instruments (C-SSRS, IS PATH WARM) identify populations at elevated risk and guide intervention and disposition ; they do not forecast who will die and when — actuarial prediction of individual suicide is poor. This is the same prediction critique raised against Tarasoff-style dangerousness prediction in Unit 3 ( study-tarasoff ). Assess to intervene and manage risk , not to prophesy. S1 S3 S5 Asking about suicide does not plant the idea. The clinician's fear of "putting the thought in their head" is not supported; direct, plain questioning is safe and may reduce distress. The real danger is avoidance . S4 No-suicide contracts are not evidence-based and can create false reassurance and defensive practice; collaborative safety planning (with means reduction) has replaced them. S6 S7 Means restriction works at the population level despite the substitution objection. Critics argue people substitute methods; the evidence is that substitution is incomplete , crises are often transient/impulsive , and case fatality differs so much by method that reducing access to the most lethal means saves lives. S8 Trauma neurobiology: read the direction, not the details. The amygdala-up / hippocampus-and-PFC- down picture and the explicit/implicit memory split are well supported in direction, but cortisol findings are inconsistent and not a clean biomarker, and the window of tolerance and polyvagal theory are clinically useful heuristics , not validated brain states. van der Kolk's Body Keeps the Score is popular-press — corroborate its mechanisms (done here against S14/ S15) and treat the strong "trauma stored in the body" and recovered-memory claims as contested. S14 S15 S16 S17 Trauma-informed ≠ trauma treatment. A trauma-informed approach (SAMHSA's 4 Rs / 6 principles) is a universal stance to avoid re-traumatization that any counselor adopts and that does not require the client to disclose or process the trauma; trauma treatment (PE, CPT, TF-CBT, EMDR) is a specific, trained modality that reduces symptoms. Conflating them leads beginners to "dig for the trauma story," which is exactly what trauma-informed care restrains (ties to the don't-probe stance from aux-psychological-first-aid and concept-intake-interview ). S12 S13 The cost-of-the-work terms overlap. VT (schema disruption from empathic exposure), STS (PTSD-like symptoms from indirect exposure), compassion fatigue (STS + burnout), burnout (general overload), and countertransference (from the counselor's own history) are distinct constructs with fuzzy edges in the literature; the unit teaches the discriminations while noting the overlap. Self-care is an ethical duty (ACA C.2.g) , and prevention is organizational, not only personal . S18 S19 S20 S21 Provenance caveats. James & Gilliland and Herman are offline (books) and cited via reputable secondary summaries; the SAMHSA framework's exact wording was confirmed across two secondary summaries plus the primary publication record; the HPA-axis review (S14) and the Trippany/Kress counseling article (S19) were read in full via pypdf. Firearm case-fatality and crisis-duration figures are order-of-magnitude public-health estimates from Means Matter, not precise constants.
