pages.title: Unit 12 sources — Research Methods & Program Evaluation
pages.html:
Unit 12 sources — Research Methods & Program Evaluation

Evidence base for Unit 12 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1].

Researched 2026-07-20. Tier 3 "rounding out" unit — the final unit of the 12-unit spine. CACREP core area Research & Program Evaluation (§2.F.8). The syllabus objective is deliberately practical: read and critically evaluate counseling research, understand outcome measurement, and know research ethics. Per the course-map, the unit quizzes choosing the method, not executing it — no hand-calculation of statistics; the skill is telling designs apart, reading an effect size, ranking evidence, and spotting a threat to validity. Six substantive areas: experimental vs. correlational (vs. quasi-experimental) designs and the requirements for a causal claim; threats to validity (Cook & Campbell's four validities); effect size vs. statistical vs. clinical significance (and what a p-value does and does not mean); evidence-based practice (APA's three-legged definition, the evidence hierarchy, empirically-supported-treatment tiers, and the replication crisis / allegiance & publication bias); single-case designs and progress monitoring; program evaluation (formative/summative, process/outcome, needs assessment); and research ethics / the IRB (the Belmont Report, the historical abuses behind it, and ACA Section G). Anchored on open psychology-methods textbooks (Price et al., Research Methods in Psychology), primary/canonical methodology (Cook & Campbell; Chambless & Hollon; Jacobson & Truax; the Open Science Collaboration), government/regulatory primaries (the Belmont Report, the Common Rule), and the profession's own documents (APA 2006 EBP policy; the ACA Code of Ethics; CACREP 2016). Contested threads carried at evaluate level: the replication crisis and questionable research practices; allegiance/publication bias (already met in Units 9–10); the gap between a group average and the individual client (nomothetic vs. idiographic); and the limits of the evidence hierarchy itself.

The unit's stance thread — the Unit-wide "resist the urge to fix" caution, translated for research — is "the number is not the person": evidence informs clinical judgment, it does not replace it, and being a discerning consumer means resisting both credulity and cynicism.

Tier: research designs and causation

  • Price, P. C., Jhangiani, R., Chiang, I.-C. A., Leighton, D. C., & Cuttler, C. Research Methods in Psychology (open textbook; multiple editions — OpenTextBC / Saylor / WSU Pressbooks mirrors). https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_research-methods-in-psychology/ · https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/ Widely adopted, peer-reviewed open psychology-methods textbook; the anchor for designs, single-subject research, and validity. Authority: high (educational primary). Experiments are the design that supports causal claims; correlational studies show association, not causation. The directionality problem (which variable caused which?) and the third-variable problem (a lurking common cause) are why "correlation ≠ causation." Random assignment (equating groups at the outset — an internal-validity move) is distinct from random sampling/selection (drawing a representative sample — an external-validity move).
  • "What's the difference between correlational and experimental research?" Scribbr; David Schuster, Research Methods Course Pack, Ch. 4 "Causality" (San José State). https://www.scribbr.com/frequently-asked-questions/correlational-vs-experimental-research/ · https://www.davidschuster.info/books/methods/causality.html Orientation-tier teaching resources; used for the three requirements of a causal inference. Cross-checked against S1. Authority: moderate (corroborated). A causal claim requires three things: (1) covariation (the variables are related), (2) temporal precedence (the cause precedes the effect), and (3) no plausible alternative explanation (confounds ruled out — the job random assignment does).
  • "Quasi-experimental designs." EBSCO Research Starters (Health and Medicine). https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/health-and-medicine/quasi-experimental-designs Encyclopedic research-reference entry; used for the quasi-experimental definition. Authority: moderate. A quasi-experiment has a manipulation (an intervention/treatment) but no random assignment — participants fall into groups by a pre-existing characteristic or by convenience. It sits between correlational studies and true experiments on internal validity: better than correlational (there is an intervention) but weaker than an RCT (selection confounds are not controlled by randomization). Common in real-world/field settings where randomizing is impossible or unethical.

Tier: threats to validity (the Campbellian system)

  • Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (1979). Quasi-Experimentation: Design & Analysis Issues for Field Settings; extended in Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference. The canonical taxonomy of the four validities and their threats. Books, offline — the framework is corroborated via the peer-reviewed and educational secondaries below. Authority: very high (foundational). Four kinds of validity, each with characteristic threats: statistical-conclusion validity (is there a real covariation, analyzed correctly?), internal validity (did the treatment, not something else, cause the change?), construct validity (do the measures/operations match the intended constructs?), and external validity (do the findings generalize to other people, settings, times?). Classic internal-validity threats: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, statistical regression (regression to the mean), selection, attrition/mortality, and their interactions.
  • García-Pérez, M. A. (2012). Statistical Conclusion Validity: Some Common Threats and Simple Remedies. Frontiers in Psychology, 3, 325 (PMC3429930). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3429930/ Peer-reviewed methods review. Authority: high (statistical-conclusion validity + the four-validity frame). Statistical-conclusion validity concerns whether the data can reasonably be regarded as revealing a link (or its absence) between variables on statistical grounds — threats include low power, violated assumptions, unreliable measures, and fishing/error-rate inflation from multiple tests.
  • Trochim, Research Methods Knowledge Base (conjointly.com); "Threats to Validity of Research Design," Portland State (B. Stipak); "Threats to Internal / Statistical Conclusion Validity" (C. Rakes teaching slides). https://web.pdx.edu/~stipakb/download/PA555/ResearchDesign.html Widely cited educational treatments of the Campbellian threats; used to enumerate/define the internal-validity threats and the internal↔external validity tradeoff. Cross-checked against S4/S5. Authority: moderate (corroborated). The tradeoff: tightly controlled lab experiments maximize internal validity but can sacrifice external validity (artificial setting); naturalistic field studies maximize external validity but admit confounds. No single study optimizes both — which is one reason replication across contexts matters.

Tier: effect size, significance, and clinical significance

  • Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.); operationalized in Sullivan, G. M., & Feinn, R. (2012). Using Effect Size—or Why the P Value Is Not Enough. J. Grad. Med. Educ., 4(3), 279–282. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3444174/ Cohen is the canonical source for effect-size conventions; the JGME paper is the standard peer-reviewed "why effect size" teaching reference. Authority: high. Effect size = the magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size. Cohen's d (standardized mean difference) rule-of-thumb: ≈0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large (a d below ~0.2 is trivial); Pearson r ≈ 0.1/0.3/0.5. The p-value depends on both effect size and sample size, so a large study can make a trivial effect "significant"; effect size answers the question a p-value cannot — how big?
  • Nahm, F. S. (2017). What the P values really tell us. / "Alternatives to P value: confidence interval and effect size" (PMC5133225); Andrade, C. (2019). The P value and statistical significance: misunderstandings, explanations, challenges… (PubMed 29337724). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5133225/ · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29337724/ Peer-reviewed statistics-education articles. Authority: high (p-value definition + its misinterpretations, CIs). A p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the observed one if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability the null (or the hypothesis) is true, not the probability the result is due to chance, and not a measure of effect size or importance. p < .05 is a conventional (arbitrary) threshold, not a law of nature. A 95% confidence interval conveys the precision of the estimate (and if it excludes the null value, the result is "significant" at .05) — more informative than a bare p-value because it shows the plausible range and the magnitude.
  • Wasserstein, R. L., & Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose. The American Statistician, 70(2), 129–133. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108 The American Statistical Association's formal consensus statement — the authoritative word on p-value (mis)use. Authority: very high. Six principles, in spirit: p-values can indicate incompatibility with a null model, but they do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or the size/importance of an effect; scientific conclusions should not be based only on whether p crosses a threshold; proper inference requires full reporting and transparency; and "statistical significance ≠ scientific, human, or economic significance."
  • Jacobson, N. S., & Truax, P. (1991). Clinical significance: a statistical approach to defining meaningful change in psychotherapy research. J. Consult. Clin. Psychol., 59(1), 12–19 (PubMed 1619094); overview at PSYCTC.org (RCSC). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1619094/ · https://www.psyctc.org/psyctc/root/stats/rcsc/ The canonical operationalization of clinical (vs. statistical) significance in psychotherapy; the Reliable Change Index. Authority: high (heavily cited — the bridge to Unit 7 outcome monitoring). Clinically significant change = movement from a score typical of the dysfunctional population to one typical of the functional population. The Reliable Change Index (RCI) = the pre-to-post change divided by the standard error of the difference — it asks whether an individual's change exceeds what measurement error alone would produce. Combining the two classifies clients as recovered / improved / unchanged / deteriorated. This is the individual-client meaning of "did it work," and the statistical backbone of measurement-based care (Unit 7).

Tier: evidence-based practice, the evidence hierarchy, and empirically supported treatments

  • APA Presidential Task Force on Evidence-Based Practice (2006). Evidence-based practice in psychology. American Psychologist, 61(4), 271–285. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4832531/ (three-legged-stool corroboration) · https://www.apa.org/practice/resources/evidence The profession's official EBP policy (primary); corroborated via peer-reviewed secondaries. Authority: very high. EBPP = "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences" (p. 273). Three co-equal legs — best available research + clinical expertise + client characteristics/values — that must be integrated; research evidence is one leg, not the master leg. (This is the same definition Unit 9's unit09-modalities hub uses: "evidence-based" is not a horse race between brand-name therapies.)
  • Chambless, D. L., & Hollon, S. D. (1998). Defining empirically supported therapies. J. Consult. Clin. Psychol., 66(1), 7–18 (Div. 12 PDF). https://www.div12.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Chambless-Hollon-1998-Defining-Empirically-Supported-Therapies.pdf The standard criteria behind APA Division 12's list of empirically supported treatments. Authority: high. Well-established: efficacy shown in ≥2 good between-group design experiments by independent research teams (or a large series of well-controlled single-case designs), using treatment manuals and specified samples. Probably efficacious: the lower tier — supported by fewer or non-independent studies. The load-bearing word is efficacy: it must be shown, ideally versus a placebo/rival treatment and by more than one lab (guarding against allegiance effects).
  • Evidence-based-practice library guides: UNM Health Sciences "Evidence Pyramid"; National University of Singapore "Hierarchy of Evidence & Study Types"; UC Davis "Levels of Evidence." https://www.unm.edu/~unmvclib/cascade/handouts/PICOTpyramidofevidence.pdf · https://libguides.nus.edu.sg/sysreviews/evidence Standard academic-library treatments of the evidence hierarchy. Authority: moderate–high (consensus teaching material). The evidence pyramid, strongest at the top: systematic reviews & meta-analyses > RCTs > cohort studies > case-control studies > cross-sectional/case series > case reports/expert opinion > animal/lab studies. Higher = less susceptible to bias, but rarer. Caveats carried in the reading: a bad systematic review is not better than a good RCT (the pyramid ranks design, not execution); "GRADE"-style appraisal judges quality within a level.
  • Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science, 349(6251), aac4716; Simmons, Nelson, & Simonsohn (2011). False-Positive Psychology. Psychological Science, 22(11). https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aac4716 · https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0956797611417632 The landmark reproducibility study + the paper that named researcher "degrees of freedom." Authority: very high. The OSC replicated 100 psychology studies; while ~97% of originals were "significant," only ~36% of replications reached significance and effect sizes halved on average — the empirical core of the replication crisis. Simmons et al. showed that ordinary researcher degrees of freedom (flexible stopping rules, optional covariates, selective reporting) — p-hacking — can push the false-positive rate far above 5%. Fixes: preregistration, registered reports, larger samples, open data, and valuing replication and null results. Publication bias (the file-drawer problem) and allegiance bias (the developer's own trials report the biggest effects — met in Units 9–10) both inflate the apparent evidence base.

Tier: single-case designs and progress monitoring

  • Price et al., Research Methods in Psychology, "Single-Subject Research Designs" (S1 anchor text, single-subject chapter); Kazdin, A. E. (2011). Single-Case Research Designs (2nd ed.). https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_research-methods-in-psychology/s14-02-single-subject-research-design.html Open-text chapter (fetched in full) + the canonical single-case methods reference (Kazdin, offline → corroborated). Authority: high. Single-subject / single-case experimental designs track one participant (or a few) with repeated measurement across phases. Baseline (A) = repeated measurement with no treatment; treatment (B) = the intervention. The reversal / ABAB (withdrawal) design introduces, removes, and re-introduces treatment: if the behavior tracks the phase changes, the treatment — not history/maturation — is the likely cause (the strongest single-case demonstration). The multiple-baseline design staggers treatment onset across behaviors, settings, or people, demonstrating causation without withdrawing an effective treatment (the ethical fix when reversal is inappropriate). Analysis is by visual inspection of level, trend, and latency, not (primarily) inferential statistics. Distinct from a case study (which is descriptive, no manipulation, no baseline logic). The clinical cousin — an AB design without the controls — is progress monitoring: good enough to guide this client's care, not to prove causation.
  • Fortney, J. C., et al. (2017). A Tipping Point for Measurement-Based Care. Psychiatric Services, 68(2), 179–188; Lambert's outcome-monitoring / feedback-informed treatment literature. https://ps.psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ps.201500439 Peer-reviewed; the measurement-based-care (MBC) evidence base. Authority: high (the Unit 7 ↔ Unit 12 bridge). Measurement-based care = routine, systematic symptom measurement (e.g., PHQ-9/GAD-7 — Unit 7's concept-screening-tools) used to inform and adjust treatment. It is the practice-level, single-client application of outcome measurement and the reliable-change idea ; feedback-informed treatment (routinely showing clinicians client progress, flagging "not-on-track" cases) improves outcomes, especially for clients who are deteriorating.

Tier: program evaluation

  • "Types of Evaluation" (Centre for Innovation in Campus Mental Health toolkit; Penn State CECD engagement toolkit); Astramovich & Coker (2007), Program Evaluation: The Accountability Bridge Model for Counselors, J. Counseling & Development; national survey of counselors' program-evaluation use (CORE, 2019). https://campusmentalhealth.ca/toolkits/evaluation/what-is-evaluation/types/ · https://aese.psu.edu/research/centers/cecd/engagement-toolbox/evaluating-engagement-efforts/evaluation-types Practitioner-consensus toolkits + a counseling-specific peer-reviewed model. Authority: moderate–high. Program evaluation = judging the merit/worth of a program or service (vs. research, which aims for generalizable knowledge). Types: needs assessment (what's needed, before you build), formative (improve during development/early implementation), process/implementation (was it delivered as intended, to the intended people?), summative (final judgment of worth/outcomes), and outcome/impact (did the targeted conditions actually change?). Mnemonic contrast: formative = steering the ship mid-voyage; summative = judging the whole trip on arrival. Counselors most often do single-case and outcome evaluation.

Tier: research ethics and the IRB

  • The Belmont Report (1979). National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research; U.S. DHHS Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP). https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/belmont-report/index.html The primary U.S. framework for human-subjects research ethics. Authority: very high. Three principles and their applications: Respect for persons → treat people as autonomous agents and protect those with diminished autonomy → informed consent. Beneficence → maximize benefits and minimize harms → risk/benefit assessment. Justice → distribute the burdens and benefits of research fairly → fair subject selection (don't exploit the vulnerable or convenient). IRBs enforce these.
  • The Nuremberg Code (1947); the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki (1964, rev.); the U.S. Public Health Service Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972); the Common Rule (45 CFR 46). https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/regulations/45-cfr-46/index.html · https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/common-rule Regulatory/government primaries + well-documented history (OHRP, CDC, NIJ). Authority: very high. The abuses that produced the rules: Nazi experiments → the Nuremberg Code (voluntary consent is "absolutely essential"); the Declaration of Helsinki (physician-research ethics); the Tuskegee study — Black men with syphilis were deceived and denied available penicillin for decades — the U.S. scandal that directly produced the National Research Act (1974), the Belmont Report, and the IRB/Common Rule system requiring prospective review, informed consent, and protections for vulnerable populations.
  • American Counseling Association (2014). ACA Code of Ethics, Section G: Research and Publication. https://www.counseling.org/resources/aca-code-of-ethics.pdf The counseling profession's own research-ethics standards (primary; the same document anchoring Unit 3). Authority: very high. Section G governs research: informed consent to research (voluntary; the right to decline; the purpose/procedures/risks disclosed), protecting confidentiality of research data, avoiding harm, honest reporting of results (no fabrication; report unfavorable results; correct errors), giving proper publication credit, and a boundary flag: participants who are also students/supervisees/clients must be free to decline without penalty to that relationship (ties to Unit 3 concept-dual-relationships).

Tier: the CACREP standard

  • Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs (CACREP). 2016 Standards, §2.F.8 "Research and Program Evaluation." https://www.cacrep.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/2016-CACREP-Standards-with-Glossary.pdf The accreditation body's curriculum standard. Authority: high. §2.F.8 requires counselor training in: the importance of research and how to critique research to inform practice; identification of evidence-based counseling practices; needs assessments; development of outcome measures for counseling programs; evaluation of counseling interventions and programs; qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods; research designs; statistical methods; analysis and use of data; and ethical and culturally relevant strategies for conducting/interpreting/reporting research and program evaluation. The area's framing is explicitly consumer + evaluator, not "become a statistician."

Tier: cross-unit anchors

  • Cross-references — Unit 7 concept-reliability-validity (source_units: [7, 12]), concept-screening-tools, concept-treatment-planning; Unit 9 unit09-modalities (EBP three legs; SFBT allegiance bias) and theory-solution-focused; Unit 10 theory-yalom-factors (Burlingame equivalence; group-can-harm casualty finding); Unit 3 unit03-ethics-law + concept-informed-consent + concept-dual-relationships. Unit 12 is the methods spine under the whole curriculum: it supplies the psychometrics floor Unit 7's reliability/validity page borrowed, the outcome-measurement engine behind measurement-based care, the definition of "evidence-based" Unit 9 already used, the allegiance/publication-bias caution surfaced in Units 9–10, and the research-ethics analog of Unit 3's consent/boundary rules. Being the last unit, it mostly wires back to what came before rather than being forward-referenced.
pages.text: Unit 12 sources — Research Methods & Program Evaluation Evidence base for Unit 12 readings. Each source has a one-line authority note. Inline citations in wiki pages reference these numbers, e.g. [S1] . Researched 2026-07-20. Tier 3 "rounding out" unit — the final unit of the 12-unit spine. CACREP core area Research & Program Evaluation (§2.F.8). The syllabus objective is deliberately practical: read and critically evaluate counseling research , understand outcome measurement , and know research ethics . Per the course-map, the unit quizzes choosing the method, not executing it — no hand-calculation of statistics; the skill is telling designs apart, reading an effect size, ranking evidence, and spotting a threat to validity. Six substantive areas: experimental vs. correlational (vs. quasi-experimental) designs and the requirements for a causal claim; threats to validity (Cook & Campbell's four validities); effect size vs. statistical vs. clinical significance (and what a p-value does and does not mean); evidence-based practice (APA's three-legged definition, the evidence hierarchy, empirically-supported-treatment tiers, and the replication crisis / allegiance & publication bias); single-case designs and progress monitoring ; program evaluation (formative/summative, process/outcome, needs assessment); and research ethics / the IRB (the Belmont Report, the historical abuses behind it, and ACA Section G). Anchored on open psychology-methods textbooks (Price et al., Research Methods in Psychology ), primary/canonical methodology (Cook & Campbell; Chambless & Hollon; Jacobson & Truax; the Open Science Collaboration), government/regulatory primaries (the Belmont Report, the Common Rule), and the profession's own documents (APA 2006 EBP policy; the ACA Code of Ethics; CACREP 2016). Contested threads carried at evaluate level: the replication crisis and questionable research practices; allegiance/publication bias (already met in Units 9–10); the gap between a group average and the individual client (nomothetic vs. idiographic); and the limits of the evidence hierarchy itself. The unit's stance thread — the Unit-wide "resist the urge to fix" caution, translated for research — is "the number is not the person": evidence informs clinical judgment, it does not replace it , and being a discerning consumer means resisting both credulity and cynicism. Tier: research designs and causation S1 Price, P. C., Jhangiani, R., Chiang, I.-C. A., Leighton, D. C., & Cuttler, C. Research Methods in Psychology (open textbook; multiple editions — OpenTextBC / Saylor / WSU Pressbooks mirrors). https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_research-methods-in-psychology/ · https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/ Widely adopted, peer-reviewed open psychology-methods textbook; the anchor for designs, single-subject research, and validity. Authority: high (educational primary). Experiments are the design that supports causal claims; correlational studies show association , not causation. The directionality problem (which variable caused which?) and the third-variable problem (a lurking common cause) are why "correlation ≠ causation." Random assignment (equating groups at the outset — an internal-validity move) is distinct from random sampling/selection (drawing a representative sample — an external-validity move). S2 "What's the difference between correlational and experimental research?" Scribbr; David Schuster, Research Methods Course Pack , Ch. 4 "Causality" (San José State). https://www.scribbr.com/frequently-asked-questions/correlational-vs-experimental-research/ · https://www.davidschuster.info/books/methods/causality.html Orientation-tier teaching resources; used for the three requirements of a causal inference. Cross-checked against S1. Authority: moderate (corroborated). A causal claim requires three things: (1) covariation (the variables are related), (2) temporal precedence (the cause precedes the effect), and (3) no plausible alternative explanation (confounds ruled out — the job random assignment does). S3 "Quasi-experimental designs." EBSCO Research Starters (Health and Medicine). https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/health-and-medicine/quasi-experimental-designs Encyclopedic research-reference entry; used for the quasi-experimental definition. Authority: moderate. A quasi-experiment has a manipulation (an intervention/treatment) but no random assignment — participants fall into groups by a pre-existing characteristic or by convenience. It sits between correlational studies and true experiments on internal validity: better than correlational (there is an intervention) but weaker than an RCT (selection confounds are not controlled by randomization). Common in real-world/field settings where randomizing is impossible or unethical. Tier: threats to validity (the Campbellian system) S4 Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (1979). Quasi-Experimentation: Design & Analysis Issues for Field Settings ; extended in Shadish, W. R., Cook, T. D., & Campbell, D. T. (2002). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference. The canonical taxonomy of the four validities and their threats. Books, offline — the framework is corroborated via the peer-reviewed and educational secondaries below. Authority: very high (foundational). Four kinds of validity, each with characteristic threats: statistical-conclusion validity (is there a real covariation, analyzed correctly?), internal validity (did the treatment, not something else, cause the change?), construct validity (do the measures/operations match the intended constructs?), and external validity (do the findings generalize to other people, settings, times?). Classic internal-validity threats : history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, statistical regression (regression to the mean), selection, attrition/mortality , and their interactions. S5 García-Pérez, M. A. (2012). Statistical Conclusion Validity: Some Common Threats and Simple Remedies. Frontiers in Psychology, 3, 325 (PMC3429930). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3429930/ Peer-reviewed methods review. Authority: high (statistical-conclusion validity + the four-validity frame). Statistical-conclusion validity concerns whether the data can reasonably be regarded as revealing a link (or its absence) between variables on statistical grounds — threats include low power, violated assumptions, unreliable measures, and fishing/error-rate inflation from multiple tests. S6 Trochim, Research Methods Knowledge Base (conjointly.com); "Threats to Validity of Research Design," Portland State (B. Stipak); "Threats to Internal / Statistical Conclusion Validity" (C. Rakes teaching slides). https://web.pdx.edu/~stipakb/download/PA555/ResearchDesign.html Widely cited educational treatments of the Campbellian threats; used to enumerate/define the internal-validity threats and the internal↔external validity tradeoff . Cross-checked against S4/S5. Authority: moderate (corroborated). The tradeoff : tightly controlled lab experiments maximize internal validity but can sacrifice external validity (artificial setting); naturalistic field studies maximize external validity but admit confounds. No single study optimizes both — which is one reason replication across contexts matters. Tier: effect size, significance, and clinical significance S7 Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.); operationalized in Sullivan, G. M., & Feinn, R. (2012). Using Effect Size—or Why the P Value Is Not Enough. J. Grad. Med. Educ., 4(3), 279–282. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3444174/ Cohen is the canonical source for effect-size conventions; the JGME paper is the standard peer-reviewed "why effect size" teaching reference. Authority: high. Effect size = the magnitude of a difference or relationship, independent of sample size. Cohen's d (standardized mean difference) rule-of-thumb: ≈0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large (a d below ~0.2 is trivial); Pearson r ≈ 0.1/0.3/0.5. The p-value depends on both effect size and sample size, so a large study can make a trivial effect "significant"; effect size answers the question a p-value cannot — how big? S8 Nahm, F. S. (2017). What the P values really tell us. / "Alternatives to P value: confidence interval and effect size" (PMC5133225); Andrade, C. (2019). The P value and statistical significance: misunderstandings, explanations, challenges… (PubMed 29337724). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5133225/ · https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29337724/ Peer-reviewed statistics-education articles. Authority: high (p-value definition + its misinterpretations, CIs). A p-value is the probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as the observed one if the null hypothesis were true . It is not the probability the null (or the hypothesis) is true, not the probability the result is due to chance, and not a measure of effect size or importance. p < .05 is a conventional (arbitrary) threshold, not a law of nature. A 95% confidence interval conveys the precision of the estimate (and if it excludes the null value, the result is "significant" at .05) — more informative than a bare p-value because it shows the plausible range and the magnitude. S9 Wasserstein, R. L., & Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA Statement on p-Values: Context, Process, and Purpose. The American Statistician, 70(2), 129–133. https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00031305.2016.1154108 The American Statistical Association's formal consensus statement — the authoritative word on p-value (mis)use. Authority: very high. Six principles, in spirit: p-values can indicate incompatibility with a null model, but they do not measure the probability that the hypothesis is true or the size/importance of an effect; scientific conclusions should not be based only on whether p crosses a threshold; proper inference requires full reporting and transparency ; and "statistical significance ≠ scientific, human, or economic significance." S10 Jacobson, N. S., & Truax, P. (1991). Clinical significance: a statistical approach to defining meaningful change in psychotherapy research. J. Consult. Clin. Psychol., 59(1), 12–19 (PubMed 1619094); overview at PSYCTC.org (RCSC). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/1619094/ · https://www.psyctc.org/psyctc/root/stats/rcsc/ The canonical operationalization of clinical (vs. statistical) significance in psychotherapy; the Reliable Change Index. Authority: high (heavily cited — the bridge to Unit 7 outcome monitoring). Clinically significant change = movement from a score typical of the dysfunctional population to one typical of the functional population. The Reliable Change Index (RCI) = the pre-to-post change divided by the standard error of the difference — it asks whether an individual's change exceeds what measurement error alone would produce. Combining the two classifies clients as recovered / improved / unchanged / deteriorated . This is the individual-client meaning of "did it work," and the statistical backbone of measurement-based care (Unit 7). Tier: evidence-based practice, the evidence hierarchy, and empirically supported treatments S11 APA Presidential Task Force on Evidence-Based Practice (2006). Evidence-based practice in psychology. American Psychologist, 61(4), 271–285. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4832531/ (three-legged-stool corroboration) · https://www.apa.org/practice/resources/evidence The profession's official EBP policy (primary); corroborated via peer-reviewed secondaries. Authority: very high. EBPP = "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences" (p. 273). Three co-equal legs — best available research + clinical expertise + client characteristics/values — that must be integrated ; research evidence is one leg, not the master leg. (This is the same definition Unit 9's unit09-modalities hub uses: "evidence-based" is not a horse race between brand-name therapies.) S12 Chambless, D. L., & Hollon, S. D. (1998). Defining empirically supported therapies. J. Consult. Clin. Psychol., 66(1), 7–18 (Div. 12 PDF). https://www.div12.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/Chambless-Hollon-1998-Defining-Empirically-Supported-Therapies.pdf The standard criteria behind APA Division 12's list of empirically supported treatments. Authority: high. Well-established: efficacy shown in ≥2 good between-group design experiments by independent research teams (or a large series of well-controlled single-case designs), using treatment manuals and specified samples. Probably efficacious: the lower tier — supported by fewer or non-independent studies. The load-bearing word is efficacy : it must be shown, ideally versus a placebo/rival treatment and by more than one lab (guarding against allegiance effects). S13 Evidence-based-practice library guides: UNM Health Sciences "Evidence Pyramid"; National University of Singapore "Hierarchy of Evidence & Study Types"; UC Davis "Levels of Evidence." https://www.unm.edu/~unmvclib/cascade/handouts/PICOTpyramidofevidence.pdf · https://libguides.nus.edu.sg/sysreviews/evidence Standard academic-library treatments of the evidence hierarchy. Authority: moderate–high (consensus teaching material). The evidence pyramid , strongest at the top: systematic reviews & meta-analyses > RCTs > cohort studies > case-control studies > cross-sectional/case series > case reports/expert opinion > animal/lab studies. Higher = less susceptible to bias, but rarer . Caveats carried in the reading: a bad systematic review is not better than a good RCT (the pyramid ranks design , not execution); "GRADE"-style appraisal judges quality within a level. S14 Open Science Collaboration (2015). Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science. Science, 349(6251), aac4716; Simmons, Nelson, & Simonsohn (2011). False-Positive Psychology. Psychological Science, 22(11). https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.aac4716 · https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0956797611417632 The landmark reproducibility study + the paper that named researcher "degrees of freedom." Authority: very high. The OSC replicated 100 psychology studies; while ~97% of originals were "significant," only ~36% of replications reached significance and effect sizes halved on average — the empirical core of the replication crisis . Simmons et al. showed that ordinary researcher degrees of freedom (flexible stopping rules, optional covariates, selective reporting) — p-hacking — can push the false-positive rate far above 5%. Fixes: preregistration , registered reports, larger samples, open data, and valuing replication and null results. Publication bias (the file-drawer problem) and allegiance bias (the developer's own trials report the biggest effects — met in Units 9–10) both inflate the apparent evidence base. Tier: single-case designs and progress monitoring S15 Price et al., Research Methods in Psychology , "Single-Subject Research Designs" (S1 anchor text, single-subject chapter); Kazdin, A. E. (2011). Single-Case Research Designs (2nd ed.). https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_research-methods-in-psychology/s14-02-single-subject-research-design.html Open-text chapter (fetched in full) + the canonical single-case methods reference (Kazdin, offline → corroborated). Authority: high. Single-subject / single-case experimental designs track one participant (or a few) with repeated measurement across phases. Baseline (A) = repeated measurement with no treatment; treatment (B) = the intervention. The reversal / ABAB (withdrawal) design introduces, removes, and re-introduces treatment: if the behavior tracks the phase changes, the treatment — not history/maturation — is the likely cause (the strongest single-case demonstration). The multiple-baseline design staggers treatment onset across behaviors, settings, or people , demonstrating causation without withdrawing an effective treatment (the ethical fix when reversal is inappropriate). Analysis is by visual inspection of level, trend, and latency , not (primarily) inferential statistics. Distinct from a case study (which is descriptive, no manipulation, no baseline logic). The clinical cousin — an AB design without the controls — is progress monitoring : good enough to guide this client's care, not to prove causation. S16 Fortney, J. C., et al. (2017). A Tipping Point for Measurement-Based Care. Psychiatric Services, 68(2), 179–188; Lambert's outcome-monitoring / feedback-informed treatment literature. https://ps.psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ps.201500439 Peer-reviewed; the measurement-based-care (MBC) evidence base. Authority: high (the Unit 7 ↔ Unit 12 bridge). Measurement-based care = routine, systematic symptom measurement (e.g., PHQ-9/GAD-7 — Unit 7's concept-screening-tools ) used to inform and adjust treatment. It is the practice-level, single-client application of outcome measurement and the reliable-change idea S10 ; feedback-informed treatment (routinely showing clinicians client progress, flagging "not-on-track" cases) improves outcomes, especially for clients who are deteriorating. Tier: program evaluation S17 "Types of Evaluation" (Centre for Innovation in Campus Mental Health toolkit; Penn State CECD engagement toolkit); Astramovich & Coker (2007), Program Evaluation: The Accountability Bridge Model for Counselors, J. Counseling & Development; national survey of counselors' program-evaluation use (CORE, 2019). https://campusmentalhealth.ca/toolkits/evaluation/what-is-evaluation/types/ · https://aese.psu.edu/research/centers/cecd/engagement-toolbox/evaluating-engagement-efforts/evaluation-types Practitioner-consensus toolkits + a counseling-specific peer-reviewed model. Authority: moderate–high. Program evaluation = judging the merit/worth of a program or service (vs. research, which aims for generalizable knowledge). Types: needs assessment (what's needed, before you build), formative (improve during development/early implementation), process/implementation (was it delivered as intended, to the intended people?), summative (final judgment of worth/outcomes), and outcome/impact (did the targeted conditions actually change?). Mnemonic contrast: formative = steering the ship mid-voyage; summative = judging the whole trip on arrival. Counselors most often do single-case and outcome evaluation. Tier: research ethics and the IRB S18 The Belmont Report (1979). National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research; U.S. DHHS Office for Human Research Protections (OHRP). https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/belmont-report/index.html The primary U.S. framework for human-subjects research ethics. Authority: very high. Three principles and their applications: Respect for persons → treat people as autonomous agents and protect those with diminished autonomy → informed consent . Beneficence → maximize benefits and minimize harms → risk/benefit assessment . Justice → distribute the burdens and benefits of research fairly → fair subject selection (don't exploit the vulnerable or convenient). IRBs enforce these. S19 The Nuremberg Code (1947); the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki (1964, rev.); the U.S. Public Health Service Tuskegee Syphilis Study (1932–1972); the Common Rule (45 CFR 46). https://www.hhs.gov/ohrp/regulations-and-policy/regulations/45-cfr-46/index.html · https://nij.ojp.gov/funding/common-rule Regulatory/government primaries + well-documented history (OHRP, CDC, NIJ). Authority: very high. The abuses that produced the rules: Nazi experiments → the Nuremberg Code (voluntary consent is "absolutely essential"); the Declaration of Helsinki (physician-research ethics); the Tuskegee study — Black men with syphilis were deceived and denied available penicillin for decades — the U.S. scandal that directly produced the National Research Act (1974) , the Belmont Report, and the IRB/Common Rule system requiring prospective review, informed consent, and protections for vulnerable populations. S20 American Counseling Association (2014). ACA Code of Ethics, Section G: Research and Publication. https://www.counseling.org/resources/aca-code-of-ethics.pdf The counseling profession's own research-ethics standards (primary; the same document anchoring Unit 3). Authority: very high. Section G governs research: informed consent to research (voluntary; the right to decline; the purpose/procedures/risks disclosed), protecting confidentiality of research data, avoiding harm , honest reporting of results (no fabrication; report unfavorable results; correct errors), giving proper publication credit , and a boundary flag: participants who are also students/supervisees/clients must be free to decline without penalty to that relationship (ties to Unit 3 concept-dual-relationships ). Tier: the CACREP standard S21 Council for Accreditation of Counseling and Related Educational Programs (CACREP). 2016 Standards, §2.F.8 "Research and Program Evaluation." https://www.cacrep.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/2016-CACREP-Standards-with-Glossary.pdf The accreditation body's curriculum standard. Authority: high. §2.F.8 requires counselor training in: the importance of research and how to critique research to inform practice ; identification of evidence-based counseling practices ; needs assessments ; development of outcome measures for counseling programs; evaluation of counseling interventions and programs ; qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods ; research designs ; statistical methods ; analysis and use of data ; and ethical and culturally relevant strategies for conducting/interpreting/reporting research and program evaluation. The area's framing is explicitly consumer + evaluator , not "become a statistician." Tier: cross-unit anchors S22 Cross-references — Unit 7 concept-reliability-validity ( source_units: [7, 12] ), concept-screening-tools , concept-treatment-planning ; Unit 9 unit09-modalities (EBP three legs; SFBT allegiance bias) and theory-solution-focused ; Unit 10 theory-yalom-factors (Burlingame equivalence; group-can-harm casualty finding); Unit 3 unit03-ethics-law + concept-informed-consent + concept-dual-relationships . Unit 12 is the methods spine under the whole curriculum: it supplies the psychometrics floor Unit 7's reliability/validity page borrowed, the outcome-measurement engine behind measurement-based care, the definition of "evidence-based" Unit 9 already used, the allegiance/publication-bias caution surfaced in Units 9–10, and the research-ethics analog of Unit 3's consent/boundary rules. Being the last unit, it mostly wires back to what came before rather than being forward-referenced.
